Those are the ones who went up from the rest of the tribes. And they set the altar upon its bases, etc., and they gave money to the hewers, etc. <note>Ezra 1-3</note>.

Cyrus was king for three incomplete years during the reign of Ahasuerus. At the beginning of his reign, etc., work on the house of God ceased. In the third year of his reign, he made a feast, etc. For all four years, Esther was hidden in Shushan the citadel. And Esther was taken to the king, etc. For all five years, Haman was gathering plunder for Mordechai. # Book of Fear

**Be** careful regarding the honor of your wife, as the Sages said: "He who loves his wife as himself and honors her more than himself, for it is sufficient that she raises your children and saves you from sin." Be careful regarding her tears, for her tears are frequent and the gates of tears have not been locked. Do not engage in excessive conversation with her. Regarding one's own wife, they said this is a lesser degree <note>meaning if it applies to one's own wife, how much more so with the wife of another</note>. What is considered "excessive conversation"? Like the one who asked <term>Bruriah</term> <gloss>a famous scholar mentioned in the Talmud</gloss>, "On which path shall we go to Lod?" She said to him, "Foolish Galilean! You should have said, 'On which [path] to Lod?' and not..."

<column-break/>

# Book of Fear

...that the color drains away and paleness comes <note>an expression for the shame and distress of the person being humiliated</note>, and he has no share in the World to Come. It is better for a person to cast himself into a fiery furnace than to whiten the face of his fellow in public. Even if you have rebuked a person in private many times and he did not accept it, it is permitted to shame him and whiten his face and to hate him and pursue him until he accepts it. And whoever is able to rebuke and does not, he is a sinner; but if he did rebuke him, then he has saved his soul.

<summary>This page emphasizes honoring one's wife, avoiding excessive and unnecessary speech, and details the severe spiritual repercussions of publicly shaming another individual.</summary>
<keywords>Book of Fear, Honor of Wife, Bruriah, Rebuke, Public Shaming</keywords>

And be careful regarding her distress <note>original: "onatah", here referring to "ona'at devarim" or verbal mistreatment that causes emotional pain</note>, for her tears are frequent and the gates of tears are never locked <note>a reference to the Talmudic teaching that the cries of the oppressed, especially a wife, are immediately heard by Heaven</note>. And do not engage in excessive conversation with her. The Sages said this regarding one's own wife; how much more so does it apply to the wife of another. And what constitutes "excessive conversation"? It is like that man who asked Beruriah <note>a famous female scholar and the wife of Rabbi Meir</note>, "By which path shall we go to Lydda?" She said to him: "Foolish Galilean! You should have said, 'By which way to Lydda?' and not..."

<summary>This page concludes the discussion on the spiritual severity of public shaming before moving into the obligations of a husband to honor his wife and the importance of concise speech.</summary>

text:
# Book of Fear

**Be** careful with the honor of your wife, in keeping with the words of Resh Lakish <note>original abbreviation: ר"ל; the Talmud, Yevamot 62b, gives this teaching anonymously</note>: a man should love his wife as his own body and honor her more than his own body. For it is enough for you that she raises your children and saves you from sin. And be careful not to wrong her <note>the term refers to causing pain through hurtful words or mistreatment</note>, for her tears come readily, and the gates of tears are never locked. And do not talk at length with her. The sages said this of a man's own wife; how much more so, then, does it apply to the wife of his fellow. And what counts as talking at length? It is like the man who asked Beruriah <note>a learned woman of the second century, wife of Rabbi Meir, famous in the Talmud for her sharp scholarship</note>, "By which road shall we go to Lod?" She said to him, "Foolish Galilean! You should have said, 'By which to Lod?'" and not

<column-break/>

# Book of Fear

<meta>continues from previous page: the explanation of why shaming someone counts as bloodshed</meta>

the red departs and the white comes <note>original Aramaic: "דאזיל סומקא ואתי חיוורא"; the color drains from the shamed person's face, which the sages likened to the spilling of blood</note>, and he has no share in the World to Come. It is better for a person to throw himself into a fiery furnace than to whiten the face of his fellow in public. Yet if you have rebuked a person in private several times and he did not accept it, it is permitted to shame him, to whiten his face, to hate him, and to pursue him until he accepts. And one who is able to rebuke and does not rebuke is a sinner. But if he did rebuke, then he has saved his own soul.

<summary>This page instructs a man to honor his wife above himself and never to wound her with words, while also warning against excessive conversation with women, illustrated by the Talmudic story of Beruriah and the Galilean. It then finishes the teaching on public shaming, which is likened to bloodshed, and sets out the duty to rebuke a wrongdoer, first in private and only afterward openly.</summary>
<keywords>honor of one's wife, Resh Lakish, hurtful words, gates of tears, excessive talk, Beruriah, Lod, Galilean, public shaming, whitening the face, World to Come, fiery furnace, rebuke, Yonah Gerondi, Sefer ha-Yirah</keywords>

text:
Sukkah

<sig>4</sig>

<margin></margin>
<term>Ein Mishpat</term> <gloss>Legal Source</gloss> <term>Ner Mitzvah</term> <gloss>Commandment Lamp</gloss>
</margin>
<margin></margin>
[Tradition of the Shas]
* Who considers it <term>tumah</term> <gloss>ritual impurity</gloss> through intent?
* The reasoning of Rabbi Yose, who declares vessels that have significance to be impure.
* And if you say they disagree, it is sufficient to have the intent of the <term>log</term> <gloss>a liquid measure</gloss>.
* For it is written, it is favorable to him concerning them, and they thought that all purification [laws] are established by him.
* The reason is explained further on.
* [S] To the material, everything that is connected is considered <term>tumah</term> <gloss>ritual impurity</gloss>.
* [Z'L Eleazar] Because we express concern, and there is no intent for that which is near.
* [Z'L Isaac] (Impurity to) They write the intent that is near to all of them.
* [Z'L Isaac Po.] (L) How much [is it]. For 37.
</margin>

<column-break/>

<note>A printer's mark or ornament appears here.</note>

...lead to <term>tumah</term> <gloss>ritual impurity</gloss> through intent. * Who considers it <term>tumah</term> through intent? And if you say [this refers] to the impurity of vessels that are significant, it would be sufficient to have the intent of the <term>log</term> <gloss>liquid measure</gloss>. And if you say they disagree, it is sufficient to have the intent of the <term>log</term>. It is comfortable for the doubt of <term>tamei</term> <gloss>impure</gloss>: that in the sign. For standing. He explains it for him: Towers. The <term>log</term>. For it is written, it is favorable to him concerning them, and they thought that all purification laws are established by him: And if you say impurity is that all of them, the reason is explained further on: Concerning the world, that which is significant (Ezekiel 15), what is from those who roll them, vessels that are significant, because it is close, all of them, because it is close to all of them, a form of the mouth of <term>tomei</term> <gloss>the impure one</gloss> to connect all of them to all of them.

<column-break/>

Sukkah 14

->Chapter One<-

They lead to <term>tumah</term> <gloss>ritual impurity</gloss> through intent, but they do not lead every day [to] a disagreement regarding <term>tumah</term> through intent.
From their impurity, only through an act (and) the act removes, not immediately from an act and immediately from intent, intent does not remove either from an act or from intent. And if you say that they are for the purpose of eating, through intent it is done, and through intent it rises. But did we not learn in a <term>Mishnah</term> <gloss>oral law codex</gloss>: * All handles of foods that are in the stack at the threshing floor are pure (and Rabbi Yose) (Rabbi Yose declares impure). It is well for the one who says in the stack, as he teaches [they are] bundled, that is fine. But for the one who says, what is in the stack? In the stack itself, what can be said? Here too, [it refers to] those in the stack itself. If so, what is the reasoning of the Rabbis who say like Rabbi Yose? For we learned: *Rabbi Yose declares impure. But how [is this consistent]? It is well there, [because] the reason of Rabbi Yose is that of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, for Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says: Since they are fit to be turned with a pitchfork <note>original: "עתר"</note>. But here, for what is it fit? Is this what is meant, to keep them with their bodies? The main point: All handles of foods that are in the stack at the threshing floor are pure, and Rabbi Yose... Shimon ben Lakish, what is in the stack? Rabbi Yochanan says: In the stack itself. Rabbi (Eliezer) says: The clearance of the heap. [If] it is in the stack itself, Rabbi (Eliezer) who says in the stack [is] the clearance of the heap, this is why Rabbi Yose declares it impure. But Rabbi (Eliezer) [asked]: Why is the prayer of the righteous compared to a pitchfork? To tell you, just as this pitchfork turns the grain on the threshing floor from place to place, so too the prayer of the righteous turns the mind of the Holy One, blessed be He, from the attribute of judgment to the attribute of mercy. Gemara: Rav said: The <term>Mishnah</term> [refers] to boards, to planks. The house of Judah and Rabbi Meir hold that there are four [handbreadths]. All agree that if it is wide by four handbreadths, it is valid, provided that one does not sleep under it. Gemara: Rav said: The disagreement is regarding planks that have [a width of] four [handbreadths]; all agree that if it is wide by four handbreadths, it is valid. Even if it is less than [that]... these are merely reeds. Rav Papa said: This is what it means: [If] there are four [handbreadths], all agree it is invalid; [if it is] less than [four handbreadths], it is valid. "In any case, they are mere reeds." When there are [boards] from three to four [handbreadths], one master holds that since there is no [defined] measurement for space, we do not issue a decree, and one master holds that since they serve as a partition, we do issue a decree. We learned: [If] he placed a board upon it that is wide by four handbreadths, it is valid, provided that one does not sleep under it. It is well for Shmuel, who says that for those that do not have four [handbreadths] there is a disagreement, [but for those that] do have four [handbreadths] all agree it is invalid; therefore, one should not sleep under it. But for Rav, who says that for those that have four [handbreadths] there is a disagreement, but for those that do not have four [handbreadths] all agree it is valid; for Rabbi Judah, why should one not sleep under it? Do you think it is [the opinion of] all? [In] the latter clause, we arrive at Rabbi Meir. Come hear: *Two sheets join together...

<column-break/>

<note>The text continues with a discussion of the laws of Sukkah construction, specifically regarding the use of boards and the measurements required for validity.</note>

<summary>This page explores the legal status of handles on food products and the construction requirements for a Sukkah, specifically the width of planks and the legal implications of sleeping beneath them.</summary>
<keywords>Sukkah, Tumah, Intent, Rabbi Yose, Rabbi Meir, Boards, Threshing Floor, Prayer</keywords>

Sukkah

<margin>
Eye of Justice, Lamp of the Commandment
</margin>
<margin>
[Tradition of the Shas]
* Who considers it uncleanness <term>tumah</term> <gloss>ritual impurity</gloss> in thought?
* The reasoning of Rabbi Yose, who deems vessels <term>kelim</term> <gloss>utensils/objects</gloss> to be susceptible to impurity because they are significant.
* And if we say they disagree, it suffices with the thought of the <term>log</term> <gloss>a liquid measure</gloss>.
* For it is written, it is favorable to him, and they thought that since all purities <term>taharot</term> <gloss>laws of ritual purity</gloss> were established, they all apply to him.
* The reason is explained further on.
* [S] Regarding the matter of the merchant, it is all impurity.
* [R. Eliezer] As we argue, and there is no intent for the side that supports.
* [R. Isaac] (Impurity) They write the intent that supports all of them.
* [R. Isaac Pu.] (L) <unclear>stands nu. zay.</unclear>
</margin>

<column-break/>

<note>A printer's mark or ornament appears here.</note>

<unclear>Those</unclear> who lead to impurity through thought. * Who considers it impurity in thought? And if you say it concerns the impurity of vessels because they are significant, and it suffices with the thought of the <term>log</term> <gloss>a liquid measure</gloss>. And if you say it concerns the impurity of vessels because they are significant, and if we say they disagree, it suffices with the thought of the <term>log</term>. <unclear>It is easy to doubt impurity</unclear>: in the sign. The standing. It explains for him: the towers. The <term>log</term>. For it is written, it is favorable to him, and they thought that since all purities were established, they all apply to him: And if you say impurity <unclear>to him, all are yet to come</unclear>. The reason is explained further on: <unclear>Regarding the world, that which is significant</unclear> (Ezekiel 15) <unclear>what rolls them vessels since it supports all of them to all of them since it supports all of them, the form of the mouth of impurity to support all of them all of them</unclear>.

<column-break/>

Sukkah 14

->Chapter One<-

They lead to impurity through thought, and they do not bring about <unclear>the entire day</unclear> a dispute regarding impurity through thought. They are from impurities, only through an act <note>original: "מעשה"</note>. An act removes [the matter] not from an act, and not from thought. Thought does not remove [the matter], neither from an act nor from thought. And if we say that they are for the purpose of eating, through thought it is done, and through thought it is concluded. But did we not learn in the <term>Mishnah</term> <gloss>the core text of the Talmud</gloss>: * All handles of food that are in the <term>goren</term> <gloss>threshing floor</gloss> are pure. And Rabbi Yose <note>original: "ור' יוסי"</note> (Rabbi Yose declares impure). It is well for the one who says in the <term>goren</term>, for it is taught regarding their bundles, it is well. But for the one who says, what is in the <term>goren</term>, in the actual <term>goren</term>, what is there to say? Here also, it is in the actual <term>goren</term>. If so, what is the reasoning of the Sages who speak like Rabbi Yose? For we learned: *Rabbi Yose declares impure. What is this? It is well there, the reason of Rabbi Yose is that of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, who said: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish [holds this] because they are fit to turn them with a pitchfork <note>original: "עתר"</note>. But here, for what is it fit? This is to say: to gather them in their <unclear>unclear</unclear>. The body [of the law]: All handles of food that are in the <term>goren</term> are pure. And Rabbi Yose, Shimon ben Lakish, what is [meant by] in the <term>goren</term>? Rabbi Yohanan says: in the actual <term>goren</term>. Rabbi (Eliezer) says: the release of the grain that is in the actual <term>goren</term>. Rabbi (Eliezer) who says in the <term>goren</term> the release of the grain, that is [why] Rabbi Yose declares impure. But Rabbi (Eliezer) [asked]: Why is the prayer of the righteous compared to a pitchfork? To tell you, just as this pitchfork turns the grain on the <term>goren</term> from place to place, so too the prayer of the righteous turns the mind of the Holy One, blessed be He, from the attribute of judgment to the attribute of mercy. Gemara: Rav said: The <term>Mishnah</term> [speaks] of boards <note>original: "נסרים"</note>. In the house of Judah and Rabbi Meir, he holds four [handbreadths]. All agree that if it is four handbreadths wide, it is valid, provided that one does not sleep under it. Gemara: Rav said: The dispute is regarding boards that have four [handbreadths]. All agree that if it is four handbreadths wide, and even less than that, it is not just [considered] reeds. If Rav Pappa [is quoted], this is what he says: If they have four, all agree it is invalid. Less than that, it is <unclear>less than that</unclear>, all agree it is valid. In any case, they are merely reeds. When they are from three to four, one master holds: since they do not have the measurement of a place, we do not decree [against them]. And one master holds: since they are formed for a roof, we do decree [against them]. We learned: If one placed upon it a board that is four handbreadths wide, it is valid, provided that one does not sleep under it. It is well according to Shmuel, who said: when they do not have four, the dispute [applies]; [if] they have four, all agree it is invalid; that is why one should not sleep under it. But according to Rav, who said: [where] they have four, the dispute [applies], but [if] they do not have four, all agree it is valid—according to Rabbi Judah, why should one not sleep under it? Do you think it is [the opinion of] all? In the latter part [of the Mishnah], we have come to Rabbi Meir. Come hear: *Two sheets are joined.

<header>Sukkah</header>
<sig>4</sig>

<margin>
Eye of Justice, Lamp of Commandment
</margin>
<margin>
[Tradition of the Shas]
* Who considers it impurity by thought.
* The reason for Rabbi Yose, who deems utensils susceptible to impurity because they are significant.
* And if we say they disagree, it is sufficient with the thought of the <term>log</term> <gloss>a liquid measure</gloss>.
* For it is written, it is favorable to him, and they think the purity covers all that go into it.
* The reason is explained later.
* [S] For the wine, all that is within is considered impurity.
* [R’ Elazar] Thus we clarify, and there is no intent for that which is supported.
* [R’ Isaac] (Impurity to) They write intent that is supported for all of them.
* [R’ Isaac Po.] (L) They stand. 37.
</margin>

<column-break/>

<note>A printer's mark or ornament appears here.</note>

They descend into impurity through thought. * Who considers it impurity through thought? And if you say [it refers] to the impurity of utensils that are significant, it would be sufficient with the thought of the <term>log</term> <gloss>a liquid measure</gloss>. And if you say [they] disagree, is it sufficient with the thought of the <term>log</term>? It is comfortable to suspect impurity: in the sign, in the standing. The explanation is given for it: the rows, the <term>log</term>, for it is written, it is favorable to him, and they think the purity covers all that go into it. And if you say impurity... the reason is explained later: regarding the world, for that which is significant <note>Ezekiel 15</note>, that which rolls them, utensils, since the intent is to support all of them, to support all of them, the intent is the word of impurity to support all of them, all of them.

<column-break/>

Sukkah 14

->First Chapter<-

They descend into impurity through thought, but they do not produce [the state of impurity] every day; a dispute regarding impurity through thought. 
From impurities, [one is not liable] except by an act; an act brings it out [of a state of purity] immediately, an act and immediately thought, [but] thought does not bring it out [of a state of purity], neither from an act nor from thought. And if we say they are for the purpose of eating, through thought it is made, and through thought it is completed. But did we not learn: *All handles of food items that are in the stack at the threshing floor are pure, (and Rabbi Yose [says] Rabbi Yose deems them susceptible to impurity). It is well according to the one who says in the stack, as it is taught, their binding, it is well. But according to the one who says, what [is meant by] in the stack? In the stack itself? What is there to say? Here too, [it means] in the stack itself. If so, what is the reasoning of the Rabbis who say [it is pure]? For it is said like Rabbi Yose, for we learned *Rabbi Yose deems them susceptible to impurity. How is this [reconciled]? It is well there, the reason of Rabbi Yose is according to Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, for Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: Since they are fit to turn them with a pitchfork. But here, for what is it fit? It is like saying to catch them in their <unclear>grooves</unclear>. The body [of the law]: All handles of food items that are in the stack at the threshing floor are pure, and Rabbi Yose... Shimon ben Lakish. What [is meant by] in the stack? Rabbi Yohanan said: In the stack itself. Rabbi <unclear>Eliezer</unclear> says: He permitted the gathering of the stack. In the stack itself, Rabbi <unclear>Eliezer</unclear> who said in the stack, he permitted the gathering—this is why Rabbi Yose deems it susceptible to impurity. But Rabbi <unclear>Eliezer</unclear> [also said]: To what is the prayer of the righteous compared? To a pitchfork, to tell you: just as this pitchfork turns the grain on the threshing floor from place to place, so too the prayer of the righteous turns the intent of the Holy One, blessed be He, from the attribute of strict justice to the attribute of mercy. Gemara: Rav said: The Mishnah [refers to] mats made of reeds, and Rabbi Judah and Rabbi Meir hold that there are four [handbreadths]. All agree that if it is four handbreadths wide, it is valid, provided that one does not sleep under it. Gemara: Rav said: There is a dispute regarding boards that have four [handbreadths]. All agree that if it is four handbreadths wide, and even less than that, they are merely reeds. If so, <unclear>Rava</unclear> said, this is what it is saying: If they have four, all agree it is invalid. Less than three, less than three, all agree it is valid. In any case, they are merely reeds. If [the width] is between three and four, one master holds: since they do not have the measurement of a place, we do not issue a decree. And one master holds: since they are destined for the <term>bur</term> <gloss>storage pit</gloss>, we do issue a decree. We learned: If one placed a board on it that is four handbreadths wide, it is valid, provided that one does not sleep under it. It is well according to Samuel, who said: If they do not have four [handbreadths], there is a dispute; [if] they have four, all agree it is invalid; for that reason, one should not sleep under it. But according to Rav, who said: If they have four, there is a dispute, but if they do not have four, all agree it is valid—according to Rabbi Judah, why should one not sleep under it? Do you think it is [a ruling] on which all agree? The end [of the clause] refers us to Rabbi Meir. Come hear: *Two sheets join together...

<column-break/>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>

<margin>Source Reference: Ner Mitzvah</margin>
<margin>
Tradition of the Shas:
* Who considers it susceptible to ritual impurity through intention alone.
* The reasoning of Rabbi Yose, who declares vessels that are significant to be susceptible to impurity.
* And if we say they disagree, it would be sufficient for it to have the status of a vessel through intention alone.
* As it is written, he is pleased with them, and they thought to establish all purities through them.
* The reason is explained later.
* [S] To the donkey-driver, everything that covers is considered impurity.
* [Zechariah Elazar] Thus says Marmerginun, and you have no intention for the support.
* [Zechariah Isaac] (Impurity to) They write the intention since it supports all of them.
* [Zechariah Isaac 86:] (Later) 56. 37.
</margin>

<column-break/>

<note>Small circular decorative printer's ornament used as a separator.</note>

They descend into the status of impurity through intention. * Who considers it susceptible to impurity through intention alone? And if you say it refers to the impurity of vessels which are significant, then it would be sufficient with the intention of a vessel. And if you say it refers to the impurity of vessels which are significant, and if we say they disagree, then it would be sufficient with the intention of a vessel. It is easy to clarify the doubt regarding the impurity: as specified below. At its rising. He explains his words: Purity. A vessel. For it is written that he is pleased with them, and they thought to establish all purities, all of them ascended for him. And if you say impurity for all of them further. The reason is explained later: Generally, why are they significant (Ezekiel 15) from those that roll vessels, since they are supported by each other, for they are supported by each other, in the manner of impurity to be supported by each other.

<column-break/>

Sukkah 14

->Chapter One<-

They descend into the status of ritual impurity through intention, but they do not emerge from their status of impurity except through a change brought about by a physical action <note>Hebrew: "ma’aseh"</note>. An action removes an item from the status of a previous action or from the status of a previous intention, but intention does not remove an item from the status of an action nor from the status of a previous intention. And if we say that these items were meant for the purpose of eating, they should become susceptible through intention and lose that status through intention. But did we not learn in a Mishnah: * All handles of food that are in the stack in the threshing floor are ritually pure (and Rabbi Yose) (Rabbi Yose declares them impure). It is understandable according to the one who says the Mishnah refers to the stack, as it was taught that he bound them, that is fine. But according to the one who says: what is meant by "in the stack"? It means the actual stack of grain. What can be said? Here too, it means the actual stack. If so, what is the reasoning of the Sages? It is because they speak according to the view of Rabbi Yose, as we learned: * Rabbi Yose declares them impure. This is understandable there; the reason for Rabbi Yose’s view is according to Rabbi Simeon ben Lakish. For Rabbi Simeon ben Lakish said: Since they are fit to be turned over with a pitchfork <note>term: "atar" <gloss>pitchfork or winnowing fan</gloss></note>. But here, what are they fit for? It must be said: to catch the fallen grain with their husks. Regarding the matter itself: All handles of food that are in the stack in the threshing floor are ritually pure, and Rabbi Yose and Simeon ben Lakish said: what is meant by "in the stack"? Rabbi Yochanan said: It means the actual stack. Rabbi (Eliezer) says: To permit the pile, for it is the actual stack. Rabbi (Eliezer) who said "in the stack" meant to permit the pile, that is why Rabbi Yose declares it impure. Rather, Rabbi (Eliezer) asked: Why is the prayer of the righteous compared to a pitchfork? To tell you: just as this pitchfork turns the grain in the threshing floor from place to place, so too the prayer of the righteous turns the mind of the Holy One, Blessed be He, from the attribute of cruelty to the attribute of mercy.

Gemara: Rav said: The Mishnah's *dispute regarding covering with boards is between Rabbi Judah and Rabbi Meir. But if the board is four handbreadths wide, everyone agrees that it is valid as long as one does not sleep under it. Gemara: Rav said: The dispute concerns boards that are four handbreadths wide. For everyone agrees that if it is four handbreadths wide, it is valid. Even if it is less than this, they are just like ordinary reeds. Rav Pappa said: This is what he is saying: if they are four handbreadths wide, everyone agrees it is disqualified. If they are less than three handbreadths wide, everyone agrees it is valid, for they are like ordinary reeds. Where do they disagree? From three handbreadths to four handbreadths. One Sage <note>Rabbi Meir</note> holds: Since they do not have the minimum measurement of a "place," we do not decree against them. And the other Sage <note>Rabbi Judah</note> holds: Since they are similar to the ceiling of a house, we decree against them. We learned in the Mishnah: If one placed a board upon it that is four handbreadths wide, it is valid, provided that one does not sleep under it. This is understandable according to Shmuel, who said the dispute is when they are not four handbreadths wide, but if they are four, everyone agrees it is disqualified, and for that reason, one may not sleep under it. But according to Rav, who said the dispute is when they are four handbreadths wide, but if they are not four, everyone agrees it is valid, then according to Rabbi Judah, why should one not sleep under it? Do you think this Mishnah represents everyone's view? The latter part of the Mishnah follows the view of Rabbi Meir. Come and hear: * Two sheets join together.

<column-break/>

<note>The text continues with a discussion of the laws of Sukkah construction, specifically regarding the use of boards and the measurements required for validity.</note>

<summary>The page discusses how ritual impurity is triggered by intention versus action and explores the validity of using wide wooden boards for a Sukkah roof. It also includes a homiletic teaching comparing the prayer of the righteous to a pitchfork that turns divine judgment into mercy.</summary>
<keywords>impurity, intention, action, Sukkah, boards, pitchfork, prayer, Rabbi Yose, Rav, Shmuel</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: the discussion regarding whether wide wooden boards used for roofing a Sukkah are valid and how they might be susceptible to impurity.</meta>

<margin>
Eye of Judgment, Lamp of Commandment <note>original: "Ein Mishpat Ner Mitzvah"</note>
Tradition of the Shas <note>original: "Masoret HaShas"</note>
* Who considers it impurity through intention.
* The reason for Rabbi Yose's view that he declares vessels significant.
* And if we say they differ, intention regarding a log <term>log</term> <gloss>a liquid measure</gloss> is sufficient for him.
* As it is written: it is pleasing to him regarding them, and they thought to establish all purities for him.
* The reason is explained later.
* [S] For the one covering <term>ha-sokhen</term>, it is impurity.
* [Z'l Elazar] As we explained, and did not intend that it be adjacent.
* [Z'l Isaac] (Impurity to) They write since it is adjacent to all.
* [Z'l Isaac p. 80] (L) Later 56, 37.
</margin>

<column-break/>

<note>A small symbol or printer's ornament is depicted here.</note>

They descend to the state of impurity through intention. * Who considers it impurity through intention? And if you say for the impurity of vessels which are significant, then intention regarding a log is sufficient for him. And if we say they differ, intention regarding a log is sufficient for him. It is easy to doubt impurity: that which is in the stack. Later. One explains the words for him: purities. Log. As it is written that it is pleasing to him regarding them, and they thought to establish all purities for him: And if you say impurity for all of them further. The reason is explained later: generally because they are significant (Ezekiel 15) from the rollers, vessels, since it is adjacent to all of them, since it is adjacent to all of them, since it is adjacent to all of them, a form of impurity to be adjacent to all of them.

<column-break/>

# Sukkah 14

->Chapter One<-

They descend to the state of impurity through intention, but they do not ascend <note>from a state of impurity</note> except through a physical action. <margin>The dispute regarding impurity through intention.</margin> A physical action removes an object from the status of both a previous action and intention, but intention does not remove it from the status of either a previous action or intention. And if we say that these items are for the purpose of eating, then through intention they are prepared and through intention they should be removed? But did we not learn in a Mishnah: * All handles of food <term>yadot ha-okhalin</term> <gloss>parts of a plant, like stems, used to handle the edible portion</gloss> that are in the stack at the threshing floor are pure, but Rabbi Yose declares them susceptible to impurity? It is well according to the one who said "in the stack" refers to their binding <note>being tied together</note>, that is fine. But according to the one who said: what is meant by "in the stack"? It means literally in the stack <note>strewn about loosely</note>, what can be said? Here too, it means literally in the stack. If so, what is the reason of the Rabbis? They spoke according to the view of Rabbi Yose, for we learned: * Rabbi Yose declares them susceptible to impurity. This is well there, for the reason of Rabbi Yose is according to the view of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, for Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: Since they are fit to be turned over with a pitchfork <term>atar</term>. But here <note>in the case of the Sukkah boards</note>, what are they fit for? It can be said: for catching the grains in their husks.

Regarding the matter itself: "All handles of food that are in the stack at the threshing floor are pure, and Rabbi Yose declares them susceptible to impurity." Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish asked: What is the meaning of "in the stack"? Rabbi Yochanan said: Literally in the stack. Rabbi Elazar says: It means at the time of gathering the stack. According to the one who says "literally in the stack," that is why Rabbi Yose declares it susceptible to impurity. But Rabbi Elazar <note>asks</note>: Why is the prayer of the righteous compared to a pitchfork <term>atar</term>? To tell you: Just as this pitchfork turns the grain in the threshing floor from place to place, so too the prayer of the righteous turns the mind of the Holy One, Blessed be He, from the attribute of cruelty to the attribute of mercy.

**Gemara:** Rav said: The Mishnah's dispute <note>regarding valid roofing</note> is about covering with boards <term>nasrin</term>. This is the view of Rabbi Judah and Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Meir holds that if a board is four <note>handbreadths wide</note>, all agree it is invalid. Where they differ is when it is less than four.
**Gemara:** Rav said: The dispute is about boards that have four [handbreadths]. All agree that if it is four wide... and even less than that... aren't they just plain reeds? Rav Papa said: This is what he means: If they have four, all agree it is invalid. If they are less than three, all agree it is valid, for they are just plain reeds. Where they argue is from three handbreadths up to four. One Sage <note>Rabbi Judah</note> holds that since they do not have the minimum width of a "place" <note>four handbreadths</note>, we do not decree against them. And the other Sage <note>Rabbi Meir</note> holds that since they look like a permanent ceiling, we do decree against them.
We learned in the Mishnah: If one placed a board upon it that is four handbreadths wide, it is valid, provided one does not sleep under it. This is well according to Shmuel, who said: The dispute is when they do not have four, but if they have four, all agree it is invalid—therefore one should not sleep under it. But according to Rav, who said: The dispute is when they have four, but if they do not have four, all agree it is valid—according to Rabbi Judah, why should one not sleep under it? Do you think the final clause of the Mishnah represents everyone's view? No, the final clause follows the opinion of Rabbi Meir.
Come and hear: * Two sheets join together...

Sukkah 14

<margin>Eye of Justice, Lamp of Commandment</margin>
<margin>
[Tradition of the Shas]
* Who considers it impurity by thought.
* The reason of Rabbi Yose, who declares vessels susceptible to impurity if they are significant.
* And if we say they disagree, it is enough with the thought of the handle.
* For it is written, he is pleased with them, and they thought to establish purity; all of them come into it.
* The reason is explained later.
* [S] Regarding the word "all that you mention," this is impurity.
* [Rabbi Eliezer] Here we mention, and there is no intent for that which is adjacent.
* [Rabbi Yitzhak] (Impurity to) we write intent that is adjacent to all.
* [Rabbi Yitzhak, p.] (L) standing/arising [unclear] to them.
</margin>

<column-break/>

<note>A printer’s mark or ornament appears here.</note>

<unclear>Bring into the state of</unclear> impurity by thought. * Who considers it impurity by thought? And if you say it concerns the impurity of vessels that are significant, and it is sufficient with the thought of the handle. And if you say it concerns the impurity of vessels that are significant, and if we say they disagree, is it sufficient with the thought of the handle? It is pleasant to raise an issue: <unclear>that in the mark</unclear>. Standing. It explains it: <unclear>the fences</unclear>. Handle. For it is written, he is pleased with them, and they thought to establish purity; all of them come into it. And if you say impurity <unclear>to them all... and for</unclear>. The reason is explained later. <unclear>Regarding the world, why they are significant</unclear> (Ezekiel 15: <unclear>what the roller vessels, since it is adjacent, all to all, since it is adjacent to all, a shade of the mouth of impurity to be adjacent to all, all</unclear>.

<column-break/>

Sukkah 14

->First Chapter<-

They descend into the state of impurity by thought, and there is no dispute regarding impurity by thought. <unclear>From impurities</unclear> except by an act. An act extracts it, not immediately an act and immediately thought; thought does not extract it, not from an act and not from thought. And if we say that they are for the purpose of eating, it is done by thought and by thought it ascends. But have we not learned? * All handles of food-stuffs that are in the granary are pure, (and Rabbi Yose) (Rabbi Yose declares impure). It is well for the one who says that the term <term>b'samman</term> <gloss>in the mark/bunch</gloss> is referring to what is bundled, but for the one who says what is the meaning of <term>b'samman</term>? It is <term>b'samman</term> literally. What is there to say? Here also, it is <term>b'samman</term> literally. If so, what is the reasoning of the Sages who say like Rabbi Yose, for we have learned: * Rabbi Yose declares it impure. Why is this? It is well there, the reasoning of Rabbi Yose is that of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, for Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says: Since they are fit to be turned with a pitchfork. But here, for what is it fit? It is like saying to take them with their stalks. The matter itself: All handles of food-stuffs that are in the granary are pure, and Rabbi Yose... Shimon ben Lakish. What is <term>b'samman</term>? Rabbi Yochanan says: <term>b'samman</term> literally. Rabbi (Eliezer) says: He permitted the bundle <unclear>that in b'samman</unclear> literally. Rabbi (Eliezer) who says <term>b'samman</term>, he permitted the bundle, this is why Rabbi Yose declares it impure. But Rabbi (Eliezer) [asked]: Why is the prayer of the righteous compared to a pitchfork? To tell you, just as this pitchfork turns the grain in the granary from place to place, so too the prayer of the righteous turns the opinion of the Holy One, blessed be He, from the attribute of strict justice to the attribute of mercy. Gemara: Rav said: The Mishnah is *in boards (nesarim). Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir have [a dispute]. All agree that if it is wide four handbreadths, it is valid, provided one does not sleep underneath it. Gemara: Rav said: There is a dispute regarding boards that have four [handbreadths in them]. All agree that if it is wide four handbreadths, it is valid, and even if it is less than three [handbreadths], for they are merely reeds. Rav Papa said: This is what it means: [If] it has four, all agree it is disqualified. [If it is] less than three, it is valid. [If it is]... [it is] valid. In any case, they are merely reeds. When it fluctuates from three to four: the Master holds that since it does not have the measure of a place, we do not decree, and the Master holds that since it is like a ceiling, we do decree. We have learned: If one placed on it a board that is four handbreadths wide, it is valid, provided one does not sleep underneath it. It is well for Shmuel, who said that if they do not have four [handbreadths], there is a dispute, [and if] they do have four, all agree it is disqualified; that is why one should not sleep underneath it. But according to Rav, who says that if they have four [handbreadths], there is a dispute, but if they do not have four [handbreadths], all agree it is valid—according to Rabbi Yehuda, why should one not sleep underneath it? Do you think that [this clause] is for all? The end of the passage refers us to Rabbi Meir. Come and hear: * Two sheets may be joined together.

<column-break/>

<summary>This page discusses the laws concerning the impurity of food-stuff handles, the power of prayer in changing divine judgment, and the structural requirements for a Sukkah when using boards as roofing material.</summary>
<keywords>Sukkah, impurity, thought, act, handles of food-stuffs, granary, Rabbi Yose, Rabbi Meir, boards, four handbreadths, prayer of the righteous</keywords>

# Sukkah

<margin><term>Ein Mishpat Ner Mitzvah</term> <gloss>"Well of Justice, Lamp of the Commandment", the marginal index that links the Talmud to the later law codes</gloss></margin>

<margin>

* Does thought make it subject to impurity?
* The reason, according to Rabbi Yose who declares them impure: vessels, which are of importance.
* And if we say they disagree, it is enough for it by thought <unclear>לגי</unclear>.

Sukkah 14

->Chapter One<-

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
descend into a state of impurity by thought alone, <unclear>ואין עוללין כל יום מחלוקת לטומאה במחשבה</unclear> and they do not rise out of their impurity except through a change brought about by an act. <note>The rule concerns vessels: a person's mere intention to use an object can make it susceptible to ritual impurity, but only a physical alteration can remove that status.</note> (And) an act cancels both a prior act and a prior thought; a thought cancels neither a prior act nor a prior thought. <note>The OCR here reads "an act does not cancel", which is a misprint of the scan; the sense given follows the second half of the sentence.</note>

And if we should say that, since they serve the need of eating, their status was made by thought and by thought it departs: <note>"They" are the <term>yadot</term> <gloss>handles, that is, the stalks by which produce is held</gloss> discussed on the previous page.</note> but have we not learned in a Mishnah: * "All handles of foodstuffs that one <term>besasan</term> <gloss>a disputed word, explained below as either "trampled" or "untied"</gloss> on the threshing floor are pure, (and Rabbi Yose) (Rabbi Yose declares them impure)"?

That is well according to the one who says <term>besasan</term> means that he untied their bundle. But according to the one who says: what is <term>besasan</term>? Actually trampled them, what is there to say?

Here too, it is a case where he actually trampled them.

If so, what is the reasoning of <unclear>דאמר רבנן</unclear>? They hold like Rabbi Yose, as we learned: * "Rabbi Yose declares them impure."

What comparison is this? It is well there: the reasoning of Rabbi Yose accords with Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish. For Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: since they are fit for turning over with the <term>'atar</term> <gloss>pitchfork</gloss>. But here, what are they fit for? <unclear>הכי למימר</unclear> to hold them by their stalks.

The matter itself: "All handles of foodstuffs that one <term>besasan</term> on the threshing floor are pure, and Rabbi Yose <unclear>שמעון בן לקיש</unclear>." What is <term>besasan</term>? Rabbi Yochanan said: actually trampled them. Rabbi (Eliezer) says: he untied their bundle. <unclear>דבסמן ממש</unclear> Rabbi (Eliezer), who said <term>besasan</term> means he untied their bundle, that is why Rabbi Yose declares them impure. But Rabbi (Eliezer) <note>The OCR breaks off here and resumes in the middle of the next teaching. The connecting lines are missing.</note>

Why is the prayer of the righteous likened to a pitchfork? <note>original: "למה נמשלה תפלתן של צדיקים כעתר". The teaching plays on the Hebrew root shared by the word for "pitchfork" and the verb "to entreat".</note> To tell you: just as this pitchfork turns the grain on the threshing floor from place to place, so the prayer of the righteous turns the mind of the Holy One, blessed be He, from the attribute of harshness to the attribute of mercy.

**Mishnah.** * One may roof the sukkah with boards: these are the words of Rabbi Yehuda. And Rabbi Meir <unclear>אית ליה ארבעה דברי הכל</unclear> that is four handbreadths wide, it is valid, provided that one does not sleep beneath it.

**Gemara.** Rav said: the dispute concerns boards that have a width of four handbreadths <unclear>דברי הכל שהא רחב ארבעה דברי הכל שהא רחב ארבעה</unclear> and even less than three? But those are mere reeds!

Rav Pappa said: this is what he means. If they have four handbreadths, all agree the sukkah is invalid. If they are less than three, all agree it is valid. What is the reason? They are mere reeds. Where they disagree is from three to four. One master holds: since they do not have the measure of a "place", we do not decree against them. <note>Four handbreadths is the minimum width that counts in Jewish law as a distinct, significant area.</note> And the other master holds: since <unclear>דמהוות לבור</unclear>, we do decree.

We learned in the Mishnah: "If one placed over it a board that is four handbreadths wide, it is valid, provided that one does not sleep beneath it." That is well according to Shmuel, who said the dispute concerns boards that do not have four handbreadths, but where they have four, all agree it is invalid: for that reason one may not sleep beneath it. But according to Rav, who said the dispute concerns boards that have four, whereas if they do not have four all agree it is valid, then according to Rabbi Yehuda, why may one not sleep beneath it?

Do you think this is the opinion of all? In the latter clause we have come to the view of Rabbi Meir.

Come and hear: * "Two sheets combine

<column-break/>

<note>The text continues with a discussion of the laws of sukkah construction, specifically the use of boards (<term>nesarim</term> <gloss>planks</gloss>) and the measurements required for validity.</note>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: our King, and You are exalted as Head over all.</meta>

in their side. When He returns to the Giver, it is written: "For they shall see eye to eye when the Lord returns to Zion." And it says, "And the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together, for the mouth of the Lord has spoken." The Father of mercy, He will comfort those who are burdened and remember the covenant of the steadfast, and He will save our souls from the evil hours, and He will rebuke the <term>yetzer hara</term> <gloss>evil inclination</gloss> from those who are carried, and He will favor us for an everlasting remnant. And He will fulfill our requests with a measure of goodness, salvation, and mercy.

<note>A decorative ornament.</note>

The seat of the prophets, the book of awe, the shelters, etc.
And the Torah which Moses placed before the children of Israel, by the mouth of the Lord, by the hand of Moses.

Praise the name of the Lord, for His name alone is exalted.
His glory is upon earth and heaven. He has raised the horn for His people, a praise for all His pious ones, for the children of Israel, a people near to Him. Hallelujah.

And it says, "In the name that endures for generations," and it is written: [the initials stand for L-M and Y-D-M, meaning at the time counted for a generation that is agitated]. 

And with trust, it says, "Return, O Lord, to the tens of thousands of the families of Israel. Arise, O Lord, to Your resting place, You and the ark of Your strength. Let Your priests be clothed in righteousness, and let Your pious ones sing for joy. For the sake of David Your servant, do not turn away the face of Your anointed. For I have given you a good teaching, do not forsake My Torah. It is a tree of life to those who grasp it, and those who support it are happy. Its ways are ways of pleasantness, and all its paths are peace. Bring us back, O Lord, to You, and we will return; renew our days as of old. Happy are they, etc."

To the Chief Musician, a Psalm of David. May the Lord answer you in the day of trouble; may the name of the God of Jacob defend you. May He send your help from the sanctuary, and support you from Zion. May He remember all your offerings, and accept your burnt sacrifice, <term>selah</term> <gloss>forever/pause</gloss>. May He grant you according to your heart’s desire, and fulfill all your counsel. We will sing for joy in your salvation, and in the name of our God we will set up our banners; may the Lord fulfill all your petitions. Now I know that the Lord saves His anointed; He will answer him from His holy heaven with the mighty saving power of His right hand. Some trust in chariots, and some in horses, but we will call upon the name of the Lord our God. They have bowed down and fallen, but we have risen and stand upright. Lord, save; may the King answer us on the day we call. As for Me, this is My covenant with them, says the Lord: "My spirit that is upon you, and My words which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart out of your mouth, nor out of the mouth of your seed, nor out of the mouth of your seed’s seed," says the Lord, "from now and forever."

And You are Holy, O You who are enthroned upon the praises of Israel. And one called to another and said: "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory." And they receive one from another and say: "Holy in the highest heavens, the house of His dwelling; holy upon the earth, the work of His might; holy forever and to all eternity. The Lord of Hosts; the whole earth is full of the radiance of His glory." And a wind lifted me up, and I heard behind me the sound of a great rushing: "Blessed be the glory of the Lord from His place." And a wind lifted me up, and I heard behind me the sound of a great trembling, those who praise and say: "Blessed be the glory of the Lord from the place of the house of His dwelling." The Lord shall reign forever and to all eternity. The kingdom of the Lord endures forever and to all eternity. O Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel our fathers, keep this forever for the inclination of the thoughts of the heart of Your people, and direct their heart unto You. And He, being merciful, forgives iniquity and does not destroy; yes, He frequently turns His anger away and does not stir up all His wrath. For You, O Lord, are good and forgiving, and abundant in kindness to all who call upon You. Your righteousness is righteousness forever, and Your Torah is truth. Grant truth to Jacob, kindness to Abraham, as You have sworn to our fathers from days of old. Blessed be the Lord day by day; God bears our burden, He is our salvation, <term>selah</term>. The Lord of Hosts is with us, a fortress for us is the God of Jacob, <term>selah</term>. Lord of Hosts, happy is the man who trusts in You. Lord, save; may the King answer us on the day we call. Blessed is our God who created us for His glory, and separated us from those who go astray, and gave us the Torah of truth, and planted eternal life within us. May He open our heart to His Torah, and place in our heart His love and His awe, and to do His will, and to serve Him with a perfect heart, so that we may not labor in vain, nor bring forth for confusion. May it be Your will, O Lord our God and God of our fathers, that we keep Your statutes in this world, and that we merit to live and see and inherit goodness and blessing for the years of the days of the Messiah and for the life of the World to Come. In order that my glory may sing Your praise and not be silent; O Lord my God, I will give thanks to You forever. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his trust. Trust in the Lord forever, for in <term>Yah</term> <gloss>the Lord</gloss> the Lord is the Rock of Ages. And those who know Your name will trust in You, for You have not forsaken those who seek You, O Lord. The Lord desires, for the sake of His righteousness, to magnify the Torah and make it glorious.

<column-break/>

O Lord our Master, how majestic is Your name in all the earth.
Be strong and let your heart take courage, all you who wait for the Lord.

And now, I pray, let the power of the Lord be great, as You have spoken, saying: Remember Your mercies and Your kindnesses, for they have been from eternity.

Magnified and sanctified be His great name in the world which He has created according to His will, and may He establish His kingdom, and may He cause His salvation to flourish and bring near the [alternative reading: the end of the] Messiah. In your lifetimes and in your days and in the lifetimes of all the house of Israel, speedily and at a near time, and say, Amen. May His great name be blessed forever and to all eternity. Blessed and praised and glorified and exalted and extolled and honored and raised and lauded be the name of the Holy One, blessed is He, beyond (even more and beyond) all blessings and hymns, praises and consolations that are spoken in the world, and say, Amen. Accept, accept with mercy and favor our prayer. May the prayer and supplication of all the house of Israel be accepted before their Father who is in heaven, and say, Amen. May the name of the Lord be blessed from now and forever.

May there be abundant peace from heaven and life upon us and upon all Israel, and say, Amen. My help is from the Lord, Maker of heaven and earth. He who makes peace in His high places, He will make peace upon us and upon all Israel, and say, Amen.

A prayer of David: Incline, O Lord, Your ear, answer me, for I am poor and needy. Protect my soul, for I am pious; save Your servant, You my God, who trusts in You. Be gracious to me, O Lord, for to You I call all the day. Gladden the soul of Your servant, for to You, O Lord, I lift up my soul. For You, O Lord, are good and forgiving, and abundant in kindness to all who call upon You. Give ear, O Lord, to my prayer, and attend to the voice of my supplications. In the day of my trouble I will call upon You, for You will answer me. There is none like You among the gods, O Lord, and there are no works like Yours. All nations whom You have made shall come and bow down before You, O Lord, and they shall glorify Your name. For You are great and perform wonders; You alone are God. Teach me, O Lord, Your way, I will walk in Your truth; unite my heart to fear Your name. I will give thanks to You, O Lord my God, with all my heart, and I will glorify Your name forever. For Your kindness is great toward me, and You have delivered my soul from the lowest depths. O God, the insolent have risen against me, and a band of violent men have sought my soul, and they have not set You before them. But You, O Lord, are a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in kindness and truth. Turn to me and be gracious to me; give Your strength to Your servant and save the son of Your maidservant. Work for me a sign for good, that those who hate me may see it and be ashamed, because You, O Lord, have helped me and comforted me.

O house of Jacob, come and let us walk in the light of the Lord. For all the peoples will walk, each in the name of its god, but we will walk in the name of the Lord our God forever and ever.
May the Lord our God be with us as He was with our fathers; may He not forsake us and may He not cast us off. To incline our hearts to Him, to walk in all His ways, and to keep His commandments, and His statutes, and His ordinances which He commanded our fathers. And let these my words, which I have prayed before the Lord, be near to the Lord our God day and night, to maintain the cause of His servant and the cause of His people Israel, as each day requires. That all the peoples of the earth may know that the Lord is God; there is no other.

A Song of Ascents of David: If it had not been the Lord who was for us, let Israel now say. If it had not been the Lord who was for us when men rose up against us. Then they would have swallowed us alive when their anger was kindled against us. Then the waters would have overwhelmed us, the torrent would have gone over our soul. Then the raging waters would have gone over our soul. Blessed be the Lord who has not given us as a prey to their teeth. Our soul has escaped as a bird from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken and we have escaped. Our help is in the name of the Lord, Maker of heaven and earth.

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: ...He will see Him [as it is written] "when the Lord returns to Zion." And it is said, "The glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together, for the mouth of the Lord has spoken." The Father of mercy, He will have mercy on the burdened people, and He will remember the covenant of the steadfast <note>referring to the patriarchs</note>, and He will save our souls from the evil hours, and He will rebuke the evil inclination from those who are carried <note>meaning those who carry the burden of their own frailties</note>, and He will grant us grace for everlasting deliverance. And He will fulfill our requests with a measure of goodness, salvation, and mercy.</meta>

<note>Decorative ornament</note>

The Throne of the Prophets <note>referring to the verses recited when the Torah scroll is removed</note>... 

And this is the Torah which Moses placed before the children of Israel, by the mouth of the Lord, by the hand of Moses.

Praise the name of the Lord, for His name alone is exalted. 
His glory is upon earth and heaven. He has lifted up the horn of His people, praise for all His pious ones, for the children of Israel, the people close to Him. Hallelujah.

And it says, "His name endures forever," and it is written, "Lord, your name endures forever, Lord, your remembrance throughout all generations."
The Throne of the Prophets (The Ark, etc.).

And trust, and say, "Return, O Lord, to the tens of thousands of the thousands of Israel. Arise, O Lord, to Your resting place, You and the Ark of Your strength. Let Your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let Your pious ones sing for joy. For the sake of David Your servant, do not turn away the face of Your anointed. For I have given you a good instruction; do not forsake My Torah. It is a tree of life to those who take hold of it, and those who support it are happy. Its ways are ways of pleasantness, and all its paths are peace. Bring us back to You, O Lord, and we shall return; renew our days as of old." Blessed are those...

For the Leader, a Psalm of David. May the Lord answer you in the day of trouble; may the name of the God of Jacob set you high. May He send your help from the sanctuary, and support you from Zion. May He remember all your meal offerings, and accept your burnt offering, Selah. May He grant you your heart's desire, and fulfill all your counsel. We will sing for joy in your salvation, and in the name of our God we will set up our banners; may the Lord fulfill all your requests. Now I know that the Lord saves His anointed; He will answer him from His holy heaven with the saving power of His right hand. Some trust in chariots, and some in horses, but we will make mention of the name of the Lord our God. They have bowed down and fallen, but we have risen and stand upright. O Lord, save; may the King answer us on the day we call. As for Me, this is My covenant with them, says the Lord: My spirit that is upon you, and My words which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your seed, nor from the mouth of your seed's seed, says the Lord, from now and forever.

And You are holy, enthroned upon the praises of Israel. And one called to the other and said: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory. And they receive [the words] one from the other and say: Holy in the highest heavens, the house of His presence; holy upon the earth, the work of His might; holy forever and to all eternity. The Lord of Hosts; the whole earth is full of His radiant glory. A spirit lifted me up, and I heard behind me a sound of great rushing: Blessed be the glory of the Lord from His place. And a spirit lifted me up, and I heard behind me the sound of a great tremor, of those who praise and say: Blessed is the glory of the Lord from the place of the house of His presence. The Lord is King forever and to all eternity. The Lord’s kingdom endures forever and to all eternity. O Lord, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, our ancestors, keep this forever for the inclinations of the thoughts of the heart of Your people, and direct their hearts to You. And He, being merciful, forgives iniquity and does not destroy; He frequently turns His anger away and does not arouse all His wrath. For You, O Lord, are good, and forgiving, and abundant in kindness to all who call upon You. Your righteousness is righteousness forever, and Your Torah is truth. You will give truth to Jacob, kindness to Abraham, which You swore to our ancestors from days of old. Blessed be the Lord, day by day He bears our burden, the God of our salvation, Selah. The Lord of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our stronghold, Selah. O Lord of Hosts, happy is the man who trusts in You. O Lord, save; may the King answer us on the day we call. Blessed is our God who created us for His glory, and separated us from those who go astray, and gave us the Torah of truth, and planted eternal life within us. May He open our hearts to His Torah, and place in our hearts His love and His awe, to do His will and to serve Him with a whole heart, so that we do not labor in vain, nor bring forth for confusion. May it be Your will, O Lord our God and God of our ancestors, that we keep Your statutes in this world, and that we merit to live and see and inherit goodness and blessing for the years of the days of the Messiah and for the life of the world to come. In order that glory may sing to You and not be silent, O Lord my God, I will thank You forever. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and whose trust the Lord is. Trust in the Lord forever, for in God the Lord is a Rock of eternity. And those who know Your name will trust in You, for You have not forsaken those who seek You, O Lord. The Lord desires, for the sake of His righteousness, to make the Torah great and glorious.

<column-break/>

O Lord our Master, how glorious is Your name in all the earth.
Be strong and let your heart take courage, all you who wait for the Lord.

And now, I pray, let the power of the Lord be great, as You have spoken, saying: Remember Your mercies and Your kindnesses, for they are from old.

Magnified and sanctified be His great name. In the world which He created according to His will, and may He establish His kingdom, and cause His redemption to sprout, and bring near [the time of] His Messiah. In your lifetimes and in your days and in the lifetimes of the whole house of Israel, speedily and at a near time, and say: Amen. May His great name be blessed forever and to all eternity. Blessed and praised and glorified and exalted and elevated and honored and raised and extolled be the name of the Holy One, blessed be He. Above (far above) all the blessings and songs, praises and consolations which are uttered in the world, and say: Amen. Receive, receive with mercy and with favor our prayer. May the prayer and supplication of the whole house of Israel be accepted before their Father who is in heaven, and say: Amen. May the name of the Lord be blessed from now and forever.

May there be great peace from heaven and life for us and for all Israel, and say: Amen. My help comes from the Lord, Maker of heaven and earth. He who makes peace in His high places, He will make peace upon us and upon all Israel, and say: Amen.

A prayer of David: Incline Your ear, O Lord, and answer me, for I am poor and needy. Preserve my soul, for I am pious; save Your servant, You my God, who trusts in You. Be gracious to me, O Lord, for to You I call all the day. Gladden the soul of Your servant, for to You, O Lord, I lift up my soul. For You, O Lord, are good, and forgiving, and abundant in kindness to all who call upon You. Give ear, O Lord, to my prayer, and attend to the voice of my supplications. In the day of my trouble I will call upon You, for You will answer me. There is none like You among the gods, O Lord, and there are no works like Yours. All nations whom You have made shall come and bow down before You, O Lord, and shall honor Your name. For You are great and do wondrous things; You alone are God. Teach me Your way, O Lord, that I may walk in Your truth; unite my heart to revere Your name. I will thank You, O Lord my God, with all my heart, and I will honor Your name forever. For Your kindness is great toward me, and You have delivered my soul from the lowest depths. O God, the insolent have risen against me, and a congregation of violent men have sought my soul, and they have not set You before them. But You, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in kindness and truth. Turn to me and be gracious to me; give Your strength to Your servant, and save the son of Your handmaid. Show me a sign for good, that those who hate me may see it and be ashamed, because You, O Lord, have helped me and comforted me.

House of Jacob, come and let us walk in the light of the Lord. For all the peoples walk each in the name of its god, but we will walk in the name of the Lord our God forever and ever.
May the Lord our God be with us, as He was with our ancestors; may He not forsake us and not abandon us. To incline our hearts to Him, to walk in all His ways, and to keep His commandments, His statutes, and His ordinances, which He commanded our ancestors. And let these words of mine, which I have supplicated before the Lord, be near to the Lord our God day and night, to maintain the cause of His servant and the cause of His people Israel, as each day requires. So that all the peoples of the earth may know that the Lord is God; there is no other.

A Song of Ascents, by David: If it had not been the Lord who was for us, let Israel now say. If it had not been the Lord who was for us when men rose up against us. Then they would have swallowed us alive in the burning of their anger against us. Then the waters would have overwhelmed us, the torrent would have gone over our soul. Then the proud waters would have gone over our soul. Blessed be the Lord, who has not given us as prey to their teeth. Our soul has escaped like a bird out of the snare of the fowlers; the snare was broken, and we escaped. Our help is in the name of the Lord, Maker of heaven and earth.

Beside them, as He returns to the Giver, it is written: "For they shall see eye to eye when the Lord returns to Zion." And it says: "And the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together, for the mouth of the Lord has spoken." The Father of mercy, He shall comfort a people who are burdened, and He shall remember the covenant of the steadfast ones, and He shall save our souls from the evil hours, and He shall rebuke the evil inclination from those who are carried, and He shall favor us with an everlasting remnant. And He shall fulfill our requests with a measure of goodness, salvation, and mercy.

<note>A decorative ornament appears here.</note>

The seat of the prophets, the Book of the Sanctuary of the <term>Chufim</term> <gloss>a liturgical title for the heavenly dwelling/canopy</gloss>, etc.:
And this is the Torah that Moses set before the Children of Israel, by the word of the Lord, by the hand of Moses.

Praise the name of the Lord, for His name alone is exalted.
His glory is upon earth and heaven. He has raised a horn for His people, a praise for all His pious ones, for the Children of Israel, the people close to Him. Hallelujah.

And he says, "In the name of the One who stands for the generation," and it is written: L"M <note>abbreviation for L'Doro v'Doror, for generations</note> and V"Y"M <note>abbreviation for V'Yom, and the day</note>, and at the time as is counted, for the generation of the congregation.
The seat of the prophets, the <term>Pasuk</term> <gloss>verse</gloss> (Sanctuary of the Chufim, etc.):

And with trust he says: "Return, O Lord, to the tens of thousands of the thousands of Israel. Arise, O Lord, to Your resting place, You and the ark of Your strength. Let Your priests be clothed in righteousness, and let Your pious ones sing for joy. For the sake of David Your servant, do not turn away the face of Your anointed. For I have given you a good instruction; do not forsake My Torah. It is a tree of life to those who grasp it, and those who support it are happy. Its ways are ways of pleasantness, and all its paths are peace. Turn us back to You, O Lord, and we shall return; renew our days as of old." <term>Ashrei</term> <gloss>"Happy are they" (Psalm 145), etc.</gloss>

For the Conductor, a Psalm of David. May the Lord answer you in the day of trouble; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you. May He send your help from the sanctuary, and from Zion may He support you. May He remember all your meal offerings, and may He accept your burnt offering, <term>Selah</term> <gloss>forever/perpetually</gloss>. May He grant you your heart's desire, and fulfill all your counsel. We will sing for joy in your salvation, and in the name of our God we will raise our banners; may the Lord fulfill all your petitions. Now I know that the Lord saves His anointed; He answers him from His holy heavens with the mighty acts of salvation of His right hand. Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will call upon the name of the Lord our God. They have bowed down and fallen, but we have risen and stood upright. O Lord, save; may the King answer us on the day we call. As for Me, this is My covenant with them, says the Lord: My spirit which is upon you and My words which I have put in your mouth shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your offspring, nor from the mouth of your offspring's offspring, says the Lord, from now and forever.

And You are holy, enthroned upon the praises of Israel. And one called to another and said: "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory." And they accept this from one another and say: "Holy in the highest heavens, the house of His dwelling; holy upon the earth, the work of His might; holy forever and for all eternity. The Lord of Hosts, the whole earth is full of the radiance of His glory." Then a wind lifted me, and I heard behind me the sound of a great rushing: "Blessed is the glory of the Lord from His place." And a wind lifted me, and I heard behind me the sound of a great trembling, those who praise and say: "Blessed is the glory of the Lord from the place of the house of His dwelling." The Lord is King forever and for all eternity. The Lord's kingdom stands forever and for all eternity. O Lord, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, our ancestors, keep this forever for the impulse of the thoughts of the heart of Your people, and direct their heart to You. And He, being merciful, forgives iniquity and does not destroy, and frequently turns back His anger and does not stir up all His wrath. For You, O Lord, are good and forgiving and abundant in kindness to all who call upon You. Your righteousness is righteousness forever, and Your Torah is truth. Grant truth to Jacob, kindness to Abraham, as You have sworn to our ancestors from days of old. Blessed is the Lord day by day; the God of our salvation carries our burden, <term>Selah</term> <gloss>forever</gloss>. The Lord of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is a stronghold for us, <term>Selah</term>. O Lord of Hosts, happy is the man who trusts in You. O Lord, save; may the King answer us on the day we call. Blessed is our God who created us for His glory, and separated us from those who err, and gave us the Torah of truth, and planted eternal life within us. May He open our hearts to His Torah and place in our hearts His love and His awe, and to do His will and to serve Him with a whole heart, so that we may not labor in vain, nor give birth to confusion. May it be Your will, O Lord our God and God of our ancestors, that we keep Your statutes in this world, and that we merit to live and see and inherit goodness and blessing for the years of the Messianic era and for the life of the World to Come. In order that my glory may sing to You and not be silent; O Lord my God, I will thank You forever. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his trust. Trust in the Lord forever, for in <term>Yah</term> <gloss>the Lord</gloss>, the Lord, is the Rock of worlds. And those who know Your name will trust in You, for You have not forsaken those who seek You, O Lord. The Lord desired, for the sake of His righteousness, to make the Torah great and glorious.

<column-break/>

O Lord, our Master, how mighty is Your name in all the earth!
Be strong and let your heart take courage, all you who wait for the Lord.

And now, may the power of the Lord be great, as You have spoken, saying: Remember Your mercies and Your kindnesses, for they are from of old.

May His great name be magnified and sanctified in the world that He created according to His will; may He establish His kingdom, and may He cause His salvation to sprout and bring near <note>a marginal note says: "or: the end of"</note> His anointed, in your lifetime and in your days and in the lifetime of the entire house of Israel, speedily and at a time soon, and say: Amen. May His great name be blessed forever and for all eternity. Blessed, praised, glorified, exalted, extolled, honored, uplifted, and lauded be the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, above (at times, and above all) all the blessings and hymns, praises and consolations that are uttered in the world, and say: Amen. Receive, receive with mercy and with favor our prayer. May the prayer and supplication of the entire house of Israel be accepted before their Father who is in heaven, and say: Amen. Receive, may the name of the Lord be blessed from now and forever.

May there be great peace from heaven and life upon us and upon all Israel, and say: Amen. My help is from the Lord, Maker of heaven and earth. He who makes peace in His high places, He shall make peace upon us and upon all Israel, and say: Amen.

A prayer of David: Incline Your ear, O Lord, answer me, for I am poor and needy. Protect my soul, for I am pious; save Your servant, You my God, who trusts in You. Be gracious to me, O Lord, for I call to You all day long. Gladden the soul of Your servant, for to You, O Lord, I lift up my soul. For You, O Lord, are good and forgiving and abundant in kindness to all who call upon You. Hear, O Lord, my prayer, and listen to the voice of my supplications. In the day of my trouble I will call upon You, for You will answer me. There is none like You among the gods, O Lord, and there is nothing like Your works. All the nations that You have made shall come and bow down before You, O Lord, and they shall honor Your name. For You are great and do wondrous things; You alone are God. Teach me, O Lord, Your way, that I may walk in Your truth; unite my heart to fear Your name. I will thank You, O Lord my God, with all my heart, and I will glorify Your name forever. For Your kindness is great toward me, and You have saved my soul from the lowest depths. O God, the arrogant have risen against me, and a congregation of violent men have sought my soul, and they have not set You before them. But You, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abundant in kindness and truth. Turn to me and be gracious to me; give Your strength to Your servant, and save the son of Your handmaid. Work a sign for me for good, so that those who hate me may see and be ashamed, for You, O Lord, have helped me and comforted me.

House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord. For all the nations will walk, each in the name of its god, but we will walk in the name of the Lord our God forever and ever.
May the Lord our God be with us, as He was with our ancestors; may He not forsake us and not abandon us. To incline our hearts to Him, to walk in all His ways, and to keep His commandments and His statutes and His ordinances which He commanded our ancestors. And let these words of mine, which I have supplicated before the Lord, be near to the Lord our God day and night, to execute the judgment of His servant and the judgment of His people Israel, as each day requires. In order that all the peoples of the earth may know that the Lord is God; there is no other.

A Song of Ascents, by David: If it had not been the Lord who was for us, let Israel now say: If it had not been the Lord who was for us, when men rose up against us: Then they would have swallowed us up alive, in the heat of their anger against us: Then the waters would have overwhelmed us; a torrent would have gone over our soul: Then the arrogant waters would have passed over our soul: Blessed be the Lord, who has not given us as prey to their teeth. Our soul has escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers; the snare was broken, and we have escaped. Our help is in the name of the Lord, Maker of heaven and earth.
