Regarding this it is said, "And it came to pass that Isaac was old and his eyes dimmed" <note>Genesis 27:1</note>; that is to say, a mystery upon a mystery, for it speaks of his attribute. Therefore, the blessed One, the attribute of severe judgment, has mercy on His world and returns to the <term>ma’aseh</term> <gloss>work/act</gloss> for His occupation, for He is blessed, and this is the mystery of the attribute of severe judgment, for "all that is made is for His purpose," and this is the mystery of "Everything is turned, therefore it is pure." And in this way, you shall understand the mystery of the <term>Pachad Yitzchak</term> <gloss>Fear of Isaac</gloss>, for it is power, and it fills like the taste of the crown above, turning its face downward to shine into His great hall, covering with mercy, like the taste of "Let His face shine upon us," for it descends from the covering. And this is the mystery of "And the Lord will cause His face to shine upon you." And here I will explain to you further in this matter: know that in every place where it is written "the shining of the face" above, it is a great mystery, and it is the day of the three attributes and the crown, the face of the <term>Am</term> <gloss>People/Nation</gloss>, and all of them are attached to the Fear of Isaac and to the attribute of the Crown, turning its face, and it is attributed to all the mercies and is caught and is caught here for mercies. And this is the mystery of "God is Lord and He has given us light." And this is the mystery of the verse, "Happy is the people who know the joyful shout, O Lord, they shall walk in the light of Your countenance." And you shall understand the mystery of the verse, for Isaac was purified and his eyes dimmed from the light. And if you grasp the mystery of the <term>teki’ah</term> <gloss>blast of the shofar</gloss> in the mystery of the <term>sofer</term> <gloss>scribe/counter</gloss> in the secret of "On the day You gave us." And the mystery of the verse, "Happy is the people who know the joyful shout, O Lord, they shall walk in the light of Your countenance," and they shall be merciful from the mystery of the <term>sofer</term> <gloss>scribe/counter</gloss> of the army of Isaac. And when you understand the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss> in "the light of Your countenance they shall walk," [it is] the mystery of those who say "the remembrance of the forbearances." And the mystery of "the back of the <term>lahat</term> <gloss>flame/blazing sword</gloss>" you shall understand what is the difference between "the remembrance of the forbearances" and "all of them [are] the back of the <term>lahat</term> <gloss>flame/blazing sword</gloss>." For the remembrance of the forbearances is of the nature of the great mercies from above, in the mystery of the verse, "And the Lord will cause His face to shine." And the back of the <term>lahat</term> <gloss>flame/blazing sword</gloss> is those which are of the nature of judgment, from the attribute of the sword, as it is said, "And the spirit of God hovered over the face of the deep," and it remembers the light and the <term>chesed</term> <gloss>loving-kindness</gloss>. And therefore the attribute of God turns downward to be included in the attribute of judgment, the place where everything is formed. And this is the mystery of "And the Lord will cause His face to shine upon you." And the secret which I have made known to you here is the mystery of the attributes. Therefore, to make known to you the mystery of the attribute of the Lord, the blessed One who reconciles, in the middle, and guides you from one to the other to perfection: like the names of the <term>Sefirot</term> <gloss>divine emanations</gloss> and the blessed One who stands in the middle, the <term>tefillin</term> <gloss>phylacteries</gloss> [which include] <term>chesed</term> <gloss>loving-kindness</gloss> on the right and <term>din</term> <gloss>judgment</gloss> on the left, and they are included in the middle from the <term>chesed</term> <gloss>loving-kindness</gloss> and the judgment. And so too regarding the names of <term>chesed</term> <gloss>loving-kindness</gloss> in the middle, they are called by the names of the mercies, and their ascent is in the middle of the <term>tefillin</term> <gloss>phylacteries</gloss>, for the mercies are unified and included. And here I will explain further, know that all the names of the Holy One and the epithets and the attributes, whether they are called <term>chesed</term> <gloss>loving-kindness</gloss>, whether they are called <term>rachamim</term> <gloss>mercies</gloss>, whether they are called <term>din</term> <gloss>judgment</gloss>, you have not one of them that would be pure <term>chesed</term> <gloss>loving-kindness</gloss> or pure judgment or pure <term>rachamim</term> <gloss>mercies</gloss>, but there is in them a mixture, and everything is from below to above and from above to below. Everything is mercies and <term>chesed</term> <gloss>loving-kindness</gloss> in simple purity, without mixture in the world. And now open your eyes and give your heart to the deep secrets, for they are like the paths of the chariot and the order of the <term>Sefirot</term> <gloss>divine emanations</gloss>. And in your seeing this, you will understand the root of the <term>Sefirot</term> <gloss>divine emanations</gloss> and the names and the attributes, how they are ordered in the world. And in your understanding, the blessed One, you will understand the secret of the order of the All, the blessed One, blessed be He. Know that the names of the Upper <term>Keter</term> <gloss>Crown</gloss> are all simple names without any mixture. As for the <term>rachamim</term> <gloss>mercies</gloss> which are known, those which are adjacent to the name of <term>El</term> <gloss>God</gloss> or <term>chesed</term> <gloss>loving-kindness</gloss> adjacent to the name of <term>Elohim</term> <gloss>God/Judgment</gloss>, they are all pure and simple, there is no mixture of judgment in them, and I have fixed the mystery of what is said, "And with great mercies I will gather you." <meta>Continues from the previous page, mid-sentence. The OCR of this page is heavily corrupted (many letters misread, e.g. ס for ש, כ for ב, ל for א). The translation follows the most probable reconstruction of the Hebrew; passages that could not be securely recovered are flagged in notes.</meta>

<warning>OCR quality is poor despite the "good" scan flag. Several phrases, especially in the first lines and in the passage on "He who remembers forgotten things", are reconstructed from context and from the biblical verses quoted. Check against the page image before citing.</warning>

to destroy by judgment, and not to <note>the rest of this opening phrase is garbled in the transcription and cannot be recovered</note>. And of this it is said, "And it came to pass, when Isaac was old, and his eyes were dim" <note>Genesis 27:1</note>: that is to say, the verse speaks both of him and of his attribute. Therefore the Blessed One, in the hour of harsh judgment, has mercy on His world and returns higher and higher <note>the next few words are garbled; the sense appears to be that in the hour of harsh judgment the whole is turned toward mercy</note>. And this is the secret of "it is all turned white: he is clean" <note>Leviticus 13:13, on the leper whose whole body has turned white and who is therefore declared pure</note>. In this way, understand that the <term>Pachad Yitzchak</term> <gloss>the Fear of Isaac, the attribute of stern judgment</gloss> has no power or dominion in the hour when the supernal <term>Keter</term> <gloss>Crown, the highest sefirah</gloss> shines its face downward, because its great light covers <note>a word or two is garbled here</note> with mercy in the hour when He, may He be blessed, shines His supernal face <note>the end of this clause is garbled</note>. And this is "The Lord make His face shine upon you, and be gracious to you" <note>Numbers 6:25</note>. And I will now enlighten your eyes further, with God's help. Know that wherever you find the light of the face above, it is a great secret. It is this: there are three hundred and ten faces of wrath, and all of them cling to the Fear of Isaac. When the attribute of <term>Keter</term> shines its face and is revealed, all of them become faces of mercy, and all are turned to mercy. And this is the secret of "The Lord is God, and He has given us light" <note>Psalm 118:27; reading reconstructed from a garbled transcription</note>. And this is the meaning of "Happy is the people that know the trumpet blast; O Lord, they walk in the light of Your face" <note>Psalm 89:16</note>. By this you will understand the secret of "And it came to pass, when Isaac was old, and his eyes were dim from seeing." Then you will grasp the secret of "Blow the <term>shofar</term> <gloss>ram's horn</gloss> at the new moon, at the covered time, for our festival day" <note>Psalm 81:4, the verse associated with Rosh Hashanah, the Day of Judgment</note>, and the secret of "Happy is the people that know the trumpet blast; O Lord, they walk in the light of Your face" <note>a few words are garbled here; the sense is that mercy is aroused</note> through the <term>shofar</term> of the ram of Isaac. And when you consider the matter of "they walk in the light of Your face," <note>garbled; apparently "you will understand"</note> the secret of what we say: "He who remembers forgotten things" <note>a phrase from the Rosh Hashanah liturgy</note>. <note>The next sentence is badly garbled. It appears to contrast "He who remembers forgotten things" with a second expression, probably "from behind the darkness", and to say: then you will understand the difference between the two.</note> For "He who remembers forgotten things" is drawn from the great mercies above, in the secret of "The Lord is God, and He has given us light." But those from behind the darkness <note>reading uncertain</note> are drawn from the attribute of <term>Elohim</term> <gloss>the divine name of judgment</gloss>, from the attribute of darkness, as it is said, "and darkness was upon the face of the deep" <note>Genesis 1:2</note>, and "who forms light and creates darkness" <note>Isaiah 45:7</note>. Therefore the attribute of the Lord <note>the four-letter Name, the attribute of mercy</note> shines below, being included in the attribute of <term>Elohim</term>, the place that contains them all. And this is the secret of "May He make His face shine upon you." And now that we have informed you of this concerning these two attributes, we must inform you of the secret of the attribute of the Name <term>YHVH</term>, may He be blessed, which decides in the middle, and how He governs His world. The cognomens <note>the secondary divine titles that attach to each Name</note> of <term>YHVH</term>, may He be blessed, who stands in the middle line: on their right is <term>Chesed</term> <gloss>Loving-kindness</gloss>, on their left is <term>Din</term> <gloss>Judgment</gloss>, and they are compounded in the middle of Loving-kindness and Judgment. These cognomens that are in the middle are called the cognomens of <term>Rachamim</term> <gloss>Mercy</gloss>, and they rise in the middle, belonging to <term>YHVH</term>, which is Mercy <note>the last word of this sentence is garbled</note>.

And I will now explain, with God's help. Know that of all the holy Names, the cognomens and the attributes, whether they are called Loving-kindness, or called Mercy, or called Judgment, there is not one of them all that is complete Loving-kindness, or complete Judgment, or complete Mercy, without some mixture in it. All this holds from the Name <term>El</term> <note>reading uncertain; the transcription is garbled at this name</note> and downward. But from it and upward, all is Mercy and Loving-kindness, complete and simple, with no mixture whatsoever.

And now open your eyes and set your heart to see deep matters, which are like general rules for the orders of the <term>Merkavah</term> <gloss>the divine Chariot, the structure of the upper worlds</gloss> and the bond of the <term>Sefirot</term> <gloss>divine emanations</gloss>. When you see this, you will understand something of how the Sefirot, the Names and the attributes are bound together in the world. And when you understand this, you will understand the secret of the Creator of all, may He be blessed and exalted. Know that the Names of the supernal <term>Keter</term> are all simple Names, without mixture of anything. For example, the well-known Mercy that is attached to the Name <term>Ehyeh</term> <gloss>"I will be", the Name belonging to Keter</gloss> <note>the Name is garbled in the transcription and is restored here from context</note>, or the Loving-kindness attached to the Name <term>Ehyeh</term>: all are complete and simple, with no mixture of anything in them. And this is the secret of what is said, "and with great mercies I will gather you" <note>Isaiah 54:7</note>. And what are these "great mercies"?

<summary>Gikatilla explains that when the supernal Keter shines its face, the three hundred and ten faces of wrath attached to the Fear of Isaac are turned to mercy, which is the hidden meaning of Isaac's dim eyes, the priestly blessing, and the shofar of Rosh Hashanah. He then introduces the Name YHVH as the middle line balancing Loving-kindness and Judgment, and states that only the Names of Keter are pure mercy without any mixture.</summary>

of a sandal, and [the straps of] a phylactery for the head when it is <note>original: "cross" or "intersected"</note> crossed, and for the arm when it does not move up and down, and the ears of a skin-bag, and the ears of a pouch. **4** These are the items that require the water to reach them: the knots at the joints of the shoulder, and the rim of a coat of mail, it needs to be stretched, and the phylactery for the head when it is not crossed, and for the arm when it moves up and down, and the straps of a sandal, and the wings [of a garment]—they immerse them folded until they are submerged, and they immerse them until they bubble and rest from bubbling. **5** All handles of vessels that are long and one intends to cut them, one immerses them up to the measured place; Rabbi Judah says: until one immerses all of them. The chain of a large bucket [needs] four handbreadths, and of a small one, ten; one immerses them up to the measured place; Rabbi Tarfon says: until one immerses the entire ring. The rope tied to a basket is not considered a connection unless one has tied it [with a knot]. **6** The House of Shammai says: one may not immerse hot liquids into cold, nor cold into hot, nor [liquids of] good quality into poor, nor poor into good. The House of Hillel says: one may immerse a vessel that is full of liquid, and if one immersed it [in a pool], it is as if it were not immersed. [If it is] full of urine, we treat it as if it were water. [If it is] full of purification water <note>refers to the waters of the Red Heifer</note>, [it is invalid] until the water [of the pool] exceeds the purification water. Rabbi Jose says: even if a vessel holds a <term>kor</term> <gloss>a large dry measure</gloss> and contains only a <term>revi'it</term> <gloss>a small liquid measure</gloss>, it is as if it were not immersed. **7** All foods combine to defile the body [if they are in the amount of] half a <term>pras</term> <gloss>a measurement of half a loaf</gloss>. All liquids combine to defile the body [if they are in the amount of] a <term>revi'it</term>. This is a stringency regarding one who drinks defiled liquids compared to one who eats [defiled food], that he considers other liquids as water. **8** If one ate defiled foods and drank defiled liquids, [if] he immersed and vomited [them up], they are defiled because they are not pure in the body. If he drank pure liquids, he immersed and vomited, they are pure because they are pure in the body. [If] he swallowed a pure ring, entered the tent of the dead, and stayed, and immersed and vomited it, it is as it was. [If] he swallowed a defiled ring, he immerses and eats of the <term>terumah</term> <gloss>priestly gifts</gloss>; [if] he vomited it, it is defiled. And with respect to [a ring or object] that is cut off as a human [would be], when it is visible, it is [considered] external; if it is not visible, he immerses and eats of his <term>terumah</term>.

### Massekhet Parah

**Chapter 1**

**1** Rabbi Eliezer says: a heifer in its first year, and a cow in its second. But the Sages say: a heifer in its second year, and a cow in its third or fourth. Rabbi Meir says: even one in its fifth year is valid. An old one is [also] valid, except that we do not wait for it, lest it turn black and become disqualified. Rabbi Joshua said: I have not heard [the tradition regarding] "third." They said to him: What is the meaning of "third"? He said to them: This is how I heard it, [without elaboration]. Ben Azzai said: I will explain it. If you say "third" to another in the count, when you say "third," [it means] three years old. Similarly, they said: "fourth-year vineyard" <note>Hebrew: <term>kerem revai</term></note>. They said to him: What is the meaning of "fourth"? He said to them: This is how I heard it, [without elaboration]. Ben Azzai said: I will explain it. If you say "fourth" to another in the count, when you say "fourth-year," [it means] four years old. Similarly, they said: One who eats in a house affected by leprosy [a volume of] half a loaf from three to a <term>kab</term> <gloss>a specific dry measure</gloss>. They said to him: Say, from eighteen to a <term>seah</term> <gloss>a larger dry measure</gloss>. He said to them: This is how I heard it, [without elaboration]. Ben Azzai said: I will explain it. If you say "from three to a <term>kab</term>," it is not subject to [the dough-offering of] <term>challah</term>; and when you say "from eighteen to a <term>seah</term>," it diminishes its <term>challah</term>. **2** Rabbi Jose the Galilean says: heifers [are used] at two years old, as it is written: "And you shall take a heifer of the herd for a sin offering." But the Sages say: even those of three years. Rabbi Meir says: even those of four and five are valid, except that they do not bring old ones out of respect. **3** Sheep in their first year, and rams in their second; and all are from day to day. A thirteen-month-old [animal] is not valid, neither as a ram nor as a sheep. Rabbi Tarfon calls it <term>palgas</term> <gloss>half-grown</gloss>; Ben Azzai calls it <term>noked</term> <gloss>pasture-dweller</gloss>; Rabbi Ishmael calls it <term>farkadigma</term> <gloss>a term of obscure Greek or Latin origin</gloss>. [If] they offered it, he brings upon it the drink offerings of a ram, but it does not count for him. [An animal] of thirteen months and one day, this is a ram. **4** The communal sin offering and its burnt offerings, the individual sin offering, the sin offering of the Nazirite, and the sin offering of the leper are valid from the thirtieth day onwards, and even on the thirtieth day. And if one offered on the eighth day, they are valid. Vows, voluntary offerings, the firstborn, the tithe, and the Passover sacrifice are valid from the eighth day onwards, and even on the eighth day.

**Chapter 2**

**1** Rabbi Eliezer says: a pregnant heifer for the sin offering is valid, but the Sages disqualify it. Rabbi Eliezer says: it is not purchased from Gentiles, but the Sages validate it. And not only this, but all communal and individual sacrifices come from the Land and from outside the Land, from the new crop and from the old, except for the <term>omer</term> <gloss>the sheaf offering</gloss> and the two loaves, which only come from the new crop and from the Land. **2** A cow whose horns and hooves are black; the eyeball, the teeth, and the tongue do not disqualify the cow. And a dwarf is valid. If it had a wart and he cut it off, Rabbi Judah disqualifies it; Rabbi Simeon forbids it. Any place where he removes [a part] and no red hair has grown in its place, it is disqualified. **3** [An animal born by] cesarean section, the fee of a harlot, and the price of a dog are disqualified. Rabbi Eliezer validates them, as it is written: "You shall not bring the fee of a harlot or the price of a dog into the house of the Lord your God," and this [cow] does not come to the House. All blemishes that disqualify [other] holy offerings disqualify the cow. [If] one rode upon it, leaned upon it, hung by its tail, crossed a river with it, folded the bridle upon it, or placed his cloak upon it, it is disqualified. But if he tied it with a bridle, made a sandal for it so it would not slip, [or] spread his cloak upon it to protect it from flies, it is valid. This is the general rule: anything that is for its own needs is valid; for the needs of another, it is disqualified. **4** If a bird sat upon it, it is valid; [if] a male mounted it, it is disqualified. Rabbi Judah says: if it caused it to mount, it is disqualified, but if it did so of its own accord, it is valid. **5** If it had two black hairs...

The House of Hillel says: One may immerse a vessel that is full of liquids. If he immersed it, it is as if he did not immerse it. If it is full of urine, they view them as if they were water. They are impure because they are not pure in the body. If he drank impure water, he immersed and vomited. They are pure because they are pure in the body. If he swallowed a pure ring, entered the tent of a corpse, and then learned and immersed and vomited it, it remains as it was. If he swallowed an impure ring, he immerses and eats of the <term>terumah</term> <gloss>priestly heave-offering</gloss>. If he vomited it, it is impure. And anything outside that is severed, like a person, when it is visible, it is an interposition; and if it is not visible, he immerses and eats of his <term>terumah</term>.

### Masechet Parah <note>Red Heifer</note>

**Chapter 1**

**1** Rabbi Eliezer says: A calf of one year, and a cow of two years. The Sages say: A calf of two years, and a cow of three or four years. Rabbi Meir says: Even one of five is valid. As for the elderly, they do not wait for her lest she turn black <note>discolored</note>, and she will be disqualified. Rabbi Joshua said: I have not heard [a tradition] regarding "the third." They said to him: What is the meaning of "the third"? He said to them: This is how I heard it, without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain it. If you say "the third" to another in a count, and when you say "third," [you mean] three years old. Similarly, they spoke of a <term>kerem revai</term> <gloss>fourth-year vineyard</gloss>. They said to him: What is the meaning of "revai"? He said to them: This is how I heard it, without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain it. ### Tractate Parah

**Chapter 1**

**1** Rabbi Eliezer says: A calf <note>eglah</note> is one year old and a cow <note>parah</note> is two years old. But the Sages say: A calf is two years old and a cow is three or four. Rabbi Meir says: Even a five-year-old is valid if it is aged, but we do not wait for it <note>to age further</note> lest it grow black hairs and become disqualified. Rabbi Joshua said: I have only heard of a "third-born" <note>shlishit</note>. They said to him: What does the term "third-born" mean? He said to them: I heard it without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain; if you say "third" in the count of others, or when you say "third" meaning three years old. Similarly they said: A "fourth-year" vineyard <note>kerem revai</note>. They said to him: What does the term "fourth-year" mean? He said to them: I heard it without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain; if you say "fourth" in the count of others, or when you say "fourth-year" meaning four years old. Similarly they said: One who eats in a house afflicted with leprosy [must eat a piece of bread the size of] a <term>pras</term> <gloss>half a loaf</gloss> out of three to a <term>kav</term>. They said to him: Say instead eighteen to a <term>seah</term>. He said to them: I heard it without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain; if you say three to a <term>kav</term>, it has no <term>challah</term> <gloss>dough offering</gloss>, but when you say eighteen to a <term>seah</term>, its <term>challah</term> requirement reduces it. **2** Rabbi Yose the Galilean says: Bulls are two years old, as it is said: "And a second bull <note>par</note> of the herd you shall take for a sin offering." But the Sages say: Even three years old. Rabbi Meir says: Even four and five-year-olds are valid, but we do not bring old ones out of respect <note>for the Altar</note>. **3** Lambs are one year old and rams are two years old; and all are calculated from day to day <note>from birth</note>. A thirteen-month-old animal is not valid as either a ram or a lamb. Rabbi Tarfon calls it a <term>palgas</term> <gloss>uncertain age</gloss>. Ben Azzai calls it a <term>noked</term>. Rabbi Ishmael calls it a <term>parakadigma</term>. If one sacrificed it, he brings the drink offerings of a ram, but it does not count for his sacrifice. A thirteen-month and one-day-old animal is a ram. **4** The public sin offerings and their burnt offerings, the individual sin offering, the guilt offering of a Nazirite, and the guilt offering of a leper are valid from the thirtieth day onwards, and even on the thirtieth day. And if he sacrificed on the eighth day, they are valid. Vows, freewill offerings, the firstborn, the tithe, and the Passover lamb are valid from the eighth day onwards, and even on the eighth day.

**Chapter 2**

**1** Rabbi Eliezer says: A Red Heifer <note>Parah Adumah</note> that is pregnant is valid, but the Sages disqualify it. Rabbi Eliezer says: It may not be purchased from Gentiles, but the Sages permit it. And not only this, but all public and individual sacrifices may come from the Land [of Israel] or from outside the Land, from the new crop or from the old, except for the <term>Omer</term> <gloss>Barley Offering</gloss> and the Two Loaves <note>of Shavuot</note> which must come only from the new crop and from the Land of Israel. **2** A cow whose horns and hooves are black: if one saws them off [it is valid]. The eyeball, the teeth, and the tongue do not disqualify the heifer. A dwarf cow is valid. If there was a wart and he cut it off: Rabbi Judah disqualifies it. Rabbi Simeon forbids it in any place where the hair was removed and red hair did not grow back in its place, for it is disqualified. **3** A cow born via Caesarean section, or one given as a harlot’s hire or the price of a dog, is disqualified. Rabbi Eliezer permits it, for it is said: "You shall not bring the hire of a harlot or the price of a dog into the House of the Lord your God," and this [cow] does not enter the House <note>it is sacrificed outside the Temple</note>. All blemishes that disqualify consecrated animals disqualify the heifer. If one rode upon it, leaned upon it, hung from its tail, crossed a river with it, folded its leading rope upon it, or placed his cloak upon it—it is disqualified. But if he tied it with its rope, or made a sandal for it so it would not slip, or spread his cloak over it because of flies—it is valid. This is the general rule: anything done for its own sake <note>its own benefit or protection</note> remains valid; for the sake of another, it is disqualified. **4** If a bird rested upon it, it is valid. If a male [animal] mounted it, it is disqualified. **3** The straps of a sandal and the head-tefillin <note>phylacteries</note> when they are loose <note>original: "outside"</note>, and the arm-tefillin when it does not move up and down, and the handles of a waterskin, and the handles of a travel bag. **4** These are the things that require water to enter into them: the knot of the joints at the shoulder and the hem of a coat of mail <note>original: "siryon"</note> must be stretched out; the head-tefillin when it is not loose, and the arm-tefillin when it moves up and down; and the loops of a sandal and the wings <note>corners</note> that were immersed while covered <note>folded over</note> must be held until they sink, and must remain submerged until they bubble and cease from bubbling. **5** Regarding all handles of vessels that are long and destined to be cut off, one immerses them up to the point of the standard measure. Rabbi Judah says: One must immerse the whole thing. For the chain of a large bucket, the measure is four <term>tefachim</term> <gloss>handbreadths</gloss>, and for a small one, ten. One immerses up to the point of the measure. Rabbi Tarfon says: One must immerse the entire ring <note>the ring connecting the chain to the bucket</note>. A rope that is tied to a basket is not considered a connected part unless it is sewn. **6** The House of Shammai says: One may not immerse hot water in cold, nor cold in hot, nor good <note>clean</note> water in bad <note>foul</note>, nor bad in good. The House of Hillel says: One may immerse. If a vessel is full of liquids and one immersed it, it is as if it did not immerse. If it was full of urine, it is viewed as if it were water. If it was full of purification water <note>water mixed with the ashes of the Red Heifer</note>, it is not pure until the [immersion] water exceeds the purification water. Rabbi Yose says: Even a vessel that holds a <term>kor</term> <gloss>a large volume, approx. 390 liters</gloss> but contains only a <term>revi'it</term> <gloss>a quarter-log, approx. 86ml</gloss> of liquid, it is as if it did not immerse. **7** All foods join together to disqualify the body <note>making it unfit to eat sacred food</note> if they equal the volume of half a <term>paras</term> <gloss>half a loaf, approx. the volume of two or three eggs</gloss>. All liquids join together to disqualify the body if they equal a <term>revi'it</term>. This is a stringency regarding one who drinks impure liquids over one who eats them, for in this case other liquids are treated like water. **8** If one ate impure food or drank impure liquids and then immersed and vomited them up, they are still impure because they were not purified within the body. If one drank impure water and then immersed and vomited it up, it is pure because it was purified within the body <note>the person's immersion counts for the water inside him</note>. If one swallowed a pure ring and entered a tent containing a corpse <note>which spreads ritual impurity</note>, and stayed there and immersed, and then vomited the ring, it remains as it was <note>pure</note>. If one swallowed an impure ring, one may immerse and eat <term>terumah</term> <gloss>the priestly tithe</gloss>; if he vomits it up, it is still impure. If its thickness is visible on the outside <note>protruding under the skin</note>, it is like a person when it is visible on the outside, but if it is not visible, he may immerse and eat his <term>terumah</term>.

### Tractate Parah

**Chapter 1**

**1** Rabbi Eliezer says: A calf <note>original: "eglah"</note> is a one-year-old and a cow <note>original: "parah"</note> is a two-year-old. The Sages say: A calf is a two-year-old and a cow is a three-year-old or a four-year-old. Rabbi Meir says: Even a five-year-old is valid; they only call it "old" because they do not wait for it to age further, lest its hair turn black and it becomes disqualified <note>the Red Heifer must be entirely red</note>. Rabbi Joshua said: I have only heard the term "third" <note>original: "shlishit"</note>. They said to him: What does the term "third" mean? He said to them: Thus I heard it without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain it; if you say "third" it refers to its order in a sequence, but when you say "a three-year-old" <note>shlishit</note> it means three years old. Similarly, they said: "A fourth-year vineyard" <note>kerem reva'i</note>. They asked him: What does the term "reva'i" mean? He said to them: Thus I heard it without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain it; if you say "fourth" it refers to its order in a sequence, but when you say "reva'i" it means four years old. Similarly, they said: One who eats in a house afflicted with leprosy <note>original: "tzara'at"</note> must stay for the time it takes to eat a <term>paras</term> <gloss>half-loaf</gloss> of three to a <term>kav</term>. They said to him: Say instead "eighteen to a <term>seah</term>." He said to them: Thus I heard it without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain it; if you say "three to a <term>kav</term>," there is no <term>challah</term> <gloss>dough offering</gloss> taken from it, but when you say "eighteen to a <term>seah</term>," its <term>challah</term> reduces the volume. **2** Rabbi Yose the Galilean says: Bulls <note>original: "parim"</note> are two-year-olds, as it is said: "And take a second bull, a young of the herd, for a sin offering." The Sages say: Even three-year-olds. Rabbi Meir says: Even four-year-olds and five-year-olds are valid, but they do not bring old animals out of respect <note>for the Altar</note>. **3** Lambs are one-year-olds and rams are two-year-olds, and all are measured from day to day <note>from their literal birth date</note>. An animal of thirteen months is not valid as either a ram or a lamb. Rabbi Tarfon calls it a <term>palgas</term> <gloss>an intermediate or "half" animal</gloss>. Ben Azzai calls it a <term>noked</term>. Rabbi Ishmael calls it a <term>parachadigma</term> <note>a specimen or example</note>. If one sacrificed it, he must bring the drink offerings of a ram, but his sacrifice does not count toward his obligation. Once it is thirteen months and one day old, it is considered a ram. **4** The communal sin offerings and their burnt offerings, the individual sin offering, the guilt offering of a <term>Nazirite</term> <gloss>one who takes a vow of abstinence</gloss>, and the guilt offering of a leper are valid from the thirtieth day onwards, and even on the thirtieth day itself. And if one sacrificed them on the eighth day, they are valid. Vows, voluntary offerings, the firstborn, the tithe, and the Passover lamb are valid from the eighth day onwards, and even on the eighth day itself.

**Chapter 2**

**1** Rabbi Eliezer says: A pregnant Red Heifer is valid, but the Sages disqualify it. Rabbi Eliezer says: It may not be purchased from gentiles, but the Sages permit it. And not only this, but all communal and individual sacrifices may come from within the Land <note>of Israel</note> or from outside the Land, from the new crop or from the old, except for the <term>Omer</term> <gloss>measure of barley</gloss> and the Two Loaves, which must only come from the new crop and from the Land. **2** A cow whose horns and hooves are black, they should be chopped off. The eyeball, the teeth, and the tongue do not disqualify the cow. A dwarf cow is valid. If it had a wart and he cut it off, Rabbi Judah disqualifies it. Rabbi Simeon forbids it in any place where the removal does not result in red hair growing back in its place; then it is disqualified. **3** One born from a Caesarean section, or the hire of a harlot, or the price of a dog is disqualified. Rabbi Eliezer validates them, as it is said: "You shall not bring the hire of a harlot or the price of a dog into the house of the Lord your God," and this [the Red Heifer] does not enter the "House" <note>it is prepared outside the Temple</note>. All blemishes that disqualify other consecrated animals also disqualify the cow. If one rode upon it, leaned upon it, hung from its tail, crossed a river with it, folded its leading rope over it, or placed his cloak upon it—it is disqualified. But if he tied it with a rope, or made a sandal for it so that it would not slip, or spread his cloak over it because of flies, it remains valid. This is the general rule: anything done for the cow's own sake, it remains valid; but if done for another's need, it is disqualified. **4** If a bird rested upon it, it remains valid. If a male <note>bull</note> mounted it, it is disqualified. Rabbi Judah says: If the person brought the male up onto it, it is disqualified; but if it happened on its own, it is valid. **5** If it had two black hairs...

If he drank unclean water, he immersed and vomited: it is pure, because they are pure in the body. ### Masechet Parah

**Chapter 1**

**1** Rabbi Eliezer says: a heifer in its first year, and a cow in its second year. But the Sages say: a heifer in its second year, and a cow in its third or fourth year. Rabbi Meir says: even a five-year-old is valid. An old one is valid, but we do not wait for it, lest it turn black and become disqualified. Rabbi Joshua said: I have not heard regarding the term "third." They said to him: what is the meaning of "third"? He said to them: thus I heard, without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain it. If you say "third" to another in a count, and when you say "third," it is three years old. Similarly, they said "fourth-year vineyard" <note>referring to *kerem reva'i*</note>. They said to him: what is the meaning of "fourth-year"? He said to them: thus I heard, without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain it. If you say "fourth" to another in a count, and when you say "fourth-year," it is four years old. Similarly, they said: one who eats in a plague-stricken house a *pras* from three to a *kab* <gloss>measures of volume</gloss>. They said to him: say from eighteen to a *seah*. He said to them: thus I heard, without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain it. If you say "from three to a *kab*," it does not contain *challah* <gloss>priestly dough-offering</gloss>, and when you say "from eighteen to a *seah*," the *challah* is diminished. **2** Rabbi Yose the Galilean says: bulls in their second year, as it is written, "And take a bull-calf of the herd for a sin-offering." But the Sages say: even in their third year. Rabbi Meir says: even in their fourth and fifth years they are valid, but one does not bring old ones out of respect. **3** Sheep in their first year, and rams in their second, and all are from day to day. A thirteen-month-old is not valid, neither as a ram nor as a sheep. Rabbi Tarfon calls it *palgas* <gloss>a transitional age</gloss>; Ben Azzai calls it *noked* <gloss>a shepherd's term</gloss>; Rabbi Ishmael calls it *parchedigma* <gloss>a term of Greek origin</gloss>. If one offered it, he brings the drink-offerings of a ram, but it is not credited to his altar. A thirteen-month-and-one-day-old is a ram. **4** The public sin-offering and its burnt-offerings, the individual's sin-offering, the guilt-offering of a Nazirite, and the guilt-offering of a leper are valid from the thirtieth day and onwards, and even on the thirtieth day. And if one offered them on the eighth day, they are valid. Vows and freewill offerings, the firstborn, the tithe, and the Passover sacrifice are valid from the eighth day and onwards, and even on the eighth day.

**Chapter 2**

**1** Rabbi Eliezer says: a pregnant red heifer <note>the *parah adumah* used for purification</note> is valid, but the Sages disqualify it. Rabbi Eliezer says: it is not to be purchased from the Gentiles, but the Sages declare it valid. And not only this, but all public and individual sacrifices come from the land [of Israel] and from outside the land, from the new crop and from the old, except for the *Omer* <gloss>barley offering</gloss> and the Two Loaves, which come only from the new crop and from the land. **2** A cow whose horns or hooves are black; the pupil of the eye, the teeth, and the tongue do not disqualify the cow. A dwarf cow is valid. If it had a wart and one cut it off, Rabbi Judah disqualifies it; Rabbi Shimon forbids it. Any place from which it is removed, if red hair did not grow in its place, it is disqualified. **3** One born by Caesarean section, or one received as a harlot's hire or the price of a dog, is disqualified. Rabbi Eliezer declares it valid, as it is written, "You shall not bring the hire of a harlot or the price of a dog into the house of the Lord your God," and this one does not come into the House. All the blemishes that disqualify dedicated animals disqualify the red heifer. If one rode upon it, leaned upon it, hung onto its tail, crossed a river with it, folded its bridle over it, or placed his garment upon it, it is disqualified. But if he tied it with a bridle, made for it a sandal so it would not slip, or spread his garment over it to protect it from flies, it is valid. This is the rule: whatever is for its benefit is valid; for the benefit of another, it is disqualified. **4** If a bird sat upon it, it is valid. If a male mounted it, it is disqualified. Rabbi Judah says: if he made it mount, it is disqualified; if it was of its own accord, it is valid. **5** If it had two black hairs...

### Tractate Parah

**Chapter 1**

**1** Rabbi Eliezer says: The heifer <note>the heifer whose neck is broken, Deuteronomy 21</note> is in its first year, and the cow <note>the red heifer of Numbers 19</note> is in its second. But the Sages say: The heifer is in its second year, and the cow is in its third or its fourth. Rabbi Meir says: Even one in its fifth year is valid. An old one is valid, except that one does not wait for it, lest it grow black hairs, so that it should not become unfit. Rabbi Joshua said: I have heard only the word <term>shelashit</term> <gloss>"third-ling", an unusual form for a three-year-old</gloss>. They said to him: What is the meaning of the expression <term>shelashit</term>? He said to them: This is how I heard it, without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain. If you say <term>shelishit</term> <gloss>"third"</gloss>, it means the third compared with others in a count; but when you say <term>shelashit</term>, it means one that is three years old. In the same way they said: a <term>kerem reva'i</term> <gloss>a vineyard in its fourth year</gloss>. They said to him: What is the meaning of the expression <term>reva'i</term>? He said to them: This is how I heard it, without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain. If you say <term>revi'i</term> <gloss>"fourth"</gloss>, it means the fourth compared with others in a count; but when you say <term>reva'i</term>, it means one that is four years old. In the same way they said: One who eats in a house afflicted with <term>tzara'at</term> <gloss>the plague of the house described in Leviticus 14</gloss> half a loaf from loaves of three to the <term>kav</term> <gloss>a dry measure</gloss>. They said to him: Say rather, from eighteen to the <term>se'ah</term> <gloss>a measure of six kav</gloss>. He said to them: This is how I heard it, without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain. If you say "from three to the <term>kav</term>", no <term>challah</term> <gloss>the dough offering</gloss> has been taken from it; but when you say "from eighteen to the <term>se'ah</term>", its <term>challah</term> has reduced it. **2** Rabbi Yose the Galilean <note>the print reads "the days of the Galilean day", a typographical slip</note> says: Bulls are in their second year, as it is said, "And a second young bull of the herd you shall take for a sin offering" <note>Numbers 8:8</note>. But the Sages say: Even those in their third year. Rabbi Meir says: Even those in their fourth and fifth years are valid, except that old ones are not brought, out of respect. **3** Lambs are in their first year and rams in their second, and all of them are counted from day to day. One that is thirteen months old is valid neither as a ram nor as a lamb. Rabbi Tarfon calls it <term>palgas</term> <gloss>a half-grown animal, between lamb and ram</gloss>. Ben Azzai calls it <term>noked</term> <gloss>a term of uncertain sense, perhaps "marked one"</gloss>. Rabbi Ishmael calls it <term>parakhadigma</term> <gloss>from the Greek, perhaps "a false stamp" or "a counterfeit coin"</gloss>. If one offered it, one brings with it the drink offerings of a ram, yet it is not credited to that person as their sacrifice. One that is thirteen months and one day old is a ram. **4** The sin offerings of the community and their burnt offerings, the sin offering of an individual, the guilt offering of a <term>nazir</term> <gloss>one under a vow of abstinence</gloss> and the guilt offering of a <term>metzora</term> <gloss>one afflicted with the skin disease of Leviticus 13</gloss> are valid from the thirtieth day onward, and even on the thirtieth day itself. And if they were offered on the eighth day, they are valid. Vow offerings and freewill offerings, the firstborn, the animal tithe and the Passover offering are valid from the eighth day onward, and even on the eighth day itself.

**Chapter 2**

**1** Rabbi Eliezer says: A heifer of purification <note>the red heifer</note> that is pregnant is valid. But the Sages declare it unfit. Rabbi Eliezer says: It may not be bought from non-Jews. But the Sages declare it valid. And not this alone, but all offerings of the community and of the individual may come from the Land and from outside the Land, from the new produce and from the old, except for the <term>omer</term> <gloss>the sheaf of first barley</gloss> and the two loaves <note>of the festival of Shavuot</note>, which come only from the new produce and from the Land. **2** A cow whose horns and hooves are black: one cuts them down <note>the print reads "yagur"; the standard text has "yagod", "one cuts off"</note>. The eyeball, the teeth and the tongue do not make a cow unfit. And a dwarf cow is valid. If it had a wart and it was cut off, Rabbi Judah declares it unfit. Rabbi Simeon says <note>the print reads "forbids"</note>: Wherever it was removed and red hair did not grow back in its place, it is unfit. **3** One born by caesarean section, or one given as a prostitute's fee or as the price of a dog, is unfit. Rabbi Eliezer declares it valid, as it is said, "You shall not bring the fee of a prostitute or the price of a dog into the house of the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 23:19</note>, and this one does not come into the House. All blemishes that make consecrated animals unfit also make the cow unfit. If one rode on it, leaned on it, hung on its tail, crossed a river with its help, folded its lead rope upon it, or placed one's cloak on it, it is unfit. But if one tied it with a lead rope, made it a sandal so that it would not slip, or spread one's cloak over it because of the flies, it is valid. This is the rule: Whatever is done for its own need, it is valid; for any other need, it is unfit. **4** If a bird rested on it, it is valid. If a male mounted it, it is unfit. Rabbi Judah says: If someone brought the male to it, it is unfit; but if it came of its own accord, it is valid. **5** If it had two black hairs

Y³ ¶ And their fats ¶ and Moses burned them on the altar. **17** And the bull and his skin and his flesh he burned with fire outside the camp, as the Lord commanded Moses. —

**18** And he brought the ram of the burnt offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands upon the head of the ram, and he slaughtered it. **19** And Moses sprinkled the blood on the altar round about. **20** And he cut the ram into its pieces, and Moses burned the head and the pieces and the fat and the entrails. **21** And the legs he washed in water, and Moses burned the whole ram on the altar; it was a burnt sacrifice for a sweet aroma, an offering made by fire to the Lord, as the Lord commanded Moses. —

**22** And he brought the second ram, the ram of ordination, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands upon the head of the ram, and he slaughtered it. **23** And Moses took some of its blood and put it on the tip of Aaron's right ear, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot. **24** § And he brought Aaron's sons, and Moses put some of the blood on the tip of their right ear, and on the thumb of their right hand, and on the big toe of their right foot, and Moses sprinkled the blood on the altar round about. **25** And he took the fat and the fat tail and all the fat that was upon the entrails and the lobe of the liver and the two kidneys and their fats and the right thigh. **26** And from the basket of unleavened bread that was before the Lord he took one unleavened cake, and one cake of bread with oil, and one wafer, and put them on the fats and on the right thigh. **27** And he put all upon the hands of Aaron and upon the hands of his sons, and waved them as a wave offering before the Lord. **28** And Moses took them from their hands and burned them on the altar upon the burnt offering; they were an ordination for a sweet aroma, an offering made by fire to the Lord. —

# LEVITICUS VIII 16-28

Y³ ¶ and their fat portions. ¶ And Moses burned them on the altar. **17** But the bull and its hide, its flesh, and its offal <note>original: "peresh", the contents of the stomach or intestines</note>, he burned with fire outside the camp, as the Lord commanded Moses. —

**18** And he brought the ram of the burnt offering near, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the ram. And it was slaughtered. **19** And Moses dashed the blood against the altar all around. **20** And he cut the ram into its pieces, and Moses burned the head, the pieces, the fat, and the innards. **21** And the legs he washed in water, and Moses burned the entire ram on the altar. It was a burnt offering for a pleasing aroma, a fire-offering to the Lord, as the Lord commanded Moses. —

**22** And he brought near the second ram, the ram of ordination <note>term: milluim, literally "fillings", referring to the consecration of the priests</note>, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the ram. And it was slaughtered. **23** And Moses took some of its blood and put it on the tip of Aaron's right ear, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot. **24** Then he brought near the sons of Aaron, and Moses put some of the blood on the tips of their right ears, and on the thumbs of their right hands, and on the big toes of their right feet; and Moses dashed the blood against the altar all around. **25** And he took the fat, and the fat tail, and all the fat that was on the innards, and the lobe of the liver, and the two kidneys and their fat, and the right thigh. **26** And from the basket of unleavened bread that was before the Lord, he took one unleavened cake, one cake of oiled bread, and one wafer, and placed them on the fat portions and on the right thigh. **27** And he put all of these on the palms of Aaron and on the palms of his sons, and waved them as a wave offering before the Lord. **28** Then Moses took them from their palms and burned them on the altar upon the burnt offering. They were an ordination offering for a pleasing aroma, a fire-offering to the Lord. —

# The Letter of Ibn Tufayl <note>original: Epistola Ebn Tophail</note>

And at that point, we saw ourselves as worthy of producing words to be transmitted from us, and it became incumbent upon us that you be the first whom we present with what we have and the first to whom we disclose what we possess, because of your sincere friendship and the purity of your attention <note>literally: the purity of your inclination or ear</note>. However, if we were to cast upon you the ultimate conclusions we have reached before establishing the principles with you, it would benefit you no more than a summary matter of tradition <term>taqlid</term> <gloss>the acceptance of authority without proof or personal experience</gloss>. This would only be possible if you maintained a good opinion of us based on affection and familiarity, rather than because we deserve to have our words accepted on their own merit. We do not desire for you anything less than a rank higher than this, nor are we satisfied for you with such a status, as it is not sufficient for salvation, let alone for attaining the highest degrees.

Rather, we wish to lead you upon the paths that our own journey <term>suluk</term> <gloss>spiritual path or conduct</gloss> previously followed, and to swim with you in the sea that we crossed first, so that it may lead you to where we have arrived. Then you will witness what we witnessed and realize through the insight of your own soul <term>basirah</term> <gloss>spiritual perception or inner sight</gloss> everything that we realized, becoming independent of linking your knowledge <term>ma'rifah</term> <gloss>experiential knowledge or gnosis</gloss> to what we have known. 

This requires a specific and significant amount of time, freedom from distractions, and applying one's entire resolve <term>himmah</term> <gloss>spiritual ambition or intense focus</gloss> to this art. If this resolve is sincere in you, and your intention is sound to strive for this objective, then "at morning light you will praise your nocturnal journey" <note>An Arabic proverb: 'Inda al-sabah yahmadu al-qawmu al-sura'. It means that the exhaustion of a night's travel is forgotten and praised once the destination is reached at dawn; here it refers to the success of spiritual effort</note>. You will attain the blessing of your endeavor; you will have pleased your Lord, and He will have pleased you. text:
Epistola Ebn Tophail

And when we saw ourselves worthy of setting down words that would outlive us, it became incumbent upon us that you be the first whom we present with what we possess, and whom we inform of what we hold. This is because there is no one more sincere, more pure, or more refined in character than you. However, were we to cast before you the ultimate ends we have reached in this matter before establishing the principles with you, it would offer you nothing more than an act of blind imitation <note>original: "taqlid"</note>, which is entirely summary. This would only occur if you held a favorable opinion of us due to our friendship and affinity, and not because you felt we deserved to have our words accepted. We are not satisfied for you to remain at such a level, nor are we content for you to dwell in this station, as it is insufficient for salvation, let alone for attaining the highest degrees.

We intend to lead you along the paths upon which we have traveled, and to have you swim in the sea that we ourselves crossed, until it brings you to where we arrived. Thus, you may witness what we witnessed, verify through your own insight everything we have verified, and dispense with the need to link your knowledge to what we have known. This requires a certain, not insignificant, amount of time, freedom from distractions, and the application of your entire resolve to this discipline. If this determination is sincere in you, and your intention is truly set on exerting yourself in this pursuit, you will praise your journey when the morning arrives, you will attain the blessing of your endeavor, and you will have pleased your Lord, and He will have pleased you. I shall be for you where you desire in your aspirations and wherever your resolve and your whole being aim. I hope to guide you along the most direct path, and the one most secure from perils and afflictions. Now, I shall offer a brief glimpse to awaken your desire.

<summary>The author explains his intent to guide his correspondent toward personal verification of truth rather than blind imitation, emphasizing that true wisdom requires dedication, time, and solitude.</summary>
<keywords>Ibn Tufayl, knowledge, personal verification, salvation, spiritual journey, resolve, imitation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Ibn Rushd’s critique of the Ash’arite theologians (the Mutakallimun). Having previously addressed the "principle of possibility," he now turns to their specific arguments regarding the Divine Will and the creation of the world within a "void." He is currently dissecting the logical relationship between an eternal Will and a temporally created object.</meta>

<page-num>43</page-num>

-># The Discovery of the Methods of Proof Regarding the Beliefs of the Faith<-

<header>The Discovery of the Methods of Proof Regarding the Beliefs of the Faith</header>

...the atmosphere in which it was created—meaning the **void** <term>Void: *al-khalā’*, an empty space or vacuum that theologians hypothesized existed before or outside the world</term>—due to it being in a different position within that void. From this, they concluded that the world was created through an act of **will**. 

The premise stating that the **will** is what specifies one of two identical options is correct. However, the premise stating that the world exists within a void surrounding it is either false or, at the very least, not self-evident. Furthermore, an absurd consequence follows from their position on this void: it would have to be **eternal** <term>Eternal: *qadīm*, having no beginning in time</term>. This is because if the void itself were created, it would require another void to exist within, leading to an infinite regress.

As for the premise stating that nothing but a **temporally created** <term>Temporally created: *muḥdath*, something that began to exist after not existing</term> object can proceed from the will, that is not self-evident. This is because the will in **actuality** <term>Actuality: *bi-l-fi‘l*, the state of being fully realized or active</term> exists simultaneously with the action of the willed object itself. This is because "will" belongs to the category of **relative terms** <term>Relative terms: *al-mudāf*, concepts that can only be defined in relation to one another</term>. It has been demonstrated that when one of two relative terms exists in actuality, the other must also exist in actuality—just as the existence of a **father** implies the existence of a **son**. 

If one exists in **potency** <term>Potency: *bi-l-quwwah*, the capacity or potential for something to exist or happen</term>, the other exists in potency. Therefore, if the will in actuality is eternal, then the willed object in actuality must necessarily be eternal. If the will in actuality were created, then the willed object must also be created in actuality.

As for the will that precedes the willed object, that is the "will in potency"—meaning a will whose object has not yet emerged into actuality because the specific action required for the object's creation has not yet been joined to that will. It is therefore evident that when its willed object does emerge, the will enters a state of existence it was not in before the object's actualization. This is because the will is the cause of the object’s creation through the mediation of the act. Thus, if the **theologians** <term>Theologians: *al-Mutakallimūn*, scholars who used dialectical reasoning to defend Islamic tenets</term> were to posit that the will is created, it would follow by necessity that the willed object is created.

The apparent sense of the **Religious Law** <term>Religious Law: *al-Shar‘*, referring to the divine revelation or scripture</term> is that it did not delve into such technical depths with the general public. For this reason, it did not explicitly state whether the Divine Will is eternal or created. Instead, it expressed the most apparent view: that the Will is what brings created beings into existence. This is seen in the words of the Almighty: ﴾*Verily, Our word unto a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say unto it: "Be," and it is*﴿ <note>Quran 16:40; original Arabic: *innamā amrunā li-shay’in idhā aradnāhu an naqūla lahu kun fa-yakūn*</note>. This is because the masses do not understand how temporally created beings can proceed from an eternal will. Rather, the truth is that the Religious Law remained silent on the eternity or temporality of the Will because this is...

<summary>Ibn Rushd critiques the theological view that a world created in time proves an eternal Divine Will, arguing instead that a truly "active" will must coexist with its object. He notes that the Quran avoids these complex philosophical definitions of "eternal" versus "temporal" to remain accessible to common believers.</summary>

<keywords>Ibn Rushd, Divine Will, Theologians (Mutakallimun), Eternal vs. Temporal, Void (Khala'), Creation, Quranic Interpretation, Kun fa-yakun</keywords>

text:
Exposition of the Methods of Proof Concerning the Doctrines of the Religious Community

Page 43

The atmosphere in which it was created, or rather the void in which it was created, since he posits a place other than that void, leads to the conclusion that the world was created by will. The premise stating that will is what distinguishes one of two identical things is correct, whereas the premise stating that the world is in a void surrounding it is false or not self-evident. Furthermore, his postulation of this void necessitates a position they consider abhorrent, which is that the void itself must be eternal, for if it were created, it would require a void of its own.

As for the premise that will can only result in a created object of will, this is not self-evident. Will in its actual state exists alongside the act of the object of will itself, because will belongs to the category of relative terms <note>i.e., relational attributes that require a counterpart</note>. It has been established that when one relative term exists in actuality, the other exists in actuality, such as a father and a son; and when one exists in potentiality, the other exists in potentiality. If the will that is in actuality is created, then the object of will is necessarily created in actuality. If the will that is in actuality is eternal, then the object of will that is in actuality is eternal.

The will that precedes the object of will is the will in potentiality, meaning the will whose object has not yet been brought into act, as the act necessitating the creation of the object of will has not accompanied that will. Therefore, it is evident that when its object is brought forth, the will exists in a manner it did not possess before the object was brought into act, as it was the cause of the object’s creation through the medium of the act. Thus, if the theologians <term>Mutakallimun</term> <gloss>scholastic theologians</gloss> posit that the will is created, then the object of will must necessarily be created.

It is apparent that the revealed Law does not delve into such depth with the general public. Therefore, it does not explicitly state whether the will is eternal or created. Instead, it explicitly states what makes it clear that the will brings created entities into existence, as in His, the Almighty’s, saying: "Our command to a thing when We intend it is only that We say to it 'Be,' and it is." This is so because the general public does not understand how created entities can arise from an eternal will. The truth is that the Law does not explicitly mention either the creation or the eternity of the will, as this is among...

<summary>Averroes analyzes the theological debates surrounding the nature of Divine Will, arguing that the concepts of "created" versus "eternal" will are logically problematic and that the religious Law intentionally avoids such complex technical speculation for the sake of the public.</summary>

text:
<header>Al-Biruni's Book | On the Verification of What Pertains to India</header>

The truth is lost because the hearts of the common people are more inclined toward superstitions, and thus the reports became confused. Then, another calamity came from the direction of the heretics (<term>Zanadiqa</term>), the followers of <term>Mani</term>, such as Ibn al-Muqaffa', 'Abd al-Karim ibn Abi al-'Awja', and their likes. They cast doubt in the minds of the weak-willed regarding the "First One" through the concepts of modification and possibility, drawing them toward dualism and adorning the life of Mani in their eyes until they grasped his rope. He was a man not content with the ignorance of his own doctrine, but spoke of the structure of the world with deceptions that became widespread in speech. Added to this were the previous Jewish intrigues, so it became a view attributed to Islam—God is far above such a thing. Whoever opposes it and holds to the truth that conforms to the Qur'an is labeled an infidel and an atheist, with their blood judged as lawful to be spilled, and they are not permitted to have their speech heard. And this is worse than what is heard from the speech of Pharaoh: "I am your lord most high" <note>Qur'an 79:24</note>, "and I know of no other god for you besides me" <note>Qur'an 28:38</note>. Fanaticism may lead us away from the ideal path due to excessive zeal, but God will make firm the steps of the one who intends Him and intends the truth. As for the Indians, their religious books and the informational <term>Puranas</term> all speak on the structure of the world in a way that contradicts the truth evident to their own astronomers. However, the people are compelled by the necessity of performing their rituals and leading the vast majority of the public to follow them toward astrological calculations and judicial predictions. Thus, they show inclination toward them, speak of their virtues, seek blessing in meeting them, and declare with certainty that they are among the people of Paradise and that none of them will enter Hell. Their astronomers reciprocate by confirming and matching what they are upon, even if most of it contradicts the truth, and they support them...

<summary>Al-Biruni discusses the corruption of historical and geographical knowledge through political and religious factionalism, specifically critiquing how Indian astrological traditions are compromised by religious and social necessity.</summary>
<keywords>heretics, Mani, Ibn al-Muqaffa', Islam, idolatry, Puranas, astrological calculations</keywords>

text:
# We set the distance

from midday <term>nisf al-nahar</term> because adjusting for birth times <term>al-milad</term> with it is easier than working with local horizons. The longest daylight hours for the latitude of Jerusalem <term>Bayt al-Maqdis</term> are fourteen hours and some fraction. The Jewish method using seasonal hours <term>al-saʿat al-zamaniyyah</term> <gloss>hours that vary in length depending on the season</gloss> is not sound unless the conjunction for the start of Tishrei <note>the first month of the Jewish civil year</note> coincides exactly with the autumnal equinox. However, it never occurs exactly with it; rather, it precedes or follows it by a significant amount, as we demonstrated previously.

When we extract the time of conjunction using the calculation provided by the Jews in the table we analyzed according to their view, we then proceed from that to determine the start of the year and its quality—whether it is deficient <term>naqisan</term>, regular <term>muʿtadilan</term>, or complete <term>tamaman</term>. We already know whether the year is common <term>basitah</term> or leap <term>kabisah</term>. We look in the Table of Limits <term>jadwal al-hudud</term> for a duration of weekdays whose two boundaries encompass the time our calculation yielded for the conjunction. We look on the "leap" side if it is a leap year, and on the "common" side if it is a common year. When we find it, we find alongside it the first day of the week for that year and its quality. Once we know the start of the year and its quality, and we combine that quality with whether it is common or leap, we can determine the start of the following year.

text:
# Why We Set the Distance

We have set the distance from noon <note>original: "nisf al-nahar"</note> because adjusting for birth times is easier this way than working with horizons. Furthermore, the hours of the longest day for the latitude of Jerusalem <note>original: "Bayt al-Maqdis"</note> are fourteen hours and some change. The Jewish practice using seasonal hours <note>term: al-sa'at al-zamaniyya <gloss>hours of unequal length that vary based on the duration of daylight</gloss></note> is not correct unless the conjunction <note>term: al-ijtima' <gloss>the astronomical new moon or syzygy</gloss></note> for the start of the month of Tishrei <note>note: the first month of the Jewish civil year</note> happens exactly at the autumnal equinox. However, it never occurs exactly with it. Instead, it precedes or follows it by a significant amount, as we have explained previously.

When we extract the time of the conjunction using the calculation provided by the Jews in the table we analyzed according to their view, we then proceed from that to the knowledge of the first day of the year and its character, whether it be deficient, regular, or complete <note>note: these refer to the three possible lengths of the Jewish year: "chaserah," "kesidrah," and "shlemah"</note>. We already have the prior knowledge of whether the year is common <note>term: basita <gloss>a regular 12-month year</gloss></note> or embolismic <note>term: kabisa <gloss>a 13-month leap year</gloss></note>.

Next, we look in the Table of Limits <note>original: "jadwal al-hudud"</note> for a duration of days of the week whose two boundaries encompass the time we found for the conjunction. We look on the side for leap years if it is a leap year, and on the side for common years if it is a common year. When we find it, we find next to it the first day of the year in the week and its specific character. Once we know the first day of the year and its character, and we combine that character with its status as common or leap, we can determine from that the arrival of the first day of the following year.

# The Reason We Set the Distance

We have placed the distance starting from <term>nisf al-nahar</term> <gloss>noon</gloss> because the <term>ta'dil</term> <gloss>correction</gloss> for the <term>milad</term> <gloss>birth of the moon</gloss> is easier to calculate this way than by using local horizons. The longest daylight hours for the latitude of <term>Beit al-Maqdis</term> <gloss>Jerusalem</gloss> are fourteen hours and a fraction. The Jewish system of using <term>al-sa'at al-zamaniyya</term> <gloss>temporal hours</gloss> <note>hours that vary in length according to the season</note> is only accurate if the <term>al-ijtima'</term> <gloss>conjunction</gloss> for the start of the month of <term>Tishri</term> <gloss>the first month of the Jewish civil year</gloss> coincides exactly with the autumnal equinox. However, it never actually coincides with it; rather, it occurs significantly before or after it, as we have demonstrated previously.

When we determine the time of the conjunction using the calculations provided by the Jews in the table we have analyzed according to their methods, we can then proceed to determine the start of the year and its specific character—whether it is <term>nuqsan</term> <gloss>deficient</gloss>, <term>i'tidal</term> <gloss>regular</gloss>, or <term>tamam</term> <gloss>complete</gloss> <note>referring to the varying number of days in the months of Heshvan and Kislev</note>. We already know whether the year is <term>basita</term> <gloss>ordinary</gloss> or <term>kabisa</term> <gloss>leap</gloss> <note>an intercalary year with an extra month</note>. 

We then look in the <term>Jadwal al-Hudud</term> <gloss>Table of Limits</gloss> for the specific period within the days of the week. The two boundaries of this period must contain the time we calculated for the conjunction. We look under the section for leap years if the year is a leap year, or the section for ordinary years if it is an ordinary year. Once found, we will see alongside it the day of the week on which the year begins and its specific character. By knowing the start of the year and its character, and combining this with whether the year is ordinary or leap, we can determine the starting point of the following year.

text:
# Kalila and Dimna

<note>Decorative floral-style border elements at the top and bottom of the page.</note>

When the Lion rose the next day, the judge entered to see him, accompanied by a group of the notables of his companions, with a document of what Dimna had said in his defenses. The Lion took that document and ordered them to depart from him.

Then he sent for his mother and read the document to her. It troubled her, and she said: "If I am harsh with you, O King, do not be angry."

The Lion said: "I will not be angry, so say what you wish."

She said: "I do not see that you recognize what harms you from what benefits you. I fear that Dimna, in your long delay in resolving his matter, will incite against you something you will not be able to sit or stand for."

Then she stood and left, and she was angry. The next day, the judge sent for Dimna and brought him out, and the scholars consulted on his case, but they did not say anything.

The judge said to him: "Even if all who are present have remained silent and said nothing, their suspicions have converged that you are a criminal. There is no good for you in life after your accusation has been settled in their hearts. I see nothing better for you than to confess your sin; thus you may relieve your neck of the burden of the afterlife, and a good report of your affair may return to you for two reasons: one is your ability to find exits and fabricate excuses to defend yourself, and the other is your confession of your sin, choosing safety in the afterlife over the safety of the world. For the scholars have said: 'Death in what is honorable is better than life in what is shameful.'"

Dimna answered him, saying: "The judges do not judge by their suspicions, nor by the suspicions of the commoners or the elite. You have known that suspicion does not replace the truth in any way. For even if you all suspect that I am the author of this crime, I know my own self, and my knowledge of myself is a certainty in which there is no doubt. The only reason my affair appears ugly to you is because you suspected that I slandered..."

# Kalila and Dimna

<note>Decorative floral-style border elements at the top and bottom of the page.</note>

When the Lion woke the next morning, the Judge entered, accompanied by a group of prominent members of his court, bearing the document containing Dimna’s excuses. The Lion took the document and ordered them to withdraw.

He then sent for his mother and read the document to her. She was deeply troubled and said: "If I speak harshly to you, O King, do not be angry."

The Lion replied: "I will not be angry, so say whatever you wish."

She said: "I do not see that you distinguish what harms you from what benefits you. I fear that Dimna, through your prolonged consideration of his case, will incite a situation against you that you will be unable to withstand."

She then rose and left, visibly angry. The next day, the Judge sent for Dimna and brought him out, and he consulted the scholars regarding him, but they would not speak.

The Judge said to him: "Even if all who are present remain silent and offer no words, their suspicions have converged on the fact that you are a criminal. There is no good for you in life once this accusation is firmly established in their hearts. I see nothing better for you than to confess your guilt. This will free your soul from the consequences of the afterlife, and you may regain a good reputation for two reasons: the first is your ability to find ways out and fabricate excuses <note>original: "al-ma'adhir"</note> that defend yourself, and the second is that by confessing your sin, you choose safety in the afterlife over safety in this world. For the scholars have said: death in a manner that is honorable is better than life in a manner that is shameful."

Dimna replied to him, saying: "Judges do not pass judgment based on their own suspicions, nor on the suspicions of the common or elite people. You know that suspicion is of no avail against the truth. Even if all of you suspect that I am the author of this crime, I possess knowledge of my own soul, and my knowledge of myself is a certainty that allows for no doubt. My situation appears ugly to you only because you assume that I have conspired."

<summary>This page recounts the Lion's mother warning him against Dimna's cunning, followed by the Judge's unsuccessful attempt to pressure Dimna into confessing his crimes to avoid a shameful death.</summary>
<keywords>Dimna, The Lion, Judge, betrayal, suspicion, confession, justice, moral choice</keywords>

When the Lion awoke the following morning, the Judge and a group of his prominent companions entered his presence with a record of what Dimna had said in his defenses <note>original: "معاذيره"</note>. The Lion took the record and ordered them to depart from him.

Then he sent for his mother and read the record to her. It distressed her, and she said: "If I speak harshly to you, O King, do not be angry."

The Lion said: "I shall not be angry, so say what you wish."

She said: "I do not see you recognizing what harms you from what benefits you. I believe that by your prolonged deliberation in Dimna’s case, he will stir up against you a situation that you will be unable to withstand."

Then she stood and left in a state of anger. When the next day came, the Judge sent for Dimna and brought him out, then consulted the scholars about him, but they said nothing.

The Judge said to him: "Even if all those present remain silent and say nothing, their suspicions have united in the belief that you are a criminal. There is no good for you in life after your guilt has settled in their hearts. I see nothing better for you than to confess to your crime, thereby freeing your neck from the consequences of the Afterlife; this would also result in a better reputation for you for two reasons. One is your skill in finding ways out and fabricating excuses <note>the OCR reads "مقادير" (decrees) which is corrected in the original text to "معاذير" (excuses)</note> to defend yourself. The other is your confession of your crime, choosing safety in the Afterlife over safety in this world. For the scholars have said: Death in what is beautiful is better than life in what is ugly."

Dimna replied to him, saying: "Judges do not rule based on their own suspicions, nor on the suspicions of the common folk or the elite. I have learned that suspicion is of no avail against the truth. Even if you all suspect that I am the author of this crime, I know myself, and my knowledge of myself is a certainty in which there is no doubt. My case has only become ugly in your eyes, if it is so, because you suspected that I acted with malice."

<summary>The Lion's mother warns him against Dimna's manipulative nature while the Judge pressures Dimna to confess his crimes for the sake of his soul. Dimna maintains his innocence, arguing that legal judgments must be based on certain truth rather than collective suspicion.</summary>
