# Kalila and Dimna

<note>Decorative floral-style border elements are placed at the top and bottom of the page.</note>

When the Lion woke the next morning, the Judge and a group of his noble companions entered his presence with a book <note>original: "kitab", here referring to a written record or scroll of testimony</note> containing what Dimna said in his defense <note>original: "mu'adhirhi", his excuses or justifications</note>. The Lion took the book and ordered them to depart from him.

Then he sent for his mother and read the book to her. It troubled her, and she said, "If I am harsh with you, O King, do not be angry."

The Lion said, "I will not be angry, so say what you wish."

She said, "I do not see you recognizing what harms you from what benefits you. I suspect that with the long time you have spent deliberating over his case, Dimna will stir up against you something that you will not be able to stand against or withstand <note>an idiomatic expression meaning a situation that will leave the King powerless or unable to cope</note>."

Then she stood up and left in anger. When the next day came, the Judge sent for Dimna, brought him out, and consulted the scholars <note>original: "al-ulama", referring to legal and religious authorities</note> about him, but they said nothing.

The Judge said to him, "Even if everyone present is silent and says nothing, their suspicions have gathered that you are a criminal. There is no good for you in life after the accusation has settled in their hearts. I see nothing better for you than to confess your sin. By doing so, you may release your neck from the consequences of the Afterlife, and good words will be spoken of your case for two reasons. The first is your ability to find exits and to create excuses <note>original: "al-ma'adhir"; the text notes a variant "al-maqadir" meaning destinies or measures</note> to defend yourself. The second is your confession of your sin, choosing safety in the Afterlife over safety in this world. The scholars have said: Death in what is honorable is better than life in what is shameful <note>literally: what is ugly</note>."

Dimna answered him and said, "Judges do not rule based on their suspicions, nor on the suspicions of the common people or the elite. I have known that suspicion avails nothing against the truth. Even if you all suspect that I am the perpetrator of this crime, I know myself best, and my knowledge of myself is a certainty in which there is no doubt. My case has only become shameful in your souls, if that is the case, because you suspected that I acted with malice <term>sa'ayt</term> <gloss>strove to cause harm or slandered others</gloss>."

<note>Vocabulary: Kalila and Dimna, Ibn al-Muqaffa, the Judge, Dimna, the Lion, excuses, suspicions, the scholars.</note>

<summary>The Lion's mother warns him that Dimna is dangerous despite his written defense. The Judge urges Dimna to confess to preserve his honor and soul, but Dimna argues that suspicion is not a valid basis for a legal verdict.</summary>

Kalila and Dimna

<note>Decorative floral-style border elements at the top and bottom of the page.</note>

When the lion woke the next morning, the judge entered with a group of prominent companions, bringing a scroll containing what Dimna had said in his excuses. The lion took the scroll and ordered them to depart.

Then he sent for his mother and read the scroll to her. It distressed her, and she said, "If I speak harshly to you, O King, do not be angry."

The lion replied, "I will not be angry, so say what you wish."

She said, "I do not see that you distinguish between what harms you and what benefits you. I fear that if you continue to deliberate on Dimna’s case for too long, he will stir up against you matters you cannot withstand."

She stood and left, feeling angry. The next day, the judge sent for Dimna and brought him out. He consulted with the scholars regarding him, but they said nothing.

The judge said to him, "Even if everyone present remains silent, their suspicions have converged on the fact that you are guilty. There is no good for you in life once the accusation is settled in their hearts. I see nothing better for you than to confess your sin. By doing so, you will free yourself from the consequences of the afterlife, and a good reputation may return to you for two reasons: your ability to present arguments and fabricate excuses to defend yourself, and your confession of the sin, choosing salvation in the afterlife over safety in this world. For the scholars have said that death in a noble manner is better than life in a shameful one."

Dimna answered him, saying, "Judges do not pass sentences based on their own suspicions, nor the suspicions of the commoners or the elite. You know that suspicion does not replace truth. Even if you all suspect me of this crime, I know myself, and my knowledge of myself is a certainty in which there is no doubt. My case is only ugly in your eyes because you suspect that I have incited this."

<summary>The lion's mother warns him against delaying the judgment of Dimna, while the judge urges Dimna to confess his guilt to save his afterlife, leading to a debate on the value of suspicion versus certainty.</summary>

text:
<warning>Water stains on the left margin; slight ink bleed-through from the reverse side.</warning>
<meta>Continuity: Following Dimna’s realization that he must remove Shanzaba the Bull to regain his standing with the Lion, he continues his discourse on the nature of palace life and the pitfalls of leadership before proposing a plan based on wit rather than strength.</meta>

...seriousness. As for passion <term>al-hawā</term><note>original: "al-hawā." This refers to whims, desires, or impulsive passion that clouds judgment.</note>, it is the infatuation with women, idle talk, excessive spending, hunting, and the like. As for <gloss>eloquence</gloss>, it is ruined by excess in cursing and striking. As for the times, they are marred by drought and the failure of harvests. As for inconsistency <term>al-khulf</term>, it is the exercise of severity in a place where gentleness is required, and the exercise of kindness where severity is needed. 

Indeed, the Lion has become infatuated with **Shanzaba** <note>Spelled "Shantraba" in this specific manuscript line.</note> with an infatuation that is likely to increase.

**Kalila** said: "How can we hope to contend with **Shanzaba** when he holds a more intimate position than yours, and possesses more assistants and friends?"

**Dimna** said to him: "Do not look at it that way, for matters are not decided by strength alone. Many a weak one has achieved through his cunning <term>dahā’</term>, his strategy <term>ḥīlah</term><note>original: "ḥīlah." A central theme in these fables, referring to the use of intellect and trickery to overcome physical disadvantages.</note>, and his refinement that which many of the powerful and strong fail to do. Has it not reached you how a crow destroyed a black snake?"

**Kalila** said to him: "And how did that happen?"

**Dimna** said: "They relate that a crow had a nest in a mountain, and near it was the burrow of a black snake. Whenever the crow had chicks, the snake would eat them. When the snake had done this to him repeatedly, the crow’s grief intensified. He complained of this to a friend of his—a jackal—and said to him: 'I intend to go to the black snake and peck out its eyes while it is sleeping, that perhaps I may be relieved of it.'

His friend said to him: 'What a wretched strategy <term>al-ḥīlah</term> you have intended! Seek instead a course of action where you may attain your need without any harm reaching you. Beware lest your likeness be as the likeness of the heron <term>al-uljūm al-bajā’</term><note>original: "al-uljūm al-bajā’." Likely referring to a large water bird like a heron or pelican.</note> who wanted...'"

<summary>Dimna argues that intellect and strategy (ḥīlah) are superior to physical strength, beginning the fable of the Crow and the Snake to illustrate how a smaller creature can defeat a more powerful foe.</summary>
<keywords>strategy, cunning, Shanzaba the Bull, the Crow and the Snake, political wisdom, Ibn al-Muqaffa</keywords>

As for passion <term>al-hawā</term> <gloss>desire or whim</gloss>, it is the infatuation with women, talk, wine <note>original: "al-ṣarf." In this context, it refers to the consumption of unmixed wine or general worldly indulgence.</note>, hunting, and similar things. As for folly <note>The OCR reads "al-faṣāḥah" (eloquence), but the context of "insulting and striking" suggests "al-khurq" (clumsiness or folly), which is standard in other versions of this text.</note>, it is the excessive use of insults and striking. As for time <term>al-zamān</term> <gloss>the circumstances of the era</gloss>, it is drought and the destruction of crops. As for discord <term>al-khuluf</term>, it is the use of severity in the place of gentleness, and the use of kindness in the place of severity. 

Truly, the Lion has become infatuated with **Shantarabah** with an infatuation that is likely to grow. **Kalila** said: "How can we contend with **Shatrabah** when he holds a higher position than you and has more helpers and friends?" 

**Dimna** said to him: "Do not look at it that way, for matters are not settled by strength alone. Many a weak person has achieved, through his cunning, strategy <term>ḥīlah</term> <gloss>clever trick or stratagem</gloss>, and refinement, that which many of the powerful and strong cannot achieve. Have you not heard that a crow destroyed a black snake?" 

**Kalila** said to him: "And how was that?" 

**Dimna** said: "They say that a crow had a nest on a mountain, and near it was the burrow of a black snake. The snake ate the crow's chicks. When it had done this to him many times, the crow found the situation unbearable and complained to a friend of his, a jackal <term>ibn āwā</term> <gloss>son of the howler</gloss>. He said: 'I want to go to the snake and peck out its eyes while it is sleeping, so that perhaps I may be rid of it.' 

His friend said: 'What a wretched strategy <term>ḥīlah</term> you have intended! Seek instead a way to achieve your goal without any harm coming to you. text:
<warning>Water stains on the left margin; slight ink bleed-through from the reverse side.</warning>

<margin>seriousness</margin> As for passion, it is being obsessed with women, idle talk, spending, hunting, and the like. As for eloquence, it is going to extremes in insults and violence. As for the times, it is drought and the failure of crops. As for discrepancy, it is acting with severity when one should be gentle, and acting with gentleness when one should be severe. The lion has become obsessed with <term>Shanzaba</term> <gloss>the ox</gloss> to an extent that is bound to increase. 

Kalila said to him, "How can we overcome Shanzaba when he has a higher status than you, with more supporters and friends?" 

Dimna said to him, "Do not look at that, for matters are not decided by raw strength. Often, a weak person attains through his cleverness, his cunning, and his conduct that which many strong and powerful men cannot achieve. Has word not reached you of the crow that destroyed a black snake?"

Kalila said to him, "How did that happen?" 

Dimna said, "They say that a crow had a nest on a mountain, and near it was the hole of a black snake. The black snake would eat the crow's chicks. When he did this to him repeatedly, it became unbearable for the crow, so he complained to a friend of his, a jackal, and said, 'I intend to go to the snake and peck out his eyes while he is asleep, so that perhaps I may be rid of him.' 

His friend said to him, 'That is a terrible strategy you have contemplated. Seek a matter through which you attain your need without any harm coming to you, and beware of being like the boastful toad that wanted...'

<summary>Dimna explains that intellect and cunning triumph over brute strength and status, illustrating his point with the story of a crow plotting to defeat a snake.</summary>

text:
He has no other than him. So I asked the judge: "Do you know his father?" May God protect his end. He said: "And can Abu Zayd be unknown? The one who was wounded by a tyrant <term>jabbar</term> <gloss>oppressor or giant</gloss>, and who has news and more news with every judge." At that moment, I shaved my head <note>a sign of grief or resolution</note> and woke up, but only after the time had passed. I became certain that for all of it, his evil was a trick and the house of a poem. My gaze was lowered by what I met. I swore that I would not deal with the likes of them as long as I lived. Then I did not cease to sigh over the best of my deal and the eloquence among my companions. The judge said to me, when he saw what had been transacted and it became clear that a free man had passed by: "O you, that of your wealth which has admonished you is not lost. Nor has he sinned against you who has awakened you. So take a lesson from what has come to you. Let your companions remember what befell you, so that you may forever banish your dirhams <gloss>silver coins</gloss> for the sake of memory. He who is tested and remains patient, the lesson is revealed to him and he takes heed." So I bid him farewell, not asking out of shame and sadness. The tail of loss and deception followed, and I intended to confront Abu Zayd with the news directly.

Then, I shaved my head and came to my senses, but only after the time had passed. I realized that his entire affair was a ruse and a verse of a poem. My gaze fell, humbled by what I had encountered, and I swore that I would never again deal with people like them as long as I lived. I continued to lament the poorness of my bargain and the <term>ifsah</term> <gloss>clarity/eloquence</gloss> among my companions. When the judge saw what had taken place, and it became clear that he was a free man who had gone too far, he said to me: "O man, let that which has departed from your wealth be your sermon, and let him who has awakened you not be considered a criminal. Take heed from what has come to you, and what has befallen you through your companions, so that you may always remember the disaster that struck you. May it cause you to cast away your silver coins from your memory, and may he who is tested and endures be restored, and he to whom the lesson becomes clear, may he take heed." I bade him farewell, while shame and sorrow hung heavily upon me, dragging the hem of my loss and regret, and I resolved to confront Abu Zayd with the news and speak to him plainly.

By this memory, you shall keep your dirhams <gloss>silver coins</gloss> and renew the spirit of one who was tested and remained patient, to whom the lesson was revealed and who then took heed."

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: even if a slanderer should speak against him.</meta> none other than him. So I said to the judge: "Do you know his father?" God grant him a long life. He replied: "And can <term>Abu Zayd</term> <gloss>Abu Zayd al-Saruji, the protagonist and master trickster of the Maqamat</gloss> be unknown? He is the one who has been wounded by an oppressor, and whose tales and reports are known to every judge."

At that moment, I came to my senses and woke up, but only when the time for action had already passed. I became certain that the entirety of this evil was a trick and a <term>bayt qasida</term> <gloss>the core line of a poem; idiomatically, the crux of a ruse</gloss>. What I encountered caused me to lower my gaze in shame, and I swore that I would never deal with the likes of those two again as long as I lived. Then I did not cease to groan over the loss of my bargain and the public disclosure of my folly among my companions. 

The judge said to me when he saw the state I was in—for it had become clear that the "slave" was actually a free man who had now departed: "O man, whatever of your wealth has gone to provide you a lesson is not truly lost, and he who awakened you to the truth has committed no crime against you. So take heed of what has come to you, and let your companions learn from what befell you. Always remember what overwhelmed you, so that you may exchange the memory of your lost <term>dirhams</term> <gloss>silver coins</gloss> for lasting wisdom."

He continued: "He who is tested and remains patient, and then has the moral lesson revealed to him and takes heed, has truly benefited." So I bid him farewell, filled with shame and sorrow, dragging behind me the heavy train of my own deception and loss. I then intended to confront Abu Zayd with the news in total frankness.

<margin>
The Persian commentary here explains the narrative of Abu Zayd al-Saruji and the judge in detail. It highlights the linguistic subtleties of the <term>Maqama</term> <gloss>a genre of rhymed prose</gloss> and emphasizes the moral lessons regarding the dangers of greed and the cleverness of deception.
</margin>

<summary>The narrator realizes he has been defrauded by Abu Zayd al-Saruji through an elaborate poetic ruse involving a fake slave. The judge advises the narrator to view his financial loss as a valuable payment for a lesson in wisdom and vigilance.</summary>
<keywords>Abu Zayd al-Saruji, Al-Hariri, deception, judge, wisdom, dirhams, moral lesson, Maqamat, greed, rhymed prose</keywords>

text:
...and he had no one else, so I did it for the judge. Or do you know his father, his successor, may God protect him? He said, "Is Abu Zayd unknown, he who was wounded by a tyrant, and who has stories and more stories with every judge?"

Then I shaved my head and came to my senses, but only after the time had passed. I realized that the whole thing was a ruse and a deceitful poem. I lowered my eyes in shame at what I had encountered, and I swore that I would never deal with their like as long as I lived. I continued to lament the poorness of my bargain, despite my eloquence among my companions.

The judge, seeing what had transpired and observing the man who had gone too far, said to me, "O you, what has gone from your wealth serves as a warning, and no crime has befallen you except that which has awakened you. Take heed from what has come to you, and let your companions recall what has afflicted you. You will remember forever what has befallen you, so that you may cast aside your lost dirhams for the sake of the memory. He who is tested and shows patience, and to whom the lesson becomes clear so that he learns, creates [a new self]."

I took my leave of him, not asking for anything, as shame and sorrow draped my garment of loss. I resolved to confront Abu Zayd with the news and speak to him directly.

<margin>The marginalia, written in Persian Nasta'liq, provides a detailed commentary on this passage. It explains the character of Abu Zayd al-Saruji, noting his role as a trickster archetype in the Maqamat. It further discusses the linguistic artistry of Al-Hariri, specifically the rhythm of the prose, and draws a moral lesson regarding the dangers of greed and the necessity of learning from misfortune in worldly dealings.</margin>

<summary>The narrator realizes he has been swindled by Abu Zayd al-Saruji and, after receiving counsel from the judge on the value of the lesson learned over the loss of wealth, he resolves to confront the trickster.</summary>
<keywords>Abu Zayd al-Saruji, Maqamat al-Hariri, trickery, moral lesson, greed, judicial counsel</keywords>

text: ...and wells. The Arabs used to say, "Thabir has brightened, so that we may raid [the others]." It is called Jam' and the <term>Mash'ar al-Haram</term> <gloss>The Sacred Monument</gloss>. 'Arafa is a village containing farms, greenery, and melon patches. It has fine houses for the people of Mecca, which they stay in on the day of 'Arafa. The standing place is on its plain near a mountain. There are watering places, a canal flowing through it, and a sign the Imam built behind him for prayer, with people around him. On the mountains near it are lamps. The prayer hall is on the edge of the Wadi 'Arana at the borders of 'Arafa, and standing in the valley is not permitted. Whoever goes out to it before the sun sets, a blood sacrifice becomes mandatory for him. At the edge of 'Arafa are white landmarks. In the prayer hall is a pulpit made of brick, and behind it is a large basin. Two miles before it are the two <term>Ma'zamayn</term> <gloss>the two narrow passes</gloss>, which are the boundary of the <term>Haram</term>. <term>Batn Muhassir</term> <gloss>the valley of Muhassir</gloss> is a valley between Mina and Al-Muzdalifa; it is the boundary of Al-Muzdalifa. Al-Tan'im is a place with mosques around the mosque of 'Aisha and watering places on the road to Medina, from which the Meccans enter the state of <term>ihram</term> <gloss>pilgrimage consecration</gloss> for the Umra. White landmarks surround the <term>Haram</term>. From the direction of the west, Al-Tan'im is three miles away; from the direction of Iraq, nine miles; from the direction of Yemen, seven miles; from the direction of Ta'if, eleven miles; and from the direction of the main road, ten miles. Dhu al-Hulayfa is a village near Yathrib containing a well-maintained mosque and nearby wells, but no dwellings are seen there. Al-Juhfa is a city inhabited by the Banu Ja'far; it has a fortress with two gates and a few wells. Two miles away is a spring, and it has a large cistern which sometimes lacks water, and it is plentiful.

text:
and with it. The Arabs used to say, "Thabir has shone," <note>a phrase used during the pilgrimage to signify the start of the rites at Muzdalifa</note> so that we might raid; however, the correct usage is different. It is also called <term>Jam‘</term> <gloss>the gathering place</gloss> and the <term>Mash‘ar al-Haram</term> <gloss>the Sacred Monument</gloss>. Arafat is a village containing farms, greenery, and melon fields. It has fine houses for the people of Mecca, where they stay on the Day of Arafat. The place for standing is on its morning side near a mountain <unclear>that is joined</unclear>. There are watering places and a channel that conveys water to it. A landmark has been built behind it by the Imam for supplication, with people surrounding him and on the mountains near it. The prayer hall is on the edge of the <term>Wadi ‘Arana</term> <gloss>‘Arana Valley</gloss>, on the border of Arafat. It is not permitted to stand for the rite in the valley itself; anyone who goes there before sunset must offer a blood sacrifice. On the boundary of Arafat are white markers. In the prayer hall is a pulpit made of baked brick, and behind it is a large basin. Two miles before it are the <term>Ma’zamayn</term> <gloss>the two narrow passes</gloss>, which are the boundary of the <term>Haram</term> <gloss>sacred territory</gloss>. <term>Batn Muhassir</term> <gloss>the valley of Muhassir</gloss> is a valley between Mina and Muzdalifa; it is the boundary of Muzdalifa. <term>Al-Tan‘im</term> <gloss>a place name</gloss> is a site that has mosques around the mosque of Aisha, and watering places on the road to Medina. From there, the Meccans enter the state of <term>ihram</term> <gloss>sacred state for pilgrimage</gloss> for the <term>‘Umra</term> <gloss>lesser pilgrimage</gloss>. White markers surround the <term>Haram</term>. From the west side, al-Tan‘im is three miles away; from the Iraq side, nine miles; from the Yemen side, seven miles; from the Ta'if side, eleven miles; and from the main road, ten miles. <term>Dhu al-Hulayfa</term> <gloss>a place name</gloss> is a village near <term>Yathrib</term> <gloss>Medina</gloss> with a well-maintained mosque. Nearby are wells, but no dwellings are seen there. <term>Al-Juhfa</term> <gloss>a place name</gloss> is a city inhabited by the sons of Ja‘far. It has a fortress with two gates, a few wells, and a spring two miles away. It has a large reservoir, though the water there is sometimes scarce, and it is abundant.

<summary>This page describes the geography and boundaries of sacred sites associated with the Hajj, including Arafat, Mina, Muzdalifa, al-Tan‘im, and the demarcations of the Haram.</summary>
<keywords>Arafat, Muzdalifa, Haram, Mina, pilgrimage, sacred geography, boundaries, watering places</keywords>

Batn Muhassir is a valley between Mina and Muzdalifa and is the boundary of Muzdalifa. At-Tan'im is a place that has mosques around the mosque of Aisha, and watering places on the road to Medina, from which the Meccans enter the state of <term>ihram</term> <gloss>ritual consecration</gloss> for the <term>Umra</term> <gloss>lesser pilgrimage</gloss>. White markers surround the <term>Haram</term>. From the west road, At-Tan'im is three miles away; from the Iraq road, nine miles; from the Yemen road, seven miles; from the Ta'if road, eleven miles; and from the main road, ten miles. text:
<meta>continues from previous page: It is between two mountains that overlook it. Al-Muzdalifa is a farsakh from Mina; it has a prayer hall, a watering place, a minaret, and several cisterns</meta> and on Mount Thabir <note>a mountain overlooking the valley of Mina</note>. The Arabs used to say, "O Thabir, let the sun shine so that we may depart for the slaughter" <note>original: "ashriq Thabir kay-ma nughir"</note>, referring to the disagreement <note>the pre-Islamic custom of departing after sunrise, whereas Islam changed it to departing before sunrise</note>. It is also called Jam' <gloss>the gathering place</gloss> and <term>al-Mash'ar al-Haram</term> <gloss>The Sacred Monument</gloss>. 

Arafah is a village containing farms, greenery, and melon patches. It has fine houses belonging to the people of Mecca who stay in them on the Day of Arafah. The <term>mawquf</term> <gloss>place of standing/prayer</gloss> is located on its morning side at Mount Mutalath. There are watering places there and a canal that flows through it. A marker has been built behind it for the <term>Imam</term> <gloss>prayer leader</gloss> to offer supplications, with the people surrounding him or positioned on the nearby mountains. 

The <term>musalla</term> <gloss>prayer place</gloss> is on the edge of the Valley of Urana on the borders of Arafah. It is not permissible to perform the "standing" <note>the central rite of the Hajj pilgrimage</note> within the valley itself. Anyone who enters the valley before sunset must offer a blood sacrifice <note>a penalty of a sheep or goat for a ritual error</note>. White markers define the boundary of Arafah. In the prayer place, there is a pulpit made of brick, and behind it is a large basin. 

Two miles before it lie the <term>Ma’zimayn</term> <gloss>the two narrow passes</gloss>, which mark the boundary of the <term>Haram</term> <gloss>sacred territory</gloss>. Batn Muhassir is a valley between Mina and al-Muzdalifa; it is the border of al-Muzdalifa. 

Al-Tan'im is a location containing mosques around the Mosque of Aisha, with watering places on the road to Medina. From here, the inhabitants of Mecca enter the state of <term>ihram</term> <gloss>ritual consecration</gloss> for the <term>Umrah</term> <gloss>lesser pilgrimage</gloss>. 

The Sacred Territory is surrounded by white markers. From the western road at al-Tan'im, it is three miles; from the Iraq road, nine miles; from the Yemen road, seven miles; from the Ta'if road, eleven miles; and from the main highway road, ten miles. 

Dhu al-Hulayfa is a village near Yathrib <gloss>Medina</gloss> containing a thriving mosque. There are wells nearby, but no houses are visible there. 

Al-Juhfa is a city inhabited by the Banu Ja'far. It has a fortress with two gates and a few wells. Two miles away is a spring and a large pool. Water is sometimes scarce there, though the pool is large.

<summary>Al-Muqaddasi describes the ritual geography surrounding Mecca, including the stations of Arafah, al-Muzdalifa, and al-Tan'im, as well as the distances marking the boundaries of the sacred territory.</summary>
<keywords>Arafah, Mecca, Haram, al-Muzdalifa, al-Tan'im, Dhu al-Hulayfa, al-Juhfa, Yathrib, mosques, watering places</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: it has a prayer hall, a watering place, a minaret, and several cisterns.</meta>

And Thabir <note>original: "Thabir," a prominent mountain overlooking the valley of Mina</note>. The Arabs used to say: "Shine, O Thabir, so that we may hasten to sacrifice" <note>original: "Ashriq Thabir kay-ma nughir," a pre-Islamic rhyming phrase used by pilgrims waiting for sunrise over the mountain to begin the day's rituals</note> on the contrary <note>this likely refers to the Islamic change in ritual timing compared to the pre-Islamic practice</note>. Its entirety is called Jam' and the Sacred Monument <term>al-Mash'ar al-Haram</term> <gloss>the sacred site at Muzdalifa where pilgrims pray</gloss>.

Arafat is a village containing farms, greenery, and melon fields. It has fine houses belonging to the people of Mecca, where they stay on the Day of Arafat. The standing place <term>al-mawqif</term> <gloss>the site of the central ritual of the Hajj</gloss> is located on its morning side <note>likely the eastern side</note> near a mountain called Mutalat. There are watering places there, and a canal that flows through it <note>the OCR reads "takhruhu" but footnote 'h' suggests "tajri" meaning it flows</note>. There is also a marker <term>alam</term> behind which the Imam has built a place for supplication, with the people gathered around him and upon the nearby mountains for the sacrifice <note>original: "li-adhiya"</note> and the prayer hall <term>al-musalla</term>.

The prayer hall is situated on the edge of the Urana Valley, on the borders of Arafat. It is not permissible to perform the standing <term>wuquf</term> within the valley itself; whoever enters it before the sun has set is required to offer a blood sacrifice <term>dam</term> <gloss>the ritual slaughter of an animal as an atonement for a pilgrimage error</gloss>. On the boundary of Arafat are white markers. In the prayer hall is a pulpit made of brick, and behind it is a large cistern. Two miles before this are the two mountain passes <term>al-Ma'zimayn</term>, which mark the boundary of the Sacred Territory <term>al-Haram</term>.

The Valley of Muhassir <term>Batn Muhassir</term> is a valley between Mina and al-Muzdalifa; it is the border of al-Muzdalifa.

Al-Tanim is a place containing mosques around the Mosque of Aisha and watering places on the road to Medina. From here, the residents of Mecca enter the state of ritual consecration <term>ihram</term> for the lesser pilgrimage <term>umrah</term>. White markers surround the Sacred Territory. From the western road via al-Tanim, it is three miles; from the Iraq road, nine miles; from the Yemen road, seven miles; from the Taif road, eleven miles; and from the main highway <term>al-jada</term>, ten miles.

Dhu al-Hulaifa is a village near Yathrib <note>the pre-Islamic name for Medina</note> containing a well-maintained mosque and nearby wells, though no houses are seen there. 

Al-Juhfa is a city inhabited by the Banu Ja'far. It has a fort with two gates and a few wells. Two miles away is a spring and a large pool <term>birka</term> where water might occasionally be scarce, though it is usually plentiful.

text:
And Thabir. The Arabs used to say, "Shine, Thabir, so that we may raid," which is a variation. It is called Jam' and al-Mash'ar al-Haram. Arafat is a village that contains farmlands, vegetables, and melon fields. In it are fine houses for the people of Mecca, where they stay on the Day of Arafat. The place of the standing <note>the ritual stay for the Hajj pilgrimage</note> is in a plain near the mountain of the *Muta-lat* <unclear>possibly a transcription variant for a specific peak name</unclear>. There are watering places there, an aqueduct that flows into it, and a signpost that the Imam built behind him for the supplication, with the people around him and on the nearby mountains. The prayer ground is on the edge of Wadi Arana, on the borders of Arafat; it is not permitted to stand in the valley itself. Whoever leaves toward it before the sunset must offer a blood sacrifice. At the boundary of Arafat are white markers. In the prayer ground, there is a pulpit made of baked brick, with a large basin behind it. Two miles before it are the *Ma'zamayn* <gloss>two narrow mountain passes</gloss>, which are the boundary of the Sacred Precinct. *Batn Muhassir* is a valley between Mina and Muzdalifah; it is the boundary of Muzdalifah. Al-Tan'im is a place with mosques around the Mosque of Aisha, and watering places on the Medina road; from there, the Meccans enter the state of ritual consecration for the minor pilgrimage. White markers surround the Sacred Precinct. From the direction of the west, al-Tan'im is three miles away; from the direction of Iraq, nine miles; from the direction of Yemen, seven miles; from the direction of Ta'if, eleven miles; and from the direction of the main road, ten miles. Dhu al-Hulayfah is a village near Yathrib <note>Medina</note> with a well-maintained mosque; there are wells nearby, but no houses are seen there. Al-Juhfah is a city inhabited by the Banu Ja'far; it has a fortress with two gates, a few wells, a spring two miles away, and a large reservoir, though water is sometimes scarce there and it is abundant.

text: and its ruler is the King Badr al-Din ibn Qaraman <note>original: "بفتح القاف والراء" indicating the pronunciation of Qaramān</note>. Before him, it belonged to the <term>Ispahsalār</term> <gloss>military commander</gloss> Musa, who ceded it to King al-Nasir in exchange for a compensation. He then sent a commander and an army to it, but later, Sultan Badr al-Din overcame it, built his royal residence there, and established his rule. I met this Sultan outside the city as he was returning from hunting. I dismounted from my mount, so he dismounted from his own, and I greeted him. He turned his attention to me. It is the custom of the kings of these lands that when a visitor dismounts for them, they are pleased by this action and increase their hospitality, whereas if one greets them while riding, it displeases them and does not satisfy them, potentially becoming a reason for the visitor being deprived [of favor]. This had happened to me with some of them, and I asked about it. When I greeted him and remounted, he asked about my condition and my arrival. I entered the city with him, and he ordered the best accommodation to be prepared for me. He would send much food, fruit, and sweets in silver trays, along with candles. He gave me garments, provided a mount, and was kind. Our stay with him was not long, and we departed for the city of Aksaray <note>original: "وضبطها بفتح الهمزة وسكون القاف وفتح الصاد المهمل والراء" indicating pronunciation</note>. It is one of the most beautiful and well-built cities of the Land of the Romans <note>referring to Anatolia</note>, surrounded by flowing springs and orchards on all sides. Three rivers traverse the city, and water flows through its houses. It contains trees and grapevines, and inside it are many gardens. Rugs attributed to this city are made there from sheep’s wool, which have no equal in any other land. From there, they are carried to the Levant, Egypt, Iraq, India, China, and the lands of the Turks. This city is under the obedience of the King of Iraq. I stayed there at the lodge of the <term>Sharif</term> <gloss>noble/descendant of the Prophet</gloss> Husayn, who is the deputy there for the Emir Arta. Arta is the deputy for the King of Iraq in the lands of the Romans that he has conquered. This <term>Sharif</term> is one of the <term>Fityan</term> <gloss>youths/knights of chivalry</gloss>, and he has a large group [of followers]. He honored us completely and performed the deeds of those who preceded him. It is a very populous city, though some of it has fallen into ruin. It is traversed by the river known as the Black River, which is one of the great rivers, with three bridges over it: one inside the city and two outside. text:
<meta>continues from previous page: "...to the city of Laranda, a beautiful city with much water and many orchards."</meta>

Its sultan is the King Badr al-Din ibn Qaraman <note>original: "بدر الدين بن قرمان"</note>. Before him, it belonged to the Seljuk <note>original: "اشقية" - referring to the Seljuk dynasty rulers of that region</note> Musa, but he ceded it to King al-Nasir in exchange for compensation. Al-Nasir sent a governor and an army to it, but then Sultan Badr al-Din seized it, built his royal residence there, and established his rule. I met this sultan outside the city while he was returning from hunting. I dismounted from my mount, and he also dismounted from his. I greeted him, and he received me warmly. It is the custom of the kings of these lands that if a traveler dismounts for them, they are pleased by this action and increase their hospitality. If one greets them while mounted, it offends them, does not please them, and becomes a cause for the traveler to be deprived of favors. This happened to me with some of them, and I asked for their forgiveness. When I greeted him and remounted, he asked about my situation and my journey. I entered the city with him, and he ordered the best lodging to be provided for me. He would send much food, fruit, and sweets in silver trays, along with candles. He provided me with clothes, a mount, and showed great kindness. We did not stay with him long, and we departed for the city of Aksaray <note>original: "أقسرا"</note>.

It is among the best and most well-constructed cities of the land of Rum <note>original: "الروم" - Anatolia</note>. It is surrounded by flowing springs and orchards on every side. Three rivers flow through the city, and water runs through its houses. It contains trees and grapevines, and inside it are many orchards. Rugs are made there, attributed to the city, made of sheep's wool, which have no equal in any other land. From there, they are exported to Syria, Egypt, Iraq, India, China, and the lands of the Turks. This city is under the authority of the King of Iraq. I stayed there at the lodge of the <term>Sharif</term> <gloss>noble descendant of the Prophet</gloss> Husayn, who acted there as a deputy for the Amir Arta. Arta is the deputy of the King of Iraq for the lands in Rum that he has conquered. This <term>Sharif</term> is one of the <term>Fityan</term> <gloss>knightly youths/members of chivalric orders</gloss>, and he has a large following. He honored us with complete hospitality and performed the same acts as those who preceded him.

Then we departed to the city of Nigde <note>original: "نكدة"</note>. It is in the lands of the King of Iraq, a city with much infrastructure, though some of it has fallen into ruin. A river known as the Black River <note>original: "النهر الأسود"</note> runs through it; it is one of the major rivers and has three bridges over it, one inside the city and two outside. The orchards inside and outside are irrigated by it, and fruits are plentiful there. I stayed there at the lodge of the young man Akhī Jaruq, who is the Amir of the city. He honored us according to the custom of the <term>Fityan</term>, and we stayed there for three days. Then we departed after that to the city of Kayseri, and it is among the lands of the King of Iraq, and it is one of the...

Its sultan is King Badr al-Din ibn Qaraman <note>the name is pronounced with a short 'a' on the 'q' and 'r'</note>. Before him, the city was held by Ashqiya Musa, who ceded it to King al-Nasir <note>the Mamluk Sultan of Egypt</note> in exchange for compensation. Al-Nasir sent a commander and an army there, but later Sultan Badr al-Din gained control over it and built his royal capital there, where his authority became firmly established.

I met this sultan outside the city while he was returning from a hunt. I dismounted from my animal for him, so he also dismounted from his animal and greeted me. He welcomed me warmly. It is the custom of the kings of these lands that if a traveler dismounts for them, they are pleased by his behavior and increase their honor toward him. However, if the traveler greets them while remaining mounted, they find it offensive and displeasing, and it becomes a reason for the traveler to be denied favor. This actually happened to me with one of them: I made a request and was refused. When I greeted this sultan and remounted, he asked about my circumstances and my arrival. I entered the city with him, and he ordered the finest lodgings to be prepared for me.

He would send abundant food, fruit, and sweets on silver platters, as well as candles, garments, and a mount. He treated me with great kindness. Our stay with him was not long, and we departed for the city of Aksaray <note>the name is pronounced with a short 'a' on the 'a', a silent 'q', and a short 'a' on the 's' and 'r'</note>. It is one of the most beautiful and well-constructed cities in the lands of the <term>Rum</term> <gloss>Anatolia</gloss>. It is surrounded by flowing springs and gardens on all sides. Three rivers flow through the city, and water is channeled into the houses. The city is full of trees and grapevines with many gardens inside its walls. The famous rugs named after the city are manufactured there from sheep’s wool. They have no equal in any other land and are exported from there to Syria, Egypt, Iraq, India, China, and the lands of the Turks.

This city owes its allegiance to the King of Iraq <note>the Mongol Ilkhanid ruler</note>. I stayed there at the <term>zawiya</term> <gloss>lodge or hospice</gloss> of Sharif Husayn, the deputy for Emir Arta. Arta is the deputy of the King of Iraq over the parts of the lands of the <term>Rum</term> that he has conquered. This Sharif is one of the <term>Fityan</term> <gloss>members of a chivalric youth guild</gloss> and has a large following. He treated us with total hospitality, following the example of those who came before him.

Then we traveled to the city of Niğde <note>pronounced with a short 'a' on the 'n', a silent 'k', and a short 'a' on the 'd'</note>. It is part of the lands of the King of Iraq. It is a city with many buildings, though some have fallen into ruin. It is divided by the river known as the Black River, which is a major river with three bridges: one inside the city and two outside. Waterwheels <note>original: nawa'i, likely an error for nawa'ir</note> inside and outside the city provide water for the orchards. Fruit is plentiful there. I stayed there at the <term>zawiya</term> <gloss>lodge</gloss> of the <term>Fata</term> <gloss>noble youth</gloss> Akhi Jaruq, who is the governor there. He honored us according to the custom of the <term>Fityan</term>, and we stayed there for three days. ### ACCOUNT OF THE REVOLT OF THE SHERIF JALAL AL-DIN IN THE LAND OF MA’BAR AND THE CONNECTED EVENTS CONCERNING THE KILLING OF THE VIZIER'S NEPHEW

The Sultan had appointed the Sherif Jalal al-Din Ahsan Shah as commander over the land of Ma’bar <note>original: "Ma'bar"</note> <gloss>the crossing, referring to the southeastern coast of the Indian peninsula</gloss>, which lies at a distance of six months' travel from Delhi. He rebelled, claimed the kingship for himself, killed the Sultan’s deputies and agents, and minted gold and silver coins in his own name. On one side of the dinar, he had inscribed: "The descendant of Taha and Yasin <note>These are the titles of the 20th and 36th chapters of the Quran, used here as epithets for the Prophet Muhammad</note>, the father of the poor and the destitute, Jalal al-Dunya wa al-Din." And on the other face: "He who trusts in the support of the Merciful, Ahsan Shah the Sultan."

# CHAPTER FORTY-EIGHTH

5. So that He may admit the believing men and believing women into gardens beneath which rivers flow, to abide therein forever, and remove from them their misdeeds. That is, in the sight of God, a great triumph.

6. And that He may punish the hypocritical men and hypocritical women, and the polytheistic men and polytheistic women, who assume an evil assumption about God. Upon them is a circle of evil. God has become angry with them and has cursed them, and has prepared for them Hell; and evil it is as a destination.

7. To God belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth, and God is Exalted in Might and Wise.

8. Indeed, We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good tidings, and a warner.

9. That you may believe in God and His Messenger, and honor him, respect him, and exalt Him morning and evening.

10. Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you are actually pledging allegiance to God. The hand of God is over their hands. So he who breaks his oath only breaks it to the detriment of his own soul. And he who fulfills that which he has covenanted with God, He will give him a great reward.

11. Those of the <term>A'rab</term> <gloss>Bedouin/desert Arabs</gloss> who remained behind will say to you, "Our possessions and our families occupied us, so ask forgiveness for us." They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts. Say, "Then who could prevent God from anything if He intended for you harm or intended for you benefit?" Rather, God is ever, with what you do, Acquainted.

12. But you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families, and that was made pleasing in your hearts. You assumed an evil assumption and you were a people ruined <note>original: "buran"; meaning lost or corrupt</note>.

13. And whoever does not believe in God and His Messenger, then indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers a Blaze.

text:
# CHAPTER FORTY-EIGHT

5. So that He may admit the believing men and believing women into gardens beneath which rivers flow, to abide therein forever, and to remove from them their misdeeds; and that is, in the sight of God, a great attainment. 6. And that He may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women, and the polytheist men and polytheist women, who assume an evil assumption about God. Upon them is a cycle of misfortune; and God has become angry with them and has cursed them and has prepared for them Hell, and it is an evil destination. 7. To God belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth; and God is Exalted in Might and Wise. 8. Indeed, We have sent you as a witness and a bringer of good tidings and a warner. 9. So that you may believe in God and His Messenger, and support him and honor him, and exalt Him morning and evening. 10. Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you are actually pledging allegiance to God. The hand of God is over their hands. So whoever breaks his pledge, he only breaks it against his own soul; and whoever fulfills that which he has covenanted with God, He will give him a great reward. 11. Those who remained behind of the Bedouins will say to you, "Our possessions and our families occupied us, so ask forgiveness for us." They say with their tongues what is not within their hearts. Say, "Who then could prevent God at all if He intended for you harm or intended for you benefit?" Rather, God is ever, with what you do, Acquainted. 12. But you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families, and that was made pleasing in your hearts. And you assumed an evil assumption and became a ruined people. 13. And whoever does not believe in God and His Messenger, then indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers a Blaze.

<summary>This passage details divine judgment, the nature of pledging allegiance to the Prophet, and the condemnation of those who refused to support the community.</summary>
<keywords>faith, judgment, hypocrisy, covenant, Bedouins, divine reward</keywords>

text:
<meta>This page continues the prophecy of Isaiah, following the warning that the social order and leadership of Jerusalem would collapse. The text now turns its focus to the corruption of the elite and the eventual restoration of a holy remnant under God’s protection.</meta>

<header>Isaiah * 3 * 4 *</header>
<page-num>936</page-num>

<margin>15</margin> the poor in your houses. * What do you mean by crushing my people and grinding the faces of the poor? says the Lord God of Hosts <note>original: "al-sayyid rabb al-junūd" (السيد رب الجنود) — a title emphasizing God's authority over all heavenly and earthly powers.</note>.

<margin>16</margin> And the Lord said: Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, walking with outstretched necks and glancing wantonly with their eyes, walking with mincing steps and tinkling with their feet, 
<margin>17</margin> * the Lord will bring scabs upon the crowns of the heads of the daughters of Zion, and the Lord will lay bare their nakedness. * In 
<margin>18 19</margin> that day the Lord will take away the finery of the anklets, the headbands, and the crescents; * the earrings, the bracelets, and the veils; 
<margin>21</margin> * the headdresses, the leg chains, the sashes, the perfume boxes <term>perfume boxes</term> <note>original: "hanājir al-shammāmāt" — literally 'throats of the smellers,' these were small ornamental containers for scents.</note>, and the amulets; * the rings 
<margin>22</margin> and the nose rings; * the festive robes, the capes, the cloaks, and the money purses; * the hand mirrors, 
<margin>23</margin> the linen tunics, the turbans, and the veils. * And it shall come to pass that instead of fragrance there will be a stench; instead of a sash, a rope; instead of styled hair, baldness; instead of fine silk, a loincloth of sackcloth; and branding instead of beauty. 
<margin>25 26</margin> * Your men shall fall by the sword and your heroes in war. * Her gates shall lament and mourn; and she, being empty, shall sit upon the ground.

<margin>Ch 4 v 1</margin> And seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying, "We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothes; only let us be called by your name; take away our reproach <note>This depicts a society so devastated by war that the surviving women plead for the legal protection of marriage, even without financial support.</note>."

->### Chapter Four from verse 2<-

<margin>2</margin> In that day the Branch of the Lord <term>Branch of the Lord</term> <note>A messianic reference to a future righteous ruler emerging from the lineage of Israel.</note> shall be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the earth shall be the pride and splendor of the survivors of Israel. * And it shall come to pass that he who is left in Zion and remains 
<margin>3</margin> in Jerusalem shall be called holy—everyone who is recorded for life in Jerusalem. * When the 
<margin>4</margin> Lord has washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and purged the blood of Jerusalem from her midst by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning. * Then the Lord will create over every place of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud 
<margin>5</margin> by day and smoke and the shining of a flaming fire by night. For over all the glory there will be a canopy. * And there will be a booth 
<margin>6</margin> for shade by day from the heat, and for a refuge and a shelter from the storm and rain.

->### Chapter Five<-

<margin>1</margin> Let me sing for my beloved a song of my beloved regarding his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a fertile hill.

<summary>Isaiah details the judgment against the prideful women of Jerusalem, stripping them of their luxuries, before promising a future where God purifies and protects a holy remnant in Zion. The page concludes with the beginning of the "Song of the Vineyard," a famous botanical allegory for Israel.</summary>
<keywords>Daughters of Zion, ornaments, judgment, Branch of the Lord, Mount Zion, purification, Song of the Vineyard, Jerusalem</keywords>

Isaiah 3 4

15 What is the matter with you, that you crush my people and grind the faces of the needy? says the Lord, the Lord of Hosts.

16 The Lord said: Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, walking with outstretched necks, glancing with their eyes, mincing as they walk, and jingling with their feet, 17 the Lord shall strike the heads of the daughters of Zion with a scab, and the Lord shall uncover their private parts. 18 In that day, the Lord will take away the finery of the anklets, the headbands, and the crescent ornaments; 19 the pendants, the bracelets, and the veils; 21 the headdresses, the chains, the sashes, the perfume bottles, the amulets, 22 the rings, the nose jewels, 23 the festal apparel, the mantles, the outer garments, the purses, the mirrors, the fine linen, the turbans, and the shawls. 24 Instead of perfume, there will be rottenness; instead of a sash, a rope; instead of braided hair, baldness; instead of fine robes, a girding of sackcloth; and instead of beauty, branding. 25 Your men shall fall by the sword, and your mighty men in the war. 26 Its gates shall lament and mourn; she shall be desolate and sit upon the ground.

text:
### The Fourth Art

->Chapter Four: On the Common Rules for Vomiting and Diarrhea, and an Indication of How to<-
->Attract [the Humor with] Purgative Medicines and Vomiting<-

...and other things with it. One who is being purged must not rush to consume large quantities of unwholesome food, lest nature draw it in undigested. If anything of this sort is required, it must be in very small amounts, spaced out gradually, so that what enters the body is well-digested. Phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> is a special kind of evacuation for equality <note>rebalancing the blood</note>. As for evacuation specific to an excess of a humor in quantity or corruption in quality, it is different from phlebotomy. Every evacuation that is excessive often causes harm. If the cessation of a habitual diarrhea leaves behind an ailment, the recurrence of that evacuation is often the remedy, such as when the cessation of a nosebleed causes obstructions; restoring the flow will remove them. 

Know that the remainder of the humor that needs to be evacuated is less capable of being thoroughly exhausted, and the strength of the body is depleted if one persists until it is gone. Nature often resolves that remainder on its own. As long as the humor is of the type that should be purged and the patient can bear it, do not fear excess. Sometimes you may need to purge until the patient faints. If someone has great strength and a large amount of corrupt humors, purge them little by little. This is also the case when the humor is extremely mature <note>well-digested or ready for elimination</note> or so mixed with blood that it cannot be purged all at once. This occurs in cases of sciatica, chronic joint pain, cancer, chronic scabies, and chronic boils. 

Know that diarrhea attracts from above and clears from below; thus, it agrees with the conventional method of attraction. It is also suitable after the materials have settled. If the materials are below, it draws them toward itself, clears them from where they are, and acts through attraction, and vice-versa. The state of phlebotomy differs according to the locations from which the blood is taken, as you have learned. Those who need evacuation the least are those with good digestion; inhabitants of hot climates have little need for evacuation.

We say it is recommended for one who wishes to be purged to break up or divide their food into several portions. The total amount to be taken during the day should be divided, and the foods and drinks should be varied. The stomach is prone in this state to desire to expel what is inside it, either upward or downward. As for food that is not varied—rather, relying on a single type—the stomach becomes satiated, becomes stagnant, and grips it tightly, especially if the amount is small. As for those with naturally loose bowels, none of this is needed. 

Know that the need for vomiting, diarrhea, and the like is not present in one who has a good regimen; they require things lighter than these. Perhaps exercise, massage, and cupping are sufficient for them. Then, if the body becomes filled with the best of humors, namely blood, then phlebotomy is what is needed for purification, not diarrhea. If necessity demands phlebotomy or evacuation, such as in autumn, and if it is not possible to use vomiting, it is better to use phlebotomy. This is one of the recommendations of Hippocrates and the books of the ancients, and it is the truth. Likewise, if phlegmatic humors are mixed with blood, and if the humors are uniform, viscous, and cold, phlebotomy might make them thicker and more viscous; thus, it is necessary to start with diarrhea. In summary, if the humors are uniform, prioritize phlebotomy; if they are not, evacuate the excess first until they become uniform, then perform phlebotomy. One who prioritizes medicine <note>purgative drugs</note> over phlebotomy should have performed phlebotomy for a short time first. If someone was recently bled and needs evacuation, and drinks the medicine, it will stop it. Often, taking the required medicine when phlebotomy was indicated leads to harm and agitation. If it does not subside with sedatives, phlebotomy should have been performed first. There is no evacuation required by excessive repletion as much as the severity of the ailment and the repletion—both in quality and quantity—demand. Often, good regimen takes the place of necessary phlebotomy at the time. Often, the need for evacuation arises, but an obstacle hinders it; the remedy then is fasting, sleep, and correcting the dyscrasia <note>imbalance of humors</note> in the manner of the repletion. 

There is evacuation done by way of prophylaxis, such as that required by those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other things at a known time, especially in spring. One needs to be proactive before the time arrives and perform the specific evacuation, whether phlebotomy or diarrhea. Sometimes the use of external desiccants and drying medicines is a form of evacuation, such as what is done for those with dropsy <note>edema</note>. Sometimes you are forced to use a medicine that is homogeneous in quality to the humor being evacuated, such as <term>saqmunya</term> <gloss>scammony</gloss> when you need to evacuate bile. In that case, you must mix it with something that opposes it in quality but agrees with it in purging, such as <term>halilaj</term> <gloss>myrobalan</gloss>. To correct a dyscrasia that occurs later in those with tumors in the viscera, their diarrhea may weaken them; if you are forced to do so, use things like ivy and safflower for them. As for the purgative and <term>khiyar shanbar</term> <gloss>cassia fistula</gloss>, Hippocrates said: "Whoever has a stomach that is easily moved to vomit, the first step in their purification is to use vomiting in summer or spring when the time is right." This rids the body of fatigue. Know that if the person drinking it is accustomed to a loose stool or is not accustomed to vomiting, they should avoid it in times when it is not needed. It is necessary to prepare before diarrhea by thinning the humor one wishes to evacuate and widening the passages at that time, as this rids the body of fatigue. Know that the one who drinks it—if they are accustomed to a loose stool or are not accustomed to vomiting—should [use] one of the reducing regimens before using a strong medicine. Diarrhea with abdominal flaccidity is difficult and tiring. A purgative medicine may act as a laxative if the stomach is strong, if taken during extreme hunger, or if the person is accustomed to a loose stool, or if the medicine is heavier in essence than in speed of descent. The purgative may remain, causing trouble due to the weakness of the stomach, extreme heaviness, or because the medicine irritates it, or the person has indigestion. Every purgative medicine, if it does not purge the undigested humor, stirs up the humor it is meant to purge and spreads it throughout the body, dominating the body and attracting other humors to it, increasing that humor in the body. Among the humors, some are quicker to respond to vomiting, such as bile. Some are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some have a condition like milk and stars <note>obscure metaphorical or astrological reference</note>; its diarrhea is safer in itself. Whoever has a humor flowing downward, such as those with intestinal slippage, the gripping of the intestines hinders the purgative medicine. That which is composed of medicines that are strongly different during the time of diarrhea causes the diarrhea to become agitated; the first will purge the second before the second can purge, and perhaps the first will purge the very same second. Whoever is exposed to diarrhea and their body is not cleansed of it, it must be from a drug or colic and distress that befalls them, and what is evacuated is evacuated with great difficulty. In general, if a medicine evacuates the waste, there will be no agitation with it. If it is taken with agitation, then either it is evacuating what is not waste, or if the evacuated humor changes through vomiting or diarrhea to another humor, it indicates the purification of the body from the humor intended to be evacuated.

text:
### The Fourth Art

->Chapter Four: Regarding the General Principles of Vomiting and Purging, and an Indication of How to Draw forth Purging and Emetic Medicines<-

The patient who is to be purged must not hasten to consume large or blameworthy foods, lest nature draws them in before they are digested. If any necessity requires this, it must be done little by little and with great spacing, so that it occurs gradually and what enters the body is well-digested. Phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> is the specific evacuation for the whole, whereas evacuation specific to a humor—either by excess in quantity or corruption in quality—is other than phlebotomy. Every evacuation that is excessive usually causes fainting. If the cessation of a habitual purging causes a condition, it is a sign that the evacuation should be repeated, such as in one who suffers from nasal congestion; if he makes it a habit, it will depart. Know that the remainder of the material that needs to be evacuated is less susceptible to thorough cleaning and reaching a point where the strength fails, and nature often resolves that remainder on its own. As long as the humor is of the appropriate kind and the patient bears it, do not fear excess; sometimes you may even need to purge until the point of fainting. If the patient’s strength is strong and the material of their corrupted humors is abundant, purge them little by little. This is also the case if the material is highly mature or strongly mixed with the blood and cannot be purged all at once, as in the cases of sciatica, chronic joint pains, cancer, chronic mange, and chronic boils. Know that purging draws from above and removes from below; it is consistent with the familiar method of attraction and also with the stabilization of materials after they have settled. If the materials are below, the opposite pulls them toward it, and it also removes them from where they are, by the action of attraction and vice versa. The state of phlebotomy differs according to the places from which the blood is taken, as you have learned. Those who have the least need for evacuation are those with good digestion, and inhabitants of hot climates have little need for evacuation.

We say it is recommended for someone who wishes to take a laxative to divide or space out their food. The first amount is the dosage they will test during the day in their food and drink, and they should make them varied foods and varied drinks, for the stomach is prompted by this state to desire to push what is inside it either upward or downward. As for food that is not varied but is merely more food, the stomach becomes satisfied by it, settles, and grips it firmly, especially if the amount is small. As for those with naturally soft bowels, none of this is needed. Know that the need for vomiting, purging, and the like does not arise in one who has a good regimen; such a person needs something lighter. Perhaps exercise, massage, and cupping will suffice for them. Then, if their body becomes filled, and the fill is of the best of humors, meaning blood, then phlebotomy is what is required for its purification rather than purging. When necessity dictates either phlebotomy or evacuation—such as in autumn, or by inducing vomiting—it is further removed by phlebotomy. This is one of the recommendations of Hippocrates and the books that followed it, and it is the truth. Likewise, if the phlegmatic humors are mixed with the blood. However, if the humors are uniform, viscous, and cold, phlebotomy might increase their thickness and viscosity, so one must begin with purging. In general, if the humors are uniform, prioritize phlebotomy; if an evacuation becomes necessary after that, it may be done. If they are not uniform, purge the excess first until they become uniform, then phlebotomy is performed. Whoever prioritizes medicine before phlebotomy should have prioritized phlebotomy even a little bit. Whoever was recently phlebotomized and needed an evacuation, so they drank medicine, it was held back for them. Often, drinking the medicine when phlebotomy was required resulted in fainting and distress; if it is not calmed by sedatives, then phlebotomy should have preceded it. There is no evacuation required due to excessive fullness that is not called for by the gravity of the illness and the fullness according to quality and quantity. Often, one may refrain from necessary phlebotomy due to the current management, and often the call to evacuate arises but is countered by an obstacle, in which case the only remedy is fasting, sleep, and correcting the imbalance while ignoring the fullness. Some evacuation is for the purpose of prophylaxis, such as what is needed for those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at a known time, especially in the spring. They need to be proactive before the time arrives and perform the evacuation specific to them, whether by phlebotomy or purging. Sometimes the use of external desiccants and drying medicines is a form of evacuation, as is done with those suffering from dropsy. Sometimes you are forced to use a medicine that is homogeneous in quality to the humor being evacuated, such as scammony when you need to evacuate yellow bile; in such cases, it is necessary to mix with it something that is opposite to it in quality but consistent in its purgative action, like myrobalan, and to correct the imbalance if it occurs later. In patients with visceral inflammation, their purging is weakened; if you are forced to do that, use for them things like ivy and safflower. As for the laxative and the <term>khiyar shambar</term> <gloss>cassia fistula</gloss>, Hippocrates said: "Whoever has a stomach that is easily moved to vomit, the first step in their purification is to use vomiting in summer or spring, for that rids the body of fatigue." Know that the one who is accustomed to drinking laxatives or is not accustomed to vomiting should avoid it when there is no need. It is necessary to prepare before purging by thinning the humor one wishes to evacuate and widening the passages, for that rids the body of fatigue. Know that the one who is accustomed to drinking laxatives or is not accustomed to vomiting should, before using strong medicine, follow one of the regimens of reduction. Purging while the abdomen is lean is difficult and exhausting. An emetic medicine might act as a laxative if the stomach is strong, if it is drunk on an empty stomach, or if the drinker is accustomed to laxatives, or because the medicine is heavier in substance or faster to descend. The laxative may become an emetic due to the weakness of the stomach, the intensity of the heaviness, the medicine causing nausea, or the person having indigestion. Every laxative medicine, if it does not purge the undigested matter, will stir up the humor it is meant to purge and spread it throughout the body, causing it to take over the body and attract other humors to it, thereby increasing that humor in the body. Some humors are quicker to respond to vomiting, such as yellow bile, while others are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some have a condition, such as milk or stars <note>possibly referring to planetary influences or specific herbal groupings</note>, where its laxative effect is more correct in itself. Whoever has a humor that is descending, such as those with loose bowels, the constriction of the intestines hinders the laxative medicine. What is compounded of medicines that are strongly different in the time of their purgative action will cause the bowel to be disturbed, and the first will purge the second before it purges the first, or the first might purge the second itself. Whoever is exposed to purging and their body is cleansed by it must avoid medicinal colic and distress, for if that occurs, what is evacuated is evacuated with great difficulty. In general, a medicine that evacuates the superfluous humors will not cause distress; if it is taken and distress occurs, it is either evacuating what is not superfluous, or the humor being evacuated has changed to another humor, which indicates the body has been cleansed of the humor meant to be evacuated.

text:
### Fourth Art

->Chapter Four: On Common Rules for Vomiting and Diarrhea, and an Indication of How to<-
->Attract Purging Medicine and Vomiting<-

With it others. The one being purged must not hasten to consume many or corrupt foods, for the <term>natura</term> <gloss>nature/vital force</gloss> will draw them in while they are undigested. If necessity compels any of this, it must be little by little, spaced out until it is gradual, and what enters the body must be well-digested. Phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> is the specific evacuation for blood. As for an evacuation specific to a humor that has increased in quantity or corrupted in quality, it is something other than phlebotomy. Every evacuation that is excessive causes fainting in most cases. Whoever has an episode of diarrhea interrupted should consider that a cause for the recurrence of that evacuation, as it is often induced by habits, such as one who is prone to sneezing or nosebleeds; if he becomes accustomed to them, it goes away. Know that the remainder of the material that needs to be evacuated is less susceptible to extraction, and pushing it to the point where the strength fails is ill-advised. Nature often digests that remainder. As long as the humor is of the appropriate type and the patient can bear it, do not fear excess; sometimes you may need to purge until fainting occurs. Whoever has strong vigor but much corrupted material should be purged little by little. The same applies if the material is highly matured or strongly mixed with blood and cannot be evacuated all at once. This occurs in cases of sciatica, chronic joint pain, cancer, chronic scabies, and chronic boils. Know that diarrhea draws from above and clears from below, so it is consistent with familiar attraction and is also effective after the materials have settled. If the materials are below, it draws them to itself conversely and clears them from where they are by the act of attraction, and vice versa. The state of phlebotomy differs according to the places from which the blood is taken, as you have learned. The people least in need of evacuation are those with good digestion, and inhabitants of hot climates have little need for evacuation.

We say it is recommended for someone who wishes to be purged to consume or space out their food in small amounts. The total amount to be experienced in a day should be in segments, and the foods and drinks should be varied. The stomach is moved by this situation to desire to expel what is within it, either upward or downward. As for food that is not varied, but rather one type of food, the stomach becomes satisfied with it, rests, and holds onto it tightly, especially if the quantity is small. As for those with a naturally laxative constitution, nothing of this is necessary. Know that the need for vomiting, diarrhea, and the like does not arise in one who follows a good regimen, as they require something milder. Perhaps exercise, massage, and cupping will suffice for them. Then, if their body is filled with the most abundant quantity of the best humors—meaning blood—then phlebotomy is what is needed for purification, not diarrhea. If necessity demands phlebotomy or evacuation, and the season is autumn, and the choice is between vomiting or phlebotomy, then phlebotomy is further away <note>from causing harm</note>. This is one of Hippocrates' maxims, and it is written in his books, and it is the truth. This is also the case if phlegmatic humors are mixed with blood. However, if the humors are equal, viscous, and cold, phlebotomy may increase their thickness and viscosity, so it is necessary to begin with diarrhea. In general, if the humors are equal, prioritize phlebotomy; if an evacuation prevails after that, then purge. If they are unequal, purge first until they are balanced, then perform phlebotomy. Whoever puts medicine before phlebotomy should have put phlebotomy before it in some small measure. Whoever is near the time of phlebotomy and needs an evacuation but drinks medicine will have it halted for him. Often, drinking medicine when phlebotomy was required results in fainting and agitation; if it is not calmed by sedatives, it was necessary to have prioritized phlebotomy. There is no evacuation required due to excessive fullness that is not called for by the gravity of the ailment and the fullness in terms of quality and quantity. Often, proper regimen prevents the need for phlebotomy at the time. Often, the need for evacuation arises, but an obstacle hinders it; the only solution is fasting, sleep, and correcting the intemperance <note>dyscrasia</note> in terms of the fullness. Some evacuation is for the purpose of prophylaxis, such as what is needed for those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at a known time, especially in the spring. One needs to be proactive before the time comes and perform the specific evacuation required, whether phlebotomy or diarrhea. Sometimes the use of external desiccants and drying medicines is a form of evacuation, as is done with those suffering from dropsy. Sometimes you are forced to use a medicine that is homogeneous to the humor being evacuated in quality, such as <term>scammony</term> <gloss>a purgative resin</gloss> when you need to evacuate yellow bile. It is then necessary to mix it with something that opposes it in quality while agreeing with it in purging, such as myrobalan. Correcting an intemperance if it happens later in patients with visceral swellings weakens their diarrhea. If you are forced to do that, use for them things like ivy and safflower. As for purgatives and cassia, that was stated by Hippocrates: whoever has a constitution that easily responds to vomiting, the first step in their purification is to use vomiting in the summer or spring when the time is right, as that clears the body of fatigue. Know that for someone accustomed to purging with milk or who is not accustomed to vomiting, they should avoid it when there is no need. One must prepare before diarrhea by softening the humor one wishes to evacuate and widening the passages, as that clears the body of fatigue. Know that one who drinks things that purge with milk or is not accustomed to vomiting, before using strong medicine, must use one of the milder regimens. Diarrhea accompanying abdominal weakness is difficult and exhausting. A medicine meant for vomiting may return as a purgative if the stomach is strong, or if it is drunk on an empty stomach, or if the drinker is accustomed to purging with milk, or because of the medicine, or if the medicine is heavier in essence and quick to descend. A purgative may remain stagnant due to stomach weakness, extreme heaviness, or because the medicine causes it distress and the user has indigestion. Every purgative medicine that does not purge while it is unripe stirs up the humor it is meant to purge and spreads it through the body, so it overcomes the body and draws other humors to it, increasing that humor in the body. Some humors are more responsive to vomiting, such as yellow bile, and some are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some have a condition such that diarrhea is better for them. Whoever has a downward-moving humor, like those with intestinal slipping <note>diarrhea/tenesmus</note>, finds that the constriction of the intestines hinders the purgative medicine. That which is composed of medicines that are strongly different in the time of purging causes the diarrhea to become agitated; the first will purge the second before the second purges, and perhaps the first will purge the very same second. Anyone who is exposed to diarrhea and their body is not cleansed will inevitably experience medicine-induced colic and distress, and what is evacuated is evacuated with great difficulty. In general, if a medicine evacuates the residues, there is no agitation with it; if it is taken and there is agitation, it is either evacuating that which is not a residue, or if the evacuated humor changes to another humor, it indicates the purification of the body from the humor intended to be evacuated.

<summary>This page outlines the complex criteria for medical purging, emphasizing the importance of humoral balance, patient strength, and the timing of maturation before evacuation.</summary>
<keywords>purging, evacuation, humors, maturation, medical regimen, Avicenna, Canon of Medicine</keywords>
