text:
A clamor arose in the entire court <note>original: dīvān</note>; anxiety stirred within that Sultan.
The commoners and nobles of the city lost their hearts; they wondered what disturbance and calamity had occurred.
"Is a powerful enemy intending to attack us? Or has some disaster for the kingdom arisen from the Unseen?"
For Dalqak <gloss>the Jester</gloss> had arrived <unclear>birān drusht</unclear>; he had killed several Arab horses on the road from his haste.
The people gathered at the palace of the King, asking why he had come in such a frantic rush.
From his speed, there was an outcry of exertion; a tumult and confusion broke out in the city of Tirmidh <note>The text uses "fād," but the context and Ottoman column confirm the city is Tirmidh</note>.
One man was raising his two hands in prayer or distress; another was wailing "Alas!" out of apprehension.
From the outcry, the turmoil, the fear, and the threat of punishment, every heart was filled with a hundred kinds of fancies.
Everyone made an omen based on their own guess: "What fire has fallen into the old clothes?" <note>A metaphor for a sudden disaster striking the state of affairs</note>.
The King quickly sought a path and granted an audience; when Dalqak kissed the ground, the King said, "Hey, what happened?"
To anyone who asked about his condition, that sour-faced man just put his finger to his lips, signaling "Hush!"
This behavior of his fueled the King's imagination; the entire assembly became stunned and dazed by his agitation.
Dalqak signaled, "O Kind King, let me be for a moment so I can catch my breath,"
"Until my wavering intellect returns to me, for I have fallen into a world of wonders."
After an hour, while the King was in the grip of suspicion and fancy, both his throat and mouth turned bitter from fear.
For he had never seen Dalqak in such a state; usually, there was no better companion than him.
He always practiced trickery and jokes; he used to keep the King happy and laughing.
He would make him laugh so much in his seat that the King would hold his belly and be unable to speak,
So that from the force of laughter his body would sweat; he would fall over from his laughing.
Yet today he is so yellow and sour-faced; he puts his finger to his lips, saying, "O King, be silent!"
Imagination upon imagination, fancy upon fancy; the King wondered what punishment was coming.
The King’s heart was filled with grief and caution, because the Khwarazm-Shah was very bloodthirsty.
He had killed many kings of that region, either by guile or by the power of that stubborn ruler.
The King of Tirmidh was trembling in his apprehension; and because of Dalqak's behavior, that fear increased.
He said, "Tell me quickly, what is the matter? From whom is this turmoil and agitation?"
Dalqak said, "I heard in the village that the King had a herald announce on every highway,"
"That 'I want someone who can reach Samarkand in three days, and if he is still there...'"
"'I have prepared treasures for him in exchange, when the purpose of the message is achieved.'"
"I hurried to the King for that reason, just to say that I do not have that ability!"
"Such a lowly person like me cannot do this; do not weave the thread of this hope upon me."

<column-break/>

A commotion arose in the entire court; anxiety was stirred in that Sultan as well.
The hearts of the nobles and commoners of the city were shaken; they wondered what disturbance and calamity had appeared.
"Has a powerful enemy shown his face? Or has a disaster come upon the kingdom from the Unseen?"
Dalqak came with great speed and twisting haste; on the road, several Arab horses were worn to nothing.
The people gathered at the palace of the King; they asked why the jester had made himself so small with haste.
With excessive and futile speed, he threw the city of Tirmidh into confusion.
One person beat their hands upon their knees; another cried "Alas!" and tore at their hair.
The turmoil and fear changed the appearance of the men; a hundred kinds of fancies fell into every heart.
An omen was taken for everything through imagination and guess; they said, "Fire has fallen into the old clothes."
The King gave him an audience and a path; he kissed the ground and the King asked for the message of the road.
To anyone who asked about his condition with great effort, he put his finger to his lips, saying, "Be silent!"
In that land, his behavior increased the fear and imagination; the agitation made everyone dazed and mute.
Dalqak signaled, "O Kind King, give me leave to catch my breath for a moment,"
"So that my mind may return to me immediately; I have fallen into a world of wonders."
An hour passed while the King was in suspicion and fancy; it made him bitter and dry, for he could not speak.
He had never seen Dalqak so distressed; there was no one more playful and lively than him.
He always used to tell jokes and pleasantries; the King was always happy and laughing with him.
He used to make the King so laugh that his hands would be doubled over.
The King would fall over from laughing; his body would sweat as he spoke.
Now he is so sour-faced and stained with distress; he puts his finger to his lips, meaning "Hush!"
Imagination upon imagination, fancy upon fancy; will the King suffer a downfall?
The King's heart was mixing grief and anxiety; the reason was that the Khwarazm-Shah was bloodthirsty.
He had made many kings non-existent, either by force or by the guile of that stubborn one.
The King of Tirmidh was terrified and fearful; the behavior of Dalqak made him even more afraid.
He said, "Who is the cause of this turmoil and distress? What is this agitation?"
Dalqak said, "I heard in the village, O King, that you made an order and a proclamation without mistake,"
"That 'I want a man who can go to Samarkand in three days to receive a reward.'"
"I will give him treasures in exchange, once the purpose is achieved from the news."
"I made haste for that reason just now, to say that I do not have the power or ability."
"There is no such strength in my character; let no one expect this service from me."

<summary>Dalqak the jester creates a city-wide panic by riding frantically to the palace, leading the King to fear an invasion by the Khwarazm-Shah. The tension is resolved through a comedic anticlimax when Dalqak reveals he only rushed there to decline a job advertisement for a fast messenger.</summary>
<keywords>Dalqak, Jester, Sultan of Tirmidh, Khwarazm-Shah, anxiety, humor, Samarkand, haste, Masnavi, Rumi</keywords>

For he had no companion more pleasant than him,
He used to keep the King happy and laughing,
He would make the King hold his sides,
He would fall down from the act of laughing,
Placing his hand on his lips: "O King, be silent,"
What anxiety might befall the King?
For the Khwarazm-Shah was very bloodthirsty,
Or due to the anger of that stubborn foe,
And by the jester's art, that anxiety increased,
Whom is this turmoil and clamor of yours from?
A herald shouted at the head of every king's road,
"I desire someone who, in three days,
I have set aside treasures to give in exchange,
I hastened to go for that reason,
Such lowliness does not befit one such as me."

<column-break/>

A disruption occurred in all the court as well,
The hearts of the noble and common citizens were in turmoil,
Or a powerful enemy had appeared,
The jester came, twisting and turning in haste,
They gathered at the gate of the King's palace,
With obscene talk and useless haste,
An elder was striking his knees,
Sedition and fear changed the men,
Every person was casting omens from conjecture and analogy,
Because the King gave permission to enter,
Whoever asked about the state of that sour-faced one,
Anxiety and imagination increased beyond measure,
The jester gestured, "O King of grace,
So that reason may return to me at once."
An hour passed, for the King was in anxiety and suspicion,
He had never seen the jester so distressed,
He would always make jokes and jests,
He would make the King laugh so much,
That from the force of laughter, he would break into a sweat,
He would always be cheerful and witty,
The King was happy and smiling at him,
He would make the King hold his sides from laughter,
He would fall down from the intensity of his laughter,
He would place his hand on his lips, meaning, "Be silent,"
Would the King feel any shame?
The cause was the bloodthirsty Khwarazm-Shah,
By his rage or the haughtiness of that stubborn one,
The jester's manner increased the anxiety,
From whom is this clamor and malaise?
He had given the order to the herald without mistake,
To go to Samarkand and receive the gift,
And when the purpose was obtained from the message,
"I do not have the power, O servant,
Do not place this service as a hope upon me."

The Absolute Manifestation is a necessary consequence of the perfection of His I-ness <note>original: "aniyyat"</note> and His Absolute Independence <gloss>ghina</gloss>. All the modes, states, and considerations of the Essence, with their rulings and requirements, are expressed in a universal manner. Glory be to Him, who manifests Himself through all the levels of instruments and cosmic realities <note>original: "haqayiq-i ali va kouni"</note>, emerging from the inner depths and the inclusion of the whole within His Oneness. They are witnessed and established in all their forms and rulings, just as they appeared and were established.

This manifestation and witnessing is an ocular and concrete vision, similar to the manifestation of the detailed within the concise. The affairs, states, and considerations of the Essence, along with their rulings and requirements, appear in a universal manner—glory be to Him—across all levels of divine and cosmic realities. These realities reveal the Essence from the depths of their hiddenness and the inclusion of the whole within His oneness. They remain witnessed and established in all their forms and rulings, just as they appeared and were fixed.

<summary>Jami explains the two modes of divine self-revelation: jala, the Essence appearing to itself, and istijla, the Essence seeing itself through the multiplicity of created forms. This process fulfills the perfection of the Divine Names across all levels of existence.</summary>

<meta>Continues from the previous page, mid-sentence: the list of worlds in which created things appear (spirits, images, senses) carries on here. The OCR of this handwritten Nasta'liq page has several likely misreadings, flagged in notes below. The page ends mid-sentence.</meta>

and the visible world <term>shahadat</term> <gloss>the realm of what is witnessed by the senses</gloss>, whether in this world <note>the OCR reads "dini" (religious), most likely a misreading of "dunya" (this world)</note> or in the hereafter. The purpose of all this is the realization and manifestation of the perfection of the Names <note>original: "kamal-i asma"</note>, which is the perfection of <term>jala</term> <gloss>disclosure, God's becoming manifest</gloss> and <term>istijla</term> <gloss>beholding that disclosure, God's witnessing of Himself</gloss>. The perfection of <term>jala</term> means His manifestation according to these considerations <term>i'tibarat</term> <gloss>aspects or relations under which the one Essence is viewed</gloss>, and the perfection of <term>istijla</term> means His witnessing of Himself according to these same considerations <note>the OCR is garbled at this point; the sense follows the parallel with the preceding clause</note>. This manifestation and witnessing is direct and concrete, like the manifestation of the summary in the detailed <note>that is, what was contained in undivided form is now spread out in distinct things</note>. It differs from the essential perfection <note>original: "kamal-i dhati"</note>, which is the manifestation of the Essence to itself, in itself and for itself, without any consideration of another or of otherness. That manifestation is one of knowledge, like the manifestation of the detailed in the summary <note>that is, all distinct things are known within the Essence while still gathered in its unity</note>. Absolute self-sufficiency <note>the OCR reads "nama-yi mutlaq", most likely a misreading of "ghana-yi mutlaq" (absolute independence or richness)</note> is a necessary consequence of that perfection <note>the OCR reads "kamal-i aniyat"; the sense requires the essential perfection just described</note>. The meaning of absolute self-sufficiency is that the modes <term>shu'un</term> <gloss>the inner states or "affairs" of the Essence</gloss>, states and considerations of the Essence, together with their rulings and their consequences, in a universal way <note>the OCR adds "subhanahu" (glory be to Him) here, possibly a misreading of "jumli" (in summary fashion)</note>, which appear in all the levels of the divine and cosmic realities, are witnessed by and established for the Essence in its inwardness and in the inclusion of all within its oneness <note>original Arabic phrase: "indiraj al-kull fi wahdatiha"</note>, with all their forms and rulings, just as they have appeared and been established

<summary>Jami explains that the purpose of creation across all worlds is the perfection of the divine Names, which consists of God's disclosure (jala) and His beholding of that disclosure (istijla). He contrasts this with the essential perfection, in which the Essence knows itself in itself without any otherness, and begins to define absolute self-sufficiency as the Essence already containing and witnessing all its modes within its own unity.</summary>

text:
<meta>Continuity: This page continues the discussion on spiritual recognition, shifting from the historical rejection of Jesus by the Jews to the metaphorical nature of sacred language and Jesus’s own prophecies concerning the one who would follow him.</meta>

<page-num>۱۳</page-num>

It should not remain hidden that some expressions, in the eyes of the masters of language, appear metaphorical <gloss>it seems</gloss>. These were mentioned in previous **Exalted Tablets** <term>Alwāh; the plural of Lawh, referring to sacred epistles or tablets of revelation</term> written for one of the friends. And now, out of a noble sense of honor and in view of your request, we mention them again in these pages, so that perhaps they may lead those thirsty in the desert of remoteness <note>original: *ṣaḥrāy-i ba‘d* — the spiritual state of being far from God’s presence</note> to the bridge of nearness, and bring those lost in the wilderness of separation and longing to the chalice of proximity and union. Thus, the clouds of error may be lifted, and the world-illuminating sun of guidance may rise from the horizon of the soul. In God is our trust, and from Him we seek help.

> Perhaps there may flow from this pen that which shall quicken the hearts <note>original: *af’idah* — the plural of *fu’ād*, referring to the seat of spiritual perception in the heart</note> of men, and cause them all to arise from the couch of their heedlessness, 
> and to inhale the sweetest fragrances of the leaves of Paradise from the **Lote-Tree** <term>Sidrah; a reference to the 'Lote-Tree beyond which there is no passing,' symbolizing the Manifestation of God</term> which has been planted in the Garden of Divinity by the hands of Power, with the leave of God.

It was known and clear to the possessors of knowledge <note>original: *ulū’l-‘ilm*</note> that when the fire of **Christian Love** <note>original: *maḥabbat-i ‘Īsavī* — referring to the spiritual spirit of the Gospel</note> consumed the veils of limitation and form, and His Holiness’s decree <note>referring to Jesus</note> became manifest to some extent, that **Unseen Beauty** <term>Jamāl-i Ghaybī</term> one day spoke to some of His spiritual companions regarding His departure. He kindled the fire of longing and said: "I go and I will come again." On another day, He said: "I go, and another shall come to speak what I have not spoken, and to complete what I have said." 

These two statements are, in truth, the essence of the signs regarding the **Manifestations of Unity** <term>Maẓāhir-i Tawḥīd</term>, which are heard and obeyed. If viewed with the eye of spiritual insight, they are in truth the promise of the Seal <note>original: *wa‘dah-i khātam* — likely referring to the promised 'Seal of the Prophets' or the ultimate fulfillment of the prophetic cycle</note>...

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: ...And in</meta>

It should not remain hidden that some of these expressions, to the masters of metaphorical language <term>arbáb-i-lisán</term> <gloss>masters of language/speech</gloss>, were mentioned in previous sacred Tablets <term>alwáh-i-mu‘ẓamah</term> <gloss>exalted Tablets</gloss> written for one of the friends. Now, in accordance with the requirement of zeal, and in view of the request of that personage, we repeat them in these pages. Perhaps this may guide the thirsty in the desert of remoteness to the bridge of nearness, and lead the lost in the wilderness of separation and distance to the destination of intimacy and reunion, so that the clouds of ignorance may disperse and the world-illuminating sun of guidance may rise from the horizon of the heart. Upon God is the reliance and from Him we seek aid.

> Perhaps there may flow from this Pen that which will quicken the hearts of the people, so that they may all arise from the bed of their heedlessness, and inhale the most fragrant leaves of Paradise from the Tree <term>sidrah</term> <gloss>the Lote-Tree of the furthest boundary</gloss> which was, by the hands of power and the permission of God, planted in the garden of Divinity.

To those firmly rooted in knowledge <note>original: *ūlu'l-'ilm* — those with deep spiritual insight</note>, it was known and clear that when the fire of the love of Jesus consumed the veils of limitation and form, and the decree of that Personage was, to some extent, fulfilled in this outward sense, one day that unseen Beauty <term>jamál-i-ghaybí</term> <gloss>unseen Beauty</gloss> spoke of separation and ignited the fire of longing. He said, "I am departing, and I shall come again." On the seventh day, He said again, "I am departing, and another shall come to say what I have not said, and to complete that which I have spoken." 

In reality, these two expressions are the essence of the manifestations of oneness <term>maẓáhiru't-tawḥíd</term> <gloss>Manifestations of God/the Manifestations of Oneness</gloss>, and they are heard and obeyed. If one views them with the eye of spiritual insight, they are, in truth, the promise of the Seal.

<summary>This page addresses the figurative nature of prophetic language, using the example of Jesus promising to return and the promise of a future Manifestation to illustrate how the Manifestations of God are fundamentally united in their mission despite variations in their outward speech.</summary>
<keywords>metaphorical language, sacred Tablets, spiritual guidance, Jesus, separation, longing, Manifestations of God, unity of the Prophets, the Seal</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta> this same manner. 

It should not remain hidden that some of these expressions <note>referring to the prophecies of old</note> may seem metaphorical to the masters of language. This was mentioned in the previous exalted Tablets <note>original: *Alwaḥ-i-mu‘azzamah* — the holy epistles or communications of the author</note> written for one of the friends, and now, out of a sense of divine honor and in response to your own request, we mention them again in these pages. Perhaps this will guide the thirsty ones in the desert of remoteness to the bridge of nearness, and lead those lost in the wilderness of separation to the cup of reunion, so that the clouds of error may be lifted and the world-illuminating sun of guidance may rise from the horizon of the soul. In God is our trust, and from Him we seek help. 

May there flow from this pen that which shall quicken the hearts of men, that they may arise as one from the slumber of their heedlessness, and inhale the sweetest fragrances of Paradise from the Divine Tree <note>original: *al-sidrah* — the Lote-tree, a symbol of the Manifestation of God</note> which was planted in the garden of Divinity by the hands of power, by the leave of God. 

To those possessed of knowledge, it is clear and evident that when the fire of Christian love <note>original: *maḥabbat-i-‘Īsavī*</note> burned away the veils of limited forms and customs, and when the authority of His Holiness <note>Jesus</note> was outwardly established, that Essence of the Unseen <note>original: *jamāl-i-ghaybī* — literally "the Unseen Beauty"</note> one day spoke of separation to some of his spiritual companions. He kindled the fire of longing and said: "I go and come again." On another occasion he said: "I go and another shall come, that he may say what I have not said, and fulfill what I have spoken." 

In truth, these two statements are the same for those who listen to the melodies of the Manifestations of Unity <note>original: *Maẓāhir-i-Tawḥīd* — the Prophets or Founders of world religions</note> and are submissive to them. And if one observes with the eye of spiritual insight, these are in truth the promise of the Seal <note>of the Prophets</note>

<page-num>13</page-num>
<margin>Small cross-like mark in bottom left margin.</margin>

It should not remain hidden that some of the phrases which, to the masters of metaphorical language <gloss>appear</gloss> as such, were mentioned in the exalted Tablets previously written for one of the friends. Now, too, in accordance with the requirement of zeal, and in view of your request, we shall mention them again in these pages, that perhaps they may guide the thirsty in the desert of remoteness to the bridge of nearness, and bring the lost ones in the wilderness of separation and distance to the goal of proximity and union, so that the clouds of error may be dispersed, and the world-illuming sun of guidance may rise from the horizon of the soul. In God do we trust, and from Him do we seek aid.

> Perhaps there shall flow from this Pen that which will quicken the hearts of the people, so that they may all arise from the bed of their heedlessness, and inhale the most fragrant scents of Paradise from the Lote-Tree that was planted by the hands of power, by the permission of God, within the Divine Garden.

It should be known and evident to the possessors of knowledge that when the fire of Christ’s love burned away the veil of limit and appearance, and the decree of that Blessed Beauty was in some measure found to be thus in outward appearance, one day that Unseen Beauty mentioned the separation to some of His spiritual companions. They kindled the fire of longing, and He said, "I am going, and I will come again." Seven days later, He said, "I am going, and another will come to say what I have not said, and to complete that which I have spoken." In truth, these two phrases are of the same essence in the Manifestations of Oneness. If they be viewed with the eye of spiritual insight, they are, in reality, the promise of the Seal.

<summary>This passage addresses the metaphorical language used in the Tablets, specifically interpreting Christ's promise of return and the succession of divine messengers as a unified spiritual truth regarding the Manifestations of God.</summary>
<keywords>Metaphorical language, Christ, Manifestations of Oneness, spiritual guidance, separation and union, promise of the Seal</keywords>

<note>The text is enclosed within an elaborate, intricate blue floral and geometric border (tazhib).</note>

The <term>Sufi</term> <gloss>mystic</gloss> sat at the foot of the wine jar in the corner of the monastery,
Until he saw the <term>muhtasib</term> <gloss>market inspector</gloss> carrying a jug on his shoulder.

I asked the wine-seller at dawn about the state,
Of the Sheikh, the judge, and the drinking of the Jews.

He said, "The matter is unspoken, even if you are a confidant,
Hold your tongue, keep the veil, and drink wine."

O cupbearer, spring is arriving and the money for wine is gone,
Think of something, for the blood of the heart is boiling with grief.

Your love is poverty, youth, and the new spring,
Accept my excuse and cover my sin with the skirt of your grace.

How long will you use your tongue like a candle?
The butterfly of desire has arrived, O silent lover.

O King of form and meaning, whom no eye has ever seen,
And no ear has ever heard the equal of.

Stay as long as the blue robe accepts it,
May your young fortune live from the ancient heaven.

Yesterday, a sharp-witted expert told me in secret,
That one should not hide anything from the wine-seller.

He said, "Take things easily, for by nature,
The world treats those who struggle hard with severity."

And then he offered a cup whose luster caused,
Venus to dance in the heavens and the harpist to perk up her ears.

With a bloody heart, bring a smiling lip like the cup,
Do not cry out like a harp when you receive a wound.

Until you become intimate, you will not hear the secrets of this veil,
The ear of the uninitiated is no place for the message of <term>Soroush</term> <gloss>the messenger angel</gloss>.

<summary>The poet reflects on the necessity of silence, the importance of ease, and the hidden nature of divine secrets.</summary>
<keywords>Sufi, Muhtasib, Cupbearer, Secrets, Divine Grace, Hafez</keywords>

The <term>Sufi</term> <gloss>mystic</gloss> sat by the base of the wine jar from the corner of the monastery,
The moment he saw the <term>Muhtasib</term> <gloss>censor of public morals</gloss> carrying a jug upon his shoulder.

The conditions of the <term>Sheikh</term> <gloss>master</gloss>, the judge, and the wine of the Jews,
I asked of the old wine-seller at the break of dawn.

He said, "The matter is not to be spoken of, even if you are a confidant,
Restrain your tongue, keep the veil, and drink your wine."

O cupbearer, spring arrives and no money for wine remains,
Think of a solution, for the heart's blood has come to a boil from grief.

Your love, poverty, youth, and the new spring,
Accept my apology and cover my sin with the hem of your generosity.

How long will you wag your tongue like a candle?
The butterfly of desire has arrived, O silent lover.

O King of form and meaning, whom no eye has ever seen,
And of whom no ear has heard the like.

Remain long enough so that the <term>khirqa-ye azraq</term> <gloss>blue robe of the dervish</gloss> may accept,
That your youthful fortune may clothe itself in the life of the ancient sky.

Last night, a sharp-witted expert whispered to me,
"It is not right to keep anything hidden from the wine-seller."

He said, "Take things easily upon yourself, for by its nature,
The world treats those who are rigid with great hardship."

Then he offered a cup whose radiance caused Venus in the heavens,
To begin dancing, and the lute-player to cover her ears.

With a bleeding heart, bring a smiling lip, just like the cup,
Do not cry out like a harp when you suffer a wound.

Until you become a familiar, you shall not hear a symbol from this veil,
The ear of the uninitiated is not the place for the message of <term>Soroush</term> <gloss>the messenger angel</gloss>.

<summary>This poem explores the tension between asceticism and the path of the heart, advocating for patience, grace, and the acceptance of divine mystery over public judgment.</summary>

The Sufi sat by the wine jar in the corner of the monastery,
The moment the <term>Muhtasib</term> <gloss>market inspector/censor of morals</gloss> saw him carrying a flagon on his shoulder.

I asked a wine-seller early in the morning
About the state of the Sheikh, the Judge, and the wine of the Jews.

He said, "It is not a story to be told, even if you are a confidant;
Hold your tongue, keep the veil, and drink your wine."

O Cupbearer, spring is arriving, and no money remains for wine,
Think of a plan, for the heart's blood has come to a boil from sorrow.

Your love, poverty, youth, and the new spring—
Accept my excuse, and cover my sin with the hem of your generosity.

How long will you speak incessantly like a candle?
The moth of desire has arrived, O lover, be silent.

O King of form and essence, for one such as you,
No eye has seen, and no ear has heard.

Stay long enough that your youthful fortune may clothe
The blue <term>khirqa</term> <gloss>dervish robe</gloss> accepted by the aged sky.

Last night, a keen-witted expert whispered to me,
"One should not hide anything from the wine-seller."

He said, "Take matters easily upon yourself, for by nature,
The world treats harshly those who are self-driven."

Then he handed me a cup whose radiance caused Venus
To dance in the sky and cover her ears against the sound of the lute.

Bring a laughing lip with a bleeding heart, just like the wine cup,
Do not cry out like a harp when you are wounded.

Until you become an initiate, you will not hear the mystery of this veil,
The ear of the uninitiated is no place for the message of <term>Soroush</term> <gloss>the messenger angel</gloss>.

<summary>This poem explores themes of spiritual intoxication, the hypocrisy of moral authorities, and the necessity of hidden wisdom, contrasting the outward piety of the orthodox with the inward truth of the initiate.</summary>

The <term>Sufi</term> <gloss>mystic</gloss> left the corner of the monastery and sat at the foot of the wine-vat,
After he saw the <term>Muhtasib</term> <gloss>moral police officer</gloss> carrying a wine-jug on his shoulder.

The state of the <term>Sheikh</term> <gloss>religious elder</gloss> and the <term>Qadi</term> <gloss>judge</gloss> and their secret drinking <note>original: "shurb al-yahudan," literally "the drinking of Jews," referring here to hypocritical or clandestine drinking</note>,
I asked of the wine-selling elder at the break of dawn.

He said: "These matters are not to be spoken, even though you are a confidant;
Draw in your tongue, keep the veil drawn, and drink your wine."

<term>Saki</term> <gloss>wine-bearer</gloss>, spring arrives and no money for wine remains;
Think of something, for the heart's blood boils with grief.

Your love, poverty, youth, and the new spring—
Accept my excuse and cover my fault with the hem of your generosity.

How long will you display your eloquence like a candle?
The moth of your desire has arrived; O lover, be silent.

O King of outward form and inner meaning, the likes of whom
No eye has ever seen and no ear has ever heard:

May you remain until your youthful fortune accepts
The blue <term>khirqa</term> <gloss>dervish robe</gloss> cast off by the aged sky.

Last night, a sharp-witted man of experience spoke to me in secret,
Saying: "It is not right to keep secrets from the wine-seller."

He said: "Take matters easily upon yourself, for by its very nature,
The world imposes hardship on those who strive too hard."

And then he gave me a cup from whose radiance in the heavens
Venus began to dance and the lute-player covered her ears <note>Venus, or Zuhra, is the celestial musician; the brilliance of the wine makes even the stars ecstatic</note>.

Bring a smiling lip with a bleeding heart, like the wine-cup;
Do not cry out like the lute if you receive a wound.

Until you become an initiate, you will not hear a mystery from behind this veil;
The ear of the stranger is no place for the message of <term>Soroush</term> <gloss>the herald angel</gloss>.

<summary>Hafez contrasts the hypocrisy of religious authorities with the honest wisdom of the wine-seller, advising the seeker to maintain a cheerful exterior despite inner suffering and to practice moderation in effort.</summary>
<keywords>Sufi, Muhtasib, Saki, Soroush, secrecy, hypocrisy, spiritual initiation</keywords>

<meta>continues from the previous page: In the era of the King who forgives faults and covers sins, Hafez became a wine-bearer and the mufti a wine-drinker.</meta>

<note>The text is enclosed within an elaborate, intricate blue floral and geometric border known as <term>tazhib</term> <gloss>the art of illumination</gloss>.</note>

The <term>Sufi</term> <gloss>mystic</gloss> left the corner of the monastery and sat at the foot of the wine jar,
Once he saw the <term>Muhtasib</term> <gloss>inspector of public morals</gloss> carrying a jug upon his own shoulder.

The condition of the <term>Sheikh</term> <gloss>religious elder</gloss>, the <term>Qadi</term> <gloss>judge</gloss>, and the secret drinking of the hypocrites,
I asked of the Elder Wine-seller at the break of dawn.

He said, "This is not to be spoken, even though you are a confidant;
Hold your tongue, keep the secret hidden, and drink your wine."

O <term>Saki</term> <gloss>cupbearer</gloss>, spring arrives and no money for wine remains;
Think of a remedy, for the heart's blood boils with grief.

Your love, my poverty, youth, and the new spring;
Accept my excuse and cover my sin with the hem of your generosity.

How long will you display your eloquence like a flickering candle?
The moth of your desire has arrived; O lover, be silent.

O King of both outward form and inner meaning, the like of whom
No eye has ever seen and no ear has ever heard.

May you remain so long that your youthful fortune
Accepts the blue cloak of authority from the aged sky and discards its tattered robes.

Last night, a sharp-witted man of affairs told me in secret,
"One should not keep secrets from you, nor from the wine-seller."

He said, "Take matters easy upon yourself, for by its very nature,
The world deals harshly with those who strive too hard."

Then he handed me a cup, from whose brilliance in the heavens
The planet Venus began to dance, lute in hand, listening closely.

Like the wine cup, bring a laughing lip even with a bleeding heart;
Do not wail like the harp when a wound touches your strings.

Until you become an intimate of the path, you will not hear the mysteries behind this veil;
The ear of the stranger is no place for the message of <term>Soroush</term> <gloss>the divine messenger angel</gloss>.

<summary>This page contains verses of Persian poetry emphasizing the hypocrisy of religious authorities and the necessity of finding spiritual truth through the "wine" of divine love and silence. It advises a stoic, joyful acceptance of life's hardships and the pursuit of inner mystical intimacy.</summary>
<keywords>Hafez, Sufism, Muhtasib, Wine-seller, Soroush, Tazhib, Mysticism, Hypocrisy</keywords>

<note>The text is enclosed within an elaborate blue floral and geometric border, known as <term>tazhib</term> <gloss>illumination</gloss>.</note>

The Sufi sat by the wine vat in the corner of the monastery,
The moment the <term>mohtasib</term> <gloss>censor of morals</gloss> saw him carrying a jar on his shoulder.

I asked the wine-seller at dawn about the state 
Of the sheikh, the judge, and the drinking of the Jews.

He said, "It is a matter that cannot be spoken, even if you are a confidant;
Hold your tongue, maintain the veil, and drink your wine."

O cupbearer, spring arrives and no money remains for wine;
Think of a solution, for the blood of my heart is boiling from sorrow.

Your love, poverty, youth, and the new spring;
Accept my excuse and cover my sin with the hem of your generosity.

How long will you speak fluently like a candle?
The moth of desire has arrived, O silent lover.

O king of form and meaning, like unto whom
No eye has seen and no ear has heard.

Remain until your youthful fortune clothes itself
In the blue robe <note>original: "خرقه ازرق"</note> accepted from the aged sky.

Last night, a sharp-witted expert whispered to me in secret,
"One should not hide anything from the wine-seller."

He said, "Take things easily upon yourself, for by its nature,
The world treats those who struggle too hard with harshness."

Then he offered a cup, from whose radiance in the heavens
Venus began to dance, and the lyre-player covered her ears.

Bring a laughing lip with a bleeding heart, just like a goblet;
Do not cry out like a harp when a wound reaches you.

Until you become familiar, you will not hear the secrets behind this veil;
The ear of the uninitiated is not the place for the message of the <term>soroush</term> <gloss>angelic herald</gloss>.

<summary>This page contains a ghazal by Hafez reflecting on the hypocrisy of religious authorities, the transience of life, and the necessity of maintaining silence regarding spiritual secrets.</summary>
<keywords>Sufi, wine-seller, Hafez, morality, secrecy, destiny, spiritual love</keywords>

Although silver and gold come from the stone,

**Poem**
Though silver and gold come out of stone,
they are not found in every stone.

| When speech reaches hardship and constraint, | You will soon see the key for the fortunate one. | The messenger returned from Sam's presence, | Bringing joy and a blessed message. |
| Much was said and heard, and finally, | Rudaba became part of this unfolding story. | She quickly gave the answer to the messenger-woman, | Who left her presence and carried the letter away. |
| She came to Rudaba as swiftly as the wind, | Full of this happiness and with glad tidings. | The fairy-faced girl showered coins upon the woman, | And seated her upon a gold-inlaid throne. |
| She gave that resourceful nurse her due: | A suit of clothing as a reward for the news. | She also prepared for the sake of the blessed Zal, | Such things as would be worthy of him. |
| She brought forward a majestic headband, | Its weave so fine the threads were invisible. | Its whole form was red rubies and pearls; | The gold was hidden beneath the gems. |
| A pair of most precious rings, | Shining like the planet Jupiter in the heavens, | She sent to Dastan <note>Another name for Zal</note>, son of Sam, | Along with many greetings and messages. |
| The woman left the chamber and reached the hallway, | When Sindukht <note>Rudaba's mother and Queen of Kabul</note> saw her. | Sindukht’s soul became filled with suspicion; | She shouted: "From where do you come? Speak!" |
| The woman turned yellow as sandarac <note>original: "sandarus," a yellow resin; a metaphor for turning pale with fear</note> from fright; | She trembled and kissed the ground. | Sindukht said to her: "O mischief-seeker, | Listen to my words and give a truthful answer." |
| "Hold your tongue before me! From where | Do you enter this chamber without looking at me?" | "My bright heart has become suspicious of you; | You will not tell me if it is the bow or the string!" <note>A Persian idiom meaning: tell me the straight truth of what is happening.</note> |
| She said to her: "I am but a seeker of solutions, | Earning my bread through searching and toil." | "I sold the price of clothes and ornaments; | My capital was what I gathered from the people." |
| "I go to the houses of the great; | From me, they buy clothes and silver at high price." | "In this chamber, Rudaba desired ornaments; | She wanted these precious gemstones." |
| "I brought her a gold-adorned crown, | And a casket full of royal jewels." | Sindukht said to her: "Show them to me, | So I may open the thoughts within my breast." |
| "I gave them to Rudaba," the woman said, | "And there was more; I will bring those now as well." | "Come," said Sindukht, "place them before my eyes; | Throw some water upon this anger of mine." |
| "The moon-faced one <note>Rudaba</note> said she would pay tomorrow," the woman replied, | "Do not seek favor from me now, I beg you." | From the woman's ill-fated words, | Sindukht's heart prepared for a confrontation. |
| Her luck did not hold out against the Queen; | Sindukht saw the deception and the woman's failing. | When she saw those precious garments, | And recognized the ornaments from Rudaba's hand, |
| She angrily seized the woman's hair in her hand, | Twisted it, and threw her down to the ground. | She dragged the resourceful woman by her hair, | Bringing her down and casting her on her face. |
| Blood filled the woman's eyes from that pain and grief; | She was dragged ignobly across the floor. | For a time Sindukht dragged her by the hair, | Then cast her on the dust like one unconscious. |
| She threw her down and bound her there; | The woman struck out with her feet and hands in pain. | From there, Sindukht entered the palace in a rage, | Filled with pain, sorrow, and deep grief. |
| She locked the palace door behind her, | Intoxicated by the anxiety of her thoughts. | She ordered her daughter to come before her, | And then she struck her own face in mourning. |
| With her two moist narcissus <note>metaphor for eyes</note>, her two roses <note>metaphor for cheeks</note> | She washed, until the flowers were stained with tears. | She said to Rudaba: "O precious moon, | Why have you chosen the pit over the throne?" |
| "What remains of goodness in the world | That I have not shown you, openly or in secret?" | "Why have you been so cruel, O moon-faced one? | Tell your mother every secret you hold." |
| "Who is this woman that comes to you? | For what purpose does she visit your side?" | "Whatever words this man and woman have crafted, | Concerning this beautiful headband and ring," |
| "From my great treasure and the lineage of the Arabs <note>referring to their descent from the serpent-king Zahhak</note>, | Much gain and loss will remain." | "You will give this bad name to the wind; | No daughter like the one I birthed was ever born!" |
| Rudaba looked at the ground and the backs of her feet; | She remained fixed in her place out of shame. | Tears of love poured from her eyes; | She adorned her face with the blood of her narcissus <note>meaning her eyes were red from crying</note>. |
| She said to her mother: "O wise one, | An army of love is laying siege to my soul." | "If my mother had not given birth to me at all, | No words of good or evil would be spoken of me." |
| "The commander Dastan (Zal) stayed in Kabul, | and he planted such love for him in my heart." | "The world became so narrow for my heart | That I wept openly and in secret." |
| "I do not wish to be alive without seeing his face; | My very life is contained in his scent." | "When he was here and sat with me, | We took an oath, hand in hand." |
| "Nothing else happened between us; | A fire was simply hidden between me and him." | "A messenger was sent to the Great Sam, | And a reply was sent back to the mighty Zal." |
| "For a time Sam was troubled and in pain; | He heard and spoke many words of counsel." | "In the end, he agreed to the union; | He has asked the ancient Mobeds <term>Mobed: A Zoroastrian priest and advisor</term> for their blessing." |

<meta>continues from previous page: Sam, through his astrologers, has consented to the union of Zal and Rudaba, and a messenger has returned with the joyful news.</meta>

# The Persian Shahnama, Volume One

| | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| When speech reached difficulty and restriction, | You will soon see the key to the happy destination. | The messenger returned from Sam, | With joy and a propitious message. |
| Much was said and heard with Rudaba's nurse, | In the end, she became in agreement. | Lightly, she handed the woman the letter, | The woman went before her and took the letter. |
| She came to Rudaba like the wind, | Happy with this joy and good news. | The fairy-faced one scattered gold upon the woman, | And seated her body upon a golden throne. |
| She granted the rights to that clever nurse, | A handful of garments for the news-bringer, | Also, for the sake of the auspicious Zal, | Whatever might be his equal in kind. |
| She brought forth a head-band <note>a crown or diadem</note>, | Its warp and woof were invisible <note>meaning so dense it appeared solid</note>. | Its entire body was red ruby and pearl, | The gold was hidden by the jewels. |
| A pair of high-value rings, | Shining like Jupiter in the sky. | She sent them to Dastan-e Sam, | With many greetings and a message. |
| The woman left the chamber and reached the doorway, | She looked and saw Sindukht <note>Rudaba's mother</note>, and saw her fortune. | Sindukht's heart became full of thoughts, | She said in a voice: "Where have you come from? Tell me." |
| From fear, the woman became like sandalwood <note>meaning pale or sickly</note>, | She grew afraid and kissed the ground. | Sindukht said to her: "O mischief-seeker, | Hear my words and give a truthful answer." |
| "Open your tongue before me as to where you are from, | You come into the chamber, why do you not look at me?" | "My bright heart has become suspicious of you, | Will you not tell me if you are a friend or a foe?" |
| She said to her: "I am one who seeks a living, | I bring bread through seeking and searching." | "I sold garments and adornments, | They had value among the people." |
| "I go to the houses of the great, | They buy clothes, silver, and gold from me." | "In this chamber, Rudaba requested adornments, | She asked for the same high-value gems." |
| "I brought her a crown decorated with gold, | A casket full of kingly jewels." | Sindukht said to her: "Show them to me, | That I may open the heart of my mind." |
| "I entrusted this and these things to Rudaba, | There was more, now I bring them too." | She said: "Come, let them pass before my eyes, | Let water pour over my anger <note>a metaphor for calming one's temper</note>." |
| "She said: 'I will give it tomorrow, moon-faced one,' | Do not come with excuses, do not seek favor from me." | Since she spoke of her ill-fated talk, | Her heart was prepared for conflict with her. |
| Her fortune did not come to the door of stability, | She was seeing loss and deficiency from her. | When she saw those high-value garments, | And saw the adornment from the hand of Rudaba, |
| She grabbed her by the hair with her hand, | She twisted it and threw her down upon the mountain <note>a metaphor for the floor/ground</note>. | The woman pulled the clever one by the hair, | She brought her and threw her upon her face. |
| Blood was in her eyes from that pain and grief, | She dragged her in humiliation upon the face of the earth. | For a while, she carried her, dragging her hair, | She threw her upon the dirt as if senseless. |
| She threw her down and tied her there, | She beat her feet and struck her hands. | From there, she entered the palace, sorrowful, | She remained with pain, sorrow, and grief. |
| She locked the door of the palace upon herself, | From the thought that she had become drunk with action <note>acting irrationally</note>. | She commanded that her daughter come before her, | She struck her hands upon her own cheeks. |
| She washed her two fresh narcissus eyes <note>poetic metaphor for eyes</note>, | Two flowers, until the flowers became wilted. | She said to Rudaba: "O high-valued moon, | Why did you choose a pit over the throne?" |
| "What is left of good-keeping in the world, | That I have not shown you, openly and secretly?" | "What kind of oppressor have you taken, O moon-faced one? | Tell all your secrets to your mother." |
| "Who is this woman who comes before you? | Why does she come to you?" | "Whatever words this man and woman have crafted, | Whether it be the beautiful head-band or the rings..." |
| "From my great treasury and the <term>Tazian</term> <gloss>Arabian</gloss> goods, | Much profit and loss remained." | "With this name, you want to give justice to the wind <note>to waste or destroy</note>, | Since I was born, a daughter like you was never born." |
| Rudaba saw the earth and the back of her feet <note>looking down in shame</note>, | She remained in place from her mother's shame. | Water of love poured from her eyes, | She decorated her face with the blood of her two narcissus eyes. |
| She said to her mother: "O wise one, | There was an army upon my life." | "If my mother had not given birth to me at all, | Good and bad words would not have gone from me." |
| "The commander Dastan has remained in Kabul, | He has planted such love in my heart." | "The world became so tight upon my heart, | That I became tearful, openly and secretly." |
| "I do not want to be alive without his face, | My life is only in the scent of him." | "Since he was with me, we sat together, | By oath, we took each other's hand in hand." |
| "Nothing went to anything else but him, | Fire was hidden between me and him." | "The messenger was sent to great Sam, | The messenger brought an answer to the great Zal." |
| For a time, she was twisted and was pained, | She spoke and listened to words at the bedside. | In the end, she became in agreement, | She asked the wise <term>Mobed</term> <gloss>Zoroastrian priest/sage</gloss> of old. |

<summary>Upon discovering the secret correspondence between Rudaba and Zal through her nurse, Sindukht is initially furious and physically chastises the nurse. However, Rudaba confesses her deep love for Zal, leading a reluctant Sindukht to eventually reconcile with the situation and seek the counsel of a Mobed.</summary>
<keywords>Rudaba, Sindukht, Zal, Dastan, Secret, Love, Mother, Mobed, Rebellion</keywords>

| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| When the talk reached difficulty and hardship, | You will soon see <term>Farrokh-Bish</term> <gloss>a name meaning "Happy-Seeker," referring here to the messenger</gloss> as the key. | The messenger returned from the presence of Sam, | With happiness and a fortunate message. |
| He spoke much and listened, and to Rudaba <note>literally: "the bread of Rudaba"</note>, | Finally, he became in agreement with the story. | Quickly he entrusted the answer to the letter to the woman; | The woman left his presence and carried the letter. |
| She came to Rudaba like the wind, | With this joy and happy with good tidings. | The fairy-faced one <note>Rudaba</note> scattered silver coins over the woman; | She seated her upon a golden-patterned chair. |
| Due to the right of that resourceful nurse, | She gave a suit of clothes to the bringer of good news. | Also likewise for the sake of the blessed Zal, | From things that would be his equal. |
| She brought forward a headband, | Where the warp and woof were invisible within it. | Its entire body was of red ruby and pearl; | The gold was all hidden by the gems. |
| A precious pair of rings, | Shining like the planet Jupiter in the heavens. | She sent them to Dastan son of Sam; | She gave many greetings and messages with them. |
| The woman left the chamber and reached the hallway; | <term>Sindukht</term> <gloss>Rudaba's mother</gloss> looked and saw her. | The soul of Sindukht became anxious because of her; | She said with a loud voice: "From where? Tell me who you are!" |
| From fear of her, the woman became like <term>sandarūs</term> <gloss>yellow resin; pale with fear</gloss>; | She was afraid and kissed the ground. | Sindukht said to her: "O seeker of mischief, | Listen to the words and give a truthful answer." |
| "Hold your tongue before me; from where | Do you enter the chamber and not look at me?" | "My bright heart has become suspicious of you; | You will not tell me until it is the string or the bow." <note>A metaphor for the truth of the matter</note> |
| She said to her: "I am a seeker of solutions; | I bring forth my bread through searching." | "The price of clothes and ornaments | I sold; people were my source of capital." |
| "I go to the houses of the great; | They buy clothes from me with silver and heavy price." | "In this chamber, Rudaba requested ornaments; | She wanted those same precious gems." |
| "I brought her a gold-patterned crown, | A small box full of kingly gems." | Sindukht said to her: "I will see; | I will open the heart of the chest and the thought." |
| "I entrusted it to Rudaba," she said, "and things | Were many; now I will bring them also." | She said: "Come, let it pass before my eyes, | Throw some water upon this anger of mine." |
| She said: "The moon-faced one will give silver tomorrow; | Do not seek an excuse to come to me." | Thus, from the ill-fortune of her speech, | She prepared her heart for battle with her. |
| She did not come out of the door of the house; | She saw in her change and decline. | When she saw those precious clothes, | And saw the ornaments from Rudaba's hand. |
| She became enraged and took her hair in her hand; | She twisted it and threw her down to the ground. | She pulled the resourceful woman by the hair; | She brought her and cast her down on her face. |
| Blood was in her eyes from that pain and grief; | In humiliation, she dragged her across the ground. | For a time, she kept dragging her by the hair; | She threw her on the dust like those who are unconscious. |
| She threw her there and bound her; | She kept stamping her feet and striking with her hands. | And from there she entered the palace, sullen; | She remained with pain and with sorrow and grief. |
| She closed the door of the palace upon herself; | From the thought, she became like one intoxicated. | She commanded that her daughter come forward; | She kept striking her own hand against her cheek. |
| Two roses with two tearful narcissi <note>metaphor for eyes weeping upon cheeks</note>, | She kept washing until the roses became colorless. | She said to Rudaba: "O precious moon, | Why did you choose the pit over the throne?" |
| "What remained of goodness in the world | That I did not show you openly and secretly?" | "O moon-faced one, what did you have as an oppressor? | Tell all the secrets to your own mother." |
| "Who is this woman who comes to you? | For what purpose does she come to you?" | "Whatever words this man and woman have made, | That there is a beautiful headband and ring." |
| "From my great treasure and the Arabs, | Much profit and loss remains." | "With this bad name, you will give the seeker to the wind; | As I have born a daughter, no one ever bore." |
| Rudaba looked at the ground and the back of her feet; | She remained in place out of shame for her mother. | The water of love poured from her eyes; | She adorned her face with the blood of two narcissi. |
| She said to her mother: "O wise one, | An army is upon my soul." | "If my mother had not given birth to me from the root, | No words of good and evil would have gone from me." |
| "The commander Dastan stayed in Kabul; | Thus his love sat upon my heart." | "The world became so narrow for my heart, | That I became weeping openly and secretly." |
| "I do not wish to be alive without his face; | My life is also in his fragrance." | "By that which he had a sitting with me, | We took his hand in hand with a covenant." |
| "Nothing else happened except for him; | Fire was hidden between me and him." | "A messenger was sent to the great Sam; | The response was sent to the great Zal." |
| "For a time he turned and was suffering; | He spoke and heard the words of the pillow." | "Finally he became in agreement; | He asked of the ancient <term>Mobad</term> <gloss>Zoroastrian priest</gloss>." |

| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| When words reached difficulty and hardship, | You will soon see the key for the fortunate one. | The messenger returned from Sam's presence, | With happiness and a fortunate message. |
| He spoke much and heard much, and Rudaba too, | Until finally she became part of the same story <note>she agreed and was delighted by the news</note>. | She quickly handed the response to the woman's letter; | The woman left her presence and took the letter. |
| She came to Rudaba like the wind, | With this joy and happy tidings. | The fairy-faced one <note>Rudaba</note> scattered silver coins upon the woman, | And seated her on a gold-decorated chair. |
| She gave the clever, resourceful nurse her due, | Providing a suit of clothes for the messenger. | Also, for the sake of the fortunate Zal, | She prepared gifts that would be worthy of him. |
| She brought forth a precious headband <note>original: "sarband," a diadem or turban ornament</note>, | Its warp and weft were hidden by decoration. | Its entire body was of red rubies and pearls; | The gold was made invisible by the gemstones. |
| A precious pair of rings, | Shining like Jupiter in the sky. | She sent them to Dastan, son of Sam, | Giving many blessings and messages with them. |
| The woman left the chamber and reached the hallway; | Sindukht <note>Rudaba's mother</note> watched and saw her. | Sindukht's soul became anxious because of her; | She called out: "From where do you come? Tell me!" |
| The woman became pale as <term>sandarac</term> <gloss>a yellow resin</gloss> from fear; | She was terrified and kissed the ground. | Sindukht said to her: "O seeker of mischief, | Hear my words and give a true answer." |
| "Tell me, from where do you come? | Why do you enter the chamber and not look at me?" | "My bright heart has become suspicious of you; | Do not hide the truth from me <note>idiom: "tell me whether it is the bow or the string"</note>." |
| She said to her: "I am a seeker of solutions; | I earn my bread through searching." | "I have been selling the price of clothes and ornaments; | I sell to people to make a living." |
| "I go to the houses of the great; | They buy clothes and silver and valuables from me." | "In this chamber, Rudaba asked for ornaments; | She requested those same precious gems." |
| "I brought her a gold-patterned crown, | And a casket full of royal jewels." | Sindukht said to her: "Show them to me, | So I may ease the thoughts in my chest." |
| "I gave them to Rudaba," she said, | "And there was more; I will bring it now." | "Come," said Sindukht, "place them before my eyes, | To pour water on this anger of mine." |
| "I will bring them tomorrow," said the moon-faced woman; | "Do not seek me now, I did not come for naught." | Because of her ill-fated words, | Sindukht prepared her heart for a confrontation. |
| Fortune did not aid the woman's plan; | Sindukht saw the deception and the loss. | When she saw those precious clothes, | And recognized the ornaments from Rudaba’s hand... |
| She grabbed the woman's hair in her hand, | Twisted it, and threw her down to the ground. | She pulled the resourceful woman by the hair; | She brought her down and threw her on her face. |
| Blood filled the woman's eyes from that pain and grief; | Sindukht dragged her in contempt across the floor. | For a time she pulled her along by her hair, | Then threw her on the dust like one unconscious. |
| She cast her down and bound her there, | Stamping her feet and striking with her hands. | From there, she entered the palace gloomily; | She was filled with pain, sorrow, and grief. |
| She closed the palace door upon herself, | Feeling like one intoxicated by her troubled thoughts. | She ordered her daughter to come before her, | While she herself struck her own face in despair. |
| Two roses <note>cheeks</note> with two moist narcissi <note>eyes</note>, | She washed with tears until the roses were stained. | She said to Rudaba: "O precious moon, | Why did you choose a pit over a throne?" |
| "What remained of goodness in the world, | That I did not show you, both openly and in secret?" | "O moon-faced one, why were you so cruel? | Tell the whole secret to your mother." |
| "Who is this woman who keeps coming? | Why does she come to see you?" | "Whatever words this man and woman have exchanged, | This beautiful headband and ring..." |
| "From my great treasury and the Arabs, | Much profit and loss remains." | "With this bad reputation, you will throw yourself to the wind; | No daughter like the one I bore was ever born." |
| Rudaba looked at the ground and her own feet; | She remained still out of shame before her mother. | The water of love poured from her eyes; | She decorated her face with the blood of two narcissi <note>tears as red as blood</note>. |
| She said to her mother: "O wise one, | An army of emotions is upon my soul." | "If my mother had not given birth to me at all, | No words of good or evil would be spoken of me." |
| "The commander Dastan <note>Zal</note> stayed in Kabul; | He planted such love for him in my heart." | "The world became so narrow for my heart, | That I wept both openly and in secret." |
| "I do not wish to be alive without seeing his face; | My life is found only in his scent." | "Know that he was here and sat with me; | We took hand in hand in a pact." |
| "Nothing else happened between him and me, | Though a fire was hidden between us." | "A messenger was sent to the great Sam, | and a reply was sent back to the great Zal." |
| "For a time Sam was troubled and pained; | He listened to advice and debated long." | "In the end, he agreed to the union; | He consulted the ancient <term>Mobed</term> <gloss>Zoroastrian priest</gloss>." |

text:
Volume I of the Persian Shahnameh

| | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| When speech reaches hardship and straitness, | You shall soon see the key to good fortune. | The messenger returned from before Sam, | With joy and a propitious message. |
| She said much and heard much, and Rudabeh, | In the end, became of one mind with her. | Lightly, she handed the woman the letter, | The woman went before her and took the letter. |
| She came to Rudabeh like the wind, | Happy with this joy and good news. | The fairy-faced one scattered gold upon the woman, | And seated her body upon a throne of gold. |
| She gave the cunning nurse her due, | And a set of clothes for the bringer of good news. | Likewise for the fortunate Zal, | Something that would be his equal. |
| She brought forth a headband <note>ornamental headpiece</note> ahead of time, | Its warp and woof had disappeared <note>meaning: it was so densely embroidered that the fabric was hidden</note>. | Its entire body was red ruby and pearl, | The gold was invisible beneath the jewels. |
| A pair of precious rings, | Shining like Jupiter in the sky, | She sent to Dastan-e-Sam <note>a title for Zal</note>, | Giving with it much praise and message. |
| The woman left the chamber and arrived at the gate, | Sindokht looked and saw her fortune <note>i.e., her secret activities</note>. | Sindokht's soul became troubled by her, | With a shout she said, "Where are you coming from? Tell me!" |
| From fear of her, the woman turned like sandalwood <note>meaning: pale/yellow</note>, | She grew afraid and kissed the ground. | Sindokht said to her, "O troublemaker, | Hear the words and give a truthful answer." |
| "Speak before me from where, | You enter the chamber and I do not see you? | My bright heart has become suspicious of you, | Will you not tell me if you are a friend or foe?" |
| She said to her, "I am a seeker of solutions, | I bring bread <note>sustenance/livelihood</note> through searching. | I sell the price of clothes and ornaments, | From the people, I have capital." |
| "I go to the houses of the great, | They buy clothes and silver and precious things from me. | Rudabeh wanted ornaments in this chamber, | And wanted those precious jewels." |
| "I brought her a crown decorated with gold, | A box full of kingly jewels." | Sindokht said to her, "Show me, | Let me open the heart and thoughts of the chest <note>i.e., reveal the contents</note>." |
| "I gave them to Rudabeh," she said, "and these things, | Were surplus; now I will bring them as well." | Come, she said, leave it before my eyes, | A tear upon the woman's face from this anger of mine. |
| "I said I would give the silver tomorrow, O moon-faced one, | Do not come for excuses, do not seek favor from me." | Since the ill-fated woman spoke, | She readied her heart for battle with her. |
| "Her fortune does not come to the door, | She saw only dwindling and loss from her." | When she saw those precious clothes, | And saw the ornaments from Rudabeh's hand, |
| She flew into a rage, seized her hair by the hand, | She twisted it and threw her face down on the ground. | The woman dragged the cunning one by the hair, | Brought her and threw her down upon her face. |
| Blood flowed in her eyes from that pain and grief, | She dragged her abjectly upon the ground. | For a while she dragged her by the hair, | And threw her on the earth as if senseless. |
| She threw her down and bound her there, | She beat her feet and struck with her hands. | And from there she went into the palace, gloomy, | She was in pain, sorrow, and grief. |
| She locked the door of the palace upon herself, | From the worry that she had become drunk with action <note>i.e., acted recklessly</note>. | She commanded her daughter to come before her, | She was striking her hands against her own cheeks. |
| Two roses <note>cheeks</note> with two moist narcissi <note>eyes</note>, | She was washing until the roses faded. | She said to Rudabeh, "O precious moon, | Why did you choose the pit instead of the throne?" |
| "What is left of goodness in the world, | That I have not shown you, openly and secretly? | What tyranny did you hold, O moon-faced one? | Tell all your secrets to your mother." |
| "Why does this woman come before you? | Why does she come to you? | The words of whatever these man and woman made, | That this beautiful headband and ring are <unclear>yours</unclear>?" |
| "From my great treasure and the Arabs <note>or "rapidly accumulated wealth"</note>, | Much profit and loss remained. | You want to cast this reputation to the wind, | Since I was born, a daughter like you was never born." |
| Rudabeh saw the ground and the backs of her feet, | She remained in shame before her mother. | Water of love poured from her eyes, | She adorned her face with the blood of two narcissi <note>crying tears of blood</note>. |
| She said to her mother, "O wise one, | The army was upon my soul. | If my mother had not given birth to me at all, | Neither good nor bad words would have gone from me." |
| "The commander Dastan <note>Zal</note> remained in Kabul, | Such love of him he planted in my heart. | The world became so narrow for my heart, | That I became weeping, openly and secretly." |
| "I do not want to be alive without his face, | My life is in the scent of him. | In that which he was with me, we sat, | By pledge, we took each other's hands." |
| "Nothing else went except for him, | Fire was hidden between me and him. | A messenger was sent to great Sam, | The messenger brought the answer to mighty Zal." |
| For a time he fretted and was pained, | He spoke and listened to words by the bedside. | In the end, he became of one mind, | He asked the ancient <term>Mobed</term> <gloss>Zoroastrian priest/sage</gloss>." |

<summary>Sindokht discovers Rudabeh's secret communications with Zal, leading to a confrontation where Rudabeh confesses her love and their secret pledge.</summary>
<keywords>Shahnameh, Rudabeh, Zal, Sindokht, Sam, secret love, Kabul</keywords>

| | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| "When a matter comes to hardship and to narrow straits, | You will soon see the key that opens it. | The messenger has come back from Sam, | With gladness and with a fortunate message." |
| "He spoke much and listened much, <note>the end of this half-line is garbled in the transcription</note> | And in the end he gave his consent." | Quickly he handed the woman the answer to the letter; | The woman left his presence and carried the letter away. |
| She came to Rudaba like the wind, | Glad with this joy and the good news. | The fairy-faced girl scattered silver coins over the woman, | And seated her on a chair figured with gold. |
| She gave that resourceful nurse | A suit of clothes as a reward for the good news; | And likewise, for the fortunate Zal, | She chose things that would be worthy of him. |
| She brought out a headband of fine cloth, | Its warp and weft hidden from sight; | Its whole surface was red ruby and pearl, | The gold quite hidden beneath the gems. |
| A pair of costly rings, | Shining like Jupiter in the heavens, | She sent to Dastan, son of Sam, <note>Dastan is another name for Zal</note> | And with them she gave many greetings and messages. |
| The woman left the chamber and reached the hall; | Sindukht looked up and caught sight of her. <note>Sindukht is Rudaba's mother, queen of Kabul</note> | Sindukht's mind grew troubled at her; | She called aloud: "Where are you from? Tell me." |
| The woman turned yellow as <term>sandarus</term> <gloss>sandarac, a pale yellow resin</gloss> from fear of her; | She was frightened and kissed the ground. | Sindukht said to her: "You maker of mischief, | Hear my words and give a true answer." |
| "Tell me plainly where you come from; | You go into the chamber and do not look at me. | My clear heart has grown suspicious of you. | Will you not tell me whether you are the bowstring or the bow?" <note>that is, what your true part in this business is</note> |
| She said to her: "I am one who lives by her wits; | I gather my bread by searching for it. | I sell clothes and ornaments; | My living comes from people." |
| "I go to the houses of the great; | They buy garments from me, and silver and costly things. | In this chamber Rudaba wanted ornaments, | And she wanted precious jewels too." |
| "I brought her a crown worked with gold, | And a casket full of royal gems." | Sindukht said to her: "Show them to me; | Set my heart and my thoughts at ease." |
| "I handed them over to Rudaba," she said, "these and other things; | There was more, and I shall bring that now as well." | "Come," she said, "set it before my eyes; | Throw some water on this anger of mine." |
| "The money," she said, "the moon-faced girl will give tomorrow; | Until I have the price, do not ask it of me." | Sindukht knew her words to be crooked, | And she set her heart on a fight with her. |
| The woman's speech did not ring true to her; | She saw in it only crookedness and falsehood. | When she saw those costly garments, | And saw the ornaments that came from Rudaba's own hand, |
| She flew into a rage, seized the woman's hair in her hand, | Twisted it, and threw her down low. | She dragged the resourceful woman by the hair, | Brought her along and flung her on her face. |
| With blood in her eyes from that pain and grief, | She dragged her in disgrace along the ground. | For a while she pulled her along by her hair, | Then cast her on the dust like one who has fainted. |

(161)
<meta>Sharafnāma, Nizami Ganjavi</meta>

At the time of turning the reins,
the seeker began another path,
for it can be counted in comparison,
Alexander said to him, "One sharp blade
A reply so noble to the army,
The news grew warmer every moment,
When Alexander knew that this swift cloud <note>original: "تند میغ", metaphor for a looming storm or threat</note>
He sent for the army from every land,
From Egypt, Africa, Rome, and Rus,
When the boundless army became a throng,
The registrar reported that three hundred thousand
When the army's preparations were complete,
The intelligent men of Rome sat,
The King, regarding the affair of Dara and his business,

<column-break/>

"Victory should not be attained through theft,
For Dara has prepared so much tallow <note>A reference to the practice of greasing or preparing weapons and armor</note>,
Those who are experts in horses,
He shreds the tallow of one hundred cows,
Arose from the noble Sovereign,
That a raging dragon has come to Rome,
He draws his lightning-like blade with speed,
To proceed to the King's door,
An army like a bride was adorned,
He requested the number of the renowned warriors,
The brave, individual horsemen arose,
He formed a council outside and [drank] wine,
They softened like wax with the King's seal,
He spoke and examined his affair,

---
(1) That is, one sword shreds the tallow and fat of a hundred cows—shreds the leather of a hundred cows—the backs of a hundred cows... [variant]
(2) That is, when Alexander knew that Dara was a swift cloud, drawing his lightning-blade towards him with the roar of thunder.
(3) That is, the reporter and army registrar announced that three hundred thousand individual horsemen had gathered—<term>mofrad savar</term> <gloss>individual horseman</gloss> and <term>yekeh savar</term> <gloss>peerless warrior</gloss>—six hundred thousand... [variant]
(4) That is, they softened their hearts like wax with the seal of Alexander's command and accepted his order—soft wax is more receptive than hard wax.

<summary>This passage describes Alexander the Great organizing his forces against Dara, involving the gathering of a vast army from diverse regions and the administrative reporting of his military strength.</summary>
<keywords>Alexander, Dara, army, military organization, Rome, leadership</keywords>

<meta>The page is set in two columns: the left column holds the first half-line of each couplet and the right column the matching second half-line, so line 1 of each column reads together. The stray "10" in the source is a printed line counter and is omitted. Footnote markers are given as (1) to (4).</meta>

For a king, when the time comes to turn his reins,
The scout began once more to report
In any number that could be reckoned up
Iskandar said to him: "A single sharp blade (1)
To the army, an answer so worthy as this
The news grew hotter with every hour
When Iskandar understood that this fierce cloud (2)
He sent out word that troops from every land
From Egypt and Africa, from <term>Rūm</term> <gloss>Rome, meaning the Greek and Byzantine lands</gloss> and from <term>Rūs</term> <gloss>the land of the Rus</gloss>,
When the boundless army had grown dense,
The <term>ʿāriż</term> <gloss>muster-master, the officer who reviews and registers the troops</gloss> reported that three hundred thousand (3)
When the business of the army was fully in order,
The wakeful minds of Rome sat down together (4)
The king, concerning Dara and the war with him,

<column-break/>

Victory is not to be won by stealth like a thief.
That Dara had mustered a host too great <note>the OCR reads "pīh" (fat) here, most likely a slip for "sipah" (army); the couplet runs on into the next line</note>
By those who are skilled in judging armies.
Cuts the fat of a hundred oxen into shreds."
Rang out loftily from the lofty king.
That a raging dragon had come against Rome.
Was drawing, with thunder, the lightning of the sword, <note>the OCR is garbled at this word; the reading "with thunder" follows the editor's footnote 2</note>
Should set out for the gate of the king.
An army was adorned like a bride.
He asked for a count of the renowned, name by name.
Brave and peerless horsemen had been tallied.
He convened a council without music or wine cup. <note>the OCR reads "bīrūn" (outside); the sense of the line points to "bī rūd", "without the lute", that is, a sober council of war</note>
And softened their wax to the seal of the king.
Spoke at length and turned the matter over.

---
(1) That is, one sword cuts the fat and grease of a hundred fattened oxen into shreds. Variant readings in other copies: "cuts the hide of a hundred oxen" and "the back of a hundred oxen".
(2) That is, when Iskandar understood that Dara is a fierce cloud who, with the roar of thunder, draws the sword of lightning against him.
(3) That is, the reviewing officer and army registrar reported that three hundred thousand lone horsemen had been gathered. <term>Mufrad-savār</term> and <term>yakka-savār</term> <gloss>"single rider": a champion without peer or equal</gloss>. Variant reading in another copy: "six hundred thousand".
(4) That is, they softened the wax of their hearts to the seal of Iskandar's command and became receptive to his order. Soft wax takes an impression more readily than hard wax.

<summary>Iskandar dismisses reports of Dara's uncountable host with the remark that one sharp blade cuts the fat of a hundred oxen, then summons troops from Egypt, Africa, Rome and Rus. With three hundred thousand horsemen mustered, he calls a sober council of his Roman advisers to plan the war. The editor's footnotes explain the imagery and record manuscript variants.</summary>
<keywords>Iskandar, Alexander, Dara, Darius, Nizami, Sharafnama, Rome, Rus, Egypt, Africa, army muster, war council, sword and oxen proverb, wax and seal metaphor, manuscript variants</keywords>

When the King finished with the pleasant delicacies, he poured wine and established a banquet of joy.
When the King had drunk two or three cups of wine, sweat rose upon his skin from the wine's heat.
He said, "O host of the golden palace, your residence is pleasant and your provisions are abundant.
Yet this sixty-step high palace, to which the heavens cast a lasso over its summit,
After sixty years have passed since you, how are you able to walk beneath its base?"
The host said, "May the King remain eternal, may the <term>Kawthar</term> <gloss>a river in Paradise</gloss> be his wine and the houris his cupbearers.
This is not remarkable for me; I am a man. How could I grow weary of such a base?"
"The remarkable thing is that there is a girl like the moon, soft and delicate like fur and fine silk.
She carries a cow like a mountain upon her neck to the place where it eats grass.
She carries the sixty-step staircase with one hand, such that she does not need to sit on any step.
That cow, moreover, is a cow like an elephant; it cannot pull its own fat for a single mile.
By God, if anyone in this land lifts a breath from the ground,
And a woman carries it to a sixty-step fortress, is it not a wondrous deed?"
When the King heard this tale from his colonel, he bit his fingertip in wonder.
He said, "How can a deed of this kind be? It cannot be, or if it is, it must be sorcery.
I will not believe this claim as truth until I see it with my own eyes first."
Then he requested from the host, the man, that he verify the claim of his speech.
When the host heard this, he went below and told the tale of the lion to the cow-slayer.

33 This is not strange for me, for I am a man; how should I grow weary of such stairs? 33
34 What is strange is that there is a girl as beautiful as the moon, as soft and delicate as the silk and ermine of a king.
35 She takes an ox as heavy as a mountain upon her neck and brings it to where it must graze.
36 She carries it up the sixty steps in one go, without pausing to rest on any stair. 36
37 And what an ox! It is like an elephant, unable to move its own weight an inch.
38 By God, if anyone else in this land could even lift its breath from the earth!
39 When a woman carries it up the sixty steps of this fortress, how can it not be a wonder?" 39
40 When the host <note>literally: the colonel</note> told this story, the King bit his fingertip in astonishment <note>a traditional gesture of amazement in Persian literature</note>.
41 He said, "How can such a deed be? It cannot be, and if it is, it must be magic.
42 I will not believe this statement to be true until I first see it with my own eyes." 42
43 He then requested of the host to prove the truth of his claim.
44 When the host heard this, he went down and told the story of the "lion" <note>referring here to the King</note> to the girl who carries the ox.

<summary>King Bahram Gur questions how his elderly host can climb the sixty steps of the pavilion, leading the host to describe a young woman who miraculously carries a full-grown ox up the same stairs every day. The King, skeptical of the feat, demands to see proof of this supposed magic.</summary>
<keywords>Bahram Gur, Fitna, sixty steps, ox-carrier, miracle of strength, pavilion banquet, amazement</keywords>
