text:
Since there is no faithfulness in the whole <note>referring to the material world or those who are not the Beloved</note>, why do you go toward any part of that whole?
All trust is placed in You, for You are the support and the chief.

If a few people cut their hands at the sight of Joseph’s face <note>a reference to the Quranic story where women were so dazzled by Joseph's beauty that they accidentally cut their hands</note>,
You have severed two hundred Josephs of the soul from heart and intellect.

From filth and from goodness, You fashion the form of a person
Who would flee for two leagues away from the odor of impurity.

Before the earthy morsel that becomes pure greenery,
It is delivered from defilement once You have breathed the spirit into it.

Come, O heart, go to the heavens; go to the pasture of God,
Since you have grazed for a while in the pasture of the cattle.

Set all your desire upon that for which you have no hope,
For it was from that initial hopelessness that you arrived at this side.

Be silent, so that the Lord, the Bestower of Speech, may speak;
For He who fashioned the door and the lock also fashioned the key.

Line 11: <note>variation</note> how much you bought

text:
When there is no fidelity in the rose, why do you turn toward every rose?
All trust is placed in you, for you are both the support and the chief.

If they cut their hands <note>a reference to the women who were so struck by the beauty of Joseph that they accidentally cut their hands with knives while peeling oranges</note> at the sight of Joseph’s face,
You have cut away two hundred Josephs of the soul from heart and reason.

From impurity and from goodness, you create the form of a person,
So that he flees two leagues away from the scent of impurity.

Make him fodder for the earth, so he may become pure greenery;
He escapes from uncleanness once you have breathed spirit into him.

Come, O heart, go to the sky, go to the pasture of God;
You have grazed long enough in the pasture of beasts.

Place all your desire on that for which you have no hope,
For it is from that initial hopelessness that you have arrived at this side.

Be silent, for the Lord who bestows speech will speak,
For He is the one who fashioned the door and the lock, and He is the one who made the key.

### Account of the revolt of the Sharif Jalal al-Din in the lands of Ma'bar, and the associated killing of the Vizier’s nephew

The Sultan had appointed the Sharif Jalal al-Din Ahsan Shah over the lands of Ma'bar <note>original: "ببلاد المعبر"</note>, which lies at a distance of six months' journey from Delhi <note>original: "دهلى"</note>. He rebelled, claimed the kingdom for himself, killed the Sultan's deputies and officials, and minted gold dinars and silver dirhams in his own name. He would write on one side of the dinar: "The descendant of Taha and Ya-Sin <note>original: "سلالة طه ويس"</note> <note>These are titles attributed to the Prophet Muhammad, taken from the opening letters of the 20th and 36th chapters of the Quran.</note>, the father of the poor and the destitute, Jalal al-Dunya wa al-Din <gloss>Glory of the World and Religion</gloss>." And on the other side: "The one who trusts <note>original: "الواثق"</note>

<column-break/>

possess, in effect, territory at the foot of the mountain, and they could not cultivate it without the permission of the sovereign of India.

OF THE UPRISING OF THE SHARIF DJELÂL EDDÎN IN THE PROVINCE OF MA'BAR, AND OF THE DEATH OF THE NEPHEW OR SON OF THE SISTER OF THE VIZIR, WHICH IS CONNECTED TO THIS REVOLT.

Djelâl eddîn rebelled, usurped power, killed the lieutenants and agents of the sovereign, and struck gold and silver coins in his own name. On one of the sides of the dînârs he had engraved the following words: « The offspring of Thâ-hâ and Yâ-sîn <note>these letters, which constitute the titles of two chapters of the Korân, the 20th and the 36th, are among the epithets given to Mahomet</note>, the father of the fakîrs <gloss>ascetics/poor</gloss> and the indigent, the illustration of the world and the religion. » And on the other face: « He who trusts

The second said: "Rather, I am its owner; for I rubbed its bearer, and kneaded his joints." The bathhouse keeper said: "Bring me the owner of the head, and I shall ask him. Is this head yours, or is it his?" They brought me to him and said: "We have a testimony from you, so appear." I stood up and came, whether I wanted to or not. The bathhouse keeper said: "O man, say nothing but the truth, and do not bear witness to anything but what is just. Tell me, to which of these two does this head belong?" I said: "May God grant you well-being, this is my head. It has accompanied me on the road, it has circled with me around the Ancient House <note>the Kaaba in Mecca</note>, and I have no doubt that it is mine." He said to me: "Be silent, you meddler!" Then he turned to one of the two disputants and said: "O man, how long will this competition over people continue with this head? Seek solace from its little worth, may you be cursed by God and the heat of His Sqar <note>a name for Hell</note>. Grant that this head is not, and that I have not seen this 'is not'."

Isa ibn Hisham said: I rose from that place ashamed, with my clothes in a state of agitation, and I slipped out of the bathhouse in a hurry. I cursed the youth with the <term>ass</term> <gloss>beating</gloss> and the <term>mass</term> <gloss>crushing</gloss>, and I pushed him with a blow like the pounding of gypsum. I said to another: "Go and bring me a cupper who will remove this burden from me." He brought me a man of fine build, handsome in attire, in the image of a doll. I felt at ease with him. He entered and said: "Peace be upon you, and from which land are you?" I said: "From Fars." He said: "May God revive you from the land of grace and prosperity, and the land of the <term>Sunnah</term> <gloss>Prophetic tradition</gloss> and the <term>Jama'ah</term> <gloss>community of believers</gloss>. I attended its congregational mosque in the month of Ramadan, when the lamps were lit and the <term>Tarawih</term> <gloss>extra evening prayers in Ramadan</gloss> were established. We did not notice until the night grew long and passed over those lanterns. But God worked for me with a light <note>referring to a shoe</note> whose tongue I had been, yet its laces did not reach its sleeve, and the boy returned to his mother after I had prayed the night prayer and the shadow had leveled. But how was your pilgrimage? Did you complete its rites as required, while they cried 'the wonder, the wonder'?" I looked at the minaret—and how easy war is for the spectators—and I found the <term>harisah</term> <gloss>a porridge dish made of meat and wheat</gloss> as it was, and I knew that the matter was by the decree and judgment of God. How long must this frustration last? Today and tomorrow, Saturday and Sunday—I shall not prolong this, and what is all this chatter? But I wanted you to know that the <term>Mubarrad</term> <gloss>a famous grammarian</gloss> regarding grammar is like the sharpness of a razor, so do not busy yourself with the talk of the commoners. Isa ibn Hisham narrated to us, saying:

He then turns upon it the heated stones until the heat meets from both sides. He said: Everyone among us stretched out toward his description, and our saliva flowed, and we smacked our lips and clicked our tongues. We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it." It has quenched its thirst with warm water, and filled itself with the shirt <note>metaphor for rich grazing</note> while it was fresh. Then we present it to you, its skin having covered a white fat upon a tray layered with thin breads like spread-out fine linen or dyed red fabric, and holes have been made in it containing juices and various seasonings. It is placed between you, sweating and smelling of broth, and smelling of broth. Do you desire it, O youths?" We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it." He said: "And your uncle, by God, dances for it." Then some of us leaped toward him with a sword and said: "What..."

I said: "May God grant you health! This is my head; it accompanied me on the road and circumambulated the Ancient House <note>the Kaaba in Mecca</note> with me, and I never doubted that it was mine."

I cursed the servant with every insult and struck him like one pounding gypsum. Then I said to another: "Go and bring me a barber to relieve me of this weight <note>the hair on his head</note>."

# The Nahid Maqama

Isa ibn Hisham narrated to us, saying:
I turned with a group of my companions toward the courtyard of a tent to seek hospitality <note>food for guests</note> from its people. A scorched-looking man <note>likely sunburnt or weather-beaten</note> came out to us and said: "Who are you?"

We said: "Guests who have not tasted an enemy <note>meaning a meal, used ironically</note> for three days."

He said: "Move aside." Then he said: "O youths, what is your opinion of some <term>nahidah</term> <gloss>thick butter or cream mixed with flour</gloss>, trembling like the crown of a bald man's head, in a wide bowl, crowned with a choice date-paste from the sides of a great, sturdy palm tree, a single one of which fills the mouth, for a group of hungry and thirsty men? The tooth vanishes into it, and its pits are like the tongues of birds. They scoop the <term>nahidah</term> with cups of milk milked from old, sturdy, well-fed camels. Do you desire it, O youths?"

We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!"

The old man laughed loudly and said: "And your uncle <note>meaning himself</note> also desires it!"

Then he said: "What is your opinion, O youths, of fine white bread <note>original: <term>darmak</term></note> like pieces of silver ingots, arranged on a leather mat smelling of mimosa? Then a bright, clever, and light youth leaps to it and kneads it without shaking it or breaking it, making it smoother than a soft king. Then he mixes it with milk or a pestle until it is thick, then he turns it and leaves it in the corner of a stone oven until it is leavened without becoming dry. Then he turns to the wood of the <term>ghada</term> tree and lights the fire. When its flame dies down, he prepares its place in the hot ashes, then takes his dough and tosses it after perfecting its color. He spreads it over the embers, then covers it until it swells and rises. He heaps over it hot stones that meet with two glows, until when he covers them in the matching embers with a lid, it cracks open transparently, its crust resembling fine parchment and its redness like the famous red dates of the Hijaz known as <term>Umm al-Jirdan</term> or <term>Adh-dhiq ibn Tab</term>. Then he sprinkles over it something white as snow <note>sugar or fat</note> until it sinks into the crevices of the fat, and the heart of the bread drinks what is upon it. I present it to you and you swallow it in great gulps. Do you desire it, O youths?"

He said: Each of us craned his neck at his description, his mouth watering, smacking his lips and tasting the air. We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!"

He said: The old man laughed and said: "And by God, your uncle does not hate it!" Then he said: "What is your opinion, O youths, of a young she-goat from Najd, high-bred and wild, that has eaten the mimosa blossoms, the Najdi wormwood, the yarrow, and dry herbage? She has sipped the summer water and filled herself with the lush grass until her sides are bursting. She is slaughtered while in prime condition, then hung in a pit-oven until she is cooked through without being scorched or underdone. Then we present her to you, her skin covering white fat, on a table arranged with thin loaves like spread fine linens or dyed cloths. She is placed between you, dripping with fat and oozing with broth. Do you desire it, O youths?"

We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!"

He said: "And by God, your uncle dances for it!"

Then one of us leaped toward him with a sword and said: "What—"

The second said: Rather, I am its owner, for I rubbed its bearer and kneaded his joints. The bathhouse attendant said: Bring me the owner of the head so I may ask him; does this head belong to you or to him? They came to me and said: We have a testimony for you to provide, so take on the burden. I stood and followed them, whether I wanted to or not. The bathhouse attendant said: Man, do not speak anything but the truth, and do not testify to anything but what is right. Tell me, to which of these two does this head belong? I said: May God preserve you, this is my head. It accompanied me on the road, it circled with me around the Ancient House <note>the Kaaba in Mecca</note>, and I have no doubt that it is mine. He said to me: Be quiet, you meddler. Then he leaned toward one of the two disputants and said: You there, how long will this contention with people continue over this head? Console yourself for its minor worth, may God’s curse and the heat of his Hell be upon it; suppose that this head is not [yours], and that we have not seen this billy goat.

Isa ibn Hisham said: I stood from that place feeling ashamed, donned my clothes trembling, and slipped out of the bath in a hurry. I cursed the boy with biting and sucking <note>insults implying base or low-class origin</note>, and I pounded him as one pounds plaster. I said to another: Go and bring me a cupper who will remove this burden from me. He brought me a man of gentle build, pretty of attire, in the image of a doll. I felt at ease with him, and he entered and said: Peace be upon you, and from what land are you? I said: From Qom. He said: May God greet you! From the land of bounty and comfort, the land of the <term>Sunnah</term> <gloss>tradition of the Prophet</gloss> and the community. I attended its mosque during the month of Ramadan when its lamps were lit and the <term>tarawih</term> <gloss>special evening prayers</gloss> were held. We were not aware of anything until the Nile rose and reached those lamps. But God worked for me with a boot I had worn while wet, so its pattern did not show on its sleeve, and the boy returned to his mother after I had prayed the night prayer and the shadow had settled. But how was your pilgrimage? Did you perform its rites as required, and did they cry "Wonderful! Wonderful!"? I looked at the minaret—and how easy war is for the spectators—and I found the <term>harisa</term> <gloss>porridge of meat and wheat</gloss> as it was, and I knew that the matter was by God’s decree and destiny. How long will this impatience last? Today and tomorrow, Saturday and Sunday; I will not lengthen this, what is this gossip? But I wanted you to know that <term>al-Mubarrad</term> <gloss>a famous 9th-century grammarian</gloss> in grammar is like a sharp razor, so do not be busy with the talk of the commoners. If the ability existed before the action, I would have shaved your head, so do you think we should begin?

Isa ibn Hisham said: I remained bewildered by his eloquence and his delirium, and I feared his sitting would be long, so I said: Until tomorrow, God willing. I asked those present about him, and they said: This is a man from the lands of Alexandria; this water did not agree with him, so <term>melancholia</term> <gloss>black bile, associated with madness</gloss> overcame him. He raves all day as you see, though he possesses much virtue. I said: I have heard of him, and his madness weighed heavily upon me, and I began to recite:

### The Nahidiyya Maqama

Isa ibn Hisham narrated to us, saying:
I leaned with a group of my companions toward the courtyard of a tent, seeking hospitality from its people. A small, bustling man came out to us and said: Who are you? We said: Guests who have not tasted any fodder for three days. He cleared his throat, then said: What is your opinion, youths, of a <term>nahida</term> <gloss>a dish of mixed curd and clarified butter</gloss> the size of a bald man’s head, in a spacious platter, crowned with the dates of Khaybar, from the clusters of a heavy-laden tree, one of which fills the mouth? It is among a group of lean, thirsty men whose molars vanish into it, as if its pits were birds’ tongues. They scoop the <term>nahida</term> with bowls that have been milked from goats, aging, thick-fleshed, and rich. Do you desire it, youths? We said: Yes, by God, we desire it. The old man laughed and said: And your uncle also desires it. Then he said: What is your opinion, youths, of fine white flour, like pieces of bullion, piled on a leather spread smelling of <term>qaraz</term> <gloss>acacia bark used for tanning</gloss>? A lithe, skillful, light-footed youth among you springs toward it, and kneads it without shaking or startling it. He clears it without <unclear>soft rubbing</unclear>, then mixes it with clarified butter or whey, a generous mixing. Then he reaches for it, twists it, and leaves it aside in the shadow. Once it ferments without being bound, he prepares branches of <term>ghada</term> <gloss>a desert tree used for firewood</gloss> and lights a fire in them. When the fire subsides, he prepares a bed for his dough, then spreads it out after having thoroughly greased it. Then he rolls it out upon it, covers it, and when it rises and puffs, he casts upon it hot stones that meet both heats. When he covers them on the glowing embers with a cover and it cracks, its crust becomes thin, and its redness is like the redness of the Hijaz date—the one famous as the "Mother of Rats" or the date of the Ibn Tab palm. He pours upon it white fat, cold as ice, until it settles into the crevices of the dough, and the heart of the flour drinks what is upon it of the fat. It is presented to you, and you snatch it like a hungry man or a glutton. Do you desire it, youths? He said: Each of us stretched out toward his description, our saliva welled up, and we smacked our lips and clicked our tongues. We said: Yes, by God, we desire it. He laughed and said: And your uncle, by God, does not despise it. Then he said: What is your opinion, youths, of a young Najdi goat, high-born and wild, that has eaten the <term>baram</term>, the Najdi wormwood, the <term>qaysum</term>, and the withered herbage? It has grazed on the heat and filled itself on <term>qasis</term> <gloss>a type of desert grass</gloss> until its marrow is hidden and its fat is rich. It is slaughtered fresh, then plunged into a cauldron until it is cooked without charring or overdoing. Then it is presented to you, its skin peeled back from white fat, upon a tray arranged with thin bread, as if it were spread-out Egyptian linen or colored <term>Quhi</term> <gloss>a fine fabric</gloss> cloth. It is filled with indentations containing mustard and various spices. It is placed between you, dripping with sweat and flowing with broth. Do you desire it, youths? We said: Yes, by God, we desire it. He said: And your uncle, by God, dances for it. Some of us jumped toward him with a sword and said: What...

The bathhouse keeper said: "O man, speak nothing but the truth, and testify to nothing but the right. Tell me: to which of these two does this head belong?" He said to me: "Silence, you meddler!" Then he turned to one of the two litigants and said: "O you, for how long will you compete with people over this head? Console yourself for its little worth; let it go to the curse of God and the heat of <term>Saqar</term> <gloss>Hellfire</gloss>. Suppose this head did not exist, and that we never saw this goat <note>referring to the protagonist</note>."

Isa ibn Hisham said: I stood up from that place in shame, dressed myself in fear, and slipped out of the bathhouse in haste. I cursed the servant boy with every insult and crushed him like gypsum <note>original: "crushed him as gypsum is crushed"</note>. Then I said to another: "Go and bring me a barber to take this weight <note>his hair</note> off me." He brought me a man of delicate build and handsome appearance, looking like a carved figurine. I felt at ease with him. He entered and said: "Peace be upon you. From which city are you?" I said: "From <term>Qum</term>." He said: "May God grant you life! From the land of blessing and prosperity, and the city of the <term>Sunnah</term> and the Community. I was present in its congregational mosque during the month of Ramadan when the lamps were lit and the <term>Tarawih</term> <gloss>night prayers</gloss> were established. We were suddenly aware of the rising of the Nile <note>an impossibility in Qum, indicating his madness</note>, which reached those lamps. But God saved me because of a boot I had worn while wet, so its embroidery did not stay on its sleeve, and the boy returned to his mother after I prayed the late evening prayer and the shadow leveled out. But how was your pilgrimage? Did you perform its rituals as required, while they cried out 'Marvel! Marvel!'? I looked at the minaret, and how easy is the war to those who merely watch! I found the <term>harisa</term> <gloss>meat and grain stew</gloss> as it was, and I knew that the matter is by the decree and fate of God. For how long shall this annoyance last? Today and tomorrow, Saturday and Sunday... I will not be long, for what is this idle talk? But I wanted you to know that <term>al-Mubarrid</term> <note>a famous 9th-century grammarian</note> in grammar is like the edge of a razor, so do not busy yourself with the talk of the common folk. If the ability existed before the deed, I would have already shaved your head; so do you think we should begin?"

## The Nahdiyya Maqama

Isa ibn Hisham narrated to us, saying:
I turned with a group of my companions to the courtyard of a tent, seeking hospitality from its people. A short, thickset man came out to us and said: "Who are you?" He cleared his throat and said: "What is your opinion, O youths, of a <term>nahida</term> <gloss>butter-and-flour dish</gloss> like a bald man's head, in a wide bowl, crowned with <term>Khaybar</term> dates from the sides of a massive palm tree, a single one of which fills the mouth? Eaten by a group of hungry, thirsty men, in which the tooth disappears, whose pits are like the tongues of birds. They scoop the <term>nahida</term> with cups of milk milked from sturdy, old, fleshy camels. Do you desire it, O youths?" We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!" The old man laughed and said: "And your uncle <note>referring to himself</note> also desires it!" 

Then he said: "What is your opinion, O youths, of fine white bread like pieces of silver ingots, piled on a leather table-mat smelling of mimosa bark? A brisk, clever, light youth leaps toward it and kneads it without shaking or rattling it, then removes it before it is fully handled, then mixes it thoroughly with skimmed milk or diluted milk. When its flame dies down, he prepares its pit, then takes his dough and flattens it after thoroughly coating it. Then he thrusts it upon the embers and covers it. When it has dried and risen, he heaps upon it glowing stones until the two heats meet. When he covers them in the matching pit with a lid, it splits open with cracks, its crust resembling thin wafers, and its redness like the redness of the Hijazi dates known as <term>Umm al-Jirdhan</term> or <term>Adhq Ibn Tab</term>. Then white honey like snow is poured over it until it sinks into the fat, and the heart of the bread drinks what is upon it of honey. It is presented to you, and you swallow it down like the swallowing of a glutton. Do you desire it, O youths?" He said: Every one of us craned his neck at his description, his mouth watered, and he smacked his lips. We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!" Then he said: "What is your opinion, O youths, of a young she-goat from Nejd, high-bred and wild, that has eaten the mimosa blossoms, the Nejdi wormwood, the yarrow, and the dry herbage? Then she is presented to you, her skin stripped away from white fat, on a table arranged with thin loaves like spread fine linen or bleached cloth. She is surrounded by bowls containing mustard sauce and various seasonings. She is placed between you, dripping with fat and flowing with gravy. Do you desire it, O youths?" We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!" He said: "And your uncle, by God, would dance for it!" At this, one of us leaped at him with a sword and said: "What..."

Its companion and follower, and its names are also many. Among them is <term>Soma</term>, because it is auspicious, and the auspicious ones are called <term>Soma-kara</term> <gloss>moon-rayed</gloss>, and the inauspicious are <term>Papa-kara</term> <gloss>evil-rayed</gloss>. Among them is <term>Nisha-isha</term>, meaning "lord of the night," and <term>Nakshatranatha</term>, meaning "lord of the mansions," and <term>Dyisha-ishvara</term>, meaning "lord of the sky," and <term>Shitanshu</term>, meaning "cold-rayed," because its sphere is moist, and in it is the comfort; so when the ray falls upon it, it cools according to its coolness, and it reflects, illuminating the darkness and cooling the night, and extinguishing what the sun had corrupted by burning. For this reason, it is also called <term>Chandra</term>. It is the left eye of <term>Narayana</term>, just as the sun is his right eye. I have deposited in this table the suns of the months and the cause of the discrepancy in them, similar to what preceded in the determination of the earths.

Its companion and follower, and its names are also many. Among them is <term>Soma</term>, because it is auspicious, and the auspicious ones are called <term>Soma-kara</term> <gloss>moon-rayed</gloss>, and the inauspicious are <term>Papa-kara</term> <gloss>evil-rayed</gloss>. Among them is <term>Nisha-isha</term>, meaning "lord of the night," and <term>Nakshatranatha</term>, meaning "lord of the mansions," and <term>Dyisha-ishvara</term>, meaning "lord of the creation/creatures," and <term>Shitanshu</term>, meaning "cold-rayed," because its sphere is moist, and in it is the comfort; so when the ray falls upon it, it cools according to its coolness, and it reflects, illuminating the darkness and cooling the night, and extinguishing what the sun had corrupted by burning. For this reason, it is also called <term>Chandra</term>. It is the left eye of <term>Narayana</term>, just as the sun is his right eye. text:
<meta>continues from previous page: Sam, through his astrologers, has consented to the union of Zal and Rudaba, and a messenger has returned with the joyful news.</meta>

# The Persian Shahnama, Volume One

| | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| When speech reached difficulty and restriction, | You will soon see the key to the happy destination. | The messenger returned from Sam, | With joy and a propitious message. |
| Much was said and heard with Rudaba's nurse, | In the end, she became in agreement. | Lightly, she handed the woman the letter, | The woman went before her and took the letter. |
| She came to Rudaba like the wind, | Happy with this joy and good news. | The fairy-faced one scattered gold upon the woman, | And seated her body upon a golden throne. |
| She granted the rights to that clever nurse, | A handful of garments for the news-bringer, | Also, for the sake of the auspicious Zal, | Whatever might be his equal in kind. |
| She brought forth a head-band <note>a crown or diadem</note>, | Its warp and woof were invisible <note>meaning so dense it appeared solid</note>. | Its entire body was red ruby and pearl, | The gold was hidden by the jewels. |
| A pair of high-value rings, | Shining like Jupiter in the sky. | She sent them to Dastan-e Sam, | With many greetings and a message. |
| The woman left the chamber and reached the doorway, | She looked and saw Sindukht <note>Rudaba's mother</note>, and saw her fortune. | Sindukht's heart became full of thoughts, | She said in a voice: "Where have you come from? Tell me." |
| From fear, the woman became like sandalwood <note>meaning pale or sickly</note>, | She grew afraid and kissed the ground. | Sindukht said to her: "O mischief-seeker, | Hear my words and give a truthful answer." |
| "Open your tongue before me as to where you are from, | You come into the chamber, why do you not look at me?" | "My bright heart has become suspicious of you, | Will you not tell me if you are a friend or a foe?" |
| She said to her: "I am one who seeks a living, | I bring bread through seeking and searching." | "I sold garments and adornments, | They had value among the people." |
| "I go to the houses of the great, | They buy clothes, silver, and gold from me." | "In this chamber, Rudaba requested adornments, | She asked for the same high-value gems." |
| "I brought her a crown decorated with gold, | A casket full of kingly jewels." | Sindukht said to her: "Show them to me, | That I may open the heart of my mind." |
| "I entrusted this and these things to Rudaba, | There was more, now I bring them too." | She said: "Come, let them pass before my eyes, | Let water pour over my anger <note>a metaphor for calming one's temper</note>." |
| "She said: 'I will give it tomorrow, moon-faced one,' | Do not come with excuses, do not seek favor from me." | Since she spoke of her ill-fated talk, | Her heart was prepared for conflict with her. |
| Her fortune did not come to the door of stability, | She was seeing loss and deficiency from her. | When she saw those high-value garments, | And saw the adornment from the hand of Rudaba, |
| She grabbed her by the hair with her hand, | She twisted it and threw her down upon the mountain <note>a metaphor for the floor/ground</note>. | The woman pulled the clever one by the hair, | She brought her and threw her upon her face. |
| Blood was in her eyes from that pain and grief, | She dragged her in humiliation upon the face of the earth. | For a while, she carried her, dragging her hair, | She threw her upon the dirt as if senseless. |
| She threw her down and tied her there, | She beat her feet and struck her hands. | From there, she entered the palace, sorrowful, | She remained with pain, sorrow, and grief. |
| She locked the door of the palace upon herself, | From the thought that she had become drunk with action <note>acting irrationally</note>. | She commanded that her daughter come before her, | She struck her hands upon her own cheeks. |
| She washed her two fresh narcissus eyes <note>poetic metaphor for eyes</note>, | Two flowers, until the flowers became wilted. | She said to Rudaba: "O high-valued moon, | Why did you choose a pit over the throne?" |
| "What is left of good-keeping in the world, | That I have not shown you, openly and secretly?" | "What kind of oppressor have you taken, O moon-faced one? | Tell all your secrets to your mother." |
| "Who is this woman who comes before you? | Why does she come to you?" | "Whatever words this man and woman have crafted, | Whether it be the beautiful head-band or the rings..." |
| "From my great treasury and the <term>Tazian</term> <gloss>Arabian</gloss> goods, | Much profit and loss remained." | "With this name, you want to give justice to the wind <note>to waste or destroy</note>, | Since I was born, a daughter like you was never born." |
| Rudaba saw the earth and the back of her feet <note>looking down in shame</note>, | She remained in place from her mother's shame. | Water of love poured from her eyes, | She decorated her face with the blood of her two narcissus eyes. |
| She said to her mother: "O wise one, | There was an army upon my life." | "If my mother had not given birth to me at all, | Good and bad words would not have gone from me." |
| "The commander Dastan has remained in Kabul, | He has planted such love in my heart." | "The world became so tight upon my heart, | That I became tearful, openly and secretly." |
| "I do not want to be alive without his face, | My life is only in the scent of him." | "Since he was with me, we sat together, | By oath, we took each other's hand in hand." |
| "Nothing went to anything else but him, | Fire was hidden between me and him." | "The messenger was sent to great Sam, | The messenger brought an answer to the great Zal." |
| For a time, she was twisted and was pained, | She spoke and listened to words at the bedside. | In the end, she became in agreement, | She asked the wise <term>Mobed</term> <gloss>Zoroastrian priest/sage</gloss> of old. |

<summary>Upon discovering the secret correspondence between Rudaba and Zal through her nurse, Sindukht is initially furious and physically chastises the nurse. However, Rudaba confesses her deep love for Zal, leading a reluctant Sindukht to eventually reconcile with the situation and seek the counsel of a Mobed.</summary>
<keywords>Rudaba, Sindukht, Zal, Dastan, Secret, Love, Mother, Mobed, Rebellion</keywords>

| "Who is this woman who comes before you? | Why does she come to you?" | "Whatever words this man and woman have crafted, | Whether it be the beautiful head-band or the rings..." |
| "From my great treasury and the <term>Tazian</term> <gloss>Arabian</gloss> goods, | Much profit and loss remained." | "With this name, you want to give justice to the wind <note>to waste or destroy</note>, | Since I was born, a daughter like you was never born." |
| Rudaba saw the earth and the back of her feet <note>looking down in shame</note>, | She remained in place from her mother's shame. | Water of love poured from her eyes, | She decorated her face with the blood of her two narcissus eyes. |
| She said to her mother: "O wise one, | There was an army upon my life." | "If my mother had not given birth to me at all, | Good and bad words would not have gone from me." |
| "The commander Dastan has remained in Kabul, | He has planted such love in my heart." | "The world became so tight upon my heart, | That I became tearful, openly and secretly." |
| "I do not want to be alive without his face, | My life is only in the scent of him." | "Since he was with me, we sat together, | By oath, we took each other's hand in hand." |
| "Nothing went to anything else but him, | Fire was hidden between me and him." | "The messenger was sent to great Sam, | The messenger brought an answer to the great Zal." |
| For a time, she was twisted and was pained, | She spoke and listened to words at the bedside. | In the end, she became in agreement, | She asked the wise <term>Mobed</term> <gloss>Zoroastrian priest/sage</gloss> of old. |

<summary>Upon discovering the secret correspondence between Rudaba and Zal through her nurse, Sindukht is initially furious and physically chastises the nurse. However, Rudaba confesses her deep love for Zal, leading a reluctant Sindukht to eventually reconcile with the situation and seek the counsel of a Mobed.</summary>

| When the talk reached difficulty and hardship, | You will soon see <term>Farrokh-Bish</term> <gloss>a name meaning "Happy-Seeker," referring here to the messenger</gloss> as the key. | The messenger returned from the presence of Sam, | With happiness and a fortunate message. |
| He spoke much and listened, and to Rudaba <note>literally: "the bread of Rudaba"</note>, | Finally, he became in agreement with the story. | Quickly he entrusted the answer to the letter to the woman; | The woman left his presence and carried the letter. |
| She came to Rudaba like the wind, | With this joy and happy with good tidings. | The fairy-faced one <note>Rudaba</note> scattered silver coins over the woman; | She seated her upon a golden-patterned chair. |
| Due to the right of that resourceful nurse, | She gave a suit of clothes to the bringer of good news. | Also likewise for the sake of the blessed Zal, | From things that would be his equal. |
| She brought forward a headband, | Where the warp and woof were invisible within it. | Its entire body was of red ruby and pearl; | The gold was all hidden by the gems. |
| A precious pair of rings, | Shining like the planet Jupiter in the heavens. | She sent them to Dastan son of Sam; | She gave many greetings and messages with them. |
| The woman left the chamber and reached the hallway; | <term>Sindukht</term> <gloss>Rudaba's mother</gloss> looked and saw her. | The soul of Sindukht became anxious because of her; | She said with a loud voice: "From where? Tell me who you are!" |
| From fear of her, the woman became like <term>sandarūs</term> <gloss>yellow resin; pale with fear</gloss>; | She was afraid and kissed the ground. | Sindukht said to her: "O seeker of mischief, | Listen to the words and give a truthful answer." |
| "Hold your tongue before me; from where | Do you enter the chamber and not look at me?" | "My bright heart has become suspicious of you; | You will not tell me until it is the string or the bow." <note>A metaphor for the truth of the matter</note> |
| She said to her: "I am a seeker of solutions; | I bring forth my bread through searching." | "The price of clothes and ornaments | I sold; people were my source of capital." |
| "I go to the houses of the great; | They buy clothes from me with silver and heavy price." | "In this chamber, Rudaba requested ornaments; | She wanted those same precious gems." |
| "I brought her a gold-patterned crown, | A small box full of kingly gems." | Sindukht said to her: "I will see; | I will open the heart of the chest and the thought." |
| "I entrusted it to Rudaba," she said, "and things | Were many; now I will bring them also." | She said: "Come, let it pass before my eyes, | Throw some water upon this anger of mine." |
| She said: "The moon-faced one will give silver tomorrow; | Do not seek an excuse to come to me." | Thus, from the ill-fortune of her speech, | She prepared her heart for battle with her. |
| She did not come out of the door of the house; | She saw in her change and decline. | When she saw those precious clothes, | And saw the ornaments from Rudaba's hand. |
| She became enraged and took her hair in her hand; | She twisted it and threw her down to the ground. | She pulled the resourceful woman by the hair; | She brought her and cast her down on her face. |
| Blood was in her eyes from that pain and grief; | In humiliation, she dragged her across the ground. | For a time, she kept dragging her by the hair; | She threw her on the dust like those who are unconscious. |
| She threw her there and bound her; | She kept stamping her feet and striking with her hands. | And from there she entered the palace, sullen; | She remained with pain and with sorrow and grief. |
| She closed the door of the palace upon herself; | From the thought, she became like one intoxicated. | She commanded that her daughter come forward; | She kept striking her own hand against her cheek. |
| Two roses with two tearful narcissi <note>metaphor for eyes weeping upon cheeks</note>, | She kept washing until the roses became colorless. | She said to Rudaba: "O precious moon, | Why did you choose the pit over the throne?" |
| "What remained of goodness in the world | That I did not show you openly and secretly?" | "O moon-faced one, what did you have as an oppressor? | Tell all the secrets to your own mother." |
| "Who is this woman who comes to you? | For what purpose does she come to you?" | "Whatever words this man and woman have made, | That there is a beautiful headband and ring." |
| "From my great treasure and the Arabs, | Much profit and loss remains." | "With this bad name, you will give the seeker to the wind; | As I have born a daughter, no one ever bore." |
| Rudaba looked at the ground and the back of her feet; | She remained in place out of shame for her mother. | The water of love poured from her eyes; | She adorned her face with the blood of two narcissi. |
| She said to her mother: "O wise one, | An army is upon my soul." | "If my mother had not given birth to me from the root, | No words of good and evil would have gone from me." |
| "The commander Dastan stayed in Kabul; | Thus his love sat upon my heart." | "The world became so narrow for my heart, | That I became weeping openly and secretly." |
| "I do not wish to be alive without his face; | My life is also in his fragrance." | "By that which he had a sitting with me, | We took his hand in hand with a covenant." |
| "Nothing else happened except for him; | Fire was hidden between me and him." | "A messenger was sent to the great Sam; | The response was sent to the great Zal." |
| "For a time he turned and was suffering; | He spoke and heard the words of the pillow." | "Finally he became in agreement; | He asked of the ancient <term>Mobad</term> <gloss>Zoroastrian priest</gloss>." |

<summary>The messenger returns to Rudaba with Zal's positive response. Sindukht discovers the secret affair, interrogates and beats the messenger, and confronts Rudaba, who tearfully confesses her love for Zal and reveals that Sam has consented to the union.</summary>

| When speech reaches difficulty and constriction, | You will soon see the key to its openness. | The messenger returned from Sam, | With joy and a auspicious message. |
| He spoke much and heard much, and exchanged stories; | In the end, he became in agreement. | Lightly, he handed the letter to the woman, | The woman went before him and took the letter. |
| She came to Rudaba like the wind, | And gave her the good news of this happiness. | The fairy-faced one scattered silver upon the woman, | And seated her body upon a throne of gold. |
| She gave to that clever nurse, | A garment from off her own body, as a reward for the news. | And also for the auspicious Zal, | Whatever might be his equal in value. |
| She brought forward a head-band <term>shara</term> <gloss>ornamental headpiece</gloss>, | The warp and woof of which were hidden from view. | Its entire surface was of red ruby and gold, | The gold itself was hidden by the jewels. |
| A pair of valuable rings, | Shining like Jupiter in the sky. | She sent them to Dastan <note>Zal</note>, son of Sam, | With many greetings and messages. |
| The woman left the chamber and reached the court, | Sindukht looked and saw her luck. | The soul of Sindukht became full of thought because of her, | She said aloud, "Tell me, where are you from?" |
| The woman became like <term>sandarous</term> <gloss>amber/pale resin</gloss> from her fear, | She grew afraid and kissed the face of the earth. | Sindukht said to her, "O seeker of sedition, | Hear my words and give me the answer." |
| "Time after time you pass before me, | You enter the chamber but do not look at me." | "My bright heart has become suspicious of you, | Will you not tell me if you are a friend or a foe?" |
| She said to her, "I am a seeker of solutions, | I bring bread <note>a livelihood</note> in several ways." | "From the price of clothes and ornaments, | I sell things and have resources from the people." |
| "I go to the houses of the great ones, | They buy clothes and jewels from me." | "In this chamber, Rudaba requested ornaments, | And requested those precious jewels." |
| "I brought her a gold-embroidered crown, | And a casket full of royal jewels." | Sindukht said to her, "Show me, | Let us open the heart closed by thought." |
| "I entrusted these two things to Rudaba, | She wanted more, so now I will bring it for her." | "She said, 'Leave the price in my sight, | Put some water <note>a bribe or payment</note> in my eyes for this anger of mine.'" |
| "She said, 'Tomorrow I will give the silver, O moon-faced one, | Do not seek the price from me until I obtain it.'" | She knew her speech was crooked, | She prepared her heart for a fight with her. |
| She came and searched her arms and sleeves, | She saw crookedness and flaws in her. | When she saw those precious garments, | And saw the ornaments from Rudaba's hand, |
| She grew angry and grabbed her hair with her hand, | She twisted it and threw her face down. | The woman grabbed the clever messenger by the hair, | She brought her and threw her down on her face. |
| She became pained in her anger at that woman, | She dragged her in humiliation upon the face of the earth. | For a time she dragged her by her hair, | She threw her on the dust like one unconscious. |
| She threw her down and bound her there, | She beat her with her feet and struck her with her hands. | And from there she entered the palace, distressed, | She remained with pain, sorrow, and grief. |
| In the palace, she locked the door upon herself, | From the thought that she had acted like one intoxicated. | She ordered her daughter to come before her, | She kept striking her hands upon her own cheeks. |
| Her two water-bright narcissus-eyes, <note>a metaphor for eyes</note> | She washed until the flowers became brilliant. | She said to Rudaba, "O precious moon, | Why have you chosen a pit over a throne?" |
| "What is left of being well-cared for in the world, | That I have not shown you, openly and secretly?" | "Why have you become a transgressor, O moon-faced one? | Tell all your secrets before your mother." |
| "From whom does this woman come to you, | And why does she come to you?" | "How is the story? Who is this man? | Who is worthy of the head-band and the ring?" |
| "From the great treasure of the crown of the Arabs, | Much gain and loss has remained with us." | "With this name, do you wish to give your honor to the wind? | Since I have given birth to a daughter, may she never be ruined." |
| Rudaba saw the earth and the back of her feet, | She remained in her place from her mother's shame. | Water of love flowed from her eyes, | She adorned her face with the blood of her two narcissus-eyes. |
| She said to her mother, "O wise one, | This love has hunted my soul." | "If my mother had not given birth to me at all, | Neither good nor bad words would have come from me." |
| "The commander Dastan <note>Zal</note> remained in Kabul, | Such love for him has set me on fire." | "The world became so narrow for my heart, | That I have become weeping, openly and secretly." |
| "I do not wish to be alive without his face, | The world is not worth one hair of his to me." | "In the place where he saw me and sat with me, | We took each other's hands in a pledge." |
| "Nothing else happened besides the meeting, | Between me and him, there was only the hot fire." | "The messenger was sent to great Sam, | The messenger returned with an answer for the great Zal." |
| "For a time he was distressed and pained, | He spoke and heard the necessary words." | "In the end, he became in agreement, | He asked the ancient <term>mobed</term> <gloss>Zoroastrian priest/wise man</gloss>." |

<summary>Sindukht discovers the secret communication between Rudaba and Zal through the messenger and, in a fit of rage, confronts her daughter. Rudaba confesses her deep, consuming love for Zal, revealing their secret meetings and the recent message from Sam.</summary>

# The Persian Shahnama, Volume One
## Page 91

| | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| When speech reached a point of hardship and narrowness, | You will soon see the key to its expansion. | The messenger returned from before Sam, | With happiness and a blessed message. |
| He spoke much, heard much, and told stories, | In the end, he <note>Sam</note> became in agreement <note>original: "ham-dastan"</note>. | Quickly he <note>Zal</note> gave the answer of the letter to the woman, | The woman left his presence and carried the letter. |
| She came to Rudaba like the wind, | She gave her the glad tidings of this joy. | The fairy-faced one <note>Rudaba</note> showered the woman with silver coins <note>term: "dirham"</note>, | And seated her upon a gold-imprinted throne. |
| She gave to that resourceful nurse, | A suit of clothes for being the bearer of glad tidings. | Likewise, for the sake of the fortunate Zal, | From things that would be his equal <note>meaning gifts of equal status</note>. |
| She brought forth a fine silken head-wrap <note>term: "shara"</note>, | Its warp and woof were invisible <note>due to the fineness of the weave</note>. | Its entire form was red ruby and gold, | The gold was all hidden by the jewels. |
| A pair of precious rings, | Shining like Jupiter in the sky. | She sent them to Dastan son of Sam, | Along with many blessings and a message. |
| The woman left the chamber and reached the palace, | Sindukht looked and saw her. | Sindukht's soul became full of thought because of her, | She said with a loud voice: "Tell me, where are you from?" |
| The woman became like sandarac <note>pale yellow</note> from fear of her, | She grew afraid and kissed the ground. | Sindukht said to her: "O seeker of mischief, | Listen to my words and give the answer. |
| From time to time you pass before me, | You enter the chamber and do not look at me. | My bright heart has become suspicious of you, | You do not tell me whether you are the bow or the string <note>a metaphor for being involved in a plot</note>." |
| She said to her: "I am a seeker of solutions, | I bring forth bread from several ways. | I sell the price of clothes and ornaments, | My capital comes from the people. |
| I go toward the houses of the great ones, | They buy clothes and also jewels from me. | In this chamber, Rudaba requested ornaments, | She requested those same precious jewels. |
| I brought her a gold-adorned crown, | And a casket full of kingly gems." | Sindukht said to her: "Show them to me, | To open my heart which is bound by thought. |
| If I delivered those two things to Rudaba," she said, | "She wanted more, and now I bring those as well." | She said: "Leave the price to my eyes, | Cast some water upon this anger of mine <note>meaning, show me the goods to calm me</note>." |
| She <note>the nurse</note> said: "Tomorrow that moon-faced one will give the money, | Do not seek the price from me until I receive it." | She <note>Sindukht</note> knew her words were crooked, | She prepared her heart for a struggle with her. |
| She came and searched her breast and sleeves, | She saw crookedness and deficiency in her. | When she saw those precious clothes, | And also the ornaments from Rudaba's hand. |
| In a rage, she took her hair in her hand, | She twisted it and threw her down upon her face. | The resourceful woman was pulled by her hair, | She brought her down and cast her on her face. |
| She became grieved by that woman in her anger, | She dragged her with contempt upon the face of the earth. | For a time she kept dragging her by the hair, | She threw her upon the dust like those who are unconscious. |
| She threw her down and bound her there, | She stamped her feet and struck with her hands. | From there she entered the palace dejectedly, | She remained in pain, sorrow, and grief. |
| She fastened the door of the palace upon herself, | She was like one drunk from the weight of her thoughts. | She commanded that her daughter come forward, | She was striking her own cheeks with her hands. |
| The two roses <note>cheeks</note> with the two tearful narcissi <note>eyes</note>, | She washed until the roses became glowing. | She said to Rudaba: "O precious moon, | Why did you choose the pit over the throne? |
| What remained of goodness in the world, | That I did not show you, openly and secretly? | Why have you become an oppressor, O moon-faced one? | Tell all your secrets before your mother. |
| From whom does this woman come, | And for what purpose does she come to you? | What is the nature of this talk? Who is this man, | For whom the head-wrap and ring are suitable? |
| From the great treasury, the crown of the Arabs <note>referring to the lineage of Zahhak</note>, | Much profit and loss has remained to us. | With this bad name, you will give it all to the wind, | May no daughter ever be born like the one I bore!" |
| Rudaba looked at the ground and the back of her feet, | She remained in her place out of shame before her mother. | The water of love poured from her eyes, | She adorned her face with the blood of two narcissi <note>bloody tears</note>. |
| She said to her mother: "O wise one, | Love is hunting my soul. | If my mother had not given birth to me from the root, | No words of good or evil would have gone from me. |
| The commander Dastan stayed in Kabul, | His love has placed me upon the fire. | The world became so narrow for my heart, | That I wept openly and secretly. |
| I do not wish to be alive without his face, | The world is not worth a single hair of his. | Since he saw me and sat with me, | We took each other's hands in a covenant. |
| Nothing else happened except for seeing, | Though between me and him the fire burned hot. | A messenger was sent to the great Sam, | And a reply was sent to the great Zal. |
| For a time he hesitated and was troubled, | He said and heard the necessary words. | In the end, he became in agreement, | And he asked the ancient priest <note>term: "mobed"</note>." |

<meta>continues from previous page</meta> as it is written: You shall not work the firstling of your ox <note>Deuteronomy 15:19</note>. 484. Not to shear the firstling, and the same applies to other consecrated animals, as it is said: You shall not shear the firstling of your sheep <note>Deuteronomy 15:19</note>. 485. Not to eat leaven on the fourteenth of Nisan after midday, as it is said: You shall not eat leavened bread with it <note>Deuteronomy 16:3</note>, meaning during the time of the Passover sacrifice, whose time is after midday. 486. Not to leave over the festive offering of the fourteenth until the third day, as it is said: Neither shall any of the meat remain <note>Deuteronomy 16:4</note>. 487. Not to offer the Passover sacrifice on a private altar, as it is said: You may not sacrifice the Passover offering within any of your gates <note>Deuteronomy 16:5</note>. 488. The commandment of rejoicing on the festivals, as it is said: And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God <note>Deuteronomy 16:11</note>. 489. The commandment of appearing <note>Pilgrimage</note>, that every male appear three times a year. 490. That we should not ascend to the Chosen House <note>The Temple</note> on a festival without a sacrifice, as it is said: And they shall not appear before the Lord empty-handed <note>Deuteronomy 16:16</note>.

### **Torah** Or <gloss>Torah Light</gloss>. These commandments mentioned in this portion are divided into three parts, which are the three pillars upon which the world stands: Torah, Divine Service, and Deeds of Loving-kindness. Torah refers to the prohibitions "do not add" and "do not subtract," which indicate the perfection of the Torah. This is as the philosophers say: a thing that is complete in the ultimate perfection cannot be said to be lacking or redundant. For if it were lacking, it would not be complete; and if it could accept an addition, it follows that it was not previously perfect. Therefore, the definition of "perfect" is that which has neither deficiency nor excess. It is known that the Torah is dependent upon His Great Name, which is <term>Yod-He-Vav-He</term> <gloss>The Tetragrammaton</gloss>, as in the verse "The Torah of the Lord <note>Y-H-V-H</note> is perfect" <note>Psalm 19:8</note>, as I have elaborated in my work on Tractate Shevuot, chapter "Torah Or." And as stated in the Zohar regarding the verse "This is My name and this is My memorial" <note>Exodus 3:15</note>: The letters <term>Yod-He</term> with "My name" <note>Sh-M-Y</note> equals 365 <note>the number of negative commandments</note>. The letters <term>Vav-He</term> with "My memorial" <note>Z-Ch-R-Y</note> equals 248 <note>the number of positive commandments</note>. And it is written: "I am the first and I am the last" <note>Isaiah 44:6</note>; He is the absolute Perfection, containing no subtraction or addition. Regarding this comes the warning: "You shall not do so to the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 12:4</note>, which is a warning against erasing the Name or breaking a stone from the Temple. Behold, the letters of the Name are like the house in which He, may He be blessed, dwells; so too the Sanctuary. And it is written: "I am the Lord, that is My name" <note>Isaiah 42:8</note>; the letters are like the enclosure of a house, and His Name, may He be blessed, is the soul within them. One who destroys His house, as it were, destroys Him. This is the secret of "You shall not do so to the Lord your God." Service <gloss>Avodah</gloss> refers to the majority of the commandments mentioned in this portion. The command came for there to be a fixed place, in the Chosen House, and the Torah gave a reason: "To His habitation shall you seek, and there you shall come" <note>Deuteronomy 12:5</note>. "To His habitation" alludes to the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss>, which is the palace of the Name <term>Y-H-V-H</term>. As it is written: "Do not fear, for she shall dwell within me," for in the Temple, the Glory <note>Kavod/Tiferet</note> unites with His people. This is "to put His name there," as the Aramaic translation <note>Targum</note> renders it: "to cause His Presence to dwell." Around the place of holiness, "the wicked walk on every side" <note>Psalm 12:9</note>, which are the <term>Kelipot</term> <gloss>husks/forces of impurity</gloss>. Therefore: "Take heed to yourself lest you offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see" <note>Deuteronomy 12:13</note>.

### **Sometimes** sparks of holiness spread outward, and it is a commandment to return them and bring them inward. This is the secret of the commandment to bring the firstlings and sacrifices from outside the city to the Chosen House. Then the branch returns to its root, and it is written of them: "There you shall offer" <note>Deuteronomy 12:14</note>, meaning there they shall have an elevation <note>aliyah</note> and not outside. Since the holiness is in the Chosen House, which is in the Holy Land, we were commanded to "turn from evil" by destroying all the places where the nations worshipped. One must uproot and eradicate them, and this was commanded specifically in the Holy Land. The secret of this alludes to the ten nations whose power is not from idols. The matter is that the nations in the Land of Israel, being under the direct rule of the Honorable Name, worship God through "cutting the plantings" <note>heresy/separation of divine attributes</note>, which is actual idolatry. However, outside the Land, they are under the rule of external forces. Just as there is a great prohibition against breaking a single stone of holiness, conversely, it is a great commandment to destroy and eliminate a "Subverted City" <note>Ir HaNidachat</note> and never to rebuild it, for its place is impure. So too with the enticer <note>Mesit</note> and subverter, one must uproot and eradicate him, for he comes from the impurity of the ancient serpent who was an enticer. The Holy One, blessed be He, immediately said "Cursed is the serpent" <note>Genesis 3:14</note>; therefore, the powers of <term>Samael</term> <note>the angel of evil</note> are never pardoned. The command came not to love him nor to listen to him, as is said of the serpent: "And I will put enmity between you and the woman" <note>Genesis 3:15</note>. A false prophet is also like an enticer. Let us return to the matter: the root of holiness is the Chosen House and Jerusalem. This is the reason for the first-fruits <term>Bikkurim</term>, that the priests have no permission to eat them until they are placed in the Chosen House. For the first-fruits, which are the "beginning," indicate great holiness, as I have written elsewhere. Therefore, they must go to the holy place, and from there they take their wisdom, for they are holy to God, and they shall eat in Jerusalem. The secret of "minor" sacrifices and the Second Tithe is that their consumption is in Jerusalem. This is the blessing of "grain, wine, and oil," which are the primary ancestors of all sustenance. It is forbidden to eat minor sacrifices until after the sprinkling of their blood, for the blood is the soul <note>nefesh</note>, and afterward comes the permission to enjoy. Know that just as the service of sacrifice is an offering to God, so too is the worshiper; for the essence of the service is that a person offers himself, in the secret of "When a man <note>Adam</note> among you brings an offering" <note>Leviticus 1:2</note>. The burnt offering is entirely consumed because it comes to atone for thoughts of the heart, which are spiritual; it is offered all night so that the serpent cannot hinder it. Minor sacrifices represent the peace of the soul and the body.

### **The secret** of the firstborn is the secret of Israel, who are called holy, as it is written: "My firstborn son, Israel" <note>Exodus 4:22</note>. He has compassion on them and guards them, and they are called "the sheep of My pasture." Therefore, the firstling is eaten only by the priests. The secret of eating sacrifices corresponds to those with blemishes. For Israel is holy and Israel is called "Man" <note>Adam</note>, which is a holy entity; afterward, a blemish fell upon him after he sinned and was clothed in "garments of skin," but he has a redemption in the secret of "I give a man in your stead." This was the secret of the <term>Azazel</term> <gloss>scapegoat</gloss>, "and he shall bear their iniquities" <note>Leviticus 16:22</note>. Our Sages of blessed memory explained: "their iniquities" <note>avonotam</note> refers to the "iniquities of the perfect ones" <note>avonot tam</note> which rest upon his head and his people. But we were commanded not to cause a blemish in a consecrated animal in order to eat them. For if one willfully casts a blemish in holy things, he also violates the prohibition of labor and shearing with holy things, for even the "broken tablets" <note>of the Ten Commandments</note> remain holy.

### **The general principle** of the matter: Divine Service is the sacrifice; however, the "inner sacrifice" is the person himself. Thus his soul is called to the Altar on High after his death, and Michael is the High Priest. This is the secret, for man was made in the image of God. Therefore, the warning was given to be careful during his life regarding damages to souls, not to kill a person except after thorough inquiry and investigation. Then he is "dead by the hand of Heaven," in the secret of "He is the Witness, He is the Judge," for the Lord, blessed be He, is a True Witness and a True Judge. So too the Sanhedrin must be; just as they are judges of truth, they must have witnesses of truth. I mean they must have clear verification of the truth of the witnesses through inquiry and investigation; then their judgment is as the judgment of Heaven, and "precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death" <note>of His pious ones</note>.

### **And since** death is precious in the eyes of the Lord—for Israel is holy from the side of their soul, so that after their death the souls attach themselves above—therefore the command came: "You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness" etc., "for you are children to the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 14:1-2</note>. This is not the case with the other nations; cutting and baldness are their customs, for it is appropriate for them since upon their death they go to destruction and have no portion in this world or the world to come. We, however, are children of God; when we depart from this world, which is a temporary dwelling, we instead have a permanent residence above with our Father in Heaven. Therefore, it is forbidden to mourn excessively or perform these acts.

### **We return** to the matter: the person who worships is himself the sacrifice, as it is written "When a man <note>Adam</note> among you brings an offering." There is a further secret in this. Even when a person descends below, in the secret of <term>Gilgul</term> <gloss>reincarnation</gloss>, "Man and beast You save, O Lord" <note>Psalm 36:7</note>. Therefore, even regarding the eating of non-sacred meat <note>basar ta'avah</note>, we were commanded regarding ritual slaughter <term>Shechitah</term> with great care to have no nick in the blade. For if so, it becomes a "carcass" <term>nevelah</term>, and a "vile thing is done in Israel." For who knows what reincarnation might be within it? "Love your fellow as yourself" <note>Leviticus 19:18</note>—choose for him a "beautiful death," meaning a slaughter without a nick. If the animal dies on its own, the power of impurity spreads and takes hold of it. But when one slaughters it properly, and the animal or pure bird contains a spark of holiness, then its soul departs in purity.

### **One who eats** a limb from a living animal is like one who eats the flesh of <unclear>...</unclear> when a soul is reincarnated there. This is the secret of "You shall not eat the soul with the flesh" <note>Deuteronomy 12:23</note>. So too the prohibition of forbidden foods and the signs of pure cattle, beasts, and birds; all indicate the spark spread within them, whether it is from the "Side of Impurity" <term>Sitra Achra</term> or the "Side of Holiness." I have elaborated on this in Parashat Shemini. When Israel conducts themselves with holiness, it is written of them: "And they shall make for Me a sanctuary and I will dwell within them" <note>Exodus 25:8</note>. For they themselves are the Tabernacle, as man is divided into three parts: the head corresponds to the Holy of Holies; the heart to the Holy place; and from the belly downward to the Courtyard of the Sanctuary, as I elaborated in Parashat Terumah. When one eats foods from the side of holiness, they are like sacrifices offered upon the Altar. Regarding this, our Sages of blessed memory said: "Now a man's table atones for him," as I have elaborated in its place.

### **Regarding** the matter of the Festival commandments and their sacrifices, I have written about each in its specific place. The command came to rejoice on the festivals, to ascend for the pilgrimage, and "three times a year shall all your males appear." One should not say that just as he comes to see, so he comes to be seen; therefore, if he wishes to be seen in the Temple where the Glory dwells, he must "turn from evil and do good" and be a faithful servant to his Creator. For without this, it is forbidden to see the face of a wicked person; how then would he wish to appear before Him, may He be blessed, bringing a burnt offering of appearance? Then he himself becomes a sacrifice through the sacrifice he offers. And it says "three times a year he shall appear"—this refers to Isaac, who was a "perfect burnt offering."

Not to shear the firstling, and the same applies to other consecrated animals, as it is said: You shall not shear the firstling of your sheep <note>Deuteronomy 15:19</note>. 485. Not to eat leaven on the fourteenth of Nisan after midday, as it is said: You shall not eat leavened bread with it <note>Deuteronomy 16:3</note>, meaning during the time of the Passover sacrifice, whose time is after midday. 486. Not to leave over the festive offering of the fourteenth until the third day, as it is said: Neither shall any of the meat remain <note>Deuteronomy 16:4</note>. 487. Not to offer the Passover sacrifice on a private altar, as it is said: You may not sacrifice the Passover offering within any of your gates <note>Deuteronomy 16:5</note>. 488. The commandment of rejoicing on the festivals, as it is said: And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God <note>Deuteronomy 16:11</note>. 489. The commandment of appearing <note>Pilgrimage</note>, that every male appear three times a year. 490. That we should not ascend to the Chosen House <note>The Temple</note> on a festival without a sacrifice, as it is said: And they shall not appear before the Lord empty-handed <note>Deuteronomy 16:16</note>.

### **Torah** Or <gloss>Torah Light</gloss>. These commandments mentioned in this portion are divided into three parts, which are the three pillars upon which the world stands: Torah, Divine Service, and Deeds of Loving-kindness. Torah refers to the prohibitions "do not add" and "do not subtract," which indicate the perfection of the Torah. This is as the philosophers say: a thing that is complete in the ultimate perfection cannot be said to be lacking or redundant. For if it were lacking, it would be complete; and if it could accept an addition, it follows that it was not previously perfect. Therefore, the definition of "perfect" is that which has neither deficiency nor excess. It is known that the Torah is dependent upon His Great Name, which is <term>Yod-He-Vav-He</term> <gloss>The Tetragrammaton</gloss>, as in the verse "The Torah of the Lord <note>Y-H-V-H</note> is perfect" <note>Psalm 19:8</note>, as I have elaborated in my work on Tractate Shevuot, chapter "Torah Or." And as stated in the Zohar regarding the verse "This is My name and this is My memorial" <note>Exodus 3:15</note>: The letters <term>Yod-He</term> with "My name" <note>Sh-M-Y</note> equals 365 <note>the number of negative commandments</note>. The letters <term>Vav-He</term> with "My memorial" <note>Z-Ch-R-Y</note> equals 248 <note>the number of positive commandments</note>. And it is written: "I am the first and I am the last" <note>Isaiah 44:6</note>; He is the absolute Perfection, containing no subtraction or addition. Regarding this comes the warning: "You shall not do so to the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 12:4</note>, which is a warning against erasing the Name or breaking a stone from the Temple. Behold, the letters of the Name are like the house in which He, may He be blessed, dwells; so too the Sanctuary. And it is written: "I am the Lord, that is My name" <note>Isaiah 42:8</note>; the letters are like the enclosure of a house, and His Name, may He be blessed, is the soul within them. One who destroys His house, as it were, destroys Him. This is the secret of "You shall not do so to the Lord your God." Service <gloss>Avodah</gloss> refers to the majority of the commandments mentioned in this portion. The command came for there to be a fixed place, in the Chosen House, and the Torah gave a reason: "To His habitation shall you seek, and there you shall come" <note>Deuteronomy 12:5</note>. "To His habitation" alludes to the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss>, which is the palace of the Name <term>Y-H-V-H</term>. As it is written: "Do not fear, for she shall dwell within me," for in the Temple, the Glory <note>Kavod/Tiferet</note> unites with His people. This is "to put His name there," as the Aramaic translation <note>Targum</note> renders it: "to cause His Presence to dwell." Around the place of holiness, "the wicked walk on every side" <note>Psalm 12:9</note>, which are the <term>Kelipot</term> <gloss>husks/forces of impurity</gloss>. Therefore: "Take heed to yourself lest you offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see" <note>Deuteronomy 12:13</note>.

### **Sometimes** sparks of holiness spread outward, and it is a commandment to return them and bring them inward. This is the secret of the commandment to bring the firstlings and sacrifices from outside the city to the Chosen House. Then the branch returns to its root, and it is written of them: "There you shall offer" <note>Deuteronomy 12:14</note>, meaning there they shall have an elevation <note>aliyah</note> and not outside. Since the holiness is in the Chosen House, which is in the Holy Land, we were commanded to "turn from evil" by destroying all the places where the nations worshipped. One must uproot and eradicate them, and this was commanded specifically in the Holy Land. The secret of this alludes to the ten nations whose power is not from idols. The matter is that the nations in the Land of Israel, being under the direct rule of the Honorable Name, worship God through "cutting the plantings" <note>heresy/separation of divine attributes</note>, which is actual idolatry. However, outside the Land, they are under the rule of external forces. Just as there is a great prohibition against breaking a single stone of holiness, conversely, it is a great commandment to destroy and eliminate a "Subverted City" <note>Ir HaNidachat</note> and never to rebuild it, for its place is impure. So too with the enticer <note>Mesit</note> and subverter, one must uproot and eradicate him, for he comes from the impurity of the ancient serpent who was an enticer. The Holy One, blessed be He, immediately said "Cursed is the serpent" <note>Genesis 3:14</note>; therefore, the powers of <term>Samael</term> <note>the angel of evil</note> are never pardoned. The command came not to love him nor to listen to him, as is said of the serpent: "And I will put enmity between you and the woman" <note>Genesis 3:15</note>. A false prophet is also like an enticer. Let us return to the matter: the root of holiness is the Chosen House and Jerusalem. This is the reason for the first-fruits <term>Bikkurim</term>, that the priests have no permission to eat them until they are placed in the Chosen House. For the first-fruits, which are the "beginning," indicate great holiness, as I have written elsewhere. Therefore, they must go to the holy place, and from there they take their wisdom, for they are holy to God, and they shall eat in Jerusalem. The secret of "minor" sacrifices and the Second Tithe is that their consumption is in Jerusalem. This is the blessing of "grain, wine, and oil," which are the primary ancestors of all sustenance. It is forbidden to eat minor sacrifices until after the sprinkling of their blood, for the blood is the soul <note>nefesh</note>, and afterward comes the permission to enjoy. Know that just as the service of sacrifice is an offering to God, so too is the worshiper; for the essence of the service is that a person offers himself, in the secret of "When a man <note>Adam</note> among you brings an offering" <note>Leviticus 1:2</note>. Minor sacrifices represent the peace of the soul and the body.

I mean they must have clear verification of the truth of the witnesses through inquiry and investigation; then their judgment is as the judgment of Heaven, and "precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death" <note>of His pious ones</note>.

### **And since** death is precious in the eyes of the Lord—for Israel is holy from the side of their soul, so that after their death the souls attach themselves above—therefore the command came: "You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness" etc., "for you are children to the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 14:1-2</note>. This is not the case with the other nations; cutting and baldness are their customs, for it is appropriate for them since upon their death they go to destruction and have no portion in this world or the world to come. We, however, are children of God; when we depart from this world, which is a temporary dwelling, we instead have a permanent residence above with our Father in Heaven. Therefore, it is forbidden to mourn excessively or perform these acts.

### **We return** to the matter: the person who worships is himself the sacrifice, as it is written "When a man <note>Adam</note> among you brings an offering." There is a further secret in this. Even when a person descends below, in the secret of <term>Gilgul</term> <gloss>reincarnation</gloss>, "Man and beast You save, O Lord" <note>Psalm 36:7</note>.
