text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
Thabir <note>A mountain near Mecca</note>, and the Arabs used to say: "Shine forth, O Thabir, so that we may depart for the slaughter." <note>An ancient pre-Islamic saying regarding the timing of the sacrifice</note> It is also called Jam'a and the <term>Mash'ar al-Haram</term> <gloss>Sacred Monument</gloss>. <margin>The boundary of Jam'a extends toward Wadi Muhassir near Mina</margin> 

Arafah is a village containing farms, greenery, and melon fields. It has fine houses belonging to the people of Mecca where they stay on the Day of Arafah. The <term>mawquf</term> <gloss>standing place</gloss> is within earshot of a rugged mountain. There are watering places, cisterns, a flowing canal <note>original: "qanat takhurr"</note>, and a built marker behind which the Imam stands to supplicate while the people surround him or stand on the low hills nearby. The prayer hall <note>original: "al-musalla"</note> is on the edge of Wadi Uranah at the borders of Arafah. Standing in the valley itself is not permitted; anyone who leaves the valley before sunset must offer a blood sacrifice <note>original: "dam," referring to the slaughter of an animal as an expiation</note>. White markers define the boundary of Arafah. In the prayer hall is a pulpit made of baked brick, and behind it is a large cistern. Two miles before it are al-Mazimayn, which mark the boundary of the <term>Haram</term> <gloss>sacred territory</gloss>. 

Batn Muhassir is a valley between Mina and al-Muzdalifa; it is the border of al-Muzdalifa. Al-Tanim is a place containing several mosques surrounding the Mosque of Aisha. There are watering places on the road to Medina from which the Meccans enter the state of <term>ihram</term> <gloss>ritual consecration</gloss> for the <term>umrah</term> <gloss>lesser pilgrimage</gloss>. <note>Other sources note the mosques of Maryam and Aisha, where the latter began her pilgrimage; the Shi'a perform their rites from the Mosque of Ali located a mile behind it.</note> 

White markers surround the <term>Haram</term>. From the western road at al-Tanim, it is three miles away. From the Iraq road, it is nine miles. From the Yemen road, it is seven miles. From the Taif road, it is eleven miles. From the main highway, it is ten miles.

Dhu al-Hulayfah is a village near Yathrib <note>the pre-Islamic name for Medina</note> containing a flourishing mosque and nearby wells, though no houses are seen there. Al-Juhfah is a populated city inhabited by the Banu Jafar. It has a fortification with two gates and a few wells. Two miles away is a spring and a large pool; water may occasionally be scarce there, though it is often plentiful.

<summary>Al-Muqaddasi describes the geographic boundaries and landmarks of the pilgrimage sites around Mecca, including Arafah, al-Tanim, and the distances of the sacred territory's borders. He also notes the stations of ihram like Dhu al-Hulayfah and al-Juhfah.</summary>
<keywords>Arafah, al-Tanim, al-Muzdalifa, Haram boundaries, Dhu al-Hulayfah, al-Juhfah, pilgrimage stations, Islamic geography</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: "...to the city of Laranda, a beautiful city with much water and many orchards."</meta>

Its sultan is the King Badr al-Din ibn Qaraman <note>original: "بدر الدين بن قرمان"</note>. Before him, it belonged to the Seljuk <note>original: "اشقية" - referring to the Seljuk dynasty rulers of that region</note> Musa, but he ceded it to King al-Nasir in exchange for compensation. Al-Nasir sent a governor and an army to it, but then Sultan Badr al-Din seized it, built his royal residence there, and established his rule. I met this sultan outside the city while he was returning from hunting. I dismounted from my mount, and he also dismounted from his. I greeted him, and he received me warmly. It is the custom of the kings of these lands that if a traveler dismounts for them, they are pleased by this action and increase their hospitality. If one greets them while mounted, it offends them, does not please them, and becomes a cause for the traveler to be deprived of favors. This happened to me with some of them, and I asked for their forgiveness. When I greeted him and remounted, he asked about my situation and my journey. I entered the city with him, and he ordered the best lodging to be provided for me. He would send much food, fruit, and sweets in silver trays, along with candles. He provided me with clothes, a mount, and showed great kindness. We did not stay with him long, and we departed for the city of Aksaray <note>original: "أقسرا"</note>.

It is among the best and most well-constructed cities of the land of Rum <note>original: "الروم" - Anatolia</note>. It is surrounded by flowing springs and orchards on every side. Three rivers flow through the city, and water runs through its houses. It contains trees and grapevines, and inside it are many orchards. Rugs are made there, attributed to the city, made of sheep's wool, which have no equal in any other land. From there, they are exported to Syria, Egypt, Iraq, India, China, and the lands of the Turks. This city is under the authority of the King of Iraq. I stayed there at the lodge of the <term>Sharif</term> <gloss>noble descendant of the Prophet</gloss> Husayn, who acted there as a deputy for the Amir Arta. Arta is the deputy of the King of Iraq for the lands in Rum that he has conquered. This <term>Sharif</term> is one of the <term>Fityan</term> <gloss>knightly youths/members of chivalric orders</gloss>, and he has a large following. text:
# CHAPTER FORTY-EIGHTH

5. So that He may admit the believing men and the believing women to gardens beneath which rivers flow, to abide therein forever, and to remove from them their misdeeds. That is, in the sight of God, a great attainment. 

6. And that He may punish the hypocritical men and the hypocritical women, and the polytheistic men and the polytheistic women, who assume an evil assumption about God. Upon them is a misfortune of evil, and God has become angry with them, and has cursed them, and has prepared for them Hell; and it is an evil destination. 

7. To God belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth, and God is Exalted in Might and Wise. 

8. Indeed, We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good tidings, and a warner. 

9. So that you may believe in God and His Messenger, and support him, and honor him, and exalt Him morning and evening. 

10. Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you are actually pledging allegiance to God. The hand of God is over their hands. So whoever breaks his pledge only breaks it against his own soul, and whoever fulfills what he has covenanted with God, He will give him a great reward. 

11. Those who remained behind of the Bedouins will say to you, "Our wealth and our families occupied us, so ask forgiveness for us." They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts. Say, "Then who could prevent God from you at all if He intended for you harm or intended for you benefit? Rather, God is ever, with what you do, Acquainted." 

12. But you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families, ever, and that was made pleasing in your hearts. You assumed an evil assumption and you became a people ruined. 

13. And whoever does not believe in God and His Messenger, then indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers a Blaze.

<summary>This passage details the divine reward for the faithful and the punishment for hypocrites and polytheists, emphasizes the validity of the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet, and rebukes the Bedouins who failed to support the cause.</summary>

text:
# CHAPTER FORTY-EIGHTH

5. So that He may admit the believing men and the believing women to gardens beneath which rivers flow, to abide therein forever, and to remove from them their misdeeds. That is, in the sight of God, a great attainment. 

6. And that He may punish the hypocritical men and the hypocritical women, and the polytheistic men and the polytheistic women, who assume an evil assumption about God. Upon them is a misfortune of evil, and God has become angry with them, and has cursed them, and has prepared for them Hell; and it is an evil destination. 

7. To God belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth, and God is Exalted in Might and Wise. 

8. Indeed, We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good tidings, and a warner. 

9. So that you may believe in God and His Messenger, and support him, and honor him, and exalt Him morning and evening. 

10. Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you are actually pledging allegiance to God. The hand of God is over their hands. So whoever breaks his pledge only breaks it against his own soul, and whoever fulfills what he has covenanted with God, He will give him a great reward. 

11. Those who remained behind of the Bedouins will say to you, "Our wealth and our families occupied us, so ask forgiveness for us." They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts. Say, "Then who could prevent God from you at all if He intended for you harm or intended for you benefit? Rather, God is ever, with what you do, Acquainted." 

12. But you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families, ever, and that was made pleasing in your hearts. You assumed an evil assumption and you became a people ruined. 

13. And whoever does not believe in God and His Messenger, then indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers a Blaze.

<summary>This passage details the divine reward for the faithful and the punishment for hypocrites and polytheists, emphasizes the validity of the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet, and rebukes the Bedouins who failed to support the cause.</summary>
<keywords>Surah Al-Fath, believers, hypocrites, polytheists, pledge of allegiance, Bedouins, divine reward, punishment</keywords>

text:
<header>Isaiah * 3 * 4 *</header>

<margin>15</margin> the poor in your houses? What do you mean by crushing my people and grinding the faces of the poor? says the Lord, the Lord of hosts.

<margin>16</margin> And the Lord said, Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with outstretched necks, glancing with their eyes, and walking with mincing steps, and making a tinkling sound with their feet;
<margin>17</margin> therefore the Lord will smite with a scab the crown of the head of the daughters of Zion, and the Lord will lay bare their private parts.
<margin>18 19</margin> In that day the Lord will take away the finery of the anklets, the headbands, and the crescents; the pendants, the bracelets, and the veils;
<margin>21</margin> the headdresses, the chains, the sashes, the perfume boxes, and the amulets; the signet rings and nose rings;
<margin>22</margin> the festival robes, the mantles, the cloaks, and the purses; the mirrors,
<margin>23</margin> the fine linen, the turbans, and the shawls. And it shall be: instead of sweet spice there shall be rot; instead of a sash, a rope; instead of well-set hair, baldness; instead of a rich robe, a girding of sackcloth; and instead of beauty, branding <note>original: "كي" (kayy) refers to branding with a hot iron.</note>.
<margin>25 26</margin> Your men shall fall by the sword, and your mighty in the war. And her gates shall lament and mourn; and she, being desolate, shall sit upon the ground.

<margin>Ch 4 v 1</margin> And seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying, "We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothing; only let us be called by your name, to take away our reproach."

->### Chapter Four, from verse 2<-

<margin>2</margin> In that day the Branch of the Lord shall be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the earth shall be excellent and comely for the survivors of Israel.
<margin>3</margin> And it shall be that he who is left in Zion and remains in Jerusalem will be called holy, everyone who is recorded for life in Jerusalem,
<margin>4</margin> when the Lord has washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and purged the blood of Jerusalem from her midst by the spirit of judgment and by the spirit of burning.
<margin>5</margin> The Lord will create above every dwelling place of Mount Zion, and above her assemblies, a cloud and smoke by day and the shining of a flaming fire by night; for over all the glory there will be a covering.
<margin>6</margin> And there will be a tabernacle for shade in the daytime from the heat, and for a place of refuge and a shelter from the storm and from rain.

->### Chapter Five<-

<margin>1</margin> Now I will sing to my beloved a song of my beloved concerning his vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill.

<summary>This page contains the prophecy against the haughty women of Jerusalem, the resulting social destruction, and the eventual promise of restoration through the Branch of the Lord.</summary>
<keywords>Isaiah, Daughters of Zion, Restoration, Branch of the Lord, Jerusalem, Judgment, Vanity, Purification</keywords>

text:
### The Fourth Art

->Chapter Four: Regarding the General Principles of Vomiting and Purging, and an Indication of How to Draw forth Purging and Emetic Medicines<-

The patient who is to be purged must not hasten to consume large or blameworthy foods, lest nature draws them in before they are digested. If any necessity requires this, it must be done little by little and with great spacing, so that it occurs gradually and what enters the body is well-digested. Phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> is the specific evacuation for the whole, whereas evacuation specific to a humor—either by excess in quantity or corruption in quality—is other than phlebotomy. Every evacuation that is excessive usually causes fainting. If the cessation of a habitual purging causes a condition, it is a sign that the evacuation should be repeated, such as in one who suffers from nasal congestion; if he makes it a habit, it will depart. Know that the remainder of the material that needs to be evacuated is less susceptible to thorough cleaning and reaching a point where the strength fails, and nature often resolves that remainder on its own. As long as the humor is of the appropriate kind and the patient bears it, do not fear excess; sometimes you may even need to purge until the point of fainting. If the patient’s strength is strong and the material of their corrupted humors is abundant, purge them little by little. This is also the case if the material is highly mature or strongly mixed with the blood and cannot be purged all at once, as in the cases of sciatica, chronic joint pains, cancer, chronic mange, and chronic boils. Know that purging draws from above and removes from below; it is consistent with the familiar method of attraction and also with the stabilization of materials after they have settled. If the materials are below, the opposite pulls them toward it, and it also removes them from where they are, by the action of attraction and vice versa. The state of phlebotomy differs according to the places from which the blood is taken, as you have learned. Those who have the least need for evacuation are those with good digestion, and inhabitants of hot climates have little need for evacuation.

We say it is recommended for someone who wishes to take a laxative to divide or space out their food. The first amount is the dosage they will test during the day in their food and drink, and they should make them varied foods and varied drinks, for the stomach is prompted by this state to desire to push what is inside it either upward or downward. As for food that is not varied but is merely more food, the stomach becomes satisfied by it, settles, and grips it firmly, especially if the amount is small. As for those with naturally soft bowels, none of this is needed. Know that the need for vomiting, purging, and the like does not arise in one who has a good regimen; such a person needs something lighter. Perhaps exercise, massage, and cupping will suffice for them. Then, if their body becomes filled, and the fill is of the best of humors, meaning blood, then phlebotomy is what is required for its purification rather than purging. When necessity dictates either phlebotomy or evacuation—such as in autumn, or by inducing vomiting—it is further removed by phlebotomy. This is one of the recommendations of Hippocrates and the books that followed it, and it is the truth. Likewise, if the phlegmatic humors are mixed with the blood. However, if the humors are uniform, viscous, and cold, phlebotomy might increase their thickness and viscosity, so one must begin with purging. In general, if the humors are uniform, prioritize phlebotomy; if an evacuation becomes necessary after that, it may be done. If they are not uniform, purge the excess first until they become uniform, then phlebotomy is performed. Whoever prioritizes medicine before phlebotomy should have prioritized phlebotomy even a little bit. Whoever was recently phlebotomized and needed an evacuation, so they drank medicine, it was held back for them. Often, drinking the medicine when phlebotomy was required resulted in fainting and distress; if it is not calmed by sedatives, then phlebotomy should have preceded it. There is no evacuation required due to excessive fullness that is not called for by the gravity of the illness and the fullness according to quality and quantity. Often, one may refrain from necessary phlebotomy due to the current management, and often the call to evacuate arises but is countered by an obstacle, in which case the only remedy is fasting, sleep, and correcting the imbalance while ignoring the fullness. Some evacuation is for the purpose of prophylaxis, such as what is needed for those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at a known time, especially in the spring. They need to be proactive before the time arrives and perform the evacuation specific to them, whether by phlebotomy or purging. Sometimes the use of external desiccants and drying medicines is a form of evacuation, as is done with those suffering from dropsy. Sometimes you are forced to use a medicine that is homogeneous in quality to the humor being evacuated, such as scammony when you need to evacuate yellow bile; in such cases, it is necessary to mix with it something that is opposite to it in quality but consistent in its purgative action, like myrobalan, and to correct the imbalance if it occurs later. In patients with visceral inflammation, their purging is weakened; if you are forced to do that, use for them things like ivy and safflower. As for the laxative and the <term>khiyar shambar</term> <gloss>cassia fistula</gloss>, Hippocrates said: "Whoever has a stomach that is easily moved to vomit, the first step in their purification is to use vomiting in summer or spring, for that rids the body of fatigue." Know that the one who is accustomed to drinking laxatives or is not accustomed to vomiting should avoid it when there is no need. It is necessary to prepare before purging by thinning the humor one wishes to evacuate and widening the passages, for that rids the body of fatigue. Know that the one who is accustomed to drinking laxatives or is not accustomed to vomiting should, before using strong medicine, follow one of the regimens of reduction. Purging while the abdomen is lean is difficult and exhausting. An emetic medicine might act as a laxative if the stomach is strong, if it is drunk on an empty stomach, or if the drinker is accustomed to laxatives, or because the medicine is heavier in substance or faster to descend. The laxative may become an emetic due to the weakness of the stomach, the intensity of the heaviness, the medicine causing nausea, or the person having indigestion. Every laxative medicine, if it does not purge the undigested matter, will stir up the humor it is meant to purge and spread it throughout the body, causing it to take over the body and attract other humors to it, thereby increasing that humor in the body. Some humors are quicker to respond to vomiting, such as yellow bile, while others are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some have a condition, such as milk or stars <note>possibly referring to planetary influences or specific herbal groupings</note>, where its laxative effect is more correct in itself. Whoever has a humor that is descending, such as those with loose bowels, the constriction of the intestines hinders the laxative medicine. What is compounded of medicines that are strongly different in the time of their purgative action will cause the bowel to be disturbed, and the first will purge the second before it purges the first, or the first might purge the second itself. Whoever is exposed to purging and their body is cleansed by it must avoid medicinal colic and distress, for if that occurs, what is evacuated is evacuated with great difficulty. In general, a medicine that evacuates the superfluous humors will not cause distress; if it is taken and distress occurs, it is either evacuating what is not superfluous, or the humor being evacuated has changed to another humor, which indicates the body has been cleansed of the humor meant to be evacuated.

<summary>This page details the procedural requirements and cautionary principles for medical purging and phlebotomy, including timing, patient constitution, and the selection of medicines based on humoral states.</summary>
<keywords>purging, phlebotomy, medical evacuation, humors, Avicenna, Canon of Medicine, medical regimen</keywords>

text:
### The Fourth Art

->Chapter Four: Regarding the General Principles of Vomiting and Purging, and an Indication of How to Draw forth Purging and Emetic Medicines<-

The patient who is to be purged must not hasten to consume large or blameworthy foods, lest nature draws them in before they are digested. If any necessity requires this, it must be done little by little and with great spacing, so that it occurs gradually and what enters the body is well-digested. Phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> is the specific evacuation for the whole, whereas evacuation specific to a humor—either by excess in quantity or corruption in quality—is other than phlebotomy. Every evacuation that is excessive usually causes fainting. If the cessation of a habitual purging causes a condition, it is a sign that the evacuation should be repeated, such as in one who suffers from nasal congestion; if he makes it a habit, it will depart. Know that the remainder of the material that needs to be evacuated is less susceptible to thorough cleaning and reaching a point where the strength fails, and nature often resolves that remainder on its own. As long as the humor is of the appropriate kind and the patient bears it, do not fear excess; sometimes you may even need to purge until the point of fainting. If the patient’s strength is strong and the material of their corrupted humors is abundant, purge them little by little. This is also the case if the material is highly mature or strongly mixed with the blood and cannot be purged all at once, as in the cases of sciatica, chronic joint pains, cancer, chronic mange, and chronic boils. Know that purging draws from above and removes from below; it is consistent with the familiar method of attraction and also with the stabilization of materials after they have settled. If the materials are below, the opposite pulls them toward it, and it also removes them from where they are, by the action of attraction and vice versa. The state of phlebotomy differs according to the places from which the blood is taken, as you have learned. Those who have the least need for evacuation are those with good digestion, and inhabitants of hot climates have little need for evacuation.

We say it is recommended for someone who wishes to take a laxative to divide or space out their food. The first amount is the dosage they will test during the day in their food and drink, and they should make them varied foods and varied drinks, for the stomach is prompted by this state to desire to push what is inside it either upward or downward. As for food that is not varied but is merely more food, the stomach becomes satisfied by it, settles, and grips it firmly, especially if the amount is small. As for those with naturally soft bowels, none of this is needed. Know that the need for vomiting, purging, and the like does not arise in one who has a good regimen; such a person needs something lighter. Perhaps exercise, massage, and cupping will suffice for them. Then, if their body becomes filled, and the fill is of the best of humors, meaning blood, then phlebotomy is what is required for its purification rather than purging. When necessity dictates either phlebotomy or evacuation—such as in autumn, or by inducing vomiting—it is further removed by phlebotomy. This is one of the recommendations of Hippocrates and the books that followed it, and it is the truth. Likewise, if the phlegmatic humors are mixed with the blood. However, if the humors are uniform, viscous, and cold, phlebotomy might increase their thickness and viscosity, so one must begin with purging. In general, if the humors are uniform, prioritize phlebotomy; if an evacuation prevails/is dominant after that, it may be done. If they are not uniform, purge the excess first until they become uniform, then phlebotomy is performed. Whoever prioritizes medicine before phlebotomy should have prioritized phlebotomy even a little bit. Whoever was recently phlebotomized and needed an evacuation, so they drank medicine, it was held back for them. Often, drinking the medicine when phlebotomy was required resulted in fainting and distress; if it is not calmed by sedatives, then phlebotomy should have been performed before it. There is no evacuation required due to excessive fullness that is not called for by the gravity of the illness and the fullness according to quality and quantity. Often, one may refrain from necessary phlebotomy due to the current management, and often the call to evacuate arises but is countered by an obstacle, in which case the only remedy is fasting, sleep, and correcting the imbalance while ignoring the fullness. Some evacuation is for the purpose of prophylaxis, such as what is needed for those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at a known time, especially in the spring. They need to be proactive before the time arrives and perform the evacuation specific to them, whether by phlebotomy or purging. Sometimes the use of external desiccants and drying medicines is a form of evacuation, as is done with those suffering from dropsy. Sometimes you are forced to use a medicine that is homogeneous in quality to the humor being evacuated, such as scammony when you need to evacuate yellow bile; in such cases, it is necessary to mix with it something that is opposite to it in quality but consistent in its purgative action, like myrobalan, and to correct the imbalance if it occurs later. In patients with visceral inflammation, their purging is weakened; if you are forced to do that, use for them things like ivy and safflower. As for the laxative and the <term>khiyar shambar</term> <gloss>cassia fistula</gloss>, Hippocrates said: "Whoever has a stomach that is easily moved to vomit, the first step in their purification is to use vomiting in summer or spring, for that rids the body of fatigue." Know that the one who is accustomed to drinking laxatives or is not accustomed to vomiting should avoid it when there is no need. It is necessary to prepare before purging by thinning the humor one wishes to evacuate and widening the passages, for that rids the body of fatigue. Know that the one who is accustomed to drinking laxatives or is not accustomed to vomiting should, before using strong medicine, follow one of the regimens of reduction. Purging while the abdomen is lean is difficult and exhausting. An emetic medicine might act as a laxative if the stomach is strong, if it is drunk on an empty stomach, or if the drinker is accustomed to laxatives, or because the medicine is heavier in substance or faster to descend. The laxative may become an emetic due to the weakness of the stomach, the intensity of the heaviness, the medicine causing nausea, or the person having indigestion. Every laxative medicine, if it does not purge the undigested matter, will stir up the humor it is meant to purge and spread it throughout the body, causing it to take over the body and attract other humors to it, thereby increasing that humor in the body. Some humors are quicker to respond to vomiting, such as yellow bile, while others are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some have a condition, such as milk or stars <note>possibly referring to planetary influences or specific herbal groupings</note>, where its laxative effect is more correct in itself. Whoever has a humor that is descending, such as those with loose bowels, the constriction of the intestines hinders the laxative medicine. What is compounded of medicines that are strongly different in the time of their purgative action will cause the bowel to be disturbed, and the first will purge the second before it purges the first, or the first might purge the second itself. Whoever is exposed to purging and their body is cleansed by it must avoid medicinal colic and distress, for if that occurs, what is evacuated is evacuated with great difficulty. In general, a medicine that evacuates the superfluous humors will not cause distress; if it is taken and distress occurs, it is either evacuating what is not superfluous, or the humor being evacuated has changed to another humor, which indicates the body has been cleansed of the humor meant to be evacuated.

<summary>This page details the procedural requirements and cautionary principles for medical purging and phlebotomy, including timing, patient constitution, and the selection of medicines based on humoral states.</summary>
<keywords>purging, phlebotomy, medical evacuation, humors, Avicenna, Canon of Medicine, medical regimen</keywords>

with it other things. The one who has been purged must not rush to consume many or heavy foods, lest nature <note>the body's innate power</note> attract them while they are undigested. If something of that nature is necessary, it must be introduced little by little, spaced out so that it is gradual and whatever enters the body is well-digested. **Venesection** <note>bloodletting</note> is the evacuation specific to the blood <note>original: al-saviya, referring to the balanced humor</note>. As for an evacuation specific to a humor that is excessive in quantity alone or corrupted in quality, that is not achieved by venesection. Every excessive evacuation causes vomiting in most cases. If the cessation of a habitual diarrhea causes an illness, the remedy is usually to bring back that evacuation, just as the cessation of a nosebleed or a mucus discharge causes blockages, and their return removes them. 

Know that the remainder of the matter that needs evacuation is less receptive to total extraction; to pursue it to the point of exhaustion causes the strength to fail. Often, nature itself dissolves that remainder. As long as the humor is of the type that ought to be removed and the patient can bear it, do not fear excess; sometimes you may need to evacuate until fainting occurs. He whose strength is robust and whose bad humors are many should be evacuated little by little. Likewise, when the matter is highly matured or heavily mixed with the blood and cannot be evacuated all at once, such as in cases of sciatica, chronic joint pains, cancer, chronic mange, and chronic boils. 

Know that diarrhea draws from above and uproots from below, so it aligns with the accustomed drawing of fluids and is appropriate after the materials have settled. If the materials are below, the drawing of them to the opposite direction <note>vomiting</note> and uprooting them from where they are is achieved by the action of attraction and its reverse. Venesection differs according to the sites from which the blood is taken, as you have learned. Those who least need evacuation are those with good digestion, and those in hot countries have little need for evacuation.

### Chapter Four: On the Common Laws of Vomiting and Purging and an Indication of the Method of Attracting Laxative and Emetic Medicine

We say: it is recommended for whoever wishes to take a laxative to gather or divide his food consistently. First, let the amount be what he tests in a day across different times, and let him make it of various foods and various drinks as well. For the stomach, in this state, tends to desire to push what is in it upward or downward. As for food that is not varied, the stomach becomes saturated with it, grows sluggish, and grips it tightly, especially if it is small in quantity. As for one who is naturally lax, none of this is necessary. 

Know that the need for vomiting, purging, and the like does not occur for one who follows a good regimen <term>tadbir</term>; he requires something lighter. Sometimes exercise, massage, and cupping are sufficient for him. If his body is full, and most of that fullness is of the best humors—meaning blood—then venesection is what is needed for his cleansing, not purging. If necessity demands venesection or evacuation in a season like autumn, and vomiting is also intended, then begin with venesection; this is among the recommendations of Hippocrates and the books of the ancients, and it is the truth. 

Likewise, if the phlegmatic humors are mixed with the blood. However, if the humors are equal, viscous, and cold, venesection might increase their thickness and viscosity, so it is mandatory to begin with a laxative. In general, if the humors are equal, prioritize venesection, and if an excess remains after that, evacuate. If they are unequal, evacuate the excess first until they are equal, then perform venesection. He who prioritizes medicine over venesection should have performed venesection a few days prior. He who has recently undergone venesection and needs evacuation should wait before taking medicine. Often, taking medicine when venesection was required results in vomiting and distress; if it does not settle with sedatives, it is because venesection should have preceded it. 

There is no evacuation required for excessive fullness that is not prompted by the severity of the illness and the fullness in terms of quality and quantity. Often, a good regimen <term>tadbir</term> makes the venesection required at the time unnecessary. Often, the urge for evacuation arises but an obstacle appears, so the only recourse is fasting, sleep, and correcting the imbalance <term>su' mizaj</term> caused by the fullness. 

Among evacuations are those done by way of precaution, such as what is needed for those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at a known time, especially in spring. One needs to take precautions before the time comes and perform the specific evacuation, whether it be venesection or purging. Sometimes the use of external drying agents and desiccating medicines acts as an evacuation, such as what is done for those with dropsy. You may be forced to use a medicine that matches the humor to be evacuated in quality, such as scammony when you need to evacuate yellow bile. In that case, it must be mixed with something that opposes it in quality but agrees with it in purging, like myrobalan <term>halilaj</term>. 

Correcting a bad temperament if it occurs afterward in those with tumors of the viscera may weaken their purging. If you are forced to do that, use for them things like bindweed or safflower. As for the laxative and purging cassia <term>khiyar shanbar</term>, Hippocrates said: he whose constitution is easy and whose nature responds to vomiting, the first step in his cleansing is to use vomiting in the summer or spring, for that protects the body from exhaustion. Know that one who is accustomed to a slippery or naturally lax stomach, or is unaccustomed to vomiting, should avoid it except where necessary. 

The humor one wishes to evacuate must be thinned and the channels widened before purging or vomiting. Know that for one who has a slippery stomach or is unaccustomed to vomiting, using strong medicine along with wasting of the thin abdominal walls <term>maraqq</term> is difficult and exhausting. An emetic medicine may turn into a laxative if the stomach is strong, if taken during extreme hunger, if the drinker has a naturally lax stomach, or if the medicine is of a heavy substance that descends quickly. Conversely, a laxative may become an emetic due to weakness of the stomach, extreme heaviness, the medicine being repulsive to the patient, or the patient having indigestion. 

Every laxative medicine, if it does not purge due to lack of maturation, will agitate the humor it was meant to purge and spread it through the body, taking over and drawing other humors to it, thus increasing that humor in the body. Some humors respond more quickly to vomiting, such as yellow bile; others are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some have a specific state like <unclear>...</unclear>, where purging is more correct. He whose humor is descending, such as those with intestinal slippage, the intestines will contract and struggle with laxative medicines that are composed of very different drugs in their purging time, leading to disordered purging where the first part purges the second before the second can purge, or the first purges the second itself. 

He who undergoes purging while his body is <unclear>...</unclear> will inevitably suffer from medicine that causes colic and distress, and what is evacuated will be evacuated with great difficulty. In general, when medicine evacuates waste matter, there is no distress; but if it is taken with distress, it either evacuates something other than waste, or if the humor evacuated by vomiting or purging changes to another humor, it indicates the body has been cleansed of the humor intended for evacuation.

along with others. One who is undergoing evacuation must not rush to take many raw foods, lest nature be attracted to them while they are undigested. If any such thing becomes necessary, it must be in small quantities, little by little, until it is done gradually and what enters the body is well-digested. 

Bloodletting is the evacuation specifically for the humors <note>referring to the balance of bodily fluids</note>. As for evacuation of a humor that is excessive in quantity alone or spoiled in quality, that is distinct from bloodletting. Any evacuation that is excessive often causes fever. If someone is accustomed to a condition such as an interrupted bowel movement, the recurrence of that evacuation will usually heal it, just as if the cessation of ear wax or nasal mucus caused obstructions, for their return clears them away. 

Know that leaving a remainder of the material that needs to be evacuated is less harmful than being extreme in evacuation and carrying it to the point where the strength of the body collapses. Nature often dissolves that remainder. As long as the humor is of the appropriate kind and the patient can tolerate it, do not fear excess, and you may even need to evacuate until fainting occurs. If one has strong stamina and a large amount of corrupt humors, evacuate them little by little. This is also the case if the material is highly viscous or strongly mixed with blood and cannot be evacuated all at once, as happens in sciatica, chronic joint pain, cancer, chronic mange, and chronic boils.

Know that diarrhea draws from above and cleanses from below, so it is consistent with both opposite and concordant attraction. It is also consistent after the materials have settled. If the materials are from below, it draws them in the opposite direction and clears them from where they are. Vomiting acts in the opposite way regarding attraction and cleansing. The state of bloodletting differs according to the places from which the blood is taken, as you have learned. The people with the least need for evacuation are those who have good diet and good digestion, and those in hot countries have little need for evacuation.

### Chapter Four: On the Common Rules for Vomiting and Diarrhea, and Indicating How to Draw Out Purgative and Emetic Medicines

We say that it is recommended for anyone who wishes to induce diarrhea or vomiting to divide their food, consuming the required amount for the day in several sittings, and to make these different foods and different drinks. The stomach, because of this condition, will desire to expel what is inside it either upward or downward. As for food that is not varied and is taken on top of other food, the stomach is stingy with it, holds onto it, and grips it firmly, especially if the amount is small. As for those with a loose constitution, none of this is necessary. 

Know that the need for vomiting, diarrhea, and the like does not apply to one who has a good regimen; they need what is lighter than these. Perhaps exercise, rubbing, and bathing are sufficient. Then, if their body is full, and it is full of the best humors—meaning blood—then bloodletting is what is needed for purification, rather than diarrhea. If necessity requires bloodletting and evacuation using substances like hellebore and strong medicines, one must begin with bloodletting. This is among the advice of Hippocrates in the book *Epidemics*, and it is the truth. 

This is also true if phlegmatic humors are mixed with blood, but if the humors are viscous and cold, bloodletting might increase their thickness and viscosity, so it is necessary to start with diarrhea. In general, if the humors are balanced, give precedence to bloodletting. If one dominates after that, evacuate it. If they are not balanced, evacuate the excessive matter first until it is balanced, then perform bloodletting. 

Whoever gives medicine before bloodletting when bloodletting should have been performed a few days earlier, or whoever is near the time of bloodletting and needs to evacuate—drinking medicine is more appropriate for them. Often, taking the medicine when bloodletting was required leads to fever and agitation. If it does not subside with sedatives, know that bloodletting should have been performed first. Not every evacuation is needed because of extreme fullness; rather, the magnitude of the illness may call for it, as well as fullness based on quality, not quantity. Often, an improved regimen suffices instead of bloodletting required at the time. Often, the call for evacuation arises, but an obstacle hinders it; the only remedy then is fasting, sleep, and correcting the bad temperament that the fullness caused. 

Some evacuation is done by way of precaution, such as that required by those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at a known time, especially in the spring. One must take precautions before its time and perform the evacuation specific to their illness, whether by bloodletting or diarrhea. Sometimes the use of external desiccants and drying medicines is a form of evacuation, such as what is done for those with dropsy. Sometimes you are forced to use a medicine that is homogeneous in quality to the humor being evacuated, such as scammony when you need to evacuate bile. In that case, you must mix it with something that is opposite in quality but consistent in purgation, such as myrobalan, and treat any bad temperament that occurs afterward. In those with tumors of the viscera, diarrhea and vomiting weaken them. If you are forced to do so, use for them substances like ivy and safflower. As for polypody, purging cassia, and the like—Hippocrates said that whoever is thin has a nature that responds easily to vomiting. Therefore, the priority in their purification is to use vomiting in summer, spring, or autumn, but not winter. For one with a moderate constitution, diarrhea is more appropriate for them. If a reason calls for their evacuation by vomiting, wait for the summer and avoid it when not necessary. 

It is necessary to precede diarrhea and vomiting by thinning the humor one wishes to evacuate and by widening and opening the passages, for that secures the body from exhaustion. Know that accustoming the nature to respond easily to the desired diarrhea or vomiting before using strong medicine is one of the successful regimens. Diarrhea and vomiting, when there is emaciation of the abdomen, is difficult, exhausting, and dangerous. 

An emetic medicine may act as a purgative if the stomach is strong, if it is drunk on an empty stomach, if the drinker has a loose constitution, if they are unaccustomed to vomiting, or if the medicine is heavy in substance and descends quickly. A purgative may become emetic due to a weak stomach, extreme dryness of the waste, or because the medicine is repulsive and the person has indigestion. Any purgative medicine, if it does not purge or purges undigested matter, stirs up the humor it is meant to purge and spreads it through the body, where it takes over and transforms other humors into it, thus increasing that humor in the body. 

Some humors are faster to respond to vomiting in most cases, such as bile. Some are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some vary, such as phlegm. For the feverish patient, diarrhea is safer in itself. For those whose humor is descending, such as those with intestinal flux, inducing vomiting for them is impossible. The worst purgative medicines are those composed of medicines that are strongly discordant in the time of purging, for the purging becomes agitated, and the first [medicine] purges the second before the second can purge, or perhaps the first purges the very essence of the second. Whoever is subjected to diarrhea and vomiting while their body is clean will inevitably suffer from dizziness, colic, and distress, and whatever is evacuated is evacuated with great difficulty. In general, as long as the medicine is evacuating waste, there is no agitation with it, but if it begins to agitate, it is only purging what is not waste. If the evacuated humor changes by vomiting or diarrhea to another humor, it indicates the purification of the body from the humor intended for evacuation.

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
with other things. A person who has undergone <term>evacuation</term> <gloss>medical purging of humors</gloss> must not rush into eating large amounts of food or raw foods, lest the <term>nature</term> <gloss>the body's innate healing power</gloss> attract them while they are undigested. If any such food is necessary, it must be taken little by little, thing after thing, so that it is gradual and what enters the body is well-digested.

<term>Phlebotomy</term> <gloss>bloodletting or venesection</gloss> is the evacuation specific to the <term>equable</term> <gloss>balanced humors or the blood itself</gloss>. As for the evacuation specific to a <term>humor</term> <gloss>one of the four bodily fluids</gloss> that has increased alone in quantity or corrupted in quality, that is something other than phlebotomy. Every excessive evacuation causes fever in most cases. For one who suffers an illness due to the cessation of a habitual diarrhea, repeating that evacuation usually cures them; for example, if the cessation of earwax or nasal mucus causes blockages, their return removes it. Know that leaving a remnant of the matter that needs evacuation is of less danger than being exhaustive in evacuation and reaching the point where strength fails. Often, <term>nature</term> dissolves that remnant itself. As long as the humor is of the kind that should be removed and the patient can tolerate it, do not fear excess; sometimes you may need to evacuate until fainting occurs. 

For one whose strength is high but whose bad humoral matter is plentiful, evacuate them little by little. Likewise, if the matter is very sticky or heavily mixed with the blood and cannot be evacuated all at once, as occurs in sciatica, chronic joint pains, cancer, chronic scabies, and chronic boils. Know that <term>laxatives</term> draw from above and uproot from below, so they are suitable for both types of attraction—the opposite and the corresponding—and are also suitable after the matters have settled. If the matters are below, they draw them to the opposite side and also uproot them from where they are. <term>Emetics</term> <gloss>medicines that induce vomiting</gloss> perform attraction and uprooting in the opposite manner. The status of phlebotomy differs according to the sites from which blood is taken, as you have learned. The people least in need of evacuation are those with good nutrition and good digestion, and those living in hot countries have little need for evacuation.

### Chapter Four: On Common Laws for Vomiting and Diarrhea, and an Indication of the Method of Attraction of Laxative and Emetic Medicines

->We say:<- It is recommended for one who intends to take a laxative or to vomit to divide their food, taking the amount they would consume in a day in several portions, making them different foods and different drinks as well. The stomach, in this state, tends to desire to push what is in it upwards or downwards. However, for non-varied food that enters upon other food, the stomach is stingy and tight with it, grasping it firmly, especially if it is small in quantity. But for those of a naturally soft <note>loose</note> bowel, none of this is necessary. 

Know that the need for vomiting, diarrhea, and the like does not occur for one who follows a good <term>regimen</term> <gloss>lifestyle and diet</gloss>; they require what is lighter than these. Sometimes all they need is exercise, massage, and the bath. Then, if the body is full, and most of that fullness is of the best humors—meaning blood—then phlebotomy is what is needed for its cleansing, rather than laxatives. If necessity dictates both phlebotomy and evacuation with something like <term>hellebore</term> or strong medicines, one must begin with phlebotomy. This is among the counsels of Hippocrates in the book <term>Epidemics</term> <note>original: "Epidemia"</note>, and it is the truth. 

Likewise, if the <term>phlegmatic</term> humors are mixed with the blood; however, if the humors are viscous and cold, phlebotomy might increase their thickness and viscosity, so it is necessary to begin with laxatives. In general, if the humors are equal, prioritize phlebotomy, and if a surplus remains after that, evacuate it. If they are unequal, evacuate the excess first until they are equal, then perform phlebotomy. If one prioritizes the medicine over phlebotomy when they should have prioritized phlebotomy by a few days, or if one has recently undergone phlebotomy and needs evacuation, drinking the medicine is more suitable for them. Often, taking the medicine when phlebotomy was required results in fever and agitation; if it does not settle with sedatives, know that phlebotomy should have preceded it. 

Not every evacuation is needed because of excessive fullness; rather, the severity of the illness and fullness in terms of quality, not quantity, may call for it. Often, improving the regimen suffices in place of a phlebotomy required at the time. Often a cause calls for evacuation, but an obstacle opposes it, so the only recourse is fasting, sleep, and remedying the <term>dyscrasia</term> <gloss>bad temperament</gloss> caused by the fullness. Some evacuations are by way of <term>prevention</term> <gloss>precautionary measures</gloss>, such as what is needed by those habitually afflicted by gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at a known time, especially in spring; one needs to take precautions before the time and perform the evacuation specific to their disease, whether it be phlebotomy or laxatives. 

Sometimes the use of external drying agents and desiccating medicines acts as an evacuation, as is done for those with dropsy. You may need to use a medicine that matches the humor being evacuated in quality, such as <term>scammony</term> when you need to evacuate <term>yellow bile</term>; in that case, one must mix it with something that opposes it in quality but matches it in laxative effect, such as <term>myrobalan</term> <note>original: "al-halilaj"</note>, to remedy any bad temperament that might occur afterward in those with inflammations of the viscera, which would weaken their diarrhea and vomiting. If you are forced to do that, use for them things like bindweed and safflower. As for <term>polypody</term> and <term>purging cassia</term> and the like: Hippocrates said that whoever is thin and whose nature easily responds to vomiting, it is best for their cleansing to use vomiting in summer, spring, or autumn, but not winter. One who is of moderate build, diarrhea is better for them; if a cause calls for evacuation by vomiting, let them wait for summer and avoid it where it is not needed. 

Before diarrhea and vomiting, one must precede with the <term>attenuation</term> <gloss>thinning</gloss> of the humor one wishes to evacuate, and the widening and opening of the channels, for that protects the body from exhaustion. Know that habituating the nature to softness and responding easily to the desired diarrhea or vomiting before using strong medicine is one of the successful regimens. Diarrhea and vomiting accompanied by wasting of the abdominal walls is difficult, exhausting, and dangerous. 

An emetic medicine may turn into a laxative if the stomach is strong, or if it is drunk during intense hunger, or if the drinker has a <term>relaxed</term> <gloss>naturally loose</gloss> stomach, or is unaccustomed to vomiting, or if the medicine is of a heavy substance that descends quickly. A laxative becomes an emetic because of a weak stomach, or due to the extreme dryness of the waste, or because the medicine is loathsome and the person has indigestion. Every laxative medicine, if it does not purge or purges what is immature, moves the humor it was meant to purge and spreads it through the body, thus taking over the body, and other humors transform into it, increasing that humor in the body. Some humors respond most quickly to vomiting, like yellow bile; some are resistant to vomiting, like <term>black bile</term>; and some have varying states, like phlegm. For a person with fever, diarrhea is more correct in itself. For those whose humor is descending, such as those with <term>lientery</term> <gloss>slippery intestines</gloss>, vomiting them is impossible. The worst laxative medicines are those composed of medicines that differ greatly in the timing of their purging, as they disturb the bowels, and the first purges the second before the second can purge, or the first may even purge the second itself. Whoever undergoes diarrhea or vomiting while their body is clean will inevitably suffer dizziness, colic, and distress, and what is evacuated will be evacuated with great difficulty. In general, as long as the medicine is evacuating wastes, there will be no agitation; if it begins to cause agitation, it is evacuating something other than waste. If the humor evacuated by vomiting or diarrhea changes to another humor, it indicates the body's cleansing of the humor intended for evacuation.

<summary>Ibn Sina provides detailed protocols for medical evacuation, distinguishing between bloodletting and purging. He emphasizes the need for humoral balance, the timing of treatments according to seasons, and the risks of improper medicine administration.</summary>
<keywords>phlebotomy, laxatives, emetics, humors, Hippocrates, regimen, evacuation, yellow bile, black bile, phlegm</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: He was a man of noble standing and possessed a refined manner of speech. These are the names of a group whom I have all seen, and I have learned the virtues of each one individually, and they were all people of verification. However, among the people of Ghazni and its residents, the gnostic shaykh and, in his own time, a man of justice was Abu al-Fadl ibn Asad, a venerable elder. He possessed manifest proofs and brilliant miracles; he was like a flame from the fire of love, and his life was based upon concealment. A solitary shaykh, singular and detached from attachments, was Ismail al-Shashi, a venerable elder who followed the path of blame. Shaykh Salar Tabari was one of the learned Sufis and lived a good life. The shaykh, a model of virtue and a mine of mysteries, Abu Abdullah Muhammad ibn al-Hakim, known as Murid (may God have mercy on him), was among those intoxicated by the proximity of the Divine Presence. He had no equal in his field, and his life remained hidden from the people, though he possessed manifest proofs and brilliant signs, and his company was even better than his outward appearance. A respected shaykh, and among the foremost leaders, was Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id al-Ayyar, a preserver of the Prophet's traditions; he lived a good life and saw many shaykhs. He was a man of strong state and was well-informed, yet he walked in concealment and did not reveal his inner state to anyone. A noble master, a pillar of respect and dignity, was Abu 'Ala 'Abd al-Rahim ibn Ahmad, who was a dear soul among the people and a leader of his time; my heart is well-inclined toward him, and he leads a disciplined life and is in a good state, and among...</meta>

he is knowledgeable in the arts of science. The unique shaykh Qasura ibn Muhammad al-Jardizi possesses perfect compassion for the people of the path, and every one of them holds him in honor. He has seen the shaykhs, and by virtue of the faith of the common people and the scholars of that city, I am hopeful that after this, individuals will appear whom we might regard with trust, and this group of scattered souls who have found their way into that city and rendered the image of this path ugly will be cleansed from that city. That place will then become a site frequented by the saints and those who become great, God Almighty willing. Now, we have returned to the distinction of their sects regarding doctrines and the explanation of each, and with God is the help, protection, and rectitude.

<margin>
A f. 93a.
</margin>

# Chapter on the differences of their sects, their doctrines, their signs, their stations, and their anecdotes

Before this, in the mention of Abu al-Hasan al-Nuri (may God have mercy on him), I had said that they are twelve groups: two of them are rejected and ten are accepted. Every class among them has a good practice and a praiseworthy path in spiritual struggles, and a subtle etiquette in spiritual observations. Although they differ in practices, struggles, observations, and disciplines, they are in agreement and consensus regarding the foundations and branches of the Divine Law and the profession of Divine Unity. Abu Yazid (may God be pleased with him) said: "The disagreement of the scholars is a mercy, except in the singularization of Divine Unity," and there is a famous report in agreement with this.

<margin>
B f. 102v.
</margin>

The reality of <term>Tasawwuf</term> <gloss>Sufism</gloss> lies between the reports of the shaykhs based on reality and what is divided based on metaphor and custom. Therefore, I will speak briefly and concisely in explanation of that division, and I will spread a carpet for the foundational doctrine of each one, so that the seeker may obtain knowledge of it, so that it may be a weapon for the scholars, a source of welfare for the disciples, and a path to salvation for those who love.

<summary>Al-Hujwiri introduces the classification of Sufi groups, noting their shared commitment to the fundamental principles of Islamic law and Divine Unity despite their varied spiritual practices.</summary>
<keywords>Sufism, Tasawwuf, Divine Unity, spiritual struggle, Ghazni, sectarian classification</keywords>

text:
Whoever becomes a captive of greed,
How can his eyes and heart become bright?
<margin>Whoever has greed will not find purity; the eye of the heart is not illuminated by greed.</margin>
In his eyes, the vision of status and gold
Is like a hair inside the eye.
<margin>The thought of status and gold for the greedy is like a hair in the eye or a spear point.</margin>
Except for the drunkard who is full of Truth;
Even if he is in the corner, he is the leader.
<margin>The one drunk on the love of Truth is full of it; if you give a treasure to the master of that corner, he is already rich.</margin>
Whoever has enjoyed the Vision <note>The divine encounter</note>,
This world has become a carcass in his eyes.
<margin>Whoever becomes joyful through the Vision, this world becomes a carcass to his sight.</margin>
But that Sufi was far from that drunkenness;
Inevitably, in his greed, he was night-blind.
<margin>Whoever is far from this drunken state, that fake Sufi becomes night-blind through greed.</margin>
Greed hears a hundred tales,
Yet not a single point enters the ear of greed.
<margin>Even if the greedy hear a hundred stories, they do not bring a portion of them to the ear of wisdom.</margin>

---

->The proclamation of the bankrupt man by the Judge’s heralds in the city<-
<margin>The heralds take the bankrupt man around the city by order of the Judge.</margin>

---

There was a certain homeless, bankrupt person
Stuck in prison and in relentless bonds.
<margin>There was a homeless bankrupt man who could not find his way out of the bonds of prison.</margin>
He ate the morsels of the prisoners excessively;
Upon the hearts of the people, he was like Mount Qaf out of greed.
<margin>He ate the prisoners' food for free; his greed was like a mountain, heavy on the hearts of the people.</margin>
No one had the courage to eat a morsel of bread,
For that bread-thatcher would snatch it away.
<margin>No soul had a morsel of bread because that greedy man’s hand would snatch it instantly.</margin>
Whoever is far from the invitation of the Merciful <note>God</note>,
He is a beggar even if he were a Sultan.
<margin>Whoever lacks the grace of God’s success is a beggar in spirit, even if he were a king.</margin>
Humanity was discarded because of that thief;
The prison became a hell because of that bread-snatcher.
<margin>Generosity was lost because of him; that bread-thief made the prison a hell.</margin>
If you do a kindness in hope of comfort,
From that same side, a calamity will approach.
<margin>If you hope for the corner of comfort through goodness, there is surely a calamity from one side.</margin>
There is no treasure without a trap,
There is no peace except in the private sanctuary of Truth.
<margin>There is no corner that is not a trapping ground; the sanctuary of Truth is the only true refuge.</margin>
The corner of the prison of this inevitable world
Is not without wages and the beating of the mat.
<margin>The prison corner of the world is full of types of cruelty; it has become a place of suffering and various hardships.</margin>
By God, if you crawl into a mouse hole,
You will be afflicted by the claws of a cat.
<margin>Even if your place were a mouse hole, the cat’s claws would make you drink the water of death.</margin>
A human being exists through imagination;
Let his imagination be of a beautiful possessor.
<margin>The human is comforted by imagination; let the imaginations be of beautiful states.</margin>
If unpleasantness appears in his imagination,
He melts like wax from the fire.
<margin>If terrifying imaginations arise, the soul will melt like wax in the fire.</margin>
If God keeps you among snakes and scorpions
With pleasant imaginations,
<margin>If God’s grace and beauty keep your thoughts pleasant while amidst snakes and scorpions,</margin>
The snakes and scorpions will be your companions,
For that imagination of yours is the alchemy of copper.
<margin>Snakes and scorpions become companions because your imagination is the alchemy for the copper of reality.</margin>
Sweet patience comes to you from pleasant imagination,
For that imagination of relief has come before you.
<margin>Sweet patience shows the beauty of imagination, for relief is the state that arrives beforehand.</margin>
That relief comes from faith in the heart;
Weakness of faith is despair and groaning.
<margin>The mark of relief is in the heart through faith; weakness of faith is despair and distress.</margin>
Patience is the head and crown of faith;
Where there is no patience, there is no faith.
<margin>Patience is the crown of complete faith; whoever lacks patience and endurance is incomplete.</margin>
The Prophet of God said: God has not given faith
To anyone who does not have patience in his nature.
<margin>The Prophet said: Complete faith is not for the one who lacks this character.</margin>
That one thing might be a snake in your eye,
While the same thing is a beauty in the eye of another.
<margin>In your eye, the imagination is a snake; for another, it has become a beautiful description.</margin>
For in your eye is the imagination of infidelity,
While that is the imagination of a believer in the eye of a friend.
<margin>For in your eye is the image of infidelity; sometimes it is a hook and sometimes a fish.</margin>
In this world, both actions exist;
Sometimes he is a fish, sometimes a hook.
<margin>In a single person, two forms are manifest: half is greed and half is the quality of the patient.</margin>
Half of him was a believer, half was infidelity;
Half of him brings greed, half is patience.
<margin>Half is a believer and half the mark of an infidel; half is greed and half is the quality of the patient.</margin>
Your Lord said: "Among you is a believer,"
And also: "Among you is a kaffir <gloss>disbeliever</gloss> of ancient pride."
<margin>The Truth called some "infidels" and also called others "believers" immediately.</margin>

|---|---|---|---|
| Whoever has greed becomes stuttering, | How can the eye and heart become bright with greed? | Whoever is greedy finds no clarity, | The eye of the heart does not become bright with greed. |
| Before his eye, the image of status and gold, | Is just like a hair in the sight. | The thought of status and gold for the greedy is the same, | It resembles a hair in the eye, without doubt. |
| Except for the intoxicated one who is full of God, | Even if you give him treasures, he is free. | The one intoxicated by God’s love is filled with Truth, | Even if you offer him many treasures, he remains free. |
| Whoever has become gifted with the vision, | This world has become carrion in his eyes. | Whoever has become gifted with the vision, | The world appears as carrion to his sight. |
| But that Sufi was far from intoxication, | Therefore he was night-blind in his greed. | Whoever is far from this intoxication, | Do not think the Sufi is not night-blind through greed. |
| He hears a hundred stories but is stunned by greed, | Because a point of wisdom does not enter the ear of greed. | If a hundred stories are told to the greedy, | His ear of wisdom does not grasp their meaning. |

---

The judge's town criers proclaiming the pauper
The town criers, by the judge's order, proclaim the pauper around the city

---

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| There was a pauper, homeless, | Trapped in prison and bonds, without relief. | There was a homeless pauper, | Who found no relief from the prison bonds. |
| He ate the prisoners' morsels greedily, | His greed like Mount Qaf upon the hearts of the people. | He was a free-loader of the prisoners' morsels, | His greed like a mountain, a burden on the hearts of the people. |
| No one had the heart to eat a morsel of bread, | Because that morsel would be seized by robbery. | No one had a morsel of bread, | He would seize the sustenance of others immediately. |
| Whoever is far from the invitation of the Merciful, | He has the eye of a beggar even if he is a sultan. | Whoever lacks the grace of divine success, | He is a beggar even if he is a king. |
| He trampled manliness underfoot, | Killed by the hellish prison of that stolen bread. | He placed manliness underfoot, | He made the prison a hell of stolen bread. |
| If you seek the corner of comfort, | From that direction, a calamity also comes to you. | If you seek a corner of comfort, | From one side, calamity surely comes. |
| No corner is without beasts and traps, | There is no peace except in the sanctuary of Truth. | There is no corner without a trap, | Only the sanctuary of Truth is a refuge. |
| The corner of the world's prison is unavoidable, | It is not without a heavy price and the beating of the mat. | The corner of this unfaithful world, | Is a place of suffering and various hardships. |
| By God, if you go into a mouse hole, | You will become the prey of a cat's claw. | If your place is a mouse hole, | You will drink poison from a cat's claw. |
| Man has fatness from imagination, | If his imaginations are beautiful. | Imagination is a consolation to man, even if it is only a thought, | If his imaginations are beautiful. |
| And if his imaginations show ugliness, | He melts like wax from a fire. | If the long imaginations are frightening, | Like wax in fire, he becomes consumed by soul-pain. |
| Even if you are among snakes and scorpions, | If you have good thoughts, God helps you. | If there is imagination among snakes and scorpions, | Good opinion is a help from the Lord of Glory. |
| Snakes and scorpions will be your companions, | Because your imagination was an alchemy of copper. | Snakes and scorpions become your companions, | Because your imagination is an alchemy for copper. |
| Sweet patience comes from pleasant imagination, | Because that imagination is the herald of relief. | Patience shows sweetness through beautiful imagination, | Because it is a relief that describes the state before you. |
| That relief comes from faith in the conscience, | Weakness of faith is hopelessness and distress. | Faith in the heart carries the sign of relief, | Know that weakness of faith is despair and hardship. |
| Patience finds a crown of honor from faith, | Where there is no patience, there is no faith. | Patience is a crown of beauty for faith, | Where there is no patience, there is no faith. |
| The Prophet said God does not give faith, | To whoever has no patience in his nature. | The Prophet said faith is not complete, | In whoever lacks patience and endurance. |
| That one is like a snake in your eyes, | And he is an image of beauty in the eyes of another. | In your eye, he is like a snake, | In the other's eye, he is a picture of beauty. |
| Because in your eyes, the thought of his unbelief is there, | And that imagination of a believer is in the eyes of a friend. | Because your eye imagines him as a disbeliever, | The other describes his state as faith. |
| For in this one person, both actions exist, | Sometimes he is a fish and sometimes a hook. | In one person, both forms are apparent, | Sometimes he is a hook and sometimes a fish. |
| Half of him is believer and half of him is pride, | Half of him is greedy and half of him is patient. | Half of him is believer, half is the form of an infidel, | Half is greed and half is the quality of patience. |
| Your God said, "Among you is a believer," | And again, "Among you is an infidel of old pride." | God made "among you is an infidel" clear, | And He said "among you is a believer" as well. |

<summary>This page contrasts the nature of greed, which blinds the soul and turns the world into carrion, with the state of the one intoxicated by God, whose imagination transforms reality through faith and patience, ultimately noting the dualistic nature of the human soul as described in the Quranic verses concerning believers and disbelievers.</summary>
<keywords>Greed, Faith, Patience, Imagination, Alchemy, Duality, Quran, Believer, Infidel</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
Whoever possesses greed becomes stuttering; how can the eye and heart be enlightened by greed?
In his eyes, the vision of status and gold is like a hair stuck in the eye.
Except perhaps for the drunkard who is full of God; though you give him treasures, he remains free.
Whoever has enjoyed the Vision of God, this world has become like a corpse in his eyes.
But that Sufi was far from such intoxication; therefore, in his greed, he was night-blind.
A hundred stories the one intoxicated by greed may hear, but not a single point reaches the ear of greed.

---

->Description of the judge’s heralds parading the bankrupt man through the city<-

---

There was a certain homeless, bankrupt man, lingering in prison and inescapable bonds.
He would greedily eat the morsels of the other prisoners; his greed sat on the hearts of the people like Mount Qaf.
No one had the courage to eat a morsel of bread, because that snatcher of morsels would carry it away.
Whoever is far from the invitation of the Merciful is a beggar-eyed person, even if he be a Sultan.
Having trampled chivalry underfoot, he became the prison’s hell because of his food-snatching.
If you flee to any corner in hope of comfort, an affliction will surely meet you from that side as well.
There is no corner without a beast or a trap; there is no rest except in the private sanctuary of God.
The corner of the prison of this inevitable world is not without the wages of the foot and the beating of the mat.
By God, even if you crawl into a mouse hole, you will be afflicted by the claws of a cat.
A human grows fat from imagination, if his imaginations are beautiful.
But if his imaginations show unpleasantness, he melts like wax from a fire.
If God keeps you among snakes and scorpions with pleasant imaginations,
The snakes and scorpions will be your companions, for that imagination of yours is the alchemy of copper.
Patience has become sweet through pleasant imagination, because the imagination of relief has come forward.
That relief comes into the mind from faith; weakness of faith is despair and agony.
Patience finds its head-covering from faith: "Where there is no patience, there is no faith."
The Prophet said that God has not given faith to anyone who has no patience in his nature.
That single person may be like a snake in your eye, yet he is a beautiful painting in the eye of another.
Because in your eye is the imagination of his infidelity, while that same imagination is a believer in the eye of a friend.
For in this one person both actions exist; sometimes he is the fish and sometimes he is the hook.
Half of him is a believer, half of him is old disbelief; half of him brings greed, half of him is patience.
Your Lord said: "Among you is a believer," and again: "Among you is an ancient disbeliever."

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
Like a donkey whose legs are tied, stubborn and acting out of foolishness,
he bound both his legs and went toward the head <note>meaning he prioritized his base instincts over his higher guidance</note>.
Like a blindfolded donkey, he resisted and turned away.
Then the donkey says, "One tether is enough for me."
Indeed, the action of that vile one is stitched into that moment.
The nature of the donkey is tied up in a single tether.

## In explanation of that Hadith of the Chosen One <note>original: Mustafa, the Prophet Muhammad</note>, peace be upon him, which says: "Indeed, God Almighty created the angels and placed within them Intellect; He created the beasts and placed within them Lust; and He created the children of Adam and placed within them both Intellect and Lust. Thus, he whose intellect overcomes his lust is higher than the angels, and he whose lust overcomes his intellect is lower than the beasts." The Messenger of God spoke the truth.

| | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| It has come in the tradition that the Glorious Lord | Created the world in three categories. | When the glorious Creator appeared, |
| One group was given superior intellect, knowledge, and generosity; | That is the angel, who knows nothing but prostration. | He gave one group intellect and existence. |
| Greed and passion are not in their element; | Absolute Light, living by the love of God. | Greed and passion did not exist in their element. |
| Another group is empty of knowledge, | Like an animal, focused on fodder in the pasture. | He made one group empty of knowledge; |
| They perceive nothing except the stable and fodder; | In their wretchedness, they are oblivious to honor. | Their understanding is limited to the stable and fodder. |
| This third kind is the child of Adam and mankind; | Half of him is inclined toward the celestial, | The third category is the human species; |
| Half is a donkey, inclined toward the base. | This human being is full of opposing winds. | Like beasts, he is accustomed to the low. |
| Those two groups <note>angels and animals</note> are at peace from war and strife, | While humans are divided into three communities. | These two groups became tranquil in their state. |
| And these humans are divided by the test of life. | Like Jesus, some have joined with the angels. | The test is manifest in the human species. |
| One group has become absolutely submerged <note>in God</note>; | Saved from anger, passion, and idle talk. | One group is completely submerged in the King <note>God</note>. |
| The form of a man, but the meaning of Gabriel; | Freed from self-will and the lineage of the self. | The form of a man, but the meaning of Gabriel. |
| Freed through asceticism, piety, and spiritual struggle. | They have become pure anger and absolute lust <note>referring to the base group</note>. | Those who are simple-hearted without piety or struggle; |
| Another group has joined with the beasts; | That house was narrow, and that description was lost. | The final category has the characteristics of beasts. |
| The Gabriel-like quality in them was but a ringing sound. | He became dead, like a person who is soulless. | The Gabriel-like quality in them has vanished. |

| Because the soul that does not have Him is base; | He behaves more lowly than the animals. | Since the soul is base without the Beloved, |
| He behaves more lowly than the animals; | Deceit and trickery are what he knows how to weave. | The animal soul is deep in excessive grief. |
| Deceit and trickery are what he knows how to weave; | Weaving garments of gold-thread; | The high mark is deceit and trickery. |
| Weaving garments of gold-thread; | Finding pearls at the bottom of the sea; | He makes gold-threaded garments of thyme <note>metaphor for worldly labor</note>. |
| Finding pearls at the bottom of the sea; | With astrology, medicine, and philosophy. | He draws many diagrams in the science of geometry. |
| With astrology, medicine, and philosophy; | There is no path for him to the seventh heaven. | Knowledge of medicine and astrology is also known. |
| There is no path for him to the seventh heaven; | For he was a pillar that the Ox <note>constellation</note> held up. | This is entirely a worldly attachment; |
| For he was a pillar that the Ox held up; | They named those the "secrets of the universe." | This science is a building tied to the stable. |
| They named those the "secrets of the universe." | The goal is the survival of the animal for a few days. | The goal is the survival of the animal for a few days. |

| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| He brought forth the creation in three parts: | | |
| Those who are angels, performing prostration. | | |
| They became the manifestation of God's love. | | |
| This group became entangled with animality. | | |
| They are heedless, wretched, and without honor. | | |
| They became capable of both good and evil. | | |
