| Freed from anger, passion, and idle talk. | | |
| Do not think that they are merely born of man. | | |
| Pure anger and absolute lust are the same. | | |
| The house is narrow, that high description is complete. | | |
| The soul that is without the Beloved becomes abased. | | |
| This word is the Truth's saying, let it adorn your hand. | | |
| He performs every precise task in the world. | | |
| No other animal can act like that. | | |
| Capturing jewels from the depths of the sea. | | |

<summary>Rumi explains a Hadith regarding the three types of beings: angels (intellect without lust), beasts (lust without intellect), and humans (possessing both). He describes how humans can rise above angels or fall below animals depending on whether they follow their divine intellect or base desires.</summary>
<keywords>angels, animals, humanity, intellect, lust, Nafs, Hadith, Gabriel, spiritual evolution, philosophy, worldly science</keywords>

In the interpretation of this tradition <note>original: "hadith"</note> of Mustafa, peace be upon him: "God the Exalted created the angels and implanted intellect within them; He created the beasts and implanted lust within them; and He created the children of Adam and implanted in them both intellect and lust. Thus, whoever's intellect overcomes his lust, he is higher than the angels; and whoever's lust overcomes his intellect, he is lower than the beasts." The Messenger of God spoke the truth.
This is an interpretation of the noble tradition: "God the Exalted created the angels and implanted intellect within them; He created the beasts and implanted lust within them; and He created the children of Adam and implanted in them both intellect and lust. Thus, whoever's intellect overcomes his lust, he is higher than the angels; and whoever's lust overcomes his intellect, he is lower than the beasts."

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
As a donkey, tied by its legs, struggles in its donkey-nature,
Its two feet become more entangled at the head.
When a donkey with its head tied acts rebelliously,
Its two feet only bind its own head tighter.
The donkey then says, "One bond is enough for me,"
Not knowing that those two bonds result from that wretched one's own actions.
The donkey says again, "One bond is enough for me,"
The wretch does not know that it is his own doing.

---

-> On the interpretation of this tradition of the Chosen One <note>the Prophet Muhammad</note>, peace be upon him: "Indeed, God the Exalted created the angels and instilled in them Intellect; He created the beasts and instilled in them Lust; and He created the children of Adam and instilled in them both Intellect and Lust. He whose intellect overcomes his lust is higher than the angels, and he whose lust overcomes his intellect is lower than the beasts." The Messenger of God spoke the truth. <-

---

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| It is related in the tradition that the Glorious Lord | Created the inhabitants of the world in three kinds. | In this report, it is said the Glorious Creator | Made the creatures manifest in three categories. |
| One group is entirely intellect, knowledge, and generosity; | That is the angel, who knows nothing but prostration. | To one group He gave existence with intellect, | Which are the angels who are in prostration. |
| There is no greed or desire in their element; | They are absolute light, living by the love of God. | In their element, there is no greed or desire; | They became the manifestation of the love of God. |
| Another group is void of knowledge, | Like an animal, growing fat from fodder. | One group He made void of knowledge; | They became desirous with animal nature. |
| They see nothing but the stable and the grass; | Out of misery, they are heedless of honor. | Their gnosis is the stable and the grass; | They are heedless, without misery or honor. |
| This third kind is the son of Adam and mankind; | Half of him is angel, and half of him is donkey. | The third category became the human species; | They became prepared for both good and evil. |
| The donkey-half is inclined toward the lowly; | The other half is inclined toward the sublime. | Like the beasts, half is accustomed to the lowly; | The other half is of celestial race like an angel. |
| Those two groups are at rest from war and combat, | But this human is in agony with two opposites. | Those two groups became peaceful in state; | But in man, there is conflict with two opposites. |
| And these humans were also divided by trial; | They have human forms, but have become three nations. | In the trial of the human species, it is manifest; | They were of human form, but three nations. |
| One group has become absolutely submerged; | Like Jesus, they have joined with the angels. | One division is entirely and absolutely submerged; | They joined the angelic host, in the station of Jesus. |
| The image is man, but the meaning is Gabriel; | Delivered from anger, desire, and idle talk. | The form is man, but the meaning is Gabriel; | Delivered from anger, desire, and idle talk. |
| Delivered from discipline, asceticism, and struggle; | As if they were never born of man at all. | Those who are simple-hearted without asceticism; | As if they are not born of mankind. |
| The other group joined with the donkeys; | They became pure anger and absolute lust. | The other category has the qualities of beasts; | Pure anger and absolute lust as well. |
| The Gabriel-like quality was in them and departed; | That house was narrow, and that quality was vast. | Their Gabriel-like quality suffered decline; | The house was narrow, and that quality was lofty. |
| A person who is without a soul becomes a corpse; | One becomes a donkey when their soul is without That. <note>referring to the Divine Beloved</note> | The person who is without a soul becomes a corpse; | That soul which is without the Beloved becomes a donkey. |
| Because the soul that does not have That is lowly; | This word is Truth, the Sufi has spoken it. | Since the soul without the Beloved becomes lowly; | This is the word of Truth, adorn your hand with it. |
| He exerts his soul more than the animals; | He performs subtle works in the world. | He is submerged deeper than the animal soul; | He does every precise task in the world. |
| The deceit and deception he knows how to weave, | Such does not appear from any other animal. | The pattern of knowledge, deceit, and trickery; | No other animal can act in such a way. |
| The weaving of gold-embroidered garments, | Finding pearls in the depths of the sea. | He practices crafts in gold-embroidered clothing; | Attracting jewels from the bottom of the sea. |
| The intricacies of the science of geometry, | Along with astronomy, medicine, and philosophy. | In the science of geometry, he makes many designs; | Also the known parts of philosophy, medicine, and stars. |
| Since his concern is only with this world, | He has no way to the seventh heaven. | This concern is entirely worldly; | There is no passage to the seventh heaven. |
| All this is the science of building the stable, | Which is the pillar for the ox and the camel. | This science of building is tied to the manger; | It pays attention to the ox and the camel. |

<summary>Rumi explores the tripartite nature of creation—angels (intellect), beasts (lust), and humans (both). He argues that while humans possess great worldly intellect for science and craft, this "stable-building" knowledge is worthless if it does not lead to spiritual transcendence.</summary>
<keywords>Intellect, Lust, Angels, Human Nature, Geometry, Philosophy, Spiritual Transcendence, Animal Soul, Gabriel, Jesus</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: ...The dream-teller is dying in this confusion,
Whoever has it, the effect is evident in him,
The best work is the service of good character,
The creation of mankind and jinn is to worship, that is the goal,
He was rejected from the door of Truth,
With rage, he made the bottom of the earth his place,
This ignorance became a palace of bad name,
Smoke does not lead to the fire,
Whoever has evidence of that form with physicians,
Look into the excrement while in the state of halwa,
Whoever becomes that witness is blind,
Hold me excused, for I am unseen....</meta>

A tumult fell upon the entire court,
And doubt seized the hearts of the noble and common citizens of the city.
What anxiety and calamity has occurred?
A powerful enemy is after us,
Or did a royal disaster arise from the Unseen?
He who rode a jester into the city,
Has killed several purebred horses on the road.
Gathering at the palace of the King of the people,
Why did such a rush come to the fool?
From his haste, he made a <term>fuhsh</term> <gloss>lewd/indecent</gloss> <term>ijtihad</term> <gloss>attempt/striving</gloss>,
A clamor and agitation in <term>Tirmidh</term> <gloss>a city</gloss>, the city.
That one, placing two hands upon his face,
And that other, wailing from suspicion and fear,
From the clamor, the sedition, the fear, and the punishment,
Every heart went into a hundred kinds of illusions.
Everyone was casting a fortune from speculation,
As to what fire had fallen into the cloak.
He sought a way, and the King quickly gave way,
When he kissed the earth, he said, "What was it?"
Whoever asked about the condition of that morose one,
He placed his hand upon his lips, meaning, "Hush!"
The illusion inflames his culture,
Everyone was confused by his agitation.
The jester signaled to the King of generosity,
"Allow me a moment to draw breath,"
So that the mind may return to the heart,
For I have fallen into a world of wonders.
After an hour, when the King, from illusion and suspicion,
Had become bitter in both throat and mouth,
For he had never seen the jester like this,
For there was no companion more pleasant than him.
Always he would bring jokes and witticisms,
He would keep the King happy and smiling.
He would make him laugh so much in his seat,
That the King would double over in laughter,
That from the force of laughter, his body would perspire,
That he would catch his breath, exhausted.
Today again, this yellow-faced and morose one,
Placing his hand on his lips, saying, "O King, be silent."
Illusion within illusion, and fancy within fancy,
So that the King might see what punishment comes,
For the heart of the King was with grief and abstinence,
Since <term>Khwarazm-Shah</term> <gloss>the King of Khwarazm</gloss> was very bloodthirsty.
He had killed many kings in that direction,
Either through <term>hamilah</term> <gloss>guile</gloss> or the power of that stubborn one.
This King of Tirmidh was in a state of illusion,
And by the jester’s art, that illusion was increased.
He said, "Speak quickly, what is the state?"
"Who is this turmoil and clamor from?"
He said, "I heard in the village that the King,"
"Sent a herald to every crossroads,"
"That I desire someone who, within three days,"
"Travels to Samarkand, and if still..."
"I offered corners <note>a metaphor for wealth or compensation</note> and he was rewarded,"
"When the message is received, what is the goal?"
"I hurried, go for the sake of that,"
"So that I may say I do not have the power,"
"Such humility does not come from someone like me,"
"Do not spin the thread of this hope upon me."

<column-break/>

The peace of the entire court became twofold,
The hearts of the noble and commoners of the city were in two states.
Or a powerful enemy had appeared,
The jester came, spiraling in haste.
They gathered at the palace of the King of the people,
Why did such a rush come to the fool?
A clamor and agitation occurred in Tirmidh,
With lewd acts and vain haste.
An old man was beating his knees,
Wailing and tearing his hair.
Sedition and fear changed the men,
Every heart fell into a hundredfold imagination.
In every thing, they saw omens and speculation,
As if the fire had fallen into the rags.
He gave way to the King when he entered his presence,
He kissed the earth and said, "What is the message of the path?"
Whosoever asked about the state, with great effort,
He placed his hand on his lips, saying, "Be silent."
The illusion and fancy in the city exceeded everything,
Everyone became confused and mute.
The jester signaled to the King of generosity,
"Give me permission so I may catch my breath,"
"So that the mind may return to the heart,"
"I have fallen into a wonderous state."
After an hour, when the King’s suspicion and doubt,
Had made bitter and dry [his state], like a man in agony.
He had never seen the jester so morose,
For there was no one more charming and cheerful than him.
He used to keep the King happy and smiling,
So that he would hold his stomach in laughter.
The King would double over from laughter,
That he would perspire from the exertion of his speech.
He would place his hand on his lips, meaning, "Hush,"
He was counted as a morose, confused, and senseless one.
Illusion upon illusion, fancy upon fancy,
So that the King might see what punishment comes.
The heart of the King was full of grief and doubt,
For the Khwarazm-Shah was a bloodthirsty one.
He had annihilated many kings in that direction,
Through rage or through the power of that stubborn one.
The King of Tirmidh was in a state of suspicion,
The art of the jester increased the terror.
He said, "I told you, O King,"
"From whom is this uproar and distress?"
"That I desire a person who, within three days,"
"Should go to Samarkand and receive the gift,"
"I offered him corners <note>compensation/wealth</note> as a reward,"
"Once the purpose is obtained from the news,"
"I hurried for his sake immediately,"
"But in a person like me, there is no such power,"
"Do not place hope in me for this service."

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: ...Hold me excused, for I am unseen.</meta>

A clamor arose throughout the capital,
The worry in the mind of that Sultan increased.
The hearts of the city's elite and commoners were lost,
Wondering what distress and calamity had occurred.
"A powerful enemy is intent upon us,"
"Or a heavenly disaster has arisen for the kingdom."
Because Dalqak <note>Rumi's court jester character</note> came riding in haste,
Having killed several Arabian horses along the road.
The people gathered at the King's palace:
"Why has he come with such sudden speed?"
In his haste, the extremity of his exertion
Caused a tumult and confusion in Tirmidh.
One person raised both hands in prayer,
Another wailed in fear and lamentation.
From the outcry, the sedition, the fear, and the punishment,
Every heart went toward a hundred types of suspicion.
Everyone made a prediction based on analogy:
"What fire has fallen into the woolen cloth?"
The King quickly sought a path and gave him entry;
When he kissed the ground, the King said: "Alas, what happened?"
To anyone who asked about his sour state,
He put his finger to his lips, saying: "Hush!"
This behavior of his fueled the imagination,
Everyone became stunned and confused by his distress.
Dalqak gestured: "O Gracious King,
Leave me for a moment so I may catch my breath,
Until my fleeting reason returns to me,
For I have fallen into a strange world."
After an hour, while the King was in a state of suspicion,
Both his throat and mouth turned bitter.
For he had never seen Dalqak in such a state;
There was no companion more pleasant than him.
He used to always practice trickery and jesting,
Keeping the King happy and laughing.
He would make him laugh so much in the assembly
That the King would hold his belly and double over,
Until his body would sweat from the strength of laughter,
And he would fall on his face from his laughing.
Yet today, he is so pale and sour-faced,
Putting his finger to his lips, saying: "O King, be silent!"
Suspicions upon suspicions and fantasies upon fantasies:
"What punishment will come upon the King?"
For the King’s heart was filled with grief and caution,
Since the Khwarazm-Shah <note>The ruler of the Khwarazmian Empire, known for his military campaigns</note> was very bloodthirsty.
He had killed many kings in those parts,
Either by guile or by the power of that obstinate one.
The King of Tirmidh was already in a state of dread,
And that dread increased because of Dalqak's artifice.
He said: "Speak quickly, what is the situation?
From whom is this turmoil and agitation of yours?"
He replied: "I heard in the village that the King
Issued a proclamation at every crossroads,
Saying: 'I want someone who, in three days,
Can reach Samarkand <note>A major city in Central Asia</note> and return, even now.'
'I have set aside treasures for him in exchange,
Once the purpose of the message is achieved.'
I hurried to him for that reason,
To say: 'I do not have that ability.'"
"Such a lowly task does not suit someone like me;
Do not weave this thread of hope upon me."

<column-break/>

<note>The right column contains the original Persian verses; the left column contains an Ottoman Turkish poetic translation/commentary of the same verses. Both are rendered into English below following the layout.</note>

The exhaustion made everyone appear mad,
It caused suspicion in the land for that Sultan as well.
The hearts of the elite and commoners of the city were stirred,
Wondering what distress and calamity had appeared.
"Either a powerful enemy has appeared,"
"Or a calamity has come to the kingdom from the unseen."
Dalqak came with twisting speed,
On the road, several Arabian horses were reduced to nothing.
The people gathered at the King’s palace gate:
"Why did the jester make such a display of speed?"
With excessive and futile haste,
He made Tirmidh confused and agitated.
The elders were striking their knees with their hands,
The others were crying out and tearing their hair.
The sedition and fear changed the men,
A hundred types of thoughts fell into every breast.
In everything, there was omen and analogy:
They said, "Fire has fallen into the cloth."
When the King gave him presence and a path,
He kissed the earth; the leader asked for the message of the road.
To anyone who asked about his state with great effort,
He put his hand to his lips: "Be silent!"
In that land, suspicion and fantasy grew beyond measure,
The confusion made them all stunned and mute.
Dalqak gestured: "O Gracious King,
Give me leave so I may take a breath,
Until my reason returns to me immediately,
For I have fallen into a strange state."
An hour passed in the King's suspicion and doubt,
It turned him bitter and dry; he could not speak.
He had never seen Dalqak so distressed,
None was more playful and lively than him.
He was always jesting and telling jokes,
The King was happy and laughing with him.
He would make the King so full of laughter
That he would hold his sides with both hands.
The King would fall over from laughing
As he spoke while sweating from the mirth.
Now he is so sour-faced and lost of mind,
Putting his hand to his lips, meaning: "Hush!"

"Will the King suffer some disgrace?"
The King’s heart was mixing grief and dread,
The cause was the bloodthirsty Khwarazm-Shah.
That obstinate one, through force or guile,
Had already made many kings non-existent.
The King of Tirmidh was fearful and anxious,
Dalqak's behavior increased his dread.

Tell me, what is this agitation and sorrow?"

'I want a man so that in three days,

text:
A commotion fell upon the entire court,
A disturbance fell into the imagination of that Sultan.

The hearts of the high and low of the city were lost,
Wondering what calamity and affliction had occurred.

"Either a powerful enemy has designs upon us,
Or a deadly affliction has arisen from the Unseen."

For the jester had ridden with rough haste,
And had killed several Arabian horses on the road.

The people gathered at the palace of the King,
Wondering why the jester had made such haste.

From his haste and his frantic efforts,
An uproar and anxiety fell upon Tirmidh.

One was hitting his hands against his knees,
Another was crying "Woe!" from his imagination.

From the clamor, the sedition, the fear, and the punishment,
Every heart had gone into a hundred kinds of fancies.

Each person was casting an omen based on conjecture,
Wondering what fire had fallen into the cloth.

He sought the way, and the King gave him the way quickly;
When he kissed the ground, he said to him: "Hey, what was it?"

Whoever asked him of his state in that sour mood,
He would put his finger to his lips, signaling: "Hush."

His manner increased the apprehension,
Everyone became stunned and perplexed in their anxiety.

The jester gestured: "O generous King,
Grant me a moment so that I may catch my breath.

So that my intellect may return to me for a moment,
For I have fallen into a world of wonders."

After an hour, for the King, because of the anxiety and suspicion,
Both his throat and his mouth had become bitter.

He had never seen the jester like this,
For there was no companion more pleasant to him than him.

He was always performing antics and telling jokes,
He kept the King happy and laughing.

He would make him laugh so much while sitting,
That the King would hold his belly with both hands.

For from the force of laughter his body would sweat,
And he would fall over from his laughing.

Yet today, so yellow and sour-faced,
He puts his hand to his lips saying: "O King, hush."

Anxiety upon anxiety and fancy upon fancy,
What disaster will befall the King from this?

For the King's heart was full of sorrow and caution,
Because the Khwarazm-Shah was very bloodthirsty.

He had killed many kings in that region,
Either by stratagem or by the force of that stubborn one.

This King of Tirmidh was in fear of him,
And the jester's manner only increased his fear.

He said: "Speak quickly and tell me what the situation is,
And from whom is this turmoil and clamor of yours?"

He said: "I heard in the village that the King
Had a herald cry out at every main road:

'I seek someone who will ride in three days
To Samarkand, and I will give him treasures.'

I will give him treasures in return,
Once the purpose is obtained from his message.

I rushed to you for that reason,
To say: 'I do not have that capacity.'

Such agility does not come from the likes of me;
Do not tie the thread of this hope to me."

<column-break/>

A disturbance fell upon the entire court,
It became the cause of anxiety for that Sultan also.

The hearts of the high and low of the city were in a stir,
Wondering what agitation and calamity had appeared.

"Either a powerful enemy has appeared,
Or some deadly affliction has come from the Unseen."

The jester came with speed and twisting,
Many an Arabian horse was ruined on the road.

The people gathered at the palace of the King,
Asking why the jester had made such speed.

With excessive effort and useless haste,
He made Tirmidh confused and agitated.

One was beating his knees,
Another was crying "Woe!" and tearing his hair.

Sedition and fear terrified the men,
A hundred kinds of fancies fell into every heart.

Everyone was casting omens based on fear and conjecture,
Saying, "Fire has fallen into our cloth."

When the King gave him the way to his presence,
He kissed the ground and said, "What is the message of the road?"

Whoever asked him with effort about his state,
He would say, "Finger to the lip, be silent."

His state increased the fear and fantasy,
He made everyone confused, stunned, and silent.

The jester gestured: "O generous King,
Grant me permission to take a breath.

So that my intellect may return to me again,
For I have fallen into a world of wonders."

After an hour, for the King, because of anxiety and suspicion,
His palate and mouth had become bitter and dry.

He had never seen the jester so tense,
And there was no one more delightful and witty than him.

He was always performing antics and jokes,
The King was happy and laughing with him.

He would make the King laugh so much,
That he would double over with his hands on his belly.

Laughter had made him sweat as he spoke,
The King would fall over from his laughter.

Now, so sour-faced and muddled in mind,
Putting his hand to his lips, meaning: "Hush."

Anxiety upon anxiety and fancy upon fancy,
Does this not cause distress to the King?

The King's heart was mixed with sorrow and fear,
The cause was the bloodthirsty Khwarazm-Shah.

That stubborn one had destroyed many a king,
Either by force or by stratagem.

While the King of Tirmidh was full of fear,
The jester's behavior gave him increased anxiety and dread.

He said: "Speak in haste, then, what is the state?
From whom is this uproar and this sorrow?"

He said: "I heard in the village that the King
Had given an order for a proclamation without doubt:

'I seek a man who will, within three days,
Go to Samarkand and receive a reward.'

'I will give him treasures in return,'
So that once the purpose is obtained from the message,

I rushed to you for that very reason,
To say: 'I do not have the power and strength for this.'

In one of my kind there is no such power,
Do not expect this service from me."

<note>A decorative floral border surrounds the text block.</note>

<summary>This passage recounts the arrival of a jester in the court of the King of Tirmidh; his erratic behavior and refusal to speak cause widespread panic and anxiety for the King, who fears an impending attack by the bloodthirsty Khwarazm-Shah.</summary>
<keywords>Masnavi, Jalal al-Din Rumi, Tirmidh, Khwarazm-Shah, anxiety, storytelling, courtly life</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta> and witnessing, whether in religion or in the hereafter. The objective of this is the realization and emergence of the perfection of the names, which is the perfection of <term>jala</term> <gloss>manifestation</gloss> and <term>istijla</term> <gloss>self-revelation</gloss>. The perfection of <term>jala</term> means His appearance according to these considerations, and the perfection of <term>istijla</term> means He is revealed to Himself according to these very same considerations. This appearance and witnessing is an ocular and concrete witnessing, like the appearance of the detailed within the summary, which contrasts with essential perfection. Essential perfection is the appearance of the Essence by itself, for itself, without consideration or otherness. This appearance is intellectual, like the appearance of the detailed summary. The Absolute Being necessitates the perfection of its selfhood and the richness of its absolute independence, which consists of the states, conditions, and considerations of the Essence along with their rulings and requirements in a general manner. Glorified is He, as He appears in all levels of divine and cosmic realities, representing the Essence from its hidden depths. The inclusion of the whole within its unity is witnessing and firm in all its forms and rulings, just as it appeared and was established.

<summary>This passage discusses the metaphysical concepts of manifestation (jala) and self-revelation (istijla), explaining how the Divine Essence appears through the perfection of its names and attributes in both detailed and summary forms.</summary>
<keywords>divine manifestation, jala, istijla, essential perfection, divine names, cosmic realities, unity</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
and witness, whether in this world or in the hereafter. The objective of this is the realization and manifestation of the perfection of the Names, which constitutes the perfection of clarity <term>jala</term> <gloss>the self-revelation of the Essence to itself</gloss> and the perfection of reflection <term>istijla</term> <gloss>the self-revelation of the Essence to itself in the mirrors of the many forms</gloss>. The perfection of clarity refers to His manifestation according to these conceptual considerations. The perfection of reflection occurs when He sees Himself according to the very nature of these considerations. This manifestation and witnessing is an ocular and concrete vision, similar to the manifestation of the detailed within the concise. This is in contrast to the Essential perfection, which is the manifestation of the Essence by itself and for itself, without any regard for considerations or otherness. This latter manifestation is a conceptual or cognitive one, like the manifestation of the concise within the detailed.

The absolute display is a necessary consequence of the perfection of the "I-ness" <note>original: "aniyat"</note> and the absolute richness <note>original: "ghina"</note> of the Independent One. The affairs, states, and considerations of the Essence, along with their rulings and requirements, appear in a universal manner—glory be to Him—across all levels of divine and cosmic realities. These realities reveal the Essence from the depths of their hiddenness and the inclusion of the whole within His oneness. They remain witnessed and established in all their forms and rulings, just as they appeared and were fixed.

<summary>Jami explains the two modes of divine self-revelation: jala, the Essence appearing to itself, and istijla, the Essence seeing itself through the multiplicity of created forms. This process fulfills the perfection of the Divine Names across all levels of existence.</summary>
<keywords>jala, istijla, Divine Names, Essence, manifestation, oneness, multiplicity, Sufi metaphysics</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: the world of the senses</meta> and witnessing <gloss>shahadat</gloss> whether in this world or in the hereafter. The objective of all this is the realization and manifestation of the perfection of the Names, which consists of the perfection of Radiance <term>jala</term> <gloss>the manifestation of the One in the many</gloss> and the perfection of Reflective Clarity <term>istijla</term> <gloss>the One's vision of itself in those many forms</gloss>.

The perfection of Radiance refers to His manifestation according to these conceptual considerations. The perfection of Reflective Clarity refers to His witnessing <unclear>of the forms</unclear> according to these same considerations. This is a manifestation and a witnessing that is visual and concrete, much like the manifestation and witnessing of the summarized whole within the detailed parts. This is in contrast to Essential Perfection, which is the manifestation of the Essence to itself, for itself, without any consideration of an "other" or of "otherness." That is a manifestation that is cognitive and unseen, like the manifestation of the detailed parts within the summarized whole.

Absolute Wealth <note>original: "ghina-yi mutlaq"; also translated as Self-Sufficiency</note> is a necessary attribute of Essential Perfection. The meaning of Absolute Wealth is that the modes, states, and considerations of the Essence—along with their rulings and requirements—are observed and established in their entirety. This occurs across all levels of Divine and cosmic realities. These appear to the Essence within its internal depths, where all things are folded into its Unity, according to all their forms and rulings, just as they have appeared and been established.

<summary>Jami explains the two types of Divine manifestation: Radiance, where the One appears in the many, and Reflective Clarity, where the One witnesses itself through the many. He contrasts this with the Absolute Wealth of the Essence, which contains all potential realities within its own Unity.</summary>
<keywords>jala, istijla, Divine Names, Essence, Absolute Wealth, manifestation, witnessing, Unity</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: ...And in</meta>

It should not remain hidden that some of these expressions, to the masters of metaphorical language <term>arbáb-i-lisán</term> <gloss>masters of language/speech</gloss>, were mentioned in previous sacred Tablets <term>alwáh-i-mu‘ẓamah</term> <gloss>exalted Tablets</gloss> written for one of the friends. Now, in accordance with the requirement of zeal, and in view of the request of that personage, we repeat them in these pages. Perhaps this may guide the thirsty in the desert of remoteness to the bridge of nearness, and lead the lost in the wilderness of separation and distance to the destination of intimacy and reunion, so that the clouds of ignorance may disperse and the world-illuminating sun of guidance may rise from the horizon of the heart. Upon God is the reliance and from Him we seek aid.

> Perhaps there may flow from this Pen that which will quicken the hearts of the people, so that they may all arise from the bed of their heedlessness, and inhale the most fragrant leaves of Paradise from the Tree <term>sidrah</term> <gloss>the Lote-Tree of the furthest boundary</gloss> which was, by the hands of power and the permission of God, planted in the garden of Divinity.

To those firmly rooted in knowledge <note>original: *ūlu'l-'ilm* — those with deep spiritual insight</note>, it was known and clear that when the fire of the love of Jesus consumed the veils of limitation and form, and the decree of that Personage was, to some extent, fulfilled in this outward sense, one day that unseen Beauty <term>jamál-i-ghaybí</term> <gloss>unseen Beauty</gloss> spoke of separation and ignited the fire of longing. He said, "I am departing, and I shall come again." On the seventh day, He said again, "I am departing, and another shall come to say what I have not said, and to complete that which I have spoken." 

In reality, these two expressions are the essence of the manifestations of oneness <term>maẓáhiru't-tawḥíd</term> <gloss>Manifestations of God/the Manifestations of Oneness</gloss>, and they are heard and obeyed. If one views them with the eye of spiritual insight, they are, in truth, the promise of the Seal.

<summary>This page addresses the figurative nature of prophetic language, using the example of Jesus promising to return and the promise of a future Manifestation to illustrate how the Manifestations of God are fundamentally united in their mission despite variations in their outward speech.</summary>
<keywords>metaphorical language, sacred Tablets, spiritual guidance, Jesus, separation, longing, Manifestations of God, unity of the Prophets, the Seal</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta> this same manner. 

It should not remain hidden that some of these expressions <note>referring to the prophecies of old</note> may seem metaphorical to the masters of language. This was mentioned in the previous exalted Tablets <note>original: *Alwaḥ-i-mu‘azzamah* — the holy epistles or communications of the author</note> written for one of the friends, and now, out of a sense of divine honor and in response to your own request, we mention them again in these pages. Perhaps this will guide the thirsty ones in the desert of remoteness to the bridge of nearness, and lead those lost in the wilderness of separation to the cup of reunion, so that the clouds of error may be lifted and the world-illuminating sun of guidance may rise from the horizon of the soul. In God is our trust, and from Him we seek help. 

May there flow from this pen that which shall quicken the hearts of men, that they may arise as one from the slumber of their heedlessness, and inhale the sweetest fragrances of Paradise from the Divine Tree <note>original: *al-sidrah* — the Lote-tree, a symbol of the Manifestation of God</note> which was planted in the garden of Divinity by the hands of power, by the leave of God. 

To those possessed of knowledge, it is clear and evident that when the fire of Christian love <note>original: *maḥabbat-i-‘Īsavī*</note> burned away the veils of limited forms and customs, and when the authority of His Holiness <note>Jesus</note> was outwardly established, that Essence of the Unseen <note>original: *jamāl-i-ghaybī* — literally "the Unseen Beauty"</note> one day spoke of separation to some of his spiritual companions. He kindled the fire of longing and said: "I go and come again." On another occasion he said: "I go and another shall come, that he may say what I have not said, and fulfill what I have spoken." 

In truth, these two statements are the same for those who listen to the melodies of the Manifestations of Unity <note>original: *Maẓāhir-i-Tawḥīd* — the Prophets or Founders of world religions</note> and are submissive to them. And if one observes with the eye of spiritual insight, these are in truth the promise of the Seal <note>of the Prophets</note>

<margin>+</margin>

<summary>The author explains that he is repeating certain spiritual truths to guide those seeking God. He cites the words of Jesus regarding his departure and the coming of a future Comforter as a key example of how divine messengers prophesy subsequent revelations.</summary>
<keywords>Christianity, Jesus, Manifestations of God, spiritual insight, prophecy, Divine Tree, Kitáb-i-Íqán</keywords>

These mysteries were previously mentioned in the written Tablets in the subtle melodies of the <term>Hijazi</term> <gloss>a mode of Persian music associated with the Hejaz</gloss>, which had been penned for one of the friends. Now, in response to your request, we repeat them in the sweet strains of the <term>Iraqi</term> <gloss>a mode of Persian music associated with Iraq</gloss>, that perhaps it may guide the thirsty in the deserts of remoteness to the ocean of nearness, and bring those lost in the wilderness of separation and distance to the pavilions of intimacy and union. Thus, the clouds of error may disperse, and the world-illuming sun of guidance may rise from the horizon of the heart. I rely upon God and seek His aid.

> Perchance there may flow from this Pen that which will quicken the hearts of the people, that all may rise from their beds of heedlessness, and hear the melodies of the birds of Paradise from the Lote-Tree which was, by the hands of Power, planted in the garden of the Oneness by the permission of God.

It is clear and evident to those "firmly rooted in knowledge" <note>original: *al-rāsikhūn fī’l-‘ilm*</note> that when the fire of the love of Jesus consumed the veils of the limitations of the Jews, and His decree was, to some extent, carried out according to the outward appearance, that unseen Beauty spoke one day to some of His spiritual companions of separation, and ignited the fire of longing, saying: "I go, and I will come again." And in another station, He said: "I go, and another will come who will speak what I have not spoken, and will complete what I have said."

In truth, these two utterances are one, <term>low antum fī mazāhir al-tawhīd bi-‘ayn Allāh tashhadūn</term> <gloss>if you were to witness the Manifestations of Oneness with the eye of God</gloss>. And if viewed with the eye of spiritual insight, in truth, in the era of the Seal...

<summary>The author explains that the return of the promised figures of previous religions, such as Jesus, is often described in seemingly contradictory terms that are spiritually unified. He emphasizes that literal interpretations hinder the recognition of the Manifestations of God.</summary>
<keywords>Manifestations of God, Jesus, spiritual insight, divine longing, return, unity of the Manifestations, spiritual guidance</keywords>

text:
<note>The text is enclosed within an elaborate, intricate blue floral and geometric border (tazhib).</note>

The <term>Sufi</term> <gloss>mystic</gloss> sat by the base of the wine jar from the corner of the monastery,
The moment he saw the <term>Muhtasib</term> <gloss>censor of public morals</gloss> carrying a jug upon his shoulder.

The conditions of the <term>Sheikh</term> <gloss>master</gloss>, the judge, and the wine of the Jews,
I asked of the old wine-seller at the break of dawn.

He said, "The matter is not to be spoken of, even if you are a confidant,
Restrain your tongue, keep the veil, and drink your wine."

O cupbearer, spring arrives and no money for wine remains,
Think of a solution, for the heart's blood has come to a boil from grief.

Your love, poverty, youth, and the new spring,
Accept my apology and cover my sin with the hem of your generosity.

How long will you wag your tongue like a candle?
The butterfly of desire has arrived, O silent lover.

O King of form and meaning, whom no eye has ever seen,
And of whom no ear has heard the like.

Remain long enough so that the <term>khirqa-ye azraq</term> <gloss>blue robe of the dervish</gloss> may accept,
That your youthful fortune may clothe itself in the life of the ancient sky.

Last night, a sharp-witted expert whispered to me,
"It is not right to keep anything hidden from the wine-seller."

He said, "Take things easily upon yourself, for by its nature,
The world treats those who are rigid with great hardship."

Then he offered a cup whose radiance caused Venus in the heavens,
To begin dancing, and the lute-player to cover her ears.

With a bleeding heart, bring a smiling lip, just like the cup,
Do not cry out like a harp when you suffer a wound.

Until you become a familiar, you shall not hear a symbol from this veil,
The ear of the uninitiated is not the place for the message of <term>Soroush</term> <gloss>the messenger angel</gloss>.

<summary>This poem explores the tension between asceticism and the path of the heart, advocating for patience, grace, and the acceptance of divine mystery over public judgment.</summary>
<keywords>Sufi, Muhtasib, Wine-seller, Divine Grace, Soroush, Rendi</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>

<note>The text is enclosed within an elaborate, intricate blue floral and geometric border known as <term>tazhib</term> <gloss>illumination</gloss>.</note>

The <term>Sufi</term> <gloss>mystic</gloss> left the corner of the monastery and sat at the foot of the wine-vat,
After he saw the <term>Muhtasib</term> <gloss>moral police officer</gloss> carrying a wine-jug on his shoulder.

The state of the <term>Sheikh</term> <gloss>religious elder</gloss> and the <term>Qadi</term> <gloss>judge</gloss> and their secret drinking <note>original: "shurb al-yahudan," literally "the drinking of Jews," referring here to hypocritical or clandestine drinking</note>,
I asked of the wine-selling elder at the break of dawn.

He said: "These matters are not to be spoken, even though you are a confidant;
Draw in your tongue, keep the veil drawn, and drink your wine."

<term>Saki</term> <gloss>wine-bearer</gloss>, spring arrives and no money for wine remains;
Think of something, for the heart's blood boils with grief.

Your love, poverty, youth, and the new spring—
Accept my excuse and cover my fault with the hem of your generosity.

How long will you display your eloquence like a candle?
The moth of your desire has arrived; O lover, be silent.

O King of outward form and inner meaning, the likes of whom
No eye has ever seen and no ear has ever heard:

May you remain until your youthful fortune accepts
The blue <term>khirqa</term> <gloss>dervish robe</gloss> cast off by the aged sky.

Last night, a sharp-witted man of experience spoke to me in secret,
Saying: "It is not right to keep secrets from the wine-seller."

He said: "Take matters easily upon yourself, for by its very nature,
The world imposes hardship on those who strive too hard."

And then he gave me a cup from whose radiance in the heavens
Venus began to dance and the lute-player covered her ears <note>Venus, or Zuhra, is the celestial musician; the brilliance of the wine makes even the stars ecstatic</note>.

Bring a smiling lip with a bleeding heart, like the wine-cup;
Do not cry out like the lute if you receive a wound.

Until you become an initiate, you will not hear a mystery from behind this veil;
The ear of the stranger is no place for the message of <term>Soroush</term> <gloss>the herald angel</gloss>.

<summary>Hafez contrasts the hypocrisy of religious authorities with the honest wisdom of the wine-seller, advising the seeker to maintain a cheerful exterior despite inner suffering and to practice moderation in effort.</summary>
<keywords>Sufi, Muhtasib, Saki, Soroush, secrecy, hypocrisy, spiritual initiation</keywords>

text:
<note>The text is enclosed within an elaborate, intricate blue floral and geometric border (tazhib).</note>

The Sufi sat by the corner of the monastery at the foot of the wine jar,
When the <term>Muhtasib</term> <gloss>censor of morals</gloss> saw that he was carrying a wine jug on his shoulder.

The condition of the sheikh, the judge, and their drinking of Jewish wine,
I asked of the old wine-seller at the break of dawn.

He said, "This is not a matter to be spoken of, even if you are a confidant;
Hold your tongue, keep the veil, and drink your wine."

O wine-bearer, spring is arriving and the money for wine is gone;
Think of a way, for my heart's blood is boiling from grief.

It is love, poverty, youth, and the new spring;
Accept my excuse and cover my faults with the hem of your generosity.

How long will you speak eloquently like a candle?
The moth of desire has arrived, O silent lover.

O King of form and meaning, like unto whom,
No eye has seen and no ear has heard.

Remain until your youthful fortune from the old, tattered-wearing sky,
Accepts the blue dervish cloak.

Last night, a sharp-witted expert told me in secret,
"One should not hide the wine-seller's mystery from you."

He said, "Make tasks easy upon yourself, for by nature,
The world deals harshly with those who struggle hard."

Then he gave me a cup whose brilliance caused Venus to dance in the sky,
And while playing the lute, she said, "Drink."

Bring a smiling lip with a bloody heart, just like the cup;
Do not cry out like a harp when you receive a wound.

Until you become an initiate, you will not hear the secrets behind this veil;
The ear of the uninitiated is not a place for the message of <term>Soroush</term> <gloss>the messenger angel</gloss>.

<summary>This passage contrasts the hypocrisy of religious authorities with the wisdom of the tavern, emphasizing the virtues of ease, discretion, and spiritual initiation.</summary>
<keywords>Sufi, Muhtasib, Wine-seller, Love, Spring, Soroush, Initiation</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>

<note>The text is enclosed within an elaborate, intricate blue floral and geometric border known as <term>tazhib</term> <gloss>illumination</gloss>.</note>

The <term>Sufi</term> <gloss>mystic</gloss> left the corner of the cloister and sat at the foot of the wine jar,
Once he saw that even the <term>Muhtasib</term> <gloss>town censor or moral police</gloss> carried a jug upon his shoulder.

The state of the Sheikh and the Judge, and their secret drinking like the <term>shurb al-yahud</term> <gloss>clandestine drinking associated with non-Muslims</gloss>,
I asked about this at dawn from the elder wine-seller.

He said, "This matter is not to be spoken of, even though you are a confidant;
Draw back your tongue, keep the veil drawn, and drink your wine."

<term>Saki</term> <gloss>wine-bearer</gloss>, spring is arriving and the funds for wine are gone;
Think of something, for the heart’s blood boils over with grief.

There is love, poverty, youth, and the new spring;
Accept my excuse and cover my crime with the hem of your generosity.

How long, like a candle, will you practice your eloquence?
The moth of your desire has arrived; O lover, be silent.

O King of outward form and inner meaning, the likes of whom
No eye has ever seen and no ear has ever heard:

May you remain until your youthful fortune accepts
The blue <term>khirqa</term> <gloss>dervish robe</gloss> from the old, tattered-clothed sky.

Last night, a sharp-witted man of experience told me in secret,
That the mystery of the wine-seller should not be hidden from you.

He said, "Take matters easily upon yourself, for by its nature,
The world imposes hardship upon those who strive too hard."

And then he gave me a cup, from whose radiance in the heavens,
Venus began to dance, and playing the lute, she cried out: "Drink!"

With a bleeding heart, bring a laughing lip like the wine-cup;
Do not cry out like the harp if you receive a wound.

Until you become an initiate, you will not hear a mystery from behind this veil;
The ear of a stranger is no place for the message of <term>Soroush</term> <gloss>the herald angel</gloss>.

<summary>Hafez crititiques the hypocrisy of religious authorities while advocating for a life of spiritual ease and inward joy despite outward suffering. He emphasizes that divine secrets are only revealed to those who maintain silence and embrace the trials of love.</summary>
<keywords>Sufi, Muhtasib, wine-seller, spring, Venus, Soroush, hypocrisy, silence</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: ...I did not think it chivalrous in such a state to wound the heart of the poor man <term>dervish</term> <gloss>a Sufi ascetic</gloss> with the salt of reproach.</meta>

To reproach him or to sprinkle salt upon a wound, I did not deem appropriate. I said to myself:

**Poem**
One should not be arrogant regarding the table of others.
Do not be like the locust that consumes the trees in spring;
in winter, it remains without leaf or fruit.

**Story**
A king entrusted his son to a tutor, saying, "Educate my child just as you educate your own." The tutor labored for several years and achieved success, while his own sons reached the pinnacle of knowledge. The king summoned the learned man and rebuked him, saying, "You have broken your promise and failed to fulfill the conditions." The tutor replied, "O Lord of the Earth, let it not remain hidden from your royal view that the training provided is the same for all, yet the temperaments of the pupils are different."

**Poem**
Although silver and gold come from the stone,
not every stone possesses the essence of gold.

<summary>This passage illustrates the story of a king who blames a tutor for the disparate intellectual development of the king's son versus the tutor's own children, leading to a reflection on the inherent differences in human character.</summary>
<keywords>Education, Temperament, Fate, Royal Counsel, Sa'di, Wisdom</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: Iskandar, having gathered his vast forces, contemplates the challenge of facing Dara and organizes his administration of power.</meta>

(161)

As he turned the reins of his kingdom,
He began another search,
One that can be measured by logic,
Iskandar said to him, "One sharp blade <note>original: "یک تیغ تیز"</note>
Such a noble response to the army,
The news grew hotter at every moment,
When Iskandar realized that the swift cloud <note>original: "تند میغ"</note>
He sent orders for the army from every land,
From Egypt, Africa, Rome, and Russia,
When the boundless army gathered,
The muster master reported three hundred thousand <note>original: "سیصد هزار"</note>
When the army’s preparations were complete,
The keen-minded thinkers of Rome sat down <note>original: "بیدار مغزان روم"</note>
The king, concerning Dara and his affairs,

<column-break/>

It is not proper to gain victory through theft,
That he gathered so much fat <note>original: "پیه"</note>,
Those who are experts in discerning warriors,
It would mince the fat of a hundred cows,
Arose from the lofty monarch,
That a roaring dragon had come toward Rome,
By force, it draws forth the lightning of the blade,
Proceeding toward the gate of the king,
An army was arrayed like a bride,
He requested a count of the renowned names,
Brave, peerless horsemen appeared,
He organized an assembly outside, and the cup,
They softened the wax with the king's seal,
He spoke and engaged with his affairs,

---
(1) That is, one blade of fat and the grease of a hundred cows deceives one, it shreds it—it rends the hide of a hundred cows—the backs of a hundred cows—in another version.
(2) That is, when Iskandar knew that Dara was a swift cloud, which draws the lightning of his blade toward him with the roar of thunder and lightning.
(3) That is, the reporter and army registrar announced that three hundred thousand unique horsemen had gathered—<term>mufrad-sawār</term> <gloss>peerless, singular horseman</gloss>—six hundred thousand in another version.
(4) That is, with the seal of Iskandar’s command, they softened the wax of their hearts and accepted his decree—soft wax accepts an impression faster than hard wax.

<summary>Iskandar prepares for his confrontation with Dara by organizing a massive, multi-national army and overseeing administrative details with his advisors.</summary>
<keywords>Iskandar, Dara, Army, Rome, Governance, Warfare</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
For the King, at the time of turning the reins,
Victory cannot be seized through theft.
A second researcher began to say
That Dara has prepared such a force
That it can be counted only by estimation
By those who are experts in sizing armies.
Iskandar said to him: A single sharp blade <note>original: "yek tigh-e tiz"</note>
Can slice the fat of a hundred oxen into pieces. <margin>Meaning one sword can cut through the fat of a hundred fattened oxen, or the hides or backs of a hundred oxen, according to different manuscripts.</margin>
Such a worthy answer to the army
Came from the exalted Sovereign.
The news grew warmer at every moment
That a roaring dragon <note>meaning Dara</note> was coming toward Rome.
When Iskandar realized that fierce cloud <margin>meaning Iskandar realized that Dara is like a fierce cloud drawing the lightning of his sword with the roar of thunder.</margin>
Was rarely drawing the lightning of the blade,
He sent word for the armies from every region
To set out toward the gate of the Sovereign.
From Egypt, from Africa, Rome, and Russia,
The army was adorned like a bride.
When that endless army became a multitude,
He sought a count from the register of the famous.
The muster-master reported that three hundred thousand <margin>meaning the presenter and army scribe reported that three hundred thousand elite horsemen had gathered; elite horsemen <term>mofrad savār</term> <gloss>single riders</gloss> refers to peerless heroes. Some manuscripts say six hundred thousand.</margin>
Elite, solitary horsemen had come forth.
When the preparation of the army was complete,
He held an assembly outside with the cup.
The wise minds of Rome sat down; <margin>meaning by the seal of Iskandar’s command, they softened the wax of their hearts and became receptive to his order; soft wax is more receptive than hard wax.</margin>
They softened like wax by the King’s seal.
The King spoke of the deeds of Dara
And pondered deeply upon his affair.

<summary>Iskandar dismisses the threat of Dara's superior numbers with a metaphor about a sharp blade and gathers a massive coalition of three hundred thousand elite troops from across his empire.</summary>
<keywords>Iskandar, Alexander the Great, Dara, Darius, Military Muster, Rome, Egypt, Russia, Africa, War Council</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: Iskandar (Alexander the Great) prepares for war against Dara (Darius III), reflecting on the nature of leadership and the assembly of his massive forces.</meta>

(164)

The king, when turning the reins,
Should not seek victory through theft.
The inquirer began again,
That Dara had not raised such an army
That one could count it by measure,
For those who are experts in armies.
Iskandar said to him, "A single sharp blade
Can slice the fat of a hundred oxen into pieces."
Such a noble reply from the noble king
Was high praise for the army.
The news grew hotter every moment,
That a raging dragon had come upon Rome.
When Iskandar knew that this fierce cloud
Would brandish the lightning of the sword with the thunder of rage,
He sent word so that the army from every land
Would set out toward the king's gate.
From Egypt, from the Franks, from Rome, and from the Russians,
An army was adorned like a bride.
When the boundless army became numerous,
He sought a count from the famous men.
The muster-master reported that three hundred thousand
Brave, solitary <note>meaning: elite or matchless</note> horsemen had appeared.
When the affairs of the army were fully prepared,
He held a gathering with wine and goblets.
The wise minds of Rome sat down;
With the seal of the king, they softened the wax <note>meaning: they became compliant and ready to accept his orders, like soft wax ready to receive an impression</note>.
The king spoke of the deeds of Dara and his battle,
And he deliberated upon his affair.

---

<margin>
(1) That is, one sword can slice the fat of a hundred fat oxen into pieces. <note>Variants: "can strip the hide of a hundred oxen" or "pierce the backs of a hundred oxen."</note>

(2) That is, when Iskandar knew that Dara was a fierce cloud, who with the roar of thunder and lightning draws the sword of lightning toward him.

(3) That is, the presenter and army-clerk reported that three hundred thousand elite horsemen had gathered. <term>Mufrad-sawar</term> <gloss>solitary horseman</gloss> and <term>yakka-sawar</term> <gloss>lone rider</gloss> mean a peerless or unique hero. <note>Variant: "six hundred thousand."</note> <note>Variant: "Girded his loins to seek the battlefield" in place of the second hemistich.</note>

(4) That is, with the seal of Iskandar, they softened the wax of their hearts and accepted his command. Soft wax takes an impression more quickly than hard wax.
</margin>

<summary>Iskandar prepares his vast, multi-ethnic army for war against Dara and holds a council of war with his advisors to plan the campaign.</summary>
<keywords>Iskandar, Dara, Army, Rome, Military muster, Strategy</keywords>

For a king, at the time of turning the reins toward battle, it is not fitting to seek victory through stealth.
Another investigator began to speak, saying that Dara <note>Darius III of Persia</note> has prepared an army so vast
That those who are experts in military matters cannot even estimate its number.
Alexander <note>Iskandar</note> said to him: "One sharp sword <margin>Meaning: One sword can cut the fat of a hundred fat oxen into small pieces.</margin> can mince the fat of a hundred oxen."
Such a noble response regarding the army came forth from the exalted sovereign.
The news grew more urgent at every moment: "A breath-stealing dragon has arrived from Rome."
When Alexander realized that that fierce cloud <note>referring to Dara</note> would draw the lightning of the blade with the roar of thunder,
He sent word for the armies from every region to set out toward the King's gate.
From Egypt, from the land of the Franks <note>Europeans</note>, from Rome, and from Russia, an army was adorned like a bride.
When the boundless army became a massive throng, he requested a count of the famous heroes.
The muster-master reported that three hundred thousand <note>Some manuscripts read: six hundred thousand</note> brave, elite cavalrymen had stepped forward.
When the organization of the army was complete, he held a council without the presence of wine or cups.
The wise minds of Rome sat together; they softened their hearts like wax before the King's seal <note>Meaning: They became receptive and obedient to Alexander's command, just as soft wax takes an impression more easily than hard wax.</note>.
The King spoke of Dara's affairs and his style of combat, and he deliberated deeply upon his challenge.

text:
When the King finished with the pleasant delicacies, he poured wine and established a banquet of joy.
When the King had drunk two or three cups of wine, sweat rose upon his skin from the wine's heat.
He said, "O host of the golden palace, your residence is pleasant and your provisions are abundant.
Yet this sixty-step high palace, to which the heavens cast a lasso over its summit,
After sixty years have passed since you, how are you able to walk beneath its base?"
The host said, "May the King remain eternal, may the <term>Kawthar</term> <gloss>a river in Paradise</gloss> be his wine and the houris his cupbearers.
This is not remarkable for me; I am a man. How could I grow weary of such a base?"
"The remarkable thing is that there is a girl like the moon, soft and delicate like fur and fine silk.
She carries a cow like a mountain upon her neck to the place where it eats grass.
She carries the sixty-step staircase with one hand, such that she does not need to sit on any step.
That cow, moreover, is a cow like an elephant; it cannot pull its own fat for a single mile.
By God, if anyone in this land lifts a breath from the ground,
And a woman carries it to a sixty-step fortress, is it not a wondrous deed?"
When the King heard this tale from his colonel, he bit his fingertip in wonder.
He said, "How can a deed of this kind be? It cannot be, or if it is, it must be sorcery.
I will not believe this claim as truth until I see it with my own eyes first."
Then he requested from the host, the man, that he verify the claim of his speech.
When the host heard this, he went below and told the tale of the lion to the cow-slayer.

<summary>The King, while enjoying a banquet, is amazed by his host's claim that a delicate girl carries both a massive cow and the palace's sixty-step staircase with ease. Finding this feat impossible or magical, the King demands to witness it himself, prompting the host to go and prepare for the demonstration.</summary>
<keywords>Haft Paykar, Nizami Ganjavi, King, host, sixty-step palace, cow, physical prowess, skepticism, sorcery</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
When the King had finished with the pleasant delicacies, he set the wine flowing and established a joyful banquet. After the King had drunk two or three goblets of wine, sweat broke out on his forehead like rosewater. 

He said, "O host of the golden palace, your dwelling is pleasant and your provisions are abundant. But this high pavilion of sixty steps, which the sky itself would need a lasso to reach: after sixty years of your life have passed, how can you traverse them beneath your feet?"

The host replied, "May the King live forever! May his wine be from the <term>Kawsar</term> <gloss>a river in Paradise</gloss> and may a <term>Houri</term> <gloss>a maiden of Paradise</gloss> be his cupbearer. This is not strange for me, for I am a man; how could I be weary of such steps? The strange thing is that there is a girl, beautiful as the moon, soft and delicate as royal silk and ermine. She places a bull, heavy as a mountain, upon her neck and brings it to its feeding place. She climbs those sixty steps in one go, such that she never rests upon any step. And what a bull! It is like an elephant; it cannot move its own fat a single inch. By God, if anyone in this land could even lift it for a single breath from the ground! That a woman should carry it up sixty steps of a fortress—how is this not a wondrous thing?"

When the colonel told this story to the King, the King bit his fingertip in amazement. He said, "How can such a deed be? It is not possible, and if it were, it would be sorcery. I cannot believe this word is true until I first see it with my own eyes."

Then he requested the host to prove the claim of his speech true. When the host heard this, he went down and told the Lion’s <note>the King’s</note> story to the "Bull-slayer" <note>Fitna, the slave girl</note>.

<summary>King Bahram Gur questions how his aging host climbs the sixty-step pavilion, leading the host to describe a delicate girl who carries a full-grown bull up the stairs daily. Skeptical, the King demands to see the feat himself to prove it is not sorcery.</summary>
<keywords>Bahram Gur, Fitna, sixty steps, the bull and the girl, strength vs. practice, Nizami Ganjavi, Persian poetry</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
When the King finished his pleasant meal, he poured the wine and began a celebration of joy.
After the King had drunk two or three goblets of wine, sweat appeared upon his forehead like roses.
He said, "O host of the golden palace, your home is pleasant and your provisions are abundant.
But this sixty-step high palace, whose head reaches for the sky as if with a lasso,
after sixty years have passed for you, how can you traverse it under your feet?"
The host said, "May the King remain forever; may his wine be from the <term>Kawsar</term> <gloss>the river of Paradise</gloss> and his cupbearer a <term>Houri</term> <gloss>celestial maiden</gloss>.
This is not a wonder from me, for I am a man; how could I grow tired of such a climb?
The wonder is that there is a girl, beautiful as the moon, soft and delicate as the King’s silk and ermine.
She takes a bull, massive as a mountain, upon her neck and brings it here at the time of feeding.
She climbs those sixty steps in one go, without pausing to rest on any step.
And what a bull! It is like an elephant; it cannot even drag its own fat along.
By God, if anyone in this land could even lift it for a single breath from the ground—
yet a woman carries it up a sixty-step fortress! How could this work not be a marvel?"
When the host told this story to the King, the King bit his fingertip in amazement.
He said, "How can a deed of this kind be possible? It is either not true, or if it is, it must be sorcery.
I cannot truly believe this word until I first see it with my own eyes."
Then he requested of the host that he prove the truth of his claim.
When the host heard this, he went down and told the Lion <note>Bahram Gur</note>'s story to the Bull-bearer <note>Fitna</note>.

<summary>King Bahram Gur questions how his host manages the steep sixty-step climb at his age, leading the host to reveal the even greater feat of a young woman carrying a bull up the stairs. The King, skeptical of such strength, demands to see the proof himself.</summary>
<keywords>Bahram Gur, Fitna, sixty steps, bull, feat of strength, skepticism, palace, Nizami Ganjavi</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>

**Rabbi Eleazar** explained all of these things. **Rabbi Eleazar** spoke to Isaac, saying, "Who is the <term>din</term> <gloss>Judgment</gloss>? It is the bent/constricted one." Isaac said, "The <term>din</term> is the part that is hidden; heaven forbid that I should be angry if it is not my portion." And yet, is Isaac not <term>chesed</term> <gloss>Loving-kindness</gloss>? It is bent, and the Holy One, blessed be He, is all <term>din</term>; He is <term>rachamim</term> <gloss>Mercy</gloss> that is bent, and Mercy is hidden. He inherits the <term>chesed</term> because the <term>chesed</term> is bent. And Isaac, as <term>din</term>, is <term>chesed</term>. Isaac is bent by Mercy, which is severe <term>din</term>. And in this, it was above, this from that, and it went forth from that until everything became known as one, and from one all are suspended. And everything is not found as one unless the heavens are forever and ever. **Rabbi Eleazar** made it known that there are no traces <unclear>that can be seen</unclear> when we see it, and one desires both to understand everything, such as Jacob, and this is what is written:
> "The middle bolt in the midst of the boards shall pass through from end to end." <note>Exodus 26:28</note>

It is a complete vessel, for if it were not called from this side and from this side, everything would not be known. Everything is able to be in one balance; it neither rises nor changes, as it is written:
> "For I the Lord do not change." <note>Malachi 3:6</note>

**Rabbi Yehuda** said: All of them are shining sparks, from here and from here they are suspended, and they establish the palace as one, and everything is not to be separated. And whoever separates them by his power is separated from eternal life. **Rabbi Yitzhak** said: It is written:
> "And I will give children to be their princes, and babes shall rule over them." <note>Isaiah 3:4</note>

This is what is written: "And they are brazen-faced, the Cherubim," and this is what is written: "He who sits upon the Cherubim," and it is written: "And He rode upon a Cherub and did fly." "He who sits upon the Cherubim"—when it begins to be settled in assistance, it is written "He who sits upon the Cherubim" (this is when it is found in perfection). "And He rode upon a Cherub"—one, when the King is not settled upon His throne. "He who sits upon the Cherubim"—two. Woe to the world when one Cherub turns its face away from the other, for it is written:
> "And their faces shall look one to another." <note>Exodus 25:20</note>

When they are at peace in the world. **Rabbi Yitzhak** said: We have learned, "The nakedness of a sister and the nakedness of your daughter-in-law you shall not uncover." Woe to whoever uncovers their nakedness. In this manner, it is written regarding Jacob, "from end to end." And in this way, the portion of Israel to the Holy One, blessed be He, is found in His ornaments, in the manner of the above, as it is written:
> "Israel in whom I will be glorified." <note>Isaiah 49:3</note>

Come and see, **Rabbi Yitzhak** said: In the days of the ancients, it was as when one said to his companion, "Prepare for me a portion of wheat and take from it silver." Now, a man says to his companion, "Take from it silver," and he sees it in the husk, and there is no one who tastes it, and there is no one who knows its portion, except for the few wise and light ones who are attached to the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is written:
> "And your people all of them righteous, they shall inherit the land forever, the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, that I may be glorified." <note>Isaiah 60:21</note>

Woe that it is consumed and the silver is maintained. **Rabbi Yitzhak** said: Woe, for we see that all those who are connected to the higher knots stand and observe, woe that it is consumed, and all those below are suspended. Woe. The window opens, a door, and they are changed and fixed from the knot to the order that is <unclear>upon them</unclear>. And like a book of longing, it is written: woe above, woe below, and all of them rise in one balance. He who is the longing of the book—**Rabbi Hizkiyah said**: These are the chapters that are all in the great palace, and they fill the whole earth. **Rabbi Yehuda** said: All of them are thus, and they are superior. **Rabbi** said: A curse be upon him who covers and bends, and for him who does not rise and bend them thus.

### The Parable of the Wheat

A parable of a man who lived among the villagers and did not know the dwellings of the city. He sowed wheat and ate wheat as it was. One day, he entered the city to the king's feast. He said, "Why does this man eat here?" They said, "It is the king's custom to eat." He ate and tasted a sweetness he had never known. **Rabbi** said: From what is this made? They said, "From wheat." Later, the king brought him delicacies that were in the city. He tasted them and said, "And this sweetness, what is it?" They said, "From wheat." Later, the king brought him royal delicacies that were in honey and oil. He said, "And this sweetness, what is its making?" They said, "From wheat." He said, "Certainly, this city is the secret of all the sweetness here, and it is the root of all the sweetness that is here, it is wheat." And because of that...

<summary>This page explores the mystical union of Mercy and Judgment through the imagery of the Cherubim and the "middle bolt," emphasizing the balance required for divine manifestation. It concludes with a parable of a villager who discovers that all refined royal delicacies originate from the same simple wheat, mirroring how all divine emanations derive from a single hidden source.</summary>
<keywords>Cherubim, Din, Chesed, Rachamim, Jacob, Balance, Parable of the Wheat, Divine Essence</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>of the brightness — all of them established it. **Rabbi Eleazar** spoke to Isaac: who is the "oppressed person" <note>original: *dikah katya*</note> who bent down? Isaac was thin and oppressed, he looked upon his portion; Heaven forbid he should be angry, for his portion was not like the others. And behold, Isaac is from the side of <term>Chesed</term> <gloss>Lovingkindness</gloss> which bends, yet it is said that all of them are <term>Din</term> <gloss>Judgment</gloss>. He is from the side of <term>Rachamim</term> <gloss>Mercy</gloss> which bends, and Mercy is the King. Wisdom inherits Lovingkindness, for Lovingkindness bends. And Isaac, though acting as Judgment, is from the side of Lovingkindness. Isaac bent within Mercy, yet from him comes harsh Judgment. And so it was above, this from that, and it emerged from this until that, so that all is recognized as one. All things are suspended from one another, and to find that all is one, the Heavens are needed forever and ever. **Rabbi Eleazar** recognized that there are no paths for it <note>the Divine presence</note> except when we see it as one. One desires both to complete the whole, such as Jacob, as it is written:
> And the middle bolt in the midst of the boards shall pass through from end to end. <note>Exodus 26:28</note>

This proves the whole; for if you do not read it but from this side and from that side, all is recognized. It can do all; in one <term>Metkala</term> <gloss>Scale of Balance</gloss> it rises, it does not change and shall not be altered, as it is written:
> I am the Lord, I change not. <note>Malachi 3:6</note>

**Rabbi Yehuda** [said]: all these lights shine from one another and are suspended from one another. Their foundation is one whole, not to be separated. Whoever separates them by his own strength is separated from the Life of Worlds. **Rabbi Isaac** [said]: it is written:
> And I will give children to be their princes, and babes shall rule over them. <note>Isaiah 3:4</note>

This is what is written, "fierce of face" <note>original: *azim panim*</note>, the <term>Keruvim</term> <gloss>Cherubim</gloss>. And it is written, "He who sits upon the Cherubim" <note>Psalm 80:2</note> and "He rode upon a Cherub and did fly" <note>Psalm 18:11</note>. "Sits upon the Cherubim" refers to when the Divine settles in support; it is written "Sits upon the Cherubim" <note>plural</note> when perfection is found. "He rode upon a Cherub" <note>singular</note> when the King is not settled upon His throne. "Sits upon the Cherubim" means two. Woe to the world when one Cherub turns its face away from the other, for it is written:
> And their faces shall look one to another. <note>Exodus 25:20</note>

This is when there is peace in the world. **Rabbi Isaac** said: We have learned, "the nakedness of your daughter-in-law" <note>Leviticus 18:15</note> and "the youth of your father-in-law" <note>referring to uncovering secrets</note>, you shall not reveal. Woe to him who reveals their nakedness <note>uncovering divine mysteries inappropriately</note>. In this manner it is written of Jacob that he "passed through from end to end." And thus the portion of Israel with the Holy One, blessed be He, is found in their adornment, just like the pattern above, as it is written:
> Israel, in whom I will be glorified. <note>Isaiah 49:3</note>

Come and see, **Rabbi Isaac** [said]: in former days, when one man said to another, "Show me a certain vessel and take money for it." Now a man says to another, "Take money and show me another," and there is no one to taste and no one to incline his portion, except for those few who are gathered and supreme before the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is written:
> Your people shall be all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever, the branch of my planting, the work of my hands, that I may be glorified. <note>Isaiah 60:21</note>

Woe that the silver is depleted and remains. **Rabbi Isaac** said: Woe, for I see those who are circumcised, all those who are crowned stand above in investigation. Woe that it is filled, and all these depend on the lower world. A window was opened for us and they are renovated and prepared from the incense for the arrangement that rests upon them. And as in the Book of Concealment <note>original: *Sifra de-Tzniuta*</note> it is proven: woe above and woe below, and all rise in one scale of the balance. What is the concealment of the Book? **Rabbi Hezekiah said**: These are the chapters that are all in the Great Palace and fill all the earth. **Rabbi Yehuda** said: all of them are more excellent than this. **The Rabbi said**: Woe to him who bends and bows, and to him who does not rise and bend to them so.

---

### The Parable of the Wheat

A parable of a man who lived among the fields and did not know the ways of the city dwellers. He sowed wheat and ate the wheat in its raw form. One day he entered the city, and they brought before him a good bread. He asked, "What is this for a man to eat?" They said, "It is bread, for eating." He ate it and found its taste very pleasant. **The man said**, "From what is this made?" They said, "From wheat." Later they brought him cakes kneaded in oil. He tasted them and said, "And from what are these made?" They said, "From wheat." Later they brought him the royal pastries <note>original: *tariki malkin*</note> kneaded with honey and oil. He said, "And from what are these sweets made?" They said, "From wheat." He said, "Truly, I am the master of all these things, for I eat the essence of all these, which is wheat." And because of that...

It concludes with a famous parable of a villager who fails to recognize that refined breads and pastries are made from the same raw wheat he eats, illustrating how the hidden essence of Torah is found within its outward forms.</summary>
<keywords>Cherubim, Jacob, Balance (Metkala), Judgment (Din), Mercy (Rachamim), Parable of the Wheat, Sifra de-Tzniuta, Israel</keywords>
